# How to use this guide {#howto .front}

**Start with the Essentials.** Before you open this guide, read the separate **Essentials PDF (QA_ESSENTIALS.pdf)**: the pitch, the numbers you must know by heart and the short answers to the questions you are most likely to get. Then use this full guide to go deeper: it explains every idea from zero, and it gives every answer with its follow-up and the numbers behind it. This guide is written for you, Pardheev, presenting Team Androids' solution at the Amazon ML Challenge 2026 Grand Finale on Wednesday 7 October 2026 (a 10-minute talk, then 5 minutes of questions from senior Amazon scientists). It assumes you start as a beginner and takes you to the level where you can answer a senior applied scientist calmly and exactly. Our final public F0.5 is 0.991300: say "0.9913".

**What is in it.**

- **Part A - Learn the concepts** (99 concepts in four chapters, plus a 20-stop walk through our pipeline). Every concept is taught in the same order: **In one line**, then a **Simple explanation** (an everyday picture), a **Worked example** you redo with a pen, the **Technical explanation** (the level a senior scientist expects), then **How we used it**, **Expert nuance**, **Remember** and **Judge might ask**. A0 starts from zero; A4 follows one record through the whole pipeline. The [Concept map](#concept-map) shows which concept is used at which pipeline stage.
- **Part B - The Q&A bank** (258 questions in 21 categories, numbered Q1 to Q258). Each question has *Why they ask* (what the judge is really testing), **Say** (the spoken answer, 20-35 seconds), **If they push** (the follow-up, only if asked again) and **Numbers** (with sources). Start with [the 40 most likely questions](#likely40).
- **Part C - Cheat sheet.** The numbers table, an A-Z glossary of every technical term with a link to where it is taught, the internal code names and their plain names, the honest-limitations answers in one place, and what to say when you do not know.

**How to read the badges and labels.**

| Badge or label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ★ / ★★ / ★★★ | difficulty of a question: basic / probing / hard or adversarial |
| LIKELY | a question we expect the judges to ask |
| Doc 3, Doc B.4 ... | a section or appendix of our submitted Documentation: the primary truth, safe to quote |
| CodeREADME, Evidence, Code: ..., (code) | the code package: true, but not in the Documentation; use only if asked |
| background | correct general knowledge that is not in our Documentation; use only if asked |
| derived | plain arithmetic on documented numbers, shown so you can redo it |
| toy / illustrative | invented numbers that only teach the arithmetic: **never quote them as results** |
| QA n | answer n of the talk's vetted Q&A prep sheet (the short version of Part B) |
| Qn | question n of Part B of this guide (click it) |
| A1.5, A4.17 ... | concept 5 of chapter A1, section 17 of the pipeline walk-through (click it) |

**The answer formula.** Direct answer first, then one number, then stop (2-4 sentences). If a question touches a limitation, say the limitation plainly first and then the mitigation. Use the plain names of the talk: business, incoming record, shortlist, quick rule-based filter, CatBoost ranker, the four readers (MiniLM reader, E5 reader, French MiniLM reader, French E5 reader), "what changed" features, LightGBM decision model per country, confident + clear-winner rule, second-chance searches, per-business consistency check, France rules computed by code.

**Six things never to do on stage.**

1. Never use internal code names or rule letters; they are printed only in the [code-name table](#c-names).
2. If a judge asks how the decision models reject near-identical look-alike businesses, use exactly the wording of [Q115](#q115) and add nothing; never raise the topic yourself.
3. Never invent a number, experiment, ablation or timing. If a number is missing, answer qualitatively and say what you would measure.
4. Talk only about the final submitted approach; "what didn't work" uses only the items our Documentation reports ([Q189](#q189)).
5. Never call the held-out scores an end-to-end test, never call agreement with French pseudo-labels evidence of French accuracy, and never say the 0.4 lead "was never tuned" (say: one fixed lead for every country; the threshold was tuned on fold 8).
6. Never present our AI-assisted development as a rule problem; if asked, answer briefly and factually ([Q229](#q229)).

## The 2-day plan: Monday 5 and Tuesday 6 October {#plan .front2}

Day 1 builds understanding; Day 2 turns it into fast, exact spoken answers. Each block ends with a **self-test checkpoint**: close the guide, answer aloud or on paper, then check. If you miss more than one item of a checkpoint, re-read the linked concepts before moving on. Times are a guide; take a 10-minute break every hour.

**Reading rule for a beginner.** On the first pass of a concept, read only **In one line**, **Simple explanation**, **Worked example** and **How we used it**, and redo every calculation. Read **Technical explanation** and **Expert nuance** on a second pass, for the concepts marked *must-know* below. "Skim" means: read the *In one line* and *Remember* blocks only.

# Before the finale: to do {#todo .front}

Three things to settle before you walk on stage. Tick them off on Tuesday evening at the latest.

- ☐ **Agree one accurate sentence on the team's split of work.** Agree it with Monika and Hemachand and write it into the answer to [Q228](#q228) ("Who did what in your team?"), which shows **TO FILL IN** where the sentence goes. Our documents do not record roles, so do not improvise one on stage.
- ☐ **Know what is "background" and what is Documentation.** Items marked "background" or "(code)", and facts whose source is Code, CodeREADME or Evidence, are true but are not in our submitted Documentation. Use them only if a judge asks directly; on any conflict the Documentation wins.
- ☐ **Never say a record id aloud.** The worked examples print ids such as "S1-..." (a business) or "S2-..." (an incoming record) only so that the records can be found in our files. On stage say "a US business", "an incoming record from Nantes" and so on.

# The 30-second and 2-minute pitch {#pitch .front}

Taken word for word from the end of the pipeline walk-through ([A4.20](#a4-20)). Learn the 30-second version by heart; it is the answer to "so what did you build?". The 2-minute version is for a judge who asks you to walk through the whole pipeline.

**One sentence (about 20 seconds).** "Per country, a cheap index and two pruning steps cut 6.7 trillion possible pairs to about seven candidates per business, small language-model readers and a per-country decision model score them, and we link a record only to a confident, clear winner, with second-chance searches and French rules on top."

**30 seconds (about 80 words).**
"Per country, we clean the text and a C++ inverted index pulls up businesses that share rare words, letter pieces or sounds, about 130 per business. A quick rule with no model cuts that to 21.7, and a CatBoost ranker keeps at most four per record. Cross-encoder readers score each pair, 'what changed' features describe the differences, and a LightGBM decision model links only a confident, clear winner. Second-chance searches, a consistency check and France rules finish it: public F0.5 0.9913."

**2 minutes (about 300 words).**
"We link about ten million incoming records from the US, India and France to 1.7 million businesses, each record to one business or to none. The metric is F0.5 per business, and a business with no true records scores a point only if we link nothing, so we are precision first. The pipeline runs per country and goes from cheap to expensive.

First we clean the text: lower case, abbreviations unified, Indian-script words transliterated with a word list learned from training matches, and French address and legal-form rules. A C++ inverted index then finds businesses that share rare words, letter pieces or sounds, weighted by IDF, with separate lists for name and address so one-sided matches survive. That gives about 130 candidates per business. A quick rule-based filter with no model cuts that to 21.7, at a held-out cost of 0.00003 F0.5, and a CatBoost ranker keeps at most four per record: 6.75 per business.

Cross-encoder readers, fine-tuned multilingual MiniLM and E5, read each record and candidate together. We add 'what changed' features: which numbers changed, which words were added, dropped or replaced, how rare and how close in meaning, and whether the legal form changed. A LightGBM decision model per country turns about two hundred features into a probability, and we link only a confident, clear winner: at least 0.75, or 0.82 in France, and 0.4 ahead of the runner-up.

Then targeted fixes: two second-chance searches for unlinked records, by transliterated name in India and by rare address keys, adding 9,759 and 3,137 links; a per-business consistency check; and for France, which has no labels, self-trained French readers and rules computed by code.

The final file scores 0.9913 on the public leaderboard, and close versions of our decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992 on held-out folds."

If a judge then asks for limitations, add: "We had no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file, France has no labels and its rules were designed after looking at unlabelled test records, and we kept the French E5 reader although it failed two of its four written checks."

# Part A - Learn the concepts {#part-a .part}

Five chapters, in the order of the 2-day plan's reading list: **A0** builds the machine-learning basics from zero; **A1** covers entity resolution, the metric, text cleaning and blocking; **A2** the models; **A3** training, validation and selection; **A4** follows one record through our whole pipeline and links back to the concepts it uses. The 99 concepts of A0-A3 are numbered A0.1, A0.2 ... and all have the same parts: In one line, Simple explanation, Worked example, Technical explanation, How we used it, Expert nuance, Remember and Judge might ask. Where A2 and A3 teach the same idea from two sides (early stopping, stacking, refitting, seed averaging, calibration, self-training, blending, hard examples), a grey *See also* line under the concept title links the other one.

## A0 - Machine learning from zero (the prerequisites for everything else) {#a0 .chap}

### How to read this part {#a0-how-to-read-this-part .nc}

This part assumes no background at all. It teaches the eighteen machine-learning ideas that every later part of the study guide uses, in an order where each idea builds on the earlier ones, and every idea is explained with an example from our own problem: linking messy incoming records to the right business in the US, India and France. Read it three times. First pass: only the **In one line**, **Simple explanation** and **Worked example** blocks of all eighteen concepts, with a pen, redoing the arithmetic. Second pass: the **Technical explanation**, **How we used it** and **Expert nuance** blocks; this is the level a senior applied scientist expects. Third pass: say the **Judge might ask** answers aloud until they come out in your own words. Bold words are new terms, defined where they first appear; later concepts point back to earlier ones by name ("see Decision trees").

**Three kinds of numbers.** Read this before anything else.
- **Real numbers** about our pipeline come from the submitted Documentation (tagged "Doc 3", "Doc D.1" and so on) and the shared fact sheet. They are exact and safe to say on stage. A few are marked **derived**: plain arithmetic on documented numbers, shown so you can redo it.
- **Toy numbers** appear in worked examples only to teach the arithmetic. They are always marked "toy". **Never quote them to the judges as results.**
- A few facts are marked **background**: correct general knowledge or facts read from the public models' configuration files, but not in our Documentation. Use them only if asked.

**Spoken answers** use the plain names of the v3 talk (business, incoming record, shortlist, quick rule-based filter, CatBoost ranker, the four readers, "what changed" features, LightGBM decision model per country, confident + clear-winner rule, second-chance searches, per-business consistency check, France rules computed by code). Say the final public score as "0.9913".

#### The problem in one paragraph (you will meet these words everywhere)

A **business** is a record in the reference list: 1,732,544 of them in the test files across the US, India and France. An **incoming record** is a record from one of the two other sources (9,969,589 of them) that must be linked to the one business it belongs to, or to none. A business can own several incoming records. The score is **F0.5 per business, averaged over all businesses**: a number between 0 and 1 that rewards correct links and punishes a wrong link more than a missed one (see Confusion matrix). The US and India have training **labels** (the known right answers); France has none.

#### The pipeline in one line (plain names)

clean the text → **index lookup** (find businesses that share rare words, letter pieces or sounds) → **quick rule-based filter** (no model) → **CatBoost ranker** → **shortlist** (up to 4 candidates per incoming record) → **readers** (MiniLM reader and E5 reader; for France the MiniLM reader plus the French MiniLM reader and the French E5 reader) → **"what changed" features** → **LightGBM decision model per country** → **confident + clear-winner rule** → refinements (**second-chance searches**, **per-business consistency check**, **France rules computed by code**) → two output files → the organisers' validator.

If most of these names mean nothing to you yet, that is expected; each is explained below. A short decoder for now: **CatBoost** and **LightGBM** are two widely used software libraries that build many small decision trees and add up their answers (see Decision trees and Ensembles); the **readers** are small neural language models that read an incoming record and a candidate business side by side and give one match score (see Neural networks to Pre-trained and fine-tuned models); a **threshold** is a cut-off score above which we act (see Probability scores).

### A0.1 What a model is {#a0-1 .concept}

**In one line:** A **model** is a function, learned from examples, that takes an input (for us, an incoming record paired with a candidate business) and returns an output (a match score).

**Simple explanation:** Think of a new clerk at a business registry whose job is to decide whether a scribbled form ("Joes Pizza, 410 Main St") refers to a registered business ("Joe's Pizza, 410 Main Street"). You could hand the clerk a rulebook you wrote yourself, but real forms are messy in a thousand ways no rulebook anticipates. Instead you give the clerk a big pile of old forms where the right answer is already known, and the clerk gradually works out which signs point to a match. What the clerk ends up carrying in their head is the model: not a copy of every old form, but a compact recipe that turns a new form into a judgement. In a computer the recipe is a set of numbers (for example the split points of decision trees or the weights of a neural network), and **training** is the process of finding good numbers from the examples. Using the trained model on new pairs it has never seen is called **inference** or prediction. Not everything in a system is a model: a hand-written rule such as "keep the candidate if its score is at least 60 % of the best" is also a function, but nobody learned it from data.

**Worked example (toy):** The simplest learned model is a lookup table of match rates. Suppose we have 20 labelled training pairs, each described by two clues: is the name similarity high (at least 0.85), and is the house number the same?

| Name similarity | Same house number | Training pairs | Of which true matches | Learned score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| high | yes | 6 | 6 | 6 / 6 = 1.00 |
| high | no or missing | 5 | 3 | 3 / 5 = 0.60 |
| low | yes | 4 | 1 | 1 / 4 = 0.25 |
| low | no or missing | 5 | 0 | 0 / 5 = 0.00 |

1. Group the training pairs by their clues.
2. Count the share of true matches in each group.
3. Store the four shares. These four numbers are the model's **parameters** (see Parameters and hyper-parameters).
4. Apply it to new pairs. "Joes Pizza, 410 Main St" against "Joe's Pizza, 410 Main Street": high, same number → 1.00. "Kumar Electricals, 3 Ring Road, Delhi" against "Kumar Textiles, 41 Chandni Chowk, Delhi": low, different → 0.00. "Patel Medical Store" with no address against "Patel Medical Store, 5 Station Road, Ahmedabad": high, missing → 0.60.

The examples have become a function: clues in, score out.

**Technical explanation:** In **supervised learning** (learning from examples whose right answers are known) we assume labelled examples (x, y) drawn from some distribution and choose a function f_θ from a **hypothesis class** (all lookup tables, all sums of trees of a given size, all transformer networks of a given shape) by minimising the average **loss** over the training examples (see Loss functions), hoping that it **generalises** to new draws from the same distribution. Three design choices define a model: the **representation** of the input (hand-made features, or raw text cut into tokens), the hypothesis class with its parameters θ, and the training objective with its optimiser. For pair matching, x is an (incoming record, candidate business) pair, y ∈ {0, 1} says whether the candidate is the record's true owner, and f_θ(x) estimates P(y = 1 | x). A full system wraps models in deterministic decision logic: models produce scores, rules turn scores into actions (see Probability scores). Training cost is paid once; inference cost is paid for every pair scored, and in entity resolution that dominates the design, because the number of possible pairs is enormous (6,724,569,566,212 same-country pairs in our test files, Doc 3). The assumption "new data looks like the training data" is the one that breaks most often; in our data it is weakest for France, whose address formats and legal vocabulary differ from the labelled US and Indian data and which has no labels to check against.

**How we used it:** Our system is a chain of functions, some learned and some hand-written.
- Learned from scratch on the provided labelled US/India data: the **CatBoost ranker** (76 index features → probability that the candidate is the owner); one **LightGBM decision model** per country plus a default one for unseen countries (about two hundred features → probability); and the **second-chance models** (the native-script rescue model for India; the address rescue filter and scorer for the US and India).
- Learned by fine-tuning pre-trained networks (see Pre-trained and fine-tuned models): the four **readers** (raw text of a pair → one score).
- Learned by simple counting: the Indic-to-Latin word list used in cleaning, built from labelled train matches of folds 0-5 by counting which Latin word each native-script word co-occurs with. It is a small statistical model, not a neural transliterator.
- Hand-written: text cleaning, the quick rule-based filter, the confident + clear-winner rule, the per-business consistency check, and the France rules computed by code (designed from analysis of the unlabelled French records, which our documentation discloses).

**Expert nuance:** The score that matters (public F0.5 0.991300) belongs to the whole system, not to one model, and several important choices sit in the hand-written decision layer. Learned parts adapt to data but need labels; hand-written rules are auditable but do not adapt, which is why we used rules mainly where labels were missing (France) and stated that they came from test-set analysis. A common misconception is that a model "understands" a pair: it can only use what its input shows it. A reader sees one pair at a time and cannot know that a better candidate exists, so we give that information to the decision model as competition features (see Features and labels). The toy table also shows a classic danger: "6 of 6 = 1.00" is a confident claim from only six examples (see Overfitting).

**Remember:**
- Model = a function whose numbers were learned from labelled examples; training finds the numbers, inference applies them.
- Our system mixes learned models (ranker, readers, decision models, second-chance models) with hand-written rules (filter, decision rule, consistency check, France rules).
- A model can only use what its inputs show it.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Which parts of your system are learned, and which are hand-written?* The CatBoost ranker, the four readers, one LightGBM decision model per country and the second-chance models are learned; the cleaning, the quick rule-based filter, the confident + clear-winner rule, the per-business consistency check and the France rules are code. For the US and India, the decision threshold and the consistency-check bars were tuned on held-out folds for the exact competition metric. France has no labels, so its rules came from analysing the unlabelled French records, and some of their parameters were chosen after seeing public scores, as we disclose.

---

### A0.2 Features and labels {#a0-2 .concept}

**In one line:** **Features** are the numbers we compute to describe an example; the **label** is the correct answer we want the model to learn to predict.

**Simple explanation:** A detective comparing two descriptions of a shop writes down clues: Do the names share rare words? Is the house number the same? Did "Inc" become "LLC"? Each clue, written as a number, is a feature, and the list of all clues for one pair is its **feature vector**. The label is the verdict from the closed case files: "same business" (1) or "not the same" (0). Training means showing the model many feature vectors together with their labels so it learns which patterns of clues go with which verdict. Two golden rules: a feature must be computable when the answer is unknown (otherwise the model cheats during training and fails in use), and better clues usually beat a cleverer detective.

**Worked example:** From the Documentation's US example (Doc D.1). Incoming record: "Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc)", no address. Candidate business: "Legacy Marketing Industries Inc", 2360 Airbase Road, Louisville, TN.
1. Lower-case and drop punctuation: "legacy marketing enterprises inc" against "legacy marketing industries inc".
2. Our word features ignore legal-form words, so compare {legacy, marketing, enterprises} with {legacy, marketing, industries}.
3. Words replaced: 1 (enterprises → industries); added: 0; dropped: 0; the replacement sits in the same position ("in place"): yes.
4. Plain **Jaccard overlap** = shared words / all distinct words = |{legacy, marketing}| / |{legacy, marketing, enterprises, industries}| = 2 / 4 = 0.50. Our feature weights each word by its rarity (IDF, below); the Documentation reports 0.52 for this pair.
5. Meaning similarity of the replaced word, from a pre-trained language model (see Embeddings): 0.77 (Doc D.1).
6. Legal-form relation: same (Inc and Inc). Number features: left empty (missing), because the record has no address and so no number to compare.
7. So part of this pair's feature vector reads [replaced 1, added 0, dropped 0, in place 1, IDF-weighted overlap 0.52, meaning similarity 0.77, legal form "same", number features missing, ...]: 217 numbers in all for a US pair.
8. Label: in training data it comes from the ground truth (1 if this business owns the record, else 0). Test labels are private; the decision model gave this pair 0.000088, while "Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc" in Windsor, CT got 0.965022.

**Technical explanation:** A feature vector x ∈ R^d is the model's entire view of an example; for tree models (see Decision trees) features can be on any scale, and categorical relations can be coded as integers. Our feature families are: (a) **similarity** features (string similarities, word and letter-piece overlaps, IDF-weighted overlaps); (b) **difference** features that describe the edit turning the business into the record (number deltas; words added, dropped or replaced, with position, rarity and meaning similarity; the legal-form relation); (c) **model-output** features (ranker probability, reader scores), which make the decision model a **stacked** model (see Ensembles); (d) **context** features over a record's whole shortlist (rank, best other score, margin over the best other); (e) **collective** features over the other incoming records competing for the same business (US and India only). **IDF** (inverse document frequency) measures rarity, IDF = log((N + 1) / (df + 1)) with N the number of records and df the number containing the word, so common words count less than rare ones (the index lookup uses the smoothed variant log(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1)), Doc 3); it needs no labels. In the US example the IDF-weighted overlap (0.52) differs from the plain overlap (0.50) only because the four words have different rarities. The label is defined per pair (y = 1 if candidate = owner) but the decision is per record, so the labels of one record's candidates are mutually exclusive: at most one can be 1. Unowned incoming records contribute pairs whose labels are all 0, which is how the model learns to say "none". **Leakage**, a feature that encodes the label or uses information unavailable at prediction time, is the cardinal sin: it inflates validation scores and fails in use. Missing information must be coded deliberately: our generic number differences are left missing (NaN) when there is no substituted number, and LightGBM learns which branch missing values should take; other generic features use a **sentinel** value outside their normal range (−1 for most "not applicable" cases, such as a digit edit distance or a word position when there is nothing to compare; −2 for the meaning similarities, because a real cosine can itself be as low as −1), so a single tree split can separate "not applicable" from every real value.

**How we used it:** The CatBoost ranker uses 76 features from the index lookup. The decision models use 217 features (US), 211 (India) and 158 (France and the default route); in the talk, "about two hundred features per country". Labels exist for the US and India only; France has none, which is why the French readers learned from **pseudo-labels** (see Pre-trained and fine-tuned models). Training rows for the decision models are the shortlist pairs of training records that have a candidate in business folds 6-9, labelled "candidate is the owner". We removed 21 data-specific inputs and replaced them with 25 generic "what changed" features; a code check asserts that none of the removed inputs is used.

**Expert nuance:** Similarity features alone treat two edits as equal when they cost the same number of characters, yet dropping "Inc" and swapping "Inc" for "LLC" mean very different things for identity; difference features let the model learn which edits are harmless. Our word features deliberately ignore legal-form tokens, so a legal-form change shows up only in the legal-form features and in the readers, which keeps the two kinds of edit separate. The IDF and index statistics are computed on the unlabelled test files themselves (disclosed, Doc C.1): that uses no labels, but it does adapt the pipeline to this test set. A long feature list is not a virtue in itself, and we have no feature-importance ranking prepared, so do not claim which feature matters most; show the mechanism with the US example instead.

**Remember:**
- Feature = a clue written as a number; label = the right answer from training data; a feature must never peek at the label.
- Our key idea: describe "what changed" (numbers, words added, dropped or replaced, legal form), not only "how similar".
- Labels are per pair, decisions are per record; France has no labels.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Your readers already read both texts. Why add hand-made "what changed" features?* A reader returns one number for one pair; the decision model also needs to know which edit happened, how rare the changed word is and how the candidate compares with its rivals. In our US example the legal-form features and the readers put the LLC business last although the ranker had placed it second, and the word-replacement features mark the "Industries" business, which scores 0.000088.
- *Where do your labels come from, and what exactly is one training example?* The organisers' training files give each US and Indian incoming record its owning business, or none; one example is one (incoming record, candidate) pair from the shortlist, labelled 1 if the candidate is the owner. France has no labels at all, so its readers learned from confident pseudo-labels and its decision model from US and Indian rows.

---

### A0.3 Classification, regression and ranking {#a0-3 .concept}

**In one line:** **Classification** predicts a category, **regression** predicts a number, and **ranking** predicts an order; our task needs ranking and classification together, with "none" as an allowed answer.

**Simple explanation:** Three questions a registry clerk might ask. "Is this form about this business, yes or no?" is classification. "How many forms will this business receive next month?" is regression, because the answer is a number on a scale. "Of these twenty possible businesses, which is most likely, which second, and so on?" is ranking. Our job is: for each incoming record, find the most likely business (ranking), then decide whether it is good enough to link (a yes/no classification), and otherwise answer "none". We do not treat each of the 1.7 million businesses as its own category, because that list is huge and changes; instead we ask the same yes/no question about one pair at a time.

**Worked example:** Incoming record "Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc)", no address (Doc D.1).

| Candidate business | Classification view: P(match) from the decision model | Ranking view |
|---|---|---|
| Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc, Windsor, CT | 0.965022 | 1st |
| Legacy Marketing Enterprises PC, Joshua Tree, CA | 0.088664 | 2nd |
| Legacy Marketing Industries Inc, Louisville, TN | 0.000088 | 3rd |
| Legacy Marketing Enterprises LLC, Irondequoit, NY | 0.000007 | 4th |

1. Score each pair on its own (classification).
2. Sort the scores (ranking).
3. Apply the decision rule to the top one: 0.965022 ≥ 0.75, and its lead is 0.965022 − 0.088664 = 0.876 ≥ 0.4, so the record is linked to the Windsor business only.

A regression question about the same data, which we did not model, would be "how many incoming records will this business own?"; our final file links on average 3.3805 records per business (Doc B.1).

**Technical explanation:** Binary classification models P(y = 1 | x) and is trained with log loss (see Loss functions). Multi-class classification puts a **softmax** (a function that turns K scores into K probabilities summing to 1) over K fixed classes, which is unusable when the "classes" are 1,732,544 businesses, a list that is huge, changes over time and has only a handful of examples per business, so entity resolution is normally cast as binary classification over **candidate pairs**. Regression predicts y ∈ R with losses such as squared or absolute error. **Learning to rank** has three families: **pointwise** (score each item alone with a classification or regression loss, then sort), **pairwise** (a loss on ordered pairs of items, as in RankNet) and **listwise** (a loss targeting a ranking metric over the whole list, as in LambdaMART for **NDCG**, a ranking-quality measure that rewards placing the right items near the top). Our CatBoost ranker is pointwise: a binary classifier with log loss whose probabilities are sorted. The final step is **selection with abstention**: take the **argmax** (the candidate with the highest score) over a record's candidates, then apply a **reject option** (a threshold and a margin; "reject" here means "decline to link"). The structure is many-to-one, a record links to at most one business while a business may own many records, so it is not one-to-one assignment (no Hungarian matching, the classic algorithm for pairing two lists one to one). Pointwise models never see the competitors, so list context must be supplied as features: rank, best other score and margin within the record's shortlist.

**How we used it:** The CatBoost ranker is a pointwise classifier used to rank and then cut: the top candidate always enters the shortlist, and ranks 2-4 only if their ranker probability is at least 0.001 (so at most 4 per record). The readers and the decision models are binary classifiers on pairs. The confident + clear-winner rule turns pair scores into one decision per record. The decision model receives the ranking context as features: rank, best other score, margin and group maximum of the ranker and reader scores.

**Expert nuance:** We did not use a ranking loss (LambdaMART, YetiRank or a pairwise loss), and the Documentation reports no comparison, so do not claim one would be worse. A practical point for a classification loss here: we need a probability, not just an order, because both the 0.001 shortlist floor and the decision model's input use the ranker's probability, while a listwise score is only comparable within one record's list. Injecting rank and margin features is a cheap way to make a pointwise second stage list-aware. The "none" answer is essential: about 41 % of incoming records are linked to nothing in our final file (derived from 0.5875 links per incoming record).

**Remember:**
- Classification = category, regression = number, ranking = order.
- Our ranker is a pointwise classifier (log loss) used for ranking; it is not trained with a ranking loss.
- Final decision = pick the best candidate or abstain.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Your "ranker" is a classifier. Why not a learning-to-rank objective such as LambdaMART?* Yes, it is a pointwise CatBoost classifier with log loss whose probabilities we sort. We needed a probability, not just an order: ranks 2-4 enter the shortlist only above 0.001, and the probability is an input of the decision model. We did not benchmark a ranking loss, so we do not claim it would be better or worse; what we did measure is that on held-out fold 9 the shortlist still holds the true business for at least 98.87 % of US records, against 99.37 % at the index.

---

### A0.4 Confusion matrix, precision, recall and F0.5 {#a0-4 .concept}

**In one line:** A **confusion matrix** counts the four ways a yes/no prediction can be right or wrong; **precision**, **recall** and **F0.5** summarise it, with F0.5 weighting precision more.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine auditing a clerk's links. Each link they made is either right (a **true positive**, TP) or wrong (a **false positive**, FP). Each true link they failed to make is a **false negative** (FN). Each wrong pair they correctly left alone is a **true negative** (TN); in matching there are trillions of those, so they tell us nothing. **Precision** asks "of the links you made, how many were right?"; **recall** asks "of the links you should have made, how many did you make?". F0.5 blends the two but cares more about precision, because a wrong link hurts more than a missed one. Our competition computes it separately for every business and then takes the plain average.

**Worked example (toy):** Business A, "Joe's Pizza, 410 Main St, Boston", truly owns 3 incoming records: R1, R2 and R3.

| | Truly A's record | Not A's record |
|---|---|---|
| We linked it to A | TP | FP |
| We did not link it to A | FN | TN (millions; ignored) |

1. Option 1: link R1, R2 and R7 (R7 belongs elsewhere). TP = 2, FP = 1, FN = 1. Precision = 2/3 = 0.667; recall = 2/3 = 0.667. F0.5 = 1.25 × P × R / (0.25 × P + R) = 1.25 × 0.444 / (0.167 + 0.667) = 0.667. The count form is easier by hand: F0.5 = 1.25 × TP / (predicted + 0.25 × true) = 1.25 × 2 / (3 + 0.75) = 0.667.
2. Option 2: link only R1 and R2: 1.25 × 2 / (2 + 0.75) = 0.909. (F1 would give 0.800 here; F0.5 rewards caution more.)
3. Option 3: link R1, R2, R3 and R7: 1.25 × 3 / (4 + 0.75) = 0.789.
4. Option 4: link exactly R1, R2 and R3: 1.25 × 3 / (3 + 0.75) = 1.000.
5. Macro average over three businesses: A with option 2 (0.909); B, "Kumar Textiles", which has no true records and gets nothing linked (1.000 by the competition's rule); C, "Sharma Traders", which has no true records but gets one wrong link (TP 0, predicted 1, true 0 → 0.000). Macro F0.5 = (0.909 + 1.000 + 0.000) / 3 = 0.636. One wrong link on an empty business cost a whole point.

**Technical explanation:** Precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN). F_b = (1 + b²) × P × R / (b² × P + R) = (1 + b²) × TP / ((1 + b²) × TP + b² × FN + FP). In van Rijsbergen's definition b is the relative importance of recall to precision, so with b = 0.5 (b² = 0.25) recall counts half as much as precision; equivalently F0.5 is a weighted **harmonic mean** (the reciprocal of the average of reciprocals, which is pulled towards the smaller of the two values) with weight 1 / (1 + b²) = 0.8 on precision: 1 / F = 0.8 / P + 0.2 / R. Our per-business form is F0.5 = 1.25 × TP / (predicted + 0.25 × true), defined as 1 when both predicted and true are 0. **Macro-averaging** gives each of the 1,732,544 businesses equal weight regardless of size, unlike **micro-averaging**, which pools TP, FP and FN over everything first. TN never enters an F-score, which is why accuracy (dominated by TN) is useless here. Because each incoming record has at most one owner, a wrong link creates an FP at the wrong business and leaves an FN at the true one, while abstaining creates only the FN, so a wrong link is never better than no link and usually worse (it lowers the wrong business's score unless that score is already 0). Threshold-free metrics such as **AUC** (the area under the ROC curve, which plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as the threshold moves; equivalently, the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative) summarise ranking quality over all thresholds, but the competition scores one **operating point** (one chosen threshold).

**How we used it:** This exact metric is implemented in our evaluation code: per business, macro-averaged, with the empty-row rule, and with true records that never reached our candidates still counted as misses. The labelled operating points were tuned on it: the 0.75 threshold on fold 8, the consistency-check bars on folds 8 and 9, and the second-chance thresholds on fold 8 with false positives counted twice (France's 0.82 was set without labels; see Probability scores). Results: public 0.991300; on held-out fold 9 / fold 8, close versions of our decision models (the India recipe with 3 of its 5 seeds) score US 0.991212 / 0.991545 and India 0.990046 / 0.990298 (Doc 5). 100,087 businesses (5.8 %, derived) end with an empty row.

**Expert nuance:** Under macro F0.5 the most fragile businesses are those with no true records: one wrong link takes them from 1 to 0, while missing one record of a business that owns 6 only takes it from 1 to 0.9615 (toy arithmetic: 1.25 × 5 / (5 + 1.5)). AUC can be nearly perfect while the F-score at a threshold is mediocre, and two models with almost equal AUC can produce different link files; for the French E5 reader against its base model on labelled US and Indian pairs, AUC was 0.998544 against 0.998570, a difference that says little about the final file. Recall of candidate generation (is the owner among the candidates at all?) caps the recall of everything after it, which is why we measured it at every step: 99.3694 % (US) and 98.5068 % (India) of owned fold-9 records at the index (Doc B.2).

**Remember:**
- Precision = right links / links made; recall = right links / true links; TN is irrelevant.
- Per-business F0.5 = 1.25 × TP / (predicted + 0.25 × true), and 1 for a correctly empty row; then average over businesses.
- A wrong link costs a false positive plus a miss; abstaining costs only the miss.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why does this metric push you towards abstaining?* A wrong link costs twice: the wrong business gets a false positive and the true business still misses the record, while abstaining costs only the miss; and a business with no true records scores 1 only if its row stays empty. So we link only the best candidate when it is confident and clearly ahead, and 100,087 businesses end with an empty row.
- *Why not report accuracy or AUC?* Accuracy is dominated by trillions of correct non-links, and AUC ignores the operating point. We tuned and reported the exact per-business macro F0.5; for example, the French E5 reader's AUC on US and Indian pairs was within 0.00003 of its base model's, which says little about the linked file.

---

### A0.5 Probability scores: why a score is not yet a decision {#a0-5 .concept}

**In one line:** A model gives a **score** such as 0.97 ("how likely is a match"); a separate **decision rule** turns scores into actions (link or not), and the right rule depends on what each kind of mistake costs.

**Simple explanation:** A forecast of "70 % chance of rain" does not tell you whether to carry an umbrella; that depends on how much you mind getting wet. In the same way, a model can say "97 % sure this is the same business", but whether we should link depends on the cost of a wrong link (high under F0.5) and on whether another candidate is almost as good (if two candidates both look great, the model is confused). Models also speak in different units: some output a **probability** between 0 and 1, others a **logit**, an unbounded number that the **sigmoid** function squeezes into the range 0 to 1. Our final decision is a small rule on top of the scores: link the best candidate only if it is confident enough and clearly ahead of the runner-up.

**Worked example:**
1. Logit to probability, sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). In the France example (Doc D.3), for the record "TQ COMITE SARL", "2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN, NANTES", the MiniLM reader gave the business "TQ Comite SARL", "2 RUE du Lycee, Pessac" a logit of 7.125, so sigmoid(7.125) = 0.9992 (derived). Same name, but another city. The French reader blend gave −3.2008 (sigmoid 0.039) and the decision model 0.000098. One high score was not a decision.
2. The decision rule on the US example: best 0.965022 ≥ 0.75 (confident) and 0.965022 − 0.088664 = 0.876 ≥ 0.4 (clear winner), so link. Toy counter-example: best 0.91, runner-up 0.70: confident, but the lead is 0.21 < 0.4, so no link.
3. Why the best threshold depends on context (toy). Business A owns 3 records and we already linked 2 of them correctly, so its F0.5 is 1.25 × 2 / (2 + 0.75) = 0.909. A third candidate link has match probability p. If right, F0.5 becomes 1.25 × 3 / (3 + 0.75) = 1.000, a gain of 0.091. If wrong, it becomes 1.25 × 2 / (3 + 0.75) = 0.667, a loss of 0.242. Linking pays off only if p × 0.091 > (1 − p) × 0.242, that is p > 0.727. From a different starting point the break-even moves, which is the intuition behind our per-business consistency check using different bars depending on how many other records were accepted for the same business.

**Technical explanation:** A classifier trained with log loss estimates P(y = 1 | x) on its training distribution, but tree ensembles and neural networks can be **miscalibrated** (among pairs scored 0.9, the true share of matches is not 90 %), and calibration does not survive a change of input distribution. The **logit** is z = ln(p / (1 − p)) and sigmoid is its inverse; averaging logits (as in our French blend) lets confident votes count more than averaging probabilities would. Decision theory: for one yes/no decision with costs c_FP and c_FN, act when p > c_FP / (c_FP + c_FN). F-scores are not additive costs, but a short calculation (background, not from our documents) gives a clean rule for a pooled (micro) F_b. Write F = (1 + b²) × TP / D with D = predicted + b² × true. Adding one link with match probability p leaves D + 1 in the denominator either way, so the expected score becomes (1 + b²) × (TP + p) / (D + 1), which is higher than F only if p > TP / D = F / (1 + b²). For F1 this is the known "best threshold is half the best F1" result; for F0.5 it is 0.8 × F, about 0.79 when F ≈ 0.99. Our metric is macro per business, so the break-even depends on each business's state (step 3 above); we therefore tuned thresholds empirically on held-out folds rather than deriving them. The **margin** (lead over the runner-up) is an ambiguity reject option: a record's candidates are mutually exclusive, so calibrated probabilities for one record cannot sum to more than 1, and scores of 0.9 and 0.8 signal that the model cannot separate the two. In code, a record with a single candidate treats the runner-up as minus infinity, so the lead condition passes automatically (say this only if asked); 90.59 % of incoming records have exactly one candidate in the final candidate file (Doc B.1).

**How we used it:**
- Scores in our pipeline: the ranker's probability (for the 0.001 shortlist floor, and as a decision-model input); the reader logits (for France blended in logit space, 0.35 MiniLM + 0.15 French MiniLM + 0.5 French E5); the decision model's probability (the mean of 5 seed models; a single fit on the default route).
- The decision: confident (≥ 0.75 for the US and India, tuned on fold 8; ≥ 0.82 for France and the default route) and clear winner (lead ≥ 0.4, one fixed value for every country).
- The per-business consistency check re-decides each US and Indian record with the bar 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77 for 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 or more other accepted records (chosen on folds 8 and 9).
- Second chances: native-script rescue links if its score is ≥ 0.88 with a lead ≥ 0.3 (the 0.88 chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice); address rescue US 0.86 with margin 0.0, India 0.66 with margin 0.1 (threshold and margin chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice).
- No **Platt scaling** (fitting a small logistic curve from scores to observed match rates) or **isotonic calibration** (fitting a step-wise increasing curve for the same purpose): thresholds are tuned directly on the exact metric.

**Expert nuance:** Tuning the threshold on held-out data for the exact metric makes calibration unnecessary for the decision, as long as the held-out fold resembles the test; when an input changes meaning, the threshold's meaning changes too. France is the case in point: its decision model was trained with the MiniLM reader's logits in its reader slot but at test receives the French blend, and France has no labels, so 0.82 was set label-free from the French link volume per business together with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US/India, more conservative than 0.75. Counting false positives twice when tuning the second-chance thresholds is an explicit cost weighting that reflects F0.5. Do not say the 0.4 lead was "never tuned": the Documentation does not record how it was picked; say it is one fixed lead used in every country.

**Remember:**
- Score ≠ decision; the rule (threshold + lead) encodes the cost of mistakes.
- Logit = log-odds; sigmoid turns it into a probability; France blends its readers in logit space.
- Our rule: best candidate only, ≥ 0.75 (US, India) or ≥ 0.82 (France, default), and a lead ≥ 0.4.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Are your decision-model probabilities calibrated?* We did not apply Platt or isotonic calibration; instead the thresholds were tuned directly on the exact per-business macro F0.5 on held-out fold 8, which is what the decision needs. For France, with no labels, the 0.82 bar was set label-free from the number of French links per business together with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US and Indian data.
- *Why require a lead over the runner-up instead of just a threshold?* A record's candidates compete for one slot, so two high scores mean the model cannot tell them apart, and under F0.5 a wrong link costs more than a miss. The 0.4 lead is one fixed value used in every country; the threshold itself was tuned on fold 8.

---

### A0.6 Class imbalance {#a0-6 .concept}

**In one line:** **Class imbalance** means one answer ("not a match") is vastly more common than the other, which misleads naive training and naive metrics.

**Simple explanation:** Matching is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: an incoming US record could in principle belong to any of 663,106 US businesses, and at most one is right. A lazy model that always says "no match" would be right on about 99.99985 % of pairs and completely useless. When nearly all examples are "no", a naively trained model learns mostly about easy "no" cases and too little about the rare "yes" ones. There are three standard remedies: shrink the haystack before learning, choose metrics that ignore the easy "no" answers, and choose training examples carefully. We used all three.

**Worked example (derived from documented counts):**
1. All same-country pairs: 6,724,569,566,212. Each incoming record has at most one owner, so at most 9,969,589 pairs are true: at most 1 pair in 674,508, about 1.5 per million.
2. "Always say no" accuracy for one US record: 1 − 1 / 663,106 = 99.99985 %.
3. After the index lookup and the quick rule-based filter: 37,614,782 pairs, of which true pairs can be at most 26.5 %.
4. The shortlist: 11,687,317 pairs, 1.17 per incoming record. In the final candidate file (12,293,019 pairs) our 5,856,936 links make up 47.6 % of the pairs.

So the cascade turns a one-in-a-million problem into a nearly balanced one before the expensive readers and the decision models see it.

**Technical explanation:** Imbalance hurts in three places. In learning, the average loss and its gradient are dominated by the many easy negatives, and the model's outputs inherit the training **base rate** (prior), so a model trained on a sample re-balanced towards positives over-predicts positives on the natural distribution unless the prior is corrected: subtract [log-odds of the training base rate − log-odds of the true base rate] from the logit. In evaluation, accuracy and even ROC curves look excellent when negatives dominate, because the false-positive rate divides by the huge number of negatives, so a rate that looks negligible can still mean more wrong links than right ones; precision-based metrics (precision, F-scores, precision-recall curves) stay informative because TN never enter them. In decisions, the best threshold depends on the base rate and on the costs (see Probability scores). Standard remedies: candidate generation (**blocking**) that removes obvious negatives; **informative sampling** (keep hard negatives, subsample easy ones); class weights or **focal loss** (a variant of log loss that down-weights examples the model already gets right); and tuning the threshold on a held-out set drawn like the deployment data. Hard negatives are worth far more than many easy ones because they sit next to the decision boundary.

**How we used it:**
- Blocking: index lookup → quick rule-based filter (21.7107 candidates per business) → shortlist (at most 4 per incoming record).
- Reader training sample: every "hard" training record (top ranker probability between 0.003 and 0.9995, a non-owner ranked first, or a second candidate above 0.003) plus a random 25 % of the others; candidates 1-4 if ranked first, at probability ≥ 0.001, or the owner; candidates 5-8 only if they are the owner, so the readers also see true owners that the ranker placed low.
- French E5 reader pseudo-labels: at most one positive and one negative per record, balanced classes, at most 250,000 per class.
- No class weights in any model (the training code passes no class or sample weights). The decision models train on the natural shortlist pairs of training records (folds 6-9), not on a sample re-balanced towards matches (for the US and India with the extra hard examples described in the next bullet), and their thresholds are tuned on held-out folds, so the base rate is handled at decision time.
- Only if a judge asks about hard negatives, use the QA 15 wording: "for the US and India only, the decision models were trained with extra hard examples: copies of unlinked training records that sit right next to a candidate business, with small name edits; how many to add was set from label-free counts on the test records, never from labels; the France decision model uses no such examples."

**Expert nuance:** Because the readers are trained on a deliberately hard-heavy sample, their raw scores need not be calibrated to the test base rate; that is acceptable because they are inputs to a decision model trained on other folds, which learns its own mapping from reader score to probability. Imbalance also exists at the business level: a business with no true records scores 1 only if its row stays empty, so a single false positive there costs a whole point; our final file leaves 100,087 rows empty. A common misconception is that imbalance must be "fixed" by oversampling; often the better fix is a better candidate set plus a threshold tuned for the real metric.

**Remember:**
- Raw pairs: at most about 1.5 true per million; after the shortlist: about 1.17 pairs per incoming record.
- Handle imbalance by shrinking the haystack, sampling hard examples and tuning thresholds on the true metric.
- No class weights anywhere in our pipeline.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Matching is extremely imbalanced. Did you use class weights or oversampling?* No class weights; the cascade removes most of the imbalance: of 6.7 trillion same-country pairs at most one per incoming record is true, but after the shortlist each record has on average 1.17 pairs. For the readers we sampled training records where the ranker was unsure or wrong plus a random quarter of the easy ones, and the decision thresholds were tuned on held-out folds, so the base rate is handled at decision time.

---

### A0.7 Training, validation and test data {#a0-7 .concept}

**In one line:** We learn on one part of the data (**training**), make choices on a second part (**validation**), and measure honestly on a third part that influenced nothing (**test**).

**Simple explanation:** A student preparing for an exam does textbook exercises (training), sits mock exams to decide what to revise and when to stop (validation), and then takes the real exam (test). If the student has seen the real exam paper beforehand, a high mark proves nothing. Models are the same: any data used to make a choice stops being a fair test. Matching has an extra trap: the natural unit is the business. If some records of "Sharma Traders, Pune" are in training and others in the test, the model may simply recognise Sharma Traders instead of learning how to match, and the test score looks better than reality. So we split by business: all records of a business go to the same side.

**Worked example (toy hash values):** Each labelled training business gets a **fold** number = hash(business id) mod 10, and every incoming record goes with its owner. A **hash** is a fixed scrambling function that turns an id into a large, random-looking but repeatable number; "mod 10" keeps its last digit, so the businesses spread evenly over 10 folds. (Folds split the labelled training data; the business names below are only illustrations.)

| Business | Toy hash | Fold = hash mod 10 | Its incoming records |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sharma Traders, Pune | 4,213 | 3 | 4 records, all in fold 3 |
| Joe's Pizza, Boston | 7,846 | 6 | 2 records, fold 6 |
| Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc, Windsor | 1,239 | 9 | 3 records, fold 9 |
| Patel Medical Store, Ahmedabad | 5,518 | 8 | 5 records, fold 8 |
| Green Leaf Salon, Austin | 2,990 | 0 | none |

With a record-level split, two of Sharma's four records could land in training and two in the test; the model would have seen "Sharma Traders, 12 MG Road" as a positive and would find the test copies easy. With the business-level split, fold 9 contains whole businesses the models never saw. Then each group of folds gets a job (our real plan):
1. Folds 0-5: train the Indic-to-Latin word list, the CatBoost ranker (with fold 6 for **early stopping**, i.e. deciding when to stop adding trees; see Overfitting) and the readers.
2. Folds 6-7: train the decision models; fold 8: early stopping and the 0.75 threshold; for the US and India the decision models are then refitted on folds 6-9.
3. Folds 8 and 9: choose the consistency-check bars; fold 9 (and fold 8 with a mirrored set-up): report held-out scores.

**Technical explanation:** Training data fits parameters; validation data selects hyper-parameters, early-stopping points, thresholds and model variants; test data estimates performance once. Every decision taken by looking at a dataset makes it partly training data (**adaptive overfitting**). With grouped data, splits must respect the groups (**group k-fold**); ours is fold = hash(business id, seed 20260927) mod 10, where owned records inherit their owner's fold and unowned records hash their own id. Our **stacked** design needs a second layer of hygiene: the decision model takes ranker and reader scores as inputs, and a model's scores on its own training records are over-confident, so the base models (ranker, readers) train on folds 0-5 and the decision models on folds 6-9. The usual alternative is **out-of-fold predictions** (k-fold cross-fitting of every base model); our layer-wise split costs only one training run per base model. Our held-out protocol scores fold 9 with fits on folds 6-8 that exclude every record touching fold 9, and fold 8 with fits on folds 6, 7 and 9 that exclude records touching fold 8, with each seed's iteration count fixed from its early-stopping point and scaled to the fit size. The public leaderboard is a test set to which we made 18 uploads (17 returned a score), so it was partly used as validation.

**How we used it:** As above, plus: the US and India decision models fit on folds 6-7 with early stopping on fold 8 (at most 3,000 rounds), then refit on folds 6-9 for best iteration × rows(6-9) / rows(6-7) rounds; the France and default decision models fit on 6-7 with early stopping on 8 (at most 1,500 rounds) and no refit. The native-script rescue model trains on folds 0-7 with word lists that leave out the record's own fold (**cross-fitting**, so no record benefits from its own label); the address rescue models train on folds 6-7, with thresholds on fold 8. Held-out scores of close versions of our decision models (the India recipe with 3 of its 5 seeds), fold 9 / fold 8: US 0.991212 / 0.991545, India 0.990046 / 0.990298; public 0.991300.

**Expert nuance:** Limitation first: there is no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file. The held-out scores exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules, the final US/India decision models are refitted on folds 6-9, folds 8 and 9 also chose thresholds and the consistency check, and France has no labels; the mitigation is that held-out scores from fits that leave the scored fold out sit in the same range as the public score. The pipeline also computes unsupervised statistics on the unlabelled test files (IDF, the indexes, for India a word alignment on very confident test matches, for France the geography) and self-trains the French readers on French test pseudo-labels; no labels are involved and it is disclosed (Doc C.1), but it means the system was adapted to this test set. The refit rule (scale the number of trees by the row ratio) is a heuristic, needed because no fold is left for early stopping.

**Remember:**
- Train fits, validation chooses, test judges; anything you looked at to choose is no longer a clean test.
- Split by business (hash of the business id, 10 folds); ranker and readers on folds 0-5, decision models on folds 6-9.
- Disclosed limitation: no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why split folds by business rather than by record?* The business is the unit of the metric and of several features: one business owns several records, the score is computed per business, and the consistency check looks at all records competing for the same business. A record-level split would put records of the same business on both sides and inflate the held-out score; when we score fold 9, the fits also leave out every record that touches fold 9.
- *Do you have a clean test set for the final file?* No, and our documentation says so: there is no untouched end-to-end validation; the held-out scores exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules, folds 8 and 9 also chose thresholds, and France has no labels. What we do have: close versions of our decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992 on held-out folds from fits that never saw the scored fold, the same range as the public 0.9913.

---

### A0.8 Loss functions and log loss {#a0-8 .concept}

**In one line:** A **loss function** is one number that measures how wrong a model's predictions are on the training examples; training means adjusting the model to make that number small.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine a quiz where you must also say how sure you are. Saying "99 % sure" and being wrong costs many penalty points; saying "60 % sure" and being wrong costs a few; being right and confident costs almost nothing. Over many questions, the best strategy is to be honest about your uncertainty. **Log loss** (also called **binary cross-entropy**) is exactly this penalty system, and every learned model in our pipeline is trained to collect as few penalty points as possible across its training pairs. The models never see F0.5 during training; they see log loss. We turn good scores into a good F0.5 afterwards, with the decision rule.

**Worked example (toy):** For one pair, log loss = −[y × ln(p) + (1 − y) × ln(1 − p)], where y is the label and p the predicted match probability.

| Pair | Truth y | Predicted p | Loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Joes Pizza, 410 Main St" vs "Joe's Pizza, 410 Main Street" | 1 | 0.90 | −ln 0.90 = 0.105 |
| "Patel Medical Store" (no address) vs "Patel Medical Store, 5 Station Road" | 1 | 0.60 | −ln 0.60 = 0.511 |
| "Starbucks, 200 Pine St" vs "Starbucks, 1500 Broadway" | 0 | 0.30 | −ln 0.70 = 0.357 |
| "Sunrise Pharmacy, 5 Park Ave" vs "Sunrise Bakery, 5 Park Ave" | 0 | 0.90 | −ln 0.10 = 2.303 |
| "Kumar Electricals" vs "Kumar Textiles" | 0 | 0.999 | −ln 0.001 = 6.908 |

1. Add the five losses: 10.183. Average: 10.183 / 5 = 2.037.
2. Without the last row the average is 0.819.
3. Lesson: one confidently wrong prediction dominates the total, so training pushes hardest on exactly those mistakes.

**Technical explanation:** Log loss is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model (a coin-flip model in which each pair is a match with probability p), so minimising the average log loss is **maximum-likelihood estimation**: choosing the parameters under which the observed labels are most probable. It is a **strictly proper scoring rule**: the expected loss is minimised only by predicting the true conditional probability, which is why models trained with it tend to produce probability-like scores on their training distribution. With p = sigmoid(z), the gradient with respect to the logit is simply ∂L/∂z = p − y, and the second derivative is p × (1 − p); gradient-boosting libraries build trees from exactly these two quantities (see Ensembles), and neural networks back-propagate p − y (see Gradient descent). Implementations compute the loss from the logit directly ("with logits") for numerical stability. Other losses exist for other tasks: squared error for regression, hinge loss for support-vector machines, focal loss for heavy imbalance, pairwise or listwise losses for ranking. Our evaluation metric (per-business macro F0.5) is not differentiable and does not decompose over pairs, so we optimise a smooth **surrogate** (log loss) and then optimise the metric itself at decision time by choosing thresholds. **Validation loss** on a held-out fold is also the usual signal for early stopping.

**How we used it:** Every learned model minimises log loss: the CatBoost ranker (loss "Logloss", monitored on fold 6 for early stopping), the four readers (binary cross-entropy on their single logit), the LightGBM decision models (binary objective; early stopping on fold-8 log loss with a patience of 100 rounds) and the LightGBM second-chance models (binary objective). F0.5 is used only to choose thresholds and to evaluate.

**Expert nuance:** Log loss is unbounded, so a few confidently wrong labels (label noise) can dominate training; that matters for pseudo-labels, which is one reason we kept only very confident French pseudo-labels (≥ 0.97 for matches; ≤ 0.03 for the French E5 reader's non-matches). Lower log loss does not guarantee a higher F0.5 at the chosen threshold, because log loss rewards good probabilities everywhere, including far from the threshold; that is why selection used the exact metric. Do not confuse the **loss** (what training minimises) with the **metric** (what we report).

**Remember:**
- Log loss = −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)]; confident mistakes are punished hardest.
- All our learned models minimise log loss; F0.5 chooses thresholds, it does not train anything.
- The gradient of log loss with respect to the logit is p − y.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Your models minimise log loss but the competition scores F0.5. How do you bridge the two?* Log loss is a smooth, proper objective that gives good probability-like scores; F0.5 per business is not differentiable and depends on whole businesses, so we do not train on it. We bridge the gap at decision time: on top of one fixed 0.4 lead over the runner-up, the threshold and the consistency-check bars were chosen on held-out folds for the exact per-business macro F0.5.

---

### A0.9 Gradient descent {#a0-9 .concept}

**In one line:** **Gradient descent** improves a model step by step by nudging every adjustable number in the direction that lowers the loss fastest.

**Simple explanation:** You are on a foggy hillside and want to reach the valley floor. You cannot see far, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet, so you take a small step downhill, feel again, and repeat. The slope is the **gradient**, the size of each step is the **learning rate**, and the valley floor is low loss. Steps that are too big overshoot and bounce around; steps that are too small take forever. A neural network such as our MiniLM reader has about 118 million adjustable numbers, so its hillside has 118 million directions, but calculus (a method called **backpropagation**) gives the slope in all of them at once.

**Worked example (toy):** A one-feature model p = sigmoid(w × x + b), where x is name similarity. Two training pairs: A = "Joe's Pizza" vs "Joes Pizza" (x = 0.9, y = 1) and B = "Kumar Electricals" vs "Kumar Textiles" (x = 0.2, y = 0). Start with w = 0 and b = 0; learning rate 2.
1. Predictions: p_A = p_B = sigmoid(0) = 0.5. Average log loss = ln 2 = 0.693.
2. Gradients, averaged over the two pairs: for w, the average of (p − y) × x = ((0.5 − 1) × 0.9 + (0.5 − 0) × 0.2) / 2 = (−0.45 + 0.10) / 2 = −0.175; for b, the average of (p − y) = (−0.5 + 0.5) / 2 = 0.
3. Update (step against the gradient): w = 0 − 2 × (−0.175) = 0.35; b = 0 − 2 × 0 = 0.
4. New predictions: p_A = sigmoid(0.315) = 0.578; p_B = sigmoid(0.07) = 0.517. Loss = 0.638, down from 0.693.
5. Repeat: after the second step w = 0.626, b = −0.096 and the loss is 0.597; after the third w = 0.871, b = −0.218 and the loss is 0.561. The weight w keeps growing because high name similarity goes with the match, and the bias b turns negative so that low-similarity pairs are pushed towards "no match".

**Technical explanation:** The update is θ ← θ − η × ∇L(θ), with η the learning rate. **Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent** estimates ∇L on a small batch (ours: 128 pairs) instead of the whole dataset; one **epoch** is one pass over all training pairs. **Backpropagation** applies the chain rule of calculus layer by layer, from the output back to the input, and obtains every gradient in one backward pass that costs roughly twice the forward pass. **AdamW** adapts the step for each parameter using running averages of the gradient (momentum) and of its square, and applies **weight decay** directly to the weights, decoupled from the gradient (see Regularisation). A **learning-rate schedule** with a linear **warm-up** (ours: the first 3 % of steps) followed by linear decay protects pre-trained weights from large early updates while Adam's statistics are still noisy. **Gradient clipping** rescales the whole gradient when its norm exceeds a cap (ours: 1.0), preventing rare explosive steps. **bf16 autocast** runs most arithmetic (the large matrix multiplications) in 16-bit "brain floating point", which keeps the range of 32-bit numbers with less precision, for speed and memory; the stored weights stay 32-bit and our loss is computed in 32-bit from the logit. Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space: each new tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current scores, and the boosting learning rate (0.05 for LightGBM, 0.075 for CatBoost) is the step size (see Ensembles).

**How we used it:** All four readers: AdamW with weight decay 0.01, batches of 128, one epoch, 3 % linear warm-up then linear decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, bf16 autocast, length-bucketed batches. Learning rates: 5e-5 for the encoders of the MiniLM and E5 readers and five times that for the newly added head (2.5e-4, derived); 2e-5 for the encoders of the French MiniLM and French E5 readers, again with the head at five times that rate. The French E5 reader's fine-tune took 7,419 steps (949,616 pairs / 128 per batch). Tree models: learning rate 0.05 (LightGBM) and 0.075 (CatBoost).

**Expert nuance:** The head gets the higher learning rate because it starts from random weights while the encoder is already good; the low encoder rate and the warm-up limit damage to pre-trained knowledge. One epoch is our fixed recipe, and the Documentation reports no comparison with more epochs, so do not claim it is optimal. GPU training in bf16 is not bit-deterministic (Doc A), which is one reason a clean re-run from raw data reproduced 99.82 % of the submitted links rather than all of them. The smaller learning rate for the French fine-tunes (2e-5) is a standard guard against drifting away from what the reader already knew.

**Remember:**
- Step downhill: θ ← θ − learning rate × gradient; backpropagation computes all the gradients.
- Readers: AdamW, learning rate 5e-5 (head × 5), 3 % warm-up, clipping 1.0, bf16, batch 128, one epoch.
- Boosting is gradient descent in which each step is a tree.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why a higher learning rate for the head than for the encoder?* The encoder is pre-trained and needs only gentle adjustment, while the one-layer head starts from random weights, so the head learns five times faster: 2.5e-4 against 5e-5 for the main readers. Warm-up over the first 3 % of steps and clipping at norm 1.0 keep early updates from damaging the pre-trained weights.
- *Why only one epoch?* It is our fixed recipe: one pass over a large set of training pairs focused on hard records, starting from pre-trained encoders, which kept the training of both readers to about 2.1 hours in the clean run. We did not report a comparison with more epochs, so we do not claim that one epoch is optimal.

---

### A0.10 Overfitting, underfitting, bias and variance {#a0-10 .concept}

**In one line:** **Underfitting** is a model too simple to capture the pattern; **overfitting** is a model that memorises its training examples, noise included, and does worse on new data.

**Simple explanation:** A clerk who has learned only "same name means same business" underfits: they will link every Starbucks to every other Starbucks. A clerk who has memorised the answer sheet ("form 4471 goes with business 902") overfits: perfect on old forms, lost on new ones. **Bias** is the systematic error of an overly simple model (wrong in the same way every time); **variance** is how much the model would change if trained on a slightly different sample (wrong in a different way every time). A good model balances the two, and the only way to see the balance is to check on data the model did not train on. People can overfit too: if you try many variants and keep whichever scored best on the same test, part of the "improvement" may be luck.

**Worked example (toy learning curve):** A boosted model adds trees one by one; we watch the log loss on the training folds and on held-out fold 8.

| Trees | Training loss | Fold-8 loss | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | 0.080 | 0.085 | underfitting: both high |
| 200 | 0.040 | 0.048 | improving |
| 600 | 0.020 | 0.041 | best on fold 8 |
| 1,200 | 0.008 | 0.044 | overfitting begins |
| 2,000 | 0.003 | 0.052 | training keeps improving, held-out gets worse |

1. Training loss always falls as trees are added: it cannot tell you when to stop.
2. Fold-8 loss falls, bottoms out (600 trees here), then rises: the model has started to fit noise.
3. **Early stopping** keeps the model at the best held-out round and stops once there has been no improvement for a set number of rounds (ours: 100).

A second toy: in the lookup table of "What a model is", the cell "high similarity + same number" learned 6 / 6 = 1.00 from six examples; with more data that cell might turn out to be 0.97. Trusting tiny groups is overfitting.

**Technical explanation:** For squared loss, expected test error decomposes exactly into bias² + variance + irreducible noise; the intuition carries over to classification. **Capacity** controls (tree depth or number of leaves, number of trees, minimum examples per leaf, network size, number of epochs) move a model along the bias-variance curve, and the diagnostic is the gap between training and validation performance. Variance can be reduced without adding bias by averaging models trained with different randomness (seed averaging, bagging; see Ensembles). Boosting lowers bias with every tree and therefore needs early stopping and regularisation to keep variance in check (see Regularisation). **Adaptive overfitting**, overfitting a validation set or a leaderboard through repeated selection, is a property of the research process rather than of one model: each comparison on the same data spends some of its credibility. Small score differences on a leaderboard can lie within noise, and the best of many uploads is biased upwards as an estimate of its own future score.

**How we used it:** Decision models: early stopping on fold 8 (patience 100 rounds; at most 3,000 rounds for the US and India, 1,500 for France), at least 200 rows per leaf, L2 1.0, 0.9 feature and 0.8 row sampling, mean of five seeds. Ranker: early stopping after 180 rounds without improvement on fold 6. Readers: one epoch, dropout 0.1, weight decay 0.01. Process: held-out folds as the main evidence; 18 public uploads, with the final file chosen by public score and the late public gains small (0.991114 → 0.991300). The decisions taken on public scores are listed in our Documentation: the US/India refit kept (0.990621 → 0.990676); the France refit dropped (0.990726 against 0.990748 without it); the second French self-training round dropped (0.991277 against 0.991300).

**Expert nuance:** The largest overfitting risks in our system are process-level, not model-level: the France rules came from test-set analysis with some parameters chosen after seeing public scores, and the final file was picked among 18 uploads; we disclose both. Refitting the US/India decision models on folds 6-9 trades lower variance (more data) against an iteration count that can no longer be validated (the best iteration scaled by the row ratio). Replacing data-specific inputs with generic "what changed" features guards against fitting regularities of this particular training set; on the public board the generic version cost nothing and helped slightly (0.990881 → 0.990934). Underfitting has a concrete face too: one similarity score with a threshold cannot separate businesses whose names differ by a single word, which is why the system has several stages.

**Remember:**
- Underfit = too simple (high bias); overfit = memorised noise (high variance); check on held-out data.
- Our guards: early stopping, ≥ 200 rows per leaf, subsampling, L2, five-seed averaging, one epoch.
- The biggest risk is process-level: 18 uploads and France rules tuned with test-set analysis (both disclosed).

**Judge might ask:**
- *How do you know the decision model is not overfitting?* The number of trees is set by early stopping on a fold the model does not train on, and the fits use at least 200 rows per leaf, row and feature sampling, L2 and an average of five seeds. The held-out check scores fold 9 with fits that never saw records touching fold 9, and close versions of our decision models (the India recipe with 3 of its 5 seeds) score US 0.991212 and India 0.990046 there, in line with the public 0.9913.
- *You dropped the France refit because it lost 0.00002 on the public board. Isn't that noise?* It may well be, and we say so: 0.990726 against 0.990748 is a tiny difference, and there are no French labels to confirm it. We kept the simpler France fit with the better public score; it is one of the leaderboard-driven decisions our documentation lists.

---

### A0.11 Regularisation {#a0-11 .concept}

**In one line:** **Regularisation** is any deliberate constraint that stops a model from fitting noise, trading a little training accuracy for better behaviour on new data.

**Simple explanation:** Think of the rules you would give a junior detective to stop them jumping to conclusions. "Do not form a rule from fewer than 200 cases" (a minimum number of examples per leaf). "Prefer modest conclusions unless the evidence is strong" (a penalty on large values). "Five detectives each see a random 80 % of the files, then average their verdicts" (subsampling and averaging). "Stop studying when your mock-exam marks stop improving" (early stopping). Each of these makes the detective slightly worse at reciting old cases and better at solving new ones.

**Worked example (toy):** How the L2 penalty shrinks a leaf's value in gradient boosting. With log loss, every training pair in a leaf contributes a gradient g = p − y (the slope of its loss) and a **curvature** h = p × (1 − p) (the second derivative: how quickly that slope changes, a measure of how much evidence the pair carries); the leaf's value, added to the logit of every pair that lands in it, is w = −G / (H + λ), where G and H are the sums over the leaf and λ is the L2 penalty.
1. A leaf with 4 pairs, all true matches, current p = 0.5: G = 4 × (0.5 − 1) = −2.0 and H = 4 × 0.25 = 1.0.
2. λ = 0: w = 2.0 / 1.0 = 2.0. λ = 1 (our LightGBM setting): w = 2.0 / 2.0 = 1.0. λ = 5: w = 2.0 / 6.0 = 0.33.
3. A leaf with 400 such pairs: G = −200 and H = 100. With λ = 1: w = 200 / 101 = 1.98, almost unchanged.
4. Lesson: the penalty mostly shrinks leaves built on little evidence. Our decision models also forbid leaves with fewer than 200 rows, so the 4-pair leaf could not exist at all.
