2. Micro (pooled: TP 2, predicted 3, true 2) = 1.25 × 2 / (3 + 0.5) = 0.714.
3. The single wrong link costs a full third of the macro score here.
4. A business D with 3 true records scores 0.909 with 2 correct links, 1.000 with 3 correct links, and 0.667 with 2 correct links plus 1 wrong one.

**Technical explanation:** Macro F0.5 = (1/N) Σ_b F_b over all N businesses of the test set; with N = 1,732,544 each business weighs about 5.8 × 10⁻⁷ of the score (derived). Consequences: small businesses count as much as large ones; a business with no true records drops from 1 to 0 with any link; a "link nothing" output scores exactly the share of businesses that truly own no record (unknown for the test set); singleton incoming records can only hurt when linked. Recall counts every owned record, including those that never reached the candidates, so retrieval misses lower the score even though no model saw them. The metric is not a sum over pairs: the value of one more link depends on the other links of the same business, which is why a count-dependent bar (the per-business consistency check) can help. To compare two systems on the same businesses, resample businesses with replacement and recompute the difference each time (a **paired bootstrap**), which respects the pairing and the business as the unit.

**How we used it:** Our evaluation code implements the exact metric: per business TP, predicted and true counts, F = 1.25 · TP / (pred + 0.25 · true), 1 when both are 0, averaged over the businesses of a held-out fold; every threshold and the consistency check were tuned on it. Folds are assigned per business (10 folds by a hash of the business id), so the unit of splitting matches the unit of the metric. Our held-out evaluation code (the protocol behind the Documentation's held-out table) reports 95 % intervals of differences with a paired bootstrap over businesses (2,000 resamples). The final file has 100,087 empty rows (5.8 %, derived), a direct consequence of linking only on a clear win. A diagnostic upload shows how much a group of rows matters: emptying every French row of an early upload moved the public score from 0.970125 to 0.839 (Doc B.6).

**Expert nuance:** Macro averaging changes the economics of a link: its value depends on the business it lands on (see the break-even example in Abstention). Because we cannot know which test businesses are truly empty, the safest policy is a uniformly high bar plus a lead requirement, with extra care where a business already has links. French businesses are 15.0 % of all businesses (259,452 of 1,732,544, derived), so French precision moves the score visibly; the diagnostic upload confirms French rows carry a large share of it. Per-business F values are coarse (0, 0.667, 0.909, 1, ...), so differences in the fifth decimal need paired comparisons on the same businesses before anyone believes them.

**Remember:**
- F_b = 1.25 · TP_b / (pred_b + 0.25 · true_b); empty truth plus empty prediction = 1.
- Every business weighs the same: one wrong link into an empty business costs a whole business-point.
- Tune and compare on the exact metric, per business, with paired resampling over businesses.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why is a correct empty row worth a full point, and what did that do to your design?*
  "That is the competition's definition: a business with no true records scores 1 only if we link nothing. One wrong link can turn a 1 into a 0, so we link only confident, clear winners, and 100,087 businesses end with an empty row."
- *Your variants differ in the fifth decimal. How do you know a difference is real?*
  "We compare variants on the same held-out businesses, and our held-out evaluation code uses a paired bootstrap over businesses, 2,000 resamples, for 95 % intervals of the difference. Where a difference is tiny we say so: the quick filter moved fold-9 F0.5 only from 0.990117 to 0.990086."

---

### A1.6 Scores, thresholds, precision-recall curves and AUC {#a1-6 .concept}

**In one line:** A model outputs a score, a **threshold** turns scores into yes-or-no decisions, and moving the threshold trades precision for recall.

**Simple explanation:** A smoke detector has a sensitivity knob. Turned up, every slice of toast sets it off (many false alarms, no missed fires); turned down, it stays silent even with real smoke. The knob is the threshold, and the knob position you choose is the **operating point**. A **precision-recall (PR) curve** plots precision against recall for every knob position. A **ROC curve** plots the true-positive rate (the share of real fires that set the alarm off, which is recall) against the false-positive rate (the share of non-fires, such as toast, that set it off), and **AUC** (area under the ROC curve) is one grade for how well the detector ranks real fires above toast, without choosing a knob position. In the end you still have to choose one, and the best choice depends on what mistakes cost.

**Worked example (illustrative scores):** Ten candidate links, 7 true matches in total.

| Score | 0.97 | 0.93 | 0.90 | 0.84 | 0.78 | 0.70 | 0.62 | 0.55 | 0.41 | 0.30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| True match? | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | yes | yes | no | yes | no |

| Threshold | Linked | TP | FP | Precision | Recall | F1 | F0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.80 | 4 | 4 | 0 | 1.000 | 0.571 | 0.727 | **0.870** |
| 0.70 | 6 | 5 | 1 | 0.833 | 0.714 | 0.769 | 0.806 |
| 0.60 | 7 | 6 | 1 | 0.857 | 0.857 | 0.857 | 0.857 |
| 0.50 | 8 | 6 | 2 | 0.750 | 0.857 | 0.800 | 0.769 |
| 0.40 | 9 | 7 | 2 | 0.778 | 1.000 | **0.875** | 0.814 |
| 0.25 | 10 | 7 | 3 | 0.700 | 1.000 | 0.824 | 0.745 |

Same scores, two metrics, two different best knobs: F1 prefers 0.40, F0.5 prefers 0.80.

**Technical explanation:** A threshold rule predicts "match" when the score s ≥ t. The PR curve is the set of points (R(t), P(t)); the ROC curve is (FPR(t), TPR(t)); ROC-AUC equals the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative, with ties counted as one half (the normalised Mann-Whitney statistic). AUC is invariant to any monotone transformation of the scores and uses no threshold, so it says nothing about where to operate; with extreme imbalance ROC is also dominated by true negatives, while PR is not. Our decision is not even a single threshold on pair scores: per record it is an argmax, an absolute threshold and a lead over the runner-up, followed by per-business effects. The correct procedure is therefore to simulate the exact decision rule and the exact metric on labelled held-out data for a grid of thresholds and keep the best, choosing on one fold and checking on another to limit optimism. **Calibration** maps scores to probabilities (Platt scaling fits a logistic curve to the scores; isotonic regression fits a monotone step function). For a pure threshold rule, a monotone calibration only renames the threshold, so it cannot improve the best achievable result; for a lead rule (best minus second ≥ 0.4) a non-linear calibration does change which records pass, because differences between scores are not preserved. **Cost-sensitive threshold selection** weights error types differently while choosing t; for the second-chance models we counted each false positive twice.

**How we used it:** The US and India threshold 0.75 was chosen on fold 8 for the exact per-business macro F0.5; the consistency-check bars 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77 on folds 8 and 9; the native-script rescue's 0.88 (used with a lead of 0.3) on fold 8 with false positives counted twice; the address rescue's thresholds also on fold 8 with false positives counted twice (US 0.86 with lead 0.0, India 0.66 with lead 0.1), after a filter that keeps a pair if its probability reaches the largest grid value that still keeps 98 % of the fold-8 reference links (US 0.06, India 0.015) (Doc 4). France's 0.82 was set without labels, from the French link volume per business together with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US and India (Doc C.1). AUC appears only as a sanity check of readers: on 509,260 labelled US/India pairs the French E5 reader and the E5 reader have AUC 0.998544 and 0.998570, and best F0.5 0.992782 and 0.992796 (Doc B.4). We used no Platt or isotonic calibration.

**Expert nuance:** AUC near 0.9985 for both readers shows saturation: ranking quality is excellent, yet the result still depends on where you cut and on look-alike competitors, so AUC cannot choose between operating points. A disclosed limitation: folds 8 and 9 were also used to choose the thresholds and the consistency check, so the held-out scores on them are not untouched (Doc 5). Moving a threshold to a country without labels is the hardest case; 0.82 for France is a deliberately conservative, label-free choice whose true optimum is unknown. Whenever the model changes, its threshold must be re-tuned, because scores of different models are not on a common scale.

**Remember:**
- Same scores, different metric, different best threshold (F1 0.40 against F0.5 0.80 in the toy).
- AUC is threshold-free and cannot pick an operating point; we tune on the exact metric.
- 0.75 for US and India (fold 8); 0.82 for France (label-free); false positives counted twice for the second-chance models.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why not use 0.5, or choose models by AUC?*
  "0.5 is arbitrary and AUC has no threshold at all. Our E5 reader and French E5 reader both have AUC around 0.9985 on labelled US and Indian pairs, yet what matters is per-business F0.5 at the chosen cut, so we swept thresholds on held-out fold 8 with the exact metric and got 0.75."
- *Would calibrating the scores have helped?*
  "For a single threshold, calibration only renames the cut-off, so we tuned directly on the metric instead. It would change the 0.4 lead rule, because a non-linear calibration changes score differences; we did not calibrate, and that is something we would test."

---

### A1.7 Abstention: the reject option and empty rows {#a1-7 .concept}

**In one line:** **Abstention** means deliberately outputting no link when the evidence is not strong enough, because under F0.5 a wrong answer costs more than no answer.

**Simple explanation:** Picture a quiz show where a wrong answer loses points but passing loses nothing: smart contestants answer only when they are sure. Our rule has two parts. First, the best candidate must be **confident**: its score must clear a bar. Second, it must be a **clear winner**: well ahead of the second-best candidate, because if two candidates look equally good you are guessing. If either part fails, the record stays unlinked. This is the classic **reject option** of decision theory.

**Worked example:**

Part 1, a toy break-even for business A with 3 true records and 2 correct links so far:

1. Abstain: F = 1.25 × 2 / (2 + 0.75) = 0.909.
2. Link a third record that is correct: 1.25 × 3 / (3 + 0.75) = 1.000.
3. Link a third record that is wrong: 1.25 × 2 / (3 + 0.75) = 0.667.
4. Linking pays only if the chance p of being right satisfies p × 1.000 + (1 − p) × 0.667 > 0.909, that is p > 0.727 (which is 0.909 / 1.25, the rule from F-beta). If A has no true records at all, a wrong link drops A from 1 to 0.

This is a teaching toy; our real 0.75 was found by sweeping thresholds on fold 8 with the exact metric over all businesses.

Part 2, our rule on the records of the talk (Doc D):

| Record | Best score | Runner-up | Confident? | Clear winner (lead ≥ 0.4)? | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US: "Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc)" | 0.965022 | 0.088664 | yes (≥ 0.75) | yes, 0.876 | linked to the Windsor, CT business |
| France: "TQ COMITE SARL" | 0.999837 | 0.000098 | yes (≥ 0.82) | yes, 0.999740 | accepted, then the category-swap veto drops it: no link |
| Illustrative | 0.90 | 0.70 | yes | no, 0.20 | abstain |
| India: Devanagari "Vijay Enterprises", main pass | 7.2e-6 | 6.9e-6 | no | (not reached) | unlinked; the native-script rescue then links it at 0.99994 with lead 0.99992 |

**Technical explanation:** Chow's reject rule (1970) says that with error cost 1 and rejection cost c, the Bayes-optimal classifier rejects when the largest posterior probability (the model's probability of the most likely class given the input) is below 1 − c. Our version works per record: the candidates c_1 ... c_k have decision-model scores s_i, which are pointwise binary probabilities (each pair scored on its own) and need not sum to 1 across a record's candidates; we link the argmax if s_(1) ≥ thr and s_(1) − s_(2) ≥ 0.4, and abstain otherwise. The lead condition targets ambiguity between candidates, which a per-pair probability cannot express: two near-identical businesses can both score 0.9. A softmax over a record's candidates (a function that turns a set of scores into probabilities summing to 1) would build mutual exclusivity into the model; we keep pointwise scores and enforce it in the decision rule, and the decision model also sees, per record, the rank, best-other score and margin of the ranker and reader scores as features. In code, a record with a single candidate has its runner-up treated as minus infinity, so only the threshold applies; that is the common case, since 90.59 % of incoming records have exactly one candidate in the final candidate file. Under macro F0.5 the value of a link depends on the state of its business (break-even F_b / 1.25 in the toy), which motivates the count-dependent bar of the per-business consistency check (later part). Abstention also creates a clean pool for targeted recovery: the second-chance searches run only on unlinked records, so they never undo a link.

**How we used it:** Threshold 0.75 for US and India, 0.82 for France and the unseen-country route; a lead of 0.4 for every country; consistency-check bars 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77; native-script rescue 0.88 with lead 0.3; address rescue US 0.86 with lead 0.0 and India 0.66 with lead 0.1 (Doc 4). The France rules can veto accepted links (the category-swap veto and the word-substitution veto together removed 29,021 of 887,630 accepted French links) or rescue unlinked records inside fixed score bands (Doc B.3). Outcome: 100,087 empty rows (5.8 %, derived) and 0.5875 links per incoming record, so about 41 % of incoming records are linked to nothing (derived). The Documentation does not record how 0.4 was chosen; say "one fixed lead used in every country", never "it was never tuned".

**Expert nuance:** Abstention costs recall exactly where a true owner has a near-twin; QA 14 lists "correct candidates rejected because a second one is too close" as a false-negative type. Alternatives include normalising scores across a record's candidates (softmax or listwise models), selective classification with risk-coverage curves (plotting the error rate among accepted links against the share of records accepted, and picking the point the metric prefers), or learning the reject rule itself. The empty rows are not all misses: many businesses may truly own nothing, but test labels are private, so we cannot split them. A wrong link is never better than abstaining (the owner loses the record either way, and the wrong business gains a false positive), which is why every refinement after the main decision either vetoes risky links or adds links only to unlinked records.

**Remember:**
- Link the best candidate only if confident (0.75; 0.82 in France) and a clear winner (lead at least 0.4); otherwise abstain.
- Toy break-even: a link helps business A only if its chance of being right exceeds F_A / 1.25.
- 100,087 empty rows; about 41 % of incoming records unlinked (derived).

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why require a 0.4 lead over the runner-up, not just a threshold?*
  "Two near-identical candidates can both score high, and a threshold alone would then pick one almost at random. Under F0.5 a wrong link costs more than a miss, so we link only a clear winner; 0.4 is one fixed lead for every country, and the threshold itself was tuned on fold 8."
- *How many records do you leave unlinked, and is that a problem?*
  "Our file links 0.5875 records per incoming record, so about 41 % stay unlinked, and 100,087 businesses have an empty row. Some of those records truly have no business; test labels are private, so we cannot say how many, but abstaining is never worse than a wrong link under this metric."

---

### A1.8 Text normalisation {#a1-8 .concept}

**In one line:** **Normalisation** rewrites names and addresses into one standard form, so that the same thing written differently looks the same to a computer.

**Simple explanation:** Two people copy the same shop sign: one writes "Shree Ganesh Traders & Co.", the other "SHREE GANESH TRADERS AND CO". A computer compares characters exactly, so these look different. Normalisation means rewriting both neatly in the same style before comparing: small letters only (**case folding**), punctuation removed, "&" written as "and", "Street" written as "st", "007" written as "7". It is like a teacher insisting that everyone writes dates as DD-MM-YYYY before checking homework. It must be done with care, because rewriting too aggressively can erase real differences. Four more terms: the **legal form** is the company-type word (Inc, LLC, Pvt Ltd, SARL), and the **core name** is the name with legal-form and filler words removed. **ASCII** is the basic computer alphabet of 128 characters: English letters, digits and common punctuation, with no accents and no other scripts. To **romanise** is to rewrite text from another script in Latin letters, and **unidecode** is a widely used generic library that does this character by character (it turns "é" into "e" and विजय into "vijy").

**Worked example (computed with our cleaning code):**

| Raw text | After the US/India cleaning rules |
|---|---|
| Shree Ganesh Traders & Co. | shree ganesh traders and co |
| B00K W0RLD | book world |
| Apt 007, 12 North Main Street, California | apt 7 12 n main st ca |
| Suite 0042, 5th Avenue | ste 42 5th ave |
| Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc) | legacy marketing enterprises inc |

Then, for the index, the core name drops legal and filler words:

1. "shree ganesh traders and co" → core name "shree ganesh traders" ("and" and "co" removed).
2. "legacy marketing enterprises inc" → "legacy marketing enterprises".
3. The businesses "Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc" and "Legacy Marketing Enterprises LLC" get the same core name, so the index retrieves both; the later stages must separate them (they do: 0.965022 against 0.000007 in Doc D.1).

**Technical explanation:** Our US/India cleaning rules run in this order: (1) a token containing non-ASCII characters is romanised, in names through the learned Indic-to-Latin word list with unidecode as fallback, in addresses always through unidecode; (2) lower-case; (3) "&" becomes " and "; (4) every run of characters outside a-z and 0-9 becomes one space; (5) in addresses, US and Indian state names become short codes (california → ca, maharashtra → mh) and a small table maps street, direction and unit words (road → rd, street → st, avenue → ave, north → n, suite → ste, apartment → apt, floor → fl, nagar → ngr, sector → sec), and every purely numeric token of up to 11 digits is rewritten as an integer, which drops leading zeros; (6) in names, a 0 next to a letter becomes o (repairing "leet" spellings such as B00K). The index then builds the core name by removing a fixed list of legal and filler words (inc, incorporated, llc, llp, ltd, limited, pvt, private, corp, corporation, co, company, plc, sarl, sas, sa, sci, sasu, eurl, and, the); a name made only of such words is kept as it is. The same function runs on both sides of every pair, deterministically, once per record, so its cost is linear in the data. The hand-crafted features use a separate tokeniser (lower-case, punctuation removed, Indic word list, accents stripped, legal-form words and and/et/& removed). The readers read the raw text, not the normalised text (Doc 2.2).

**How we used it:** The US/India rules serve the US, India and any unseen country (the default route); France adds French rules on top (see Address normalisation). The index lookup, the quick rule-based filter and the 76 index-lookup features all work on normalised text; the readers see the raw "name | address" text. Hand-written lists are limited to small word lists for normalisation, decision-model features, the native-script rescue and the France rules; there is no external dictionary or lookup (Doc C.6).

**Expert nuance:** Normalisation is a recall-against-precision dial: collapsing variants raises the chance of retrieving the true business but erases distinctions. We erase distinctions only where recall matters (the index keys drop legal forms) and keep them where precision matters (legal-form relation features in the decision model; the readers on raw text), which is exactly what separates the Inc from the LLC in the US example. Abbreviations depend on context: "st" is street in a US address but saint in a French name or address, and "ste" is suite in a US address but sainte in French text, which is one reason France has its own rules. Table collisions such as goa → ga and georgia → ga are harmless because every index is built per country. Dropping leading zeros is safe because both sides are transformed the same way: a ZIP code 02134 becomes 2134 everywhere and still matches.

**Remember:**
- Lower-case, & → and, punctuation → space, abbreviation and state tables, leading zeros dropped, a 0 beside a letter → o.
- Legal words are removed only for the index's core name; the legal form stays a decision feature and the readers read raw text.
- One function for both sides of every pair; one shared US/India rule set (also used for unseen countries), with French rules on top for France.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Doesn't removing Inc or LLC throw away exactly the signal that separates look-alikes?*
  "Only inside the index, where we want recall: the Inc and the LLC are both retrieved. The decision model has legal-form features and the readers read the raw text, so in our US example the Inc scores 0.965 and the LLC 0.000007."
- *Why do the readers get raw text instead of the cleaned text?*
  "Cleaning is designed for retrieval: it throws away case, punctuation and accents, and the index's core name also drops legal forms, all of which can matter for the final decision. The readers are multilingual models fine-tuned on labelled pairs, so they learn their own invariances from the original 'name | address' text."

---

### A1.9 Unicode, scripts and accent stripping {#a1-9 .concept}

**In one line:** **Unicode** gives every character a number, and Unicode normalisation makes visually identical text identical inside the computer, so that comparisons work.

**Simple explanation:** A computer stores text as numbers. The letter "é" can be stored as one number (a ready-made é) or as two (a plain "e" followed by an accent sign), and both look identical on screen while the computer sees them as different. Some characters are decorated variants of plain ones, such as the ligature "ﬁ" or a full-width "Ａ". **Unicode normalisation** is the rulebook that rewrites all of these into one standard form. **Accent stripping** then removes the accent signs, so "Société" and "Societe" compare equal. But careful: in Hindi, Tamil or Telugu, the small signs attached to letters are vowels that belong to the word; removing them destroys it.

The words you need: a **code point** is the number of one character (written U+00C9 and so on); a **script** is a writing system (Latin, Devanagari, Tamil); a **combining mark** is a character that attaches to the previous one (an accent, or an Indic vowel sign); **NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD** are the four standard normal forms.

**Worked example (computed with Python's unicodedata and text-unidecode):**

| Text | Code points | After NFKD | After deleting U+0300 to U+036F |
|---|---|---|---|
| É | U+00C9 | U+0045 U+0301 (E + combining acute) | E |
| Société Générale | | | Societe Generale |
| ﬁ (ligature) | U+FB01 | f i | fi |
| Ａ (full width) | U+FF21 | A | A |
| ① | U+2460 | 1 | 1 |
| विजय (Vijay) | 4 code points: letter VA, vowel sign I, letter JA, letter YA | unchanged | unchanged |

The Devanagari vowel sign is a combining mark, but it lives outside the block U+0300 to U+036F, so our accent stripping leaves it alone. Deleting every combining mark would turn विजय into वजय, a different word.

**Technical explanation:** Unicode assigns code points to characters grouped into scripts (Latin, Devanagari U+0900 to U+097F, Tamil, Telugu and so on). Two kinds of equivalence exist: canonical (a precomposed é against e plus a combining acute), handled by NFC (composed) and NFD (decomposed), and compatibility (ligatures, full-width forms, circled digits, superscripts), which NFKC and NFKD also fold into plain forms. Accent stripping is NFKD followed by deleting the Combining Diacritical Marks block (U+0300 to U+036F). Each character also has a general category (L letters, M marks, N numbers, P punctuation, S symbols, Z separators), which lets code clean tokens without knowing the script. Indic scripts are abugidas (writing systems in which each consonant letter carries a default vowel that attached signs change; see Transliteration), and their vowel signs (matras) and virama are combining marks (categories Mn or Mc) that carry meaning, so cleaning for those scripts must keep category M. Our code does four things: before looking a native token up in the Indic word list it keeps only characters of categories L, M and N; the feature tokeniser applies NFKD and removes only U+0300 to U+036F, after the word list; native-script names are detected by the range U+0900 to U+0DFF (Devanagari through Sinhala); and the index text is pure ASCII after cleaning (non-ASCII tokens romanised, everything outside a-z0-9 removed), so the C++ index's byte-level letter pieces are exactly character-level letter pieces.

**How we used it:** As described: accent stripping for feature tokens, category filtering for the word-list lookup, romanisation to ASCII for the index text. French accents disappear in the cleaning, because a token with non-ASCII characters is romanised by unidecode ("Comité" → "comite", "Frères" → "freres"). The readers see the raw Unicode text through a multilingual subword tokeniser (which splits text into frequent word pieces from a vocabulary covering many scripts), so accents and native scripts reach them intact, within the 128-token input limit.

**Expert nuance:** NFKD is lossy ("²" becomes "2", ligatures split), which is fine for matching and wrong for display. Accent stripping can merge distinct French words (for example "pâte" and "pate"); the index accepts that loss for recall, and the readers still see the accents. **Homoglyphs** (a Cyrillic "а" that looks like a Latin "a") differ as code points; unidecode maps them to Latin approximations. Running character algorithms on UTF-8 bytes is wrong for non-ASCII text, because one character can be several bytes; this is one reason the C++ index works only on romanised ASCII.

**Remember:**
- NFKD plus deleting U+0300 to U+036F strips Latin accents; never strip all combining marks, because Indic vowel signs are marks.
- Our index text is pure ASCII after cleaning, so byte n-grams equal character n-grams.
- The readers see the raw Unicode text.

**Judge might ask:**
- *How do you handle accents and non-Latin scripts?*
  "For the index and features everything becomes plain ASCII: French accents are stripped, and Indian-script name words go through a word list learned from labelled matches, with a generic romaniser as fallback. The readers see the original text with a multilingual tokeniser, so accents and native scripts reach them intact."

---

### A1.10 Transliteration of Indian native scripts {#a1-10 .concept}

**In one line:** **Transliteration** rewrites a word from one script into another (विजय → vijay); we learned the mapping for business-name words from labelled training matches instead of relying on a generic romaniser.

**Simple explanation:** If someone spells a name to you over a noisy phone line, you write it in English letters as best you can, and different people produce different spellings. Generic romanisers work letter by letter and often produce strange spellings, especially for English words written in Hindi letters: "एंटरप्राइजेज" is simply the English word "enterprises". Our training data already contained many correct pairs: a Devanagari incoming record and its business written in English letters. We counted which Latin word appears again and again with each Hindi word and built a small dictionary (a **lexicon**) from those counts, like learning a language from bilingual shop signs. Transliteration changes the script, not the language; **translation** would change the language.

**Worked example 1 (computed; the lexicon output is Doc D.2):**

| Native word | Generic romaniser (unidecode, lower-cased) | Learned lexicon |
|---|---|---|
| विजय | vijy | vijay |
| एंटरप्राइजेज | enttrpraaijej | enterprises |
| प्राइवेट | praaivett | private |
| लिमिटेड | limittedd | limited |

The generic output shares no word with "Vijay Enterprises Private Limited"; the lexicon output is identical to it.

**Worked example 2 (illustrative counts): how one lexicon entry is learned.** Suppose the token विजय appears in 40 labelled training records. In the true business names of those records, the Latin word "vijay" appears 38 times, "enterprises" 20 times and "traders" 6 times. Across all native-script training examples, these Latin words appear in business names 60, 2,000 and 900 times. Score = co-occurrences / (Latin word count + 1)^0.6:

| Latin word | Co-occurrences | (count + 1)^0.6 | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| vijay | 38 | 61^0.6 = 11.78 | 3.225 |
| enterprises | 20 | 2,001^0.6 = 95.66 | 0.209 |
| traders | 6 | 901^0.6 = 59.27 | 0.101 |

Checks: co-occurrences at least 3 (38, yes); purity 38 / 40 = 0.95, at least 0.35 (yes); best score at least 1.8 times the runner-up (3.225 against 1.8 × 0.209 = 0.376, yes). So the lexicon gets the entry विजय → vijay. Dividing by the Latin word's frequency stops very common words such as "enterprises" from winning for every Hindi word.

**Technical explanation:** Indic scripts are **abugidas**: each consonant letter carries an inherent vowel "a", **vowel signs (matras)** replace it, the **virama** suppresses it, and conjuncts join consonants. In Hindi the inherent vowel is often silent at the end or in the middle of a word (schwa deletion), so letter-by-letter romanisation either drops every inherent vowel ("vijy", unidecode's choice) or keeps them all ("vijaya"); the usual spelling "vijay" requires knowledge of the language. English loanwords spelled phonetically in Devanagari cannot be recovered reliably by any character-level script mapping, because the English spelling ("enterprises") is not a function of the sounds, and standard schemes such as ISO 15919 or IAST are reversible but do not produce English spellings. Our lexicon is supervised word alignment from parallel data: for every labelled training pair whose incoming name contains native script (folds 0-5 only), each native token is counted once per example against each word of its owner's normalised name (one-letter Latin words are ignored), and a token receives its best Latin word only if it co-occurs at least 3 times, its purity (the share of the token's training examples whose business name contains that Latin word) is at least 0.35, and its score n / (count of the Latin word + 1)^0.6 is at least 1.8 times the runner-up. The exponent 0.6 discounts frequent Latin words, an association statistic in the spirit of IDF or pointwise mutual information (PMI, which compares how often two words occur together with how often they would by chance); it is not a neural transliterator. Tokens without an entry fall back to unidecode. The lexicon is used for name tokens in the cleaning step and in the feature tokeniser; addresses are always romanised with unidecode.

**How we used it:** The main lexicon is learned only from labelled training pairs of folds 0-5, the same folds as the CatBoost ranker and the readers. Two other word lists exist and are disclosed. The native-script rescue uses a lexicon of training positives that keeps every alternative with at least 5 % of a native token's count, generates up to 64 transliterations per name, and is built leaving the record's own fold out when training the rescue model (Doc 3, Doc 4). For India's forensic name-comparison features, a label-free native-to-Latin alignment is computed on test records whose first-stage top candidate has probability at least 0.9 (Doc C.1; code). The native-script rescue added 9,759 links in India; in Doc D.2 the key (vijay, enterprises) plus the state Maharashtra led to a link at 0.99994.

**Expert nuance:** Coverage is the main weakness: a native token seen fewer than 3 times in labelled data stays with unidecode, and QA 14 lists "native-script names without a known transliteration" as a miss type. The consonant-skeleton channel of the index softens this, because unidecode output and Latin spellings often share a skeleton: vijy and vijay both give "vj", and enttrpraaijej ("ntrprj") and enterprises ("ntrprs") share the sound 4-grams ntrp and trpr (see Phonetic keys). The readers read the native script directly with a multilingual vocabulary and learn cross-script matches from labelled pairs. Neural transliteration models are an alternative we did not use or benchmark.

**Remember:**
- Generic romanisation: विजय → "vijy", एंटरप्राइजेज → "enttrpraaijej"; the learned lexicon gives "vijay enterprises".
- Lexicon = co-occurrence counts on labelled folds 0-5, kept if n ≥ 3, purity ≥ 0.35 and score ≥ 1.8 × runner-up; unidecode otherwise.
- The rescue lexicon leaves each record's own fold out; the label-free test alignment (probability ≥ 0.9) is disclosed.

**Judge might ask:**
- *How do you match a Devanagari name to a Latin business name?*
  "In three ways. The cleaning step maps Indian-script name words through a word list learned from labelled training matches, so विजय एंटरप्राइजेज becomes 'vijay enterprises', and the readers read the original script directly. Records that still stay unlinked get the native-script second-chance search, by transliterated name within the same state, which added 9,759 links in India."
- *Could the transliteration word lists leak labels?*
  "The main list is learned only from labelled training folds 0 to 5, and the second-chance search's list leaves each record's own fold out, so a record never benefits from its own label. One alignment is computed on test records, but it uses no labels, only confident first-stage matches, and the Documentation discloses it."

---

### A1.11 Address normalisation and parsing (US, India, France) {#a1-11 .concept}

**In one line:** **Address parsing** splits an address into its parts (house number, street type, street name, city, region), and address normalisation writes each part in one standard way.

**Simple explanation:** A postal sorter knows that "Rd", "Rd." and "Road" are the same, and that "15B" and "15 bis" mean the same house. Addresses are often the strongest evidence that two records describe the same shop: two shops can share a name, but rarely a house number and a street. Yet addresses are messy: abbreviations, typos, missing parts, different orders, different languages. So we wrote rules per country that put every address into a standard shape. In French addresses, "bis", "ter" and "quater" mark a second, third or fourth dwelling at the same number, like "15A" or "15B".

**Worked example (computed with our cleaning code):**

| Raw address | Normalised |
|---|---|
| Apt 007, 12 North Main Street, California (US rules) | apt 7 12 n main st ca |
| N° 15B R. Suzanne Lenglen (France) | 15 bis rue suzanne lenglen |
| 2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN (France; the record of Doc D.3) | 2 rue suzanne lenglen |
| 8 q Rue Victor Hugo | 8 quater rue victor hugo |
| 12 Q. Wilson | 12 quai wilson |
| 3ter Av. des Champs | 3 ter av des champs |

1. "N°" is removed before a number; the glued "15B" is split into "15 bis".
2. The token right after the house number and its suffix is the street-type position, so a lone "R" there means "rue".
3. A lone "q" means "quater" when a street type follows it ("8 q Rue ..."), but "quai" (a riverside street) when it sits in the street-type position itself ("12 Q. Wilson"): parsing depends on position.
4. The typo table: a word seen at the street-type position in incoming records but never at that position in the businesses (and almost never anywhere in them), whose closest street-type word is unique and within one or two edits, is mapped to it (illustrative: "boulevrad" is one transposition from "boulevard"). The word "rute" is one edit from both "rue" and "route", so it is ambiguous and is not mapped.

**Technical explanation:** An address has components: house number (with a suffix such as bis, ter, quater or a letter), street type (rue, avenue, boulevard; Road, Street), street name, locality or city, department, region or state, and postcode. The US/India rules map state names to codes, apply a street, direction and unit word table, and rewrite numbers as integers. The French rules (France only) remove number prefixes such as N°, No and numéro before digits; split glued suffixes (15B → 15 bis, 3ter → 3 ter) and unify bis, ter and quater; locate the street-type position as the first token after the house number(s) and suffixes; apply single-letter abbreviations only at that position (r → rue, q → quai); canonicalise multi-letter street types (avenue / ave / av → av, boulevard / blvd / bd → bd, allée → all, impasse → imp, route → rte, chemin → ch, place → pl); and apply a street-type typo table learned from the supplied test files (a word of at least 4 letters seen at the type position in incoming records, never at that position in business addresses and almost never elsewhere in them, whose closest street-type word is unique and within optimal-string-alignment distance 1 for type words of up to 6 letters, or 2 for longer ones). The French geography (regions, departments, cities) is learned without labels from how comma-separated address components co-occur in the test files, and in code the region and department components are dropped by default. French names get their own rules: S.A.R.L. → sarl, leet legal forms such as 5arl → sarl, st / ste → saint / sainte, et → and (between two words), and a few abbreviations unified (Établissements → ets, Compagnie → cie, Frs → freres). Every rule runs once per record.

**How we used it:** Normalised addresses feed the address-word channel and address score of the index lookup, the address-word and address-number statistics among its 76 features, and the address coverage used by the quick rule-based filter. Other components parse addresses in their own way: the "what changed" number features extract digit runs directly from the raw address; the France rules use their own parser of the raw French address for their "same address" tests and the street veto (which allows Damerau distance 1, or 2 for words of 8 or more characters) (code); and the address rescue retrieves businesses sharing one of a record's 3 rarest digit runs and one of its 3 rarest alphabetic address words. Disclosed: the French geography, the street-type typo table and the postcode prefixes are computed from the unlabelled test files (Doc C.1). No geocoder, postal table, business register or API was used; they were banned (Doc C.6).

**Expert nuance:** In production one would reach for a statistical address parser or a geocoder, but external data and lookups were banned, so the rules are hand-written per country plus tables learned from the supplied files. Learning tables from unlabelled test files is **transductive** (it uses the unlabelled test inputs themselves while building the system) but label-free, like computing word frequencies, and it is disclosed. House numbers are the most discriminative address tokens because digit strings are rare, which is why the address rescue starts from the rarest digit runs. Canonicalisation is limited to street types, suffixes and abbreviations; street-name words themselves are never dropped. Missing parts are common (the US example of Doc D.1 has no address at all), so every address feature must handle "empty" explicitly.

**Remember:**
- Parse first (number, suffix, type, name, city), then canonicalise each part; position matters ("q" is quater or quai).
- France: 15B → 15 bis, R. → rue, typo table and geography learned from the unlabelled test files (disclosed).
- No external postal data, geocoder or API.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Did you use a postal database, geocoder or address-parsing library?*
  "No. External data and lookups were banned and we used none. The parsing rules are hand-written per country, and the French geography and street-type typo table are learned from the supplied files without labels; the Documentation discloses that."
- *Isn't learning tables from the test files a kind of leak?*
  "It is transductive: the tables are learned from the text of the unlabelled test records, and the Documentation discloses that. It uses no labels, in the same way as computing word frequencies, and it only makes 'avenue', 'av' and their typos one token; it never decides a match on its own."

---

### A1.12 Tokens, sets and character n-grams {#a1-12 .concept}

**In one line:** To compare text we cut it into pieces, whole words (**tokens**) or short overlapping letter chunks (**character n-grams**), and compare the collections of pieces.

**Simple explanation:** Comparing two names letter by letter is fragile, because one typo pushes every later letter out of line. Instead, cut each name into pieces and count the pieces they share, like comparing two Lego models by the bricks they use. Words are big pieces: "shree ganesh" and "shri ganesh" share only one of their three different words. Letter chunks are small pieces ("shr", "hre", "ree", ...): a typo spoils only a few of them, so the two names still share most chunks. A **set** keeps each piece once and ignores order; a **bag** (multiset) also counts repeats. An n-gram of 3 letters is a 3-gram (also called a q-gram or shingle).

**Worked example (computed with our index rules; letter pieces are cut from the core name with spaces removed, sound pieces from its words sorted alphabetically):** "shree ganesh" against "shri ganesh".

| Pieces | shree ganesh | shri ganesh | Shared | Union | Jaccard |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Words | shree, ganesh | shri, ganesh | 1 | 3 | 0.333 |
| 3-grams | shr hre ree eeg ega gan ane nes esh (9) | shr hri rig iga gan ane nes esh (8) | 5 | 12 | 0.417 |
| 4-grams | shre hree reeg eega egan gane anes nesh (8) | shri hrig riga igan gane anes nesh (7) | 3 | 12 | 0.250 |
| Sound 4-grams (see Phonetic keys) | gnsh nshs shsh hshr | gnsh nshs shsh hshr | 4 | 4 | 1.000 |

A second case: "book world" against "bookworld" share no word, but their compacted letter pieces are identical.

**Technical explanation:** Tokenisation here is splitting normalised text on spaces. Sets ignore order and repetition; bags keep counts. A string of length L has L − n + 1 character n-grams; in our code a string shorter than n becomes one single gram, with no padding. The **q-gram lemma** (Ukkonen) makes n-grams a filter for typos: one edit changes at most n of a string's n-grams, so two strings within edit distance k still share at least (L − n + 1) − k · n grams, where L is the length of the longer string and grams are counted with repeats (as bags; with sets the bound is approximate). Shorter n tolerates more typos but is less selective: short grams such as "ent" are shared by many unrelated names, which makes their posting lists long. Our index keeps five kinds of pieces: name words (of the core name) and address words (unique sets), 3-grams and 4-grams of the compacted core name in its original word order, and 4-grams of the consonant skeleton; each piece is hashed (turned by a fixed formula into a 64-bit number used as its key) and tagged with its channel, so the 3-gram "gan" and a word "gan" get different keys. Each key points to a **posting list**, the list of businesses that contain that piece (see The inverted index). For name words, address words, 3-grams, 4-grams, sound grams, name numbers and address numbers, the index lookup outputs the intersection size, Jaccard, overlap coefficient and intersection over the larger set (see Set-overlap measures).

**How we used it:** Retrieval channel weights are 1 for name words and address words, 0.45 for 4-grams, 0.22 for 3-grams and 0.18 for sound grams; the posting caps and budgets are 2,500 / 15,000 for 4-grams and 1,000 / 6,000 for 3-grams (Doc 3). The set statistics above are among the 76 index-lookup features used by the CatBoost ranker and the decision models.

**Expert nuance:** Letter pieces of the compacted name handle words that are split or merged ("book world" and "bookworld"), which word tokens miss; the price is that word boundaries vanish, which is harmless in practice. Very common pieces ("ent", "ers", "ing") carry little evidence, hence lower channel weights and IDF weighting. Sets ignore order, so "ganesh shree" equals "shree ganesh", usually what we want for names; order-sensitive measures (LCS ratio) complement them. With 64-bit hashed keys, collisions are possible in principle but negligible in practice.

**Remember:**
- Words are precise but brittle; letter n-grams survive typos and split or merged words.
- One edit spoils at most n of a string's n-grams (the q-gram lemma).
- Our index uses words, 3-grams, 4-grams and sound 4-grams, each with its own weight and caps.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why add character 3-grams and 4-grams on top of words?*
  "Words miss typos and split or merged words: 'shree ganesh' and 'shri ganesh' share one word in three but five of twelve 3-grams. 4-grams are more selective and 3-grams more forgiving, so they carry weights 0.45 and 0.22 against 1 for whole words, each with its own posting cap."

---

### A1.13 Edit distances: Levenshtein, Damerau-Levenshtein and OSA {#a1-13 .concept}

**In one line:** An **edit distance** counts the smallest number of single-character changes needed to turn one string into another.

**Simple explanation:** How many keystrokes would a typist need to fix one name into the other? "shri" into "shree" needs two (change i to e, then add an e). The changes allowed are **insertion**, **deletion** and **substitution**; that count is the **Levenshtein distance**. Swapping two neighbouring letters ("gaensh" for "ganesh") is one of the most common typing slips; Levenshtein counts it as two changes, while the **Damerau-Levenshtein** distance also allows a **transposition** of neighbours and counts it as one. **OSA** (optimal string alignment) is a cheaper, restricted version of Damerau-Levenshtein.

**Worked example 1: the dynamic-programming table for "shri" → "shree".** **Dynamic programming** means solving a big problem by filling a table of small sub-problems, each computed from neighbours already filled in. Here each cell is the distance between the prefixes (the first letters) of the two words; it is the minimum of (cell above + 1: delete), (cell to the left + 1: insert), and (diagonal cell + 0 if the two letters are equal, else + 1: substitute).

| | "" | s | h | r | e | e |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| "" | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| s | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| h | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| r | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| i | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 |

The answer is the bottom-right cell: 2.

**Worked example 2 (computed with RapidFuzz):**

| Pair | Levenshtein | Damerau-Levenshtein | OSA |
|---|---|---|---|
| ganesh / gaensh | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| 1250 / 1205 (house numbers) | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| boulevard / boulevrad | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| ca / abc | 3 | 2 | 3 |

"1250" and "1205" are 45 apart as numbers but one transposition apart as digit strings: two views of the same change. The last row shows why OSA is not a true distance. A true distance (a **metric**) must obey the **triangle inequality**: going directly from one string to another never costs more than going via a third string. Here "ca" → "ac" costs 1 and "ac" → "abc" costs 1, yet OSA("ca", "abc") = 3, more than 1 + 1.

**Technical explanation:** Levenshtein distance uses unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions and is computed by dynamic programming over an (|a| + 1) × (|b| + 1) table in O(|a| · |b|) time and O(min(|a|, |b|)) memory; bit-parallel algorithms (Myers 1999, Hyyrö), which pack one column of the table into the bits of a machine word so that one CPU instruction updates up to 64 cells at once, reduce this to about ⌈|a| / 64⌉ · |b| word operations, which is how libraries such as RapidFuzz run fast. Unrestricted Damerau-Levenshtein adds adjacent transpositions and is a true metric. OSA, the restricted version, forbids editing a substring more than once; it is cheaper but violates the triangle inequality, as the "ca / abc" row shows. A normalised similarity is 1 − d / max(|a|, |b|). The **Indel distance** (insertions and deletions only) equals |a| + |b| − 2 · LCS, which links edit distances to the LCS ratio of the next concept. All of these are quadratic per pair in the worst case, so they run on candidate pairs only, never on all 6.7 trillion pairs.

**How we used it:** The Damerau-Levenshtein distance between the digit strings of the closest pair of unmatched address numbers (one only in the record, one only in the business) is one of the "what changed" number features. OSA distance builds the French street-type typo table (at most 1 for words up to 6 letters, at most 2 for longer words), and the France street veto tolerates typos up to Damerau distance 1, or 2 for words of 8 or more characters (Doc B.3). The code's forensic name comparisons include a Levenshtein distance between names. All run on shortlisted or candidate pairs only.

**Expert nuance:** An edit distance counts edits but not their meaning: inc → llc is 2 edits (computed, after lower-casing) and changes the legal entity; shree → shri is also 2 edits and is only a spelling variant; a transposed house number is 1 edit and may point to another building. That gap is the motivation for the "what changed" features, which describe which edit happened (legal form changed, word replaced, number changed and by how much) and let the decision model learn which edits are harmless. Weighted edit distances (keyboard-aware or learned costs) exist; we did not use them. Raw distances favour short strings, so lengths are given to the models as separate features.

**Remember:**
- Levenshtein = minimum insertions, deletions and substitutions; Damerau-Levenshtein adds adjacent swaps and is a metric; OSA is the restricted version and is not.
- Dynamic programming, O(|a| · |b|): fine on shortlists, impossible on 6.7 trillion pairs.
- We use Damerau-Levenshtein on digit strings and OSA / Damerau tolerance in the French typo table and street veto.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Isn't an edit distance enough to match names?*
  "It counts edits but not which edit: Inc to LLC is two edits and a different company, Shree to Shri is also two and the same shop. So beside similarities we describe what changed, legal form, words added, dropped or replaced, numbers changed, and the decision model learns which changes are harmless."
- *Why Damerau-Levenshtein for house numbers?*
  "Swapped digits are a typical copying error, and Damerau counts a swap as one edit, so 1250 against 1205 is one edit although the numbers are 45 apart. We give the model both views, the digit edit distance and the numeric difference."

---

### A1.14 LCS ratio and the RapidFuzz family {#a1-14 .concept}

**In one line:** These measures score, from 0 to 100, how much of two strings lines up in order, with variants that forgive extra words or a different word order.

**Simple explanation:** Write two names one above the other and draw lines between equal letters, never letting lines cross. The largest number of lines you can draw is the **longest common subsequence (LCS)**. The **ratio** is how much of both names those lines cover. Two popular variants: **partial ratio** asks whether the shorter name appears almost exactly inside the longer one, and **token-set ratio** ignores word order and gives full marks when all the words of one name appear in the other. **RapidFuzz** is the open-source library (MIT licence) that we used to compute them.

**Worked example (computed):**

1. LCS("shree ganesh", "shri ganesh") = "shr" + " ganesh" = 10 characters. Ratio = 2 × 10 / (12 + 11) = 0.870, which RapidFuzz reports as 86.96.
2. Three pairs:

| Record | Business | Ratio | Partial ratio | Token-set ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vijay enterprises | vijay enterprises private limited | 68.0 | 100 | 100 |
| ganesh traders | shree ganesh traders mumbai | 68.3 | 100 | 100 |
| legacy marketing enterprises | legacy marketing industries | 83.6 | 83.3 | 83.6 |

3. In the India example of Doc D.2, the chosen business has an address token-set ratio of 100 against 66.7 for each of the other four rescue candidates.

**Technical explanation:** The LCS is a subsequence, not a substring, and costs O(n · m) by dynamic programming, or O(⌈m / w⌉ · n) word operations with bit-parallel algorithms (Allison-Dix, Hyyrö). The ratio 2 · LCS / (|a| + |b|) equals 1 − Indel / (|a| + |b|), where Indel = |a| + |b| − 2 · LCS is the number of insertions and deletions; RapidFuzz's `ratio` is exactly this times 100. Our C++ index computes the same LCS ratio bit-parallel, with 128-bit masks over the first 127 characters of the shorter string and the first 192 of the longer one. Partial ratio is the best ratio between the shorter string and equally long alignments inside the longer string. Token-sort ratio sorts the words before comparing. Token-set ratio splits both strings into the shared word set I and the leftovers, compares "I" with "I + leftovers of a", "I" with "I + leftovers of b", and the two combined strings with each other, and takes the maximum, so it returns 100 when one word set contains the other (and they share at least one word). The index lookup's **token alignment** scores take, for each word of one name, its best LCS ratio against any word of the other name and average these best matches, in both directions (2 scores), and also keep, in each direction, the worst word's best match (2 more); the averages are the **Monge-Elkan** construction with LCS ratio as the inner similarity. The index code is parallelised with **OpenMP**, a standard way to spread a C++ loop over several CPU cores.

**How we used it:** Among the 76 index-lookup features are 7 LCS-ratio similarities (5 on name forms: the normalised name, the core name, the sorted core words, the compacted core name and the sound skeleton; 2 on address forms: the full address and its sorted unique words), 4 token-alignment scores and the common-prefix share of the compacted core names. RapidFuzz ratio and token-set ratio appear in the forensic name and address comparisons; ratio, partial ratio and token-set ratio in the second-chance models' features; the native-script rescue's fixed score includes the address token-set ratio; and the category-swap veto and generic-word swap veto in France require a street token-set ratio of at least 80 for "same address" (Doc B.3).

**Expert nuance:** Token-set ratio's subset rule cuts both ways: it forgives truncation (a true record that drops "Private Limited" scores 100), but it also forgives additions (a different organisation at the same address whose name is the business name plus one extra word also scores 100). A similarity score cannot tell "lost a word" from "gained a word"; the "what changed" features (words added versus dropped, and how rare they are) can, and that is the central idea of our decision features. LCS ratio respects order and set measures ignore it, so together they cover reordering and truncation. The bit-parallel LCS is effectively linear for names, because a whole name fits into one 128-bit mask.

**Remember:**
- Ratio = 2 · LCS / (|a| + |b|); RapidFuzz ratio is the same times 100; our C++ index computes it bit-parallel.
- Partial and token-set ratios forgive extra words, both truncations and additions.
- Token alignment = Monge-Elkan: the average best word match.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Which string similarity matters most in your model?*
  "We did not prepare a feature-importance ranking. The design point is that no single similarity is enough: token-set ratio gives 100 both when a true record drops 'Private Limited' and when a different organisation adds a word, so the decision model gets several similarities plus the 'what changed' features that say which side gained or lost words."
- *Why compute the similarities in C++?*
  "Because they run on every retrieved candidate, about 130 per business in our blocking study, roughly 225 million pairs for the test set (derived), each with 76 features. With a bit-parallel LCS in C++ and OpenMP, index lookup, quick filter and ranker together take about 1.3 hours on the test set."

---

### A1.15 Jaro-Winkler similarity (not used by us) {#a1-15 .concept}

**In one line:** **Jaro-Winkler** is a classic typo-tolerant similarity for short names that gives extra credit when the beginnings agree; we did not use it.

**Simple explanation:** It was designed for matching people's names in census records, where "Martha" is typed as "Marhta". It counts letters that match at nearby positions, penalises letters that appear swapped, and adds a bonus when the first few letters agree, because people rarely mistype the start of a name. It works well for short single names and less well for long multi-word business names.

**Worked example:** "martha" against "marhta".

1. Matching window = ⌊6 / 2⌋ − 1 = 2 positions; all 6 letters find a match, so m = 6.
2. In matched order the letters read m a r t h a against m a r h t a: two positions disagree, which counts as t = 2 / 2 = 1 transposition.
3. Jaro = (6/6 + 6/6 + (6 − 1)/6) / 3 = (1 + 1 + 0.833) / 3 = 0.944.
4. The common prefix "mar" has length l = 3; with the usual p = 0.1, Jaro-Winkler = 0.944 + 3 × 0.1 × (1 − 0.944) = 0.961.

Our domain (computed with RapidFuzz): shree / shri 0.848; boulevard / boulevrad 0.978 (LCS ratio 88.9); "legacy marketing enterprises" / "legacy marketing industries" 0.933 (LCS ratio 83.6).

**Technical explanation:** Two characters match if they are equal and no further apart than ⌊max(|a|, |b|) / 2⌋ − 1 positions; m is the number of matches and t half the number of matched characters that appear in a different order. Jaro = (m / |a| + m / |b| + (m − t) / m) / 3, or 0 when m = 0. Winkler's modification adds l · p · (1 − Jaro), with l the common prefix length capped at 4 and p usually 0.1 (in Winkler's original, and in RapidFuzz, the bonus is applied only when Jaro exceeds a boost threshold of 0.7). The cost is about O(|a| · window). It is not a metric. It became standard in census linkage of personal names (Winkler 1990); for multi-word strings it is often used as the inner similarity of Monge-Elkan.

**How we used it:** Not used. Our character-level similarities are the LCS ratio and the edit distances; agreement at the start of a name is a separate feature (the common-prefix share of the compacted core names, and common prefix and suffix of digit strings), so the decision model learns how much the beginning matters.

**Expert nuance:** Business names often vary at the front: honorifics such as "Shree" or "M/s", a leading "The", or the legal form written first in French names ("SARL TQ ..."), so a fixed prefix bonus can mislead. Giving prefix agreement as its own feature lets the model weight it per country. We did not benchmark Jaro-Winkler, so we do not claim it would be worse.

**Remember:**
- Jaro counts nearby matches and transpositions; Winkler adds a prefix bonus (p = 0.1, up to 4 letters).
- Built for short personal names; not used by us.
- We give prefix agreement as its own feature instead.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why not Jaro-Winkler, the classic record-linkage similarity?*
  "It is tuned for short single names whose beginnings are reliable; our names are multi-word and often vary at the front, for example the legal form written first in French names. We use LCS ratio, token-set and word-alignment measures and give the common prefix as its own feature. We did not benchmark Jaro-Winkler, so we don't claim it would be worse."

---

### A1.16 IDF, TF-IDF, BM25 and our IDF-weighted overlap {#a1-16 .concept}

**In one line:** **IDF** (inverse document frequency) gives rare words more weight than common ones, because sharing a rare word is much stronger evidence of a match.

**Simple explanation:** In a phone book, two entries sharing the word "Traders" tells you almost nothing, because thousands of shops are traders; two entries sharing "Legacy" tells you a lot. The **document frequency (df)** of a word is the number of records that contain it; IDF turns "few records contain it" into "high weight". **TF** (term frequency) counts how often a word appears inside one record. **TF-IDF** and **BM25** are standard search-engine formulas that combine both; ours is a simpler cousin built for short names, which uses IDF only.

**Worked example (N = 663,106 US test businesses; df values illustrative):**

| Word | df (illustrative) | IDF = ln(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1)) |
|---|---|---|
| legacy | 300 | 7.698 |
| marketing | 8,000 | 4.429 |
| industries | 6,000 | 4.714 |
| enterprises | 20,000 | 3.531 |
| a word in every business | 663,106 | 0.693 (= ln 2, the minimum) |
| a word in no business | 0 | 13.405 (formula value; see the note below) |

Record "legacy marketing enterprises" (no address); three businesses, each with 3 core words, so each is divided by (1 + 3)^0.22 = 1.3566:

| Business | Shared words | IDF sum | Name-word score | Share of best |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: Legacy Marketing Enterprises | all three | 15.658 | 11.542 | 1.000 |
| B: Legacy Marketing Industries | legacy, marketing | 12.127 | 8.940 | 0.775 |
| C: Marketing Enterprises Group | marketing, enterprises | 7.960 | 5.868 | 0.508 |

B beats C because they share "marketing" and differ only in the other shared word: "legacy" (7.7) is worth more than twice "enterprises" (3.5). (This shows the word channel only; real name scores also add the letter-piece and sound channels.) Note on the last IDF row: a word that no business contains has no posting list, so it retrieves nothing; when the index code totals a record's IDF for its features, it gives such an unseen term a fixed weight of 12 (code).

**Technical explanation:** The classic IDF is log(N / df); smoothed variants avoid division by zero and negative weights. Ours is log(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1)) with the natural logarithm, N the number of businesses of the country and df the number containing the term; its minimum is ln 2 when every business contains the term, and for rare and mid-frequency terms it is close to the BM25 IDF of Lucene (the open-source search library behind Elasticsearch and Solr), log(1 + (N − df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)) (both behave like ln(N / df)); they differ only for terms in almost every business, where Lucene's value falls towards 0. TF-IDF cosine builds vectors of tf · idf weights and compares them by dot product divided by both vector lengths. BM25 scores Σ idf · tf · (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 · (1 − b + b · dl / avgdl)), with k1 about 1.2 to 2 and b about 0.75: term frequency saturates and long documents are penalised. Our score has no TF, because records are sets of unique terms: it sums channel weight × IDF over shared terms and divides by (1 + the business's word or gram count)^γ, with γ = 0.22 for name words, 0.38 for the letter-piece and sound evidence (normalised by the business's 4-gram count) and 0.30 for address words. That sublinear penalty for long business names, which match many query terms by chance, plays the role of BM25's b; the query's own length does not matter, because only candidates of the same record are compared with each other. The total is ns + as + 1.2 · min(ns, as) (Doc 3). The "what changed" word features use a slightly different, also label-free IDF, log((N + 1) / (df + 1)) over all records of the country, businesses and incoming records together.

**How we used it:** IDF weights every index channel (computed over the country's businesses), the IDF-overlap features of the index lookup, the address coverage of the quick rule-based filter (the IDF share of the record's address words found in the business address), the rarity features of the "what changed" family, and the IDF containment that ranks address-rescue candidates. On the test set these statistics are computed from the unlabelled test files themselves, which the Documentation discloses (Doc C.1). We did not use BM25 or TF-IDF cosine.

**Expert nuance:** Term frequency rarely exceeds 1 in a business name, so the TF part of TF-IDF or BM25 adds little, and cosine's normalisation by query length is irrelevant when ranking the candidates of one query; a per-channel length exponent is simpler and transparent. IDF computed on the test files is transductive: a word frequent in this market gets a low weight, which is what we want, and no label is involved. A typo has df near 1 and therefore maximal IDF; that is harmless for retrieval (it matches nothing) but inflates "rarity" features, which the letter-piece channels and the decision model absorb. We did not benchmark BM25 against our scoring, so we claim nothing either way.

**Remember:**
- IDF = log(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1)): rare words weigh more; the minimum is ln 2.
- Our retrieval score is an IDF-weighted set overlap with per-channel length penalties: no TF, not BM25, not cosine.
- IDF statistics come from the unlabelled records at run time (label-free, disclosed).

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why not BM25 or TF-IDF cosine for retrieval?*
  "Names and addresses are short sets where a word rarely repeats, so the term-frequency part adds little. We use a smoothed IDF-weighted overlap with a length penalty per channel, rarest terms first. We did not benchmark BM25 against it; ours keeps the true business for 99.37 % of US and 98.51 % of Indian held-out records."
- *Where do your IDF statistics come from, train or test?*
  "From the records being processed: for the index and its features, the businesses of the country; for the 'what changed' features, all records of the country. On the test set that means the unlabelled test files; no labels are involved, and the Documentation discloses these unsupervised statistics."

---

### A1.17 Set-overlap measures: Jaccard, overlap coefficient and IDF-weighted versions {#a1-17 .concept}

**In one line:** Set-overlap measures count how many pieces two records share, relative to how many pieces they have.

**Simple explanation:** Compare two shopping lists. **Jaccard** = items on both lists divided by items on either list. **Overlap coefficient** = items on both lists divided by the length of the shorter list, so a short list contained entirely in a long one scores 1. **Dice** = twice the shared items divided by the two lengths added together. Weighted versions count rare items (saffron) more than common ones (salt), using IDF.

**Worked example:** Record words {legacy, marketing, enterprises} against business words {legacy, marketing, industries}.

1. Shared = 2; union = 4.
2. Jaccard = 2 / 4 = 0.500; overlap coefficient = 2 / 3 = 0.667; Dice = 2 × 2 / (3 + 3) = 0.667; shared over the larger set = 2 / 3.
3. IDF-weighted Jaccard with the illustrative IDFs of the previous concept: (7.698 + 4.429) / (7.698 + 4.429 + 3.531 + 4.714) = 12.127 / 20.372 = 0.595.
4. For comparison, the real IDF-weighted Jaccard of "Legacy Marketing Industries Inc" in Doc D.1 is 0.52, computed with the real IDF values.
5. Truncation case: {ganesh, traders} against {shree, ganesh, traders} gives Jaccard 2 / 3 = 0.667 but overlap coefficient 2 / 2 = 1.000.

**Technical explanation:** Jaccard J = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| (and 1 − J is a metric); Dice = 2 |A ∩ B| / (|A| + |B|); the overlap or Szymkiewicz-Simpson coefficient = |A ∩ B| / min(|A|, |B|); containment of A in B = |A ∩ B| / |A|, which is asymmetric. Weighted versions replace counts by sums of weights, for example weighted Jaccard = Σ over A ∩ B of w / Σ over A ∪ B of w. With both sets stored as sorted lists of hashed terms, each measure costs one merge, O(|A| + |B|). The index lookup outputs intersection, Jaccard, overlap coefficient and intersection over the larger set for seven sets (name words, address words, 3-grams, 4-grams, sound grams, name numbers, address numbers), plus six IDF overlaps (shared IDF, and shared IDF as a share of the record's and of the business's total, for name and for address). The quick rule-based filter uses address coverage, the IDF share of the record's address words found in the business's address, a containment measure. The "what changed" family includes the IDF-weighted Jaccard of the two core-name word sets, with legal-form words removed.

**How we used it:** As listed: in the 76 index-lookup features, in the quick filter's coverage conditions (0.95, 0.4, 0.3), and in the "what changed" features (Doc 3, Doc 4).

**Expert nuance:** The measures disagree exactly where it matters, on subsets: a truncated true record and a look-alike that adds a word both give an overlap coefficient of 1 with a lower Jaccard. Direction matters (record contained in business means the record lost words; business contained in record means the record gained words), so we give shares relative to each side plus the "what changed" features that say which side changed. Word-set measures are brittle to typos, hence the letter-piece sets. MinHash can estimate Jaccard very quickly for huge collections (see Other blocking families); with an inverted index we compute it exactly on candidates.

**Remember:**
- Jaccard = shared / union; overlap coefficient = shared / smaller set; Dice = 2 · shared / (sum of sizes).
- IDF-weighted versions make rare shared words count more.
- Symmetric measures cannot tell dropped words from added words; direction needs its own features.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why give the model both Jaccard and the overlap coefficient?*
  "They disagree exactly on subsets: a record that drops a word from the business name has overlap coefficient 1 but a lower Jaccard, and so does a record that adds a word. The model sees both, plus shares relative to each side and the 'what changed' features that say which side gained or lost words."

---

### A1.18 Phonetic keys: Soundex and Metaphone (not used) and our consonant skeleton {#a1-18 .concept}

**In one line:** A **phonetic key** writes a name roughly as it sounds, so spellings that sound alike get the same key.

**Simple explanation:** People spell what they hear: Mohammed, Mohamed; Shree, Shri. Vowels vary most between spellings, while consonants form the skeleton of a name. Our key throws away the vowels (and y) and squeezes repeated consonants, keeping a **consonant skeleton**. **Soundex** and **Metaphone** are older, English-specific versions of the same idea, with rules for how English letters sound.

**Worked example (computed with our index rules):**

| Name | Key (vowels and y removed, repeats collapsed) |
|---|---|
| shree ganesh traders | gnsh shr trdrs |
| shri ganesh traders | gnsh shr trdrs (identical) |
| mohammed traders | mhmd trdrs |
| mohamed traders | mhmd trdrs (identical) |
| vijy (generic romaniser) / vijay (Latin) | vj / vj |
| praaivett / private | prvt / prvt |
| enttrpraaijej / enterprises | ntrprj / ntrprs (share the 4-grams ntrp and trpr) |
| mona / mina | mn / mn (a false collision) |

The key is built on the sorted core words, with spaces removed, then cut into 4-grams: "gnshshrtrdrs" → gnsh, nshs, shsh, hshr, shrt, hrtr, rtrd, trdr, rdrs. The praaivett / private row shows the rule on single words only: in the index, "private" is a legal word and is removed from the core name before the key is built. For comparison, classic Soundex gives Robert → R163 and Rupert → R163.

**Technical explanation:** Soundex (patented in 1918) keeps the first letter, maps the following consonants to six digit classes, drops vowels and h, w, y, collapses repeated digits and pads to four characters. Metaphone and Double Metaphone apply dozens of English pronunciation rules; NYSIIS is similar. All of them encode English pronunciation. Our key is language-neutral: delete a, e, i, o, u and y, and collapse repeated consonants (vowels are skipped before the comparison, so consonants separated only by vowels also collapse); it is applied to the sorted unique core-name words, spaces are removed, and the result is cut into 4-grams. A skeleton shorter than 4 letters ("vj") becomes a single gram. The sound channel has the lowest weight (0.18) and the tightest posting cap and budget (800 / 4,000); the index lookup also computes one LCS-ratio similarity on the sound string and set statistics of the sound grams (Doc 3).

**How we used it:** As one of the five retrieval channels and inside the 76 index-lookup features. Soundex, Metaphone and NYSIIS are not used.

**Expert nuance:** The key is lossy by design: unrelated names collide (mona and mina both give "mn"), so it is a weak channel that only proposes candidates, and the later stages decide. It works across scripts only after romanisation, but it helps exactly there: a generic romaniser's output and the Latin spelling often share a skeleton or several sound 4-grams (vijy / vijay; enttrpraaijej / enterprises), which partly covers native-script words missing from the learned lexicon. English pronunciation rules would mishandle Indian and French names; dropping vowels is neutral across languages.

**Remember:**
- Our key: remove vowels and y, collapse repeated consonants, cut into 4-grams; weight 0.18.
- It merges spelling variants (shree / shri, mohammed / mohamed) and many romanisations; it also merges unrelated names, so it only proposes candidates.
- Soundex, Metaphone and NYSIIS are not used: they are English-centric.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why not Soundex or Metaphone?*
  "They encode English pronunciation rules, and our names are Indian, French and American, often romanised from other scripts. A language-neutral consonant skeleton catches Shree against Shri and Mohammed against Mohamed, and it is only one retrieval channel with a low weight, so its false collisions are filtered later."

---

### A1.19 Blocking and candidate generation: reduction ratio, pair completeness, pairs quality {#a1-19 .concept}

**In one line:** **Blocking** (candidate generation) quickly picks, for each incoming record, a small set of plausible businesses, so that the expensive comparison runs only on those pairs.

**Simple explanation:** A librarian asked for "Ganesh Traders, Pune" does not read all 1.7 million catalogue cards; she opens the catalogue at "Ganesh" and at "Pune" and pulls out a handful. Blocking is that catalogue step. It must be fast, it must be small (few cards pulled), and it must be safe (the right card is almost always among them). If the right card is not pulled, no amount of careful reading later can find it. The name comes from the oldest form of the idea: put records into "blocks" that share a **blocking key** (for example the same postcode) and compare only inside a block.

The words you need: the **comparison space** is the set of all possible pairs; the **reduction ratio (RR)** is the share of that space we do not keep; **pair completeness (PC)** is the share of true matches we keep (the recall of blocking); **pairs quality (PQ)** is the share of kept pairs that are true matches (the precision of blocking).

**Worked example:**

Toy (illustrative): 1,000 records × 1,000 businesses = 1,000,000 pairs, with 1,000 true matches. Blocking keeps 3,000 pairs, 950 of them true matches.

1. RR = 1 − 3,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.997.
2. PC = 950 / 1,000 = 0.95.
3. PQ = 950 / 3,000 = 0.317.

Our test set (Doc 3; per-country products derived):

| Country | Businesses × incoming records | Pairs |
|---|---|---|
| US | 663,106 × 3,817,031 | 2,531,096,158,286 |
| India | 809,986 × 4,717,565 | 3,821,161,604,090 |
| France | 259,452 × 1,434,993 | 372,311,803,836 |
| All | | 6,724,569,566,212 |

The candidate file holds 12,293,019 pairs, so RR = 1 − 12,293,019 / 6,724,569,566,212 = 0.99999817: about 1.83 pairs kept per million (derived). PC at the index lookup on labelled fold 9: 99.3694 % (US) and 98.5068 % (India).

**Technical explanation:** A blocking method maps each record to keys, or runs a ranked search, so that only pairs sharing a key or retrieved by the search become candidates. The main families are standard blocking on an exact key, multi-pass blocking (the union of several keys), token and q-gram blocking, sorted neighbourhood, canopy clustering, locality-sensitive hashing, dense vector retrieval, and ranked top-k retrieval, which is ours. The standard quality measures (Christen) are RR = 1 − |C| / |A × B|, PC = |C ∩ M| / |M| and PQ = |C ∩ M| / |C|, for a candidate set C and true matches M; a blocking method must be judged on RR and PC together, and the harmonic mean of the two is sometimes reported. In many-to-one linking it is natural to measure PC per owned incoming record: the share whose owner is among its candidates. With a capped top-k per record and capped posting lists, total work is proportional to the number of records times a bounded cost, instead of |A| · |B|. Blocking sets the recall ceiling for every later model (see Recall ceiling).

**How we used it:** All retrieval stays within one country. The funnel per business is about 130 candidates from the index lookup (blocking study of 25 Sep 2026), 21.71 after the quick rule-based filter, 6.75 in the shortlist (derived) and 7.10 in the candidate file, which also contains the second-chance candidates (Doc 3). Per incoming record that is 1.23 candidates; 90.59 % of records have exactly one, all but 2 have at least one, and 125 businesses have no candidate (Doc B.1). The size of the candidate file was itself judged (candidate efficiency), so a small file was a goal in its own right.

**Expert nuance:** RR on its own is meaningless (keeping nothing gives RR = 1), and at our scale it moves in the seventh decimal: each 0.0000001 of RR is about 672,457 pairs (derived). PQ was not reported; we would compute it on labelled folds as true matches per kept pair. Candidate counts are heavily skewed, with a median of 7 per business but a maximum of 3,182 (Doc B.1), so any average hides long tails. The blocking key choice is a modelling decision: every key encodes an assumption about how true matches can differ, which is why we combine several channels.

**Remember:**
- Blocking = a cheap search that bounds what the expensive models see; it sets the recall ceiling.
- RR 0.99999817 (12,293,019 of 6,724,569,566,212 pairs); read it only together with recall.
- Pair completeness at the index lookup on fold 9: 99.37 % US, 98.51 % India.

**Judge might ask:**
- *What is your reduction ratio, and is it meaningful on its own?*
  "0.99999817: 12.3 million candidate pairs out of 6.7 trillion same-country pairs, fewer than two per million. On its own it isn't meaningful, since keeping nothing scores 1; it matters together with recall, and the true business is still among the index results for 99.37 % of US and 98.51 % of Indian held-out records."
- *Why search only within a country?*
