  "Every record carries a country, and all our retrieval stays inside it. That shrinks the comparison space, keeps each index in memory, and lets each country use its own cleaning rules, readers and decision model."

---

### A1.20 The inverted index {#a1-20 .concept}

**In one line:** An **inverted index** maps every word (or letter piece) to the list of businesses that contain it, so candidates are found by looking words up instead of scanning everything.

**Simple explanation:** It is the index at the back of a book: "Ganesh: pages 12, 57". To find businesses that share words with an incoming record, look up each of the record's words, collect the businesses listed, and give each business points for every word it shares, more points for rarer words. Very common words, like "the" in a book, have enormous lists and say little, so we skip lists that are too long and stop once we have read enough.

The words you need: a **posting list** is the list of businesses for one word; one entry of it is a **posting**; an **accumulator** is the running score of each business during a lookup; a **posting-list cap** is the longest list we are willing to read; a **budget** is the total number of postings we read per record and channel.

**Worked example:**

A tiny index of three businesses: B1 "shree ganesh traders", B2 "ganesh sweets", B3 "vijay traders".

| Word | Posting list |
|---|---|
| ganesh | B1, B2 |
| shree | B1 |
| sweets | B2 |
| traders | B1, B3 |
| vijay | B3 |

Query "shri ganesh traders":

1. "shri" has no list (no business contains it).
2. "ganesh" adds IDF(ganesh) to B1 and B2.
3. "traders" adds IDF(traders) to B1 and B3.
4. Accumulators: B1 has both words, B2 and B3 one each, so B1 ranks first. We read 4 postings instead of comparing against every business.

Caps and budget (list lengths illustrative; the limits are the real name-channel values, cap 14,000 per list and budget 22,000 per record), with words processed rarest first:

| Query word | List length | Action | Postings used so far |
|---|---|---|---|
| vijay | 3,000 | read | 3,000 |
| shree | 9,000 | read | 12,000 |
| traders | 12,000 | skipped: 12,000 + 12,000 would exceed the 22,000 budget | 12,000 |
| enterprises | 40,000 | skipped: longer than the 14,000 cap | 12,000 |

**Technical explanation:** To build the index, each business's unique terms are hashed to 64-bit keys and the business id is appended to each term's posting list in a hash map (a table that finds the entry for a key in roughly constant time); IDF is computed once per term. A lookup accumulates scores term at a time into a per-thread dense array with one slot per business of the country, plus a list of "touched" businesses so that resetting costs only what was touched (code). Terms are processed rarest first; a term whose list is longer than the channel's cap is skipped (frequency-based stop-wording), and a term whose list would push the channel past its budget is skipped too; because lists come in increasing length, no later term of that channel can fit either. This bounds the work per record to at most 65,000 postings across the five channels plus up to 2,000 businesses from the exact-name key (derived from the budgets in Doc 3). After accumulation, the name score, address score and total are computed for the touched businesses, partial sorts pick the top lists, and the 76 features are computed for the kept candidates. Incoming records are processed in batches (20,000 by default), parallelised with OpenMP and dynamic scheduling, so that threads that finish early take more records (code). Cost: building is linear in the total number of business terms, and a lookup is linear in the postings read plus the businesses touched. Search engines also use document-at-a-time strategies with dynamic pruning (WAND, MaxScore), which skip documents that provably cannot enter the top k and so return the exact top-k; our caps are a simpler, static form of pruning that does not guarantee the exact top-k of the uncapped score.

**How we used it:** C++17 with OpenMP, one index per country over normalised business text, five channels plus the exact-name key, with the caps and budgets above (Doc 3); the lookup ran on 8 to 11 threads, and index lookup, quick filter and ranker together took about 1.3 hours on the test set (clean-run report). No embeddings, no vector search and no learned model in this stage. Recall at the index on fold 9: 99.3694 % (US) and 98.5068 % (India).

**Expert nuance:** Skipping very common terms is a recall risk for records whose words are all common ("Ganesh Traders"); the exact sorted core-name key, the letter-piece and sound channels (each with its own cap) and the address channel compensate, and the quick filter's address conditions keep address-only candidates. Unlike approximate nearest-neighbour search with randomised index construction, an inverted index with fixed caps is deterministic: it is a pruned search, not an exact top-k, but the pruning is a fixed rule, so the same input always gives the same candidates, which makes it easy to audit and reproduce (from the trained models, our inference stages rewrite both output files byte for byte). The per-thread accumulators are small compared with the posting lists, so memory is dominated by the index itself.

**Remember:**
- Posting list = term → businesses containing it; a lookup adds IDF for every shared term.
- Rarest first; skip lists longer than the cap; stop at the budget: bounded work per record.
- Deterministic and auditable (a fixed pruning rule); C++ with OpenMP; about 1.3 hours for lookup, filter and ranker on test.

**Judge might ask:**
- *What happens to a record whose words are all very common, like 'Ganesh Traders'?*
  "Very common words exceed the posting cap and are skipped, but the exact-name channel still returns every business with exactly that core name if at most 2,000 share it, and the letter-piece, sound and address channels have their own caps. Then the address usually separates them."
- *How do you bound the cost per record?*
  "Every channel has a cap per posting list and a total budget, processed rarest first, so one record reads at most about 65,000 postings plus up to 2,000 exact-name matches (derived from the budgets), and we keep a fixed number of top candidates. Cost grows linearly with the number of records."

---

### A1.21 Multi-channel retrieval and the union of top lists {#a1-21 .concept}

**In one line:** We search five ways at once (name words, address words, two kinds of letter pieces, sounds) plus an exact-name key, and keep the union of several top lists, so that a candidate strong on only one side is not lost.

**Simple explanation:** A detective questions several witnesses: one remembers the name, one the street, one only how the name sounded. If you trust only the combined story, you miss suspects that just one witness saw. So we keep the top suspects overall, plus the top suspects by name alone, plus the top suspects by address alone, plus anyone with exactly the same name. Each witness is a **channel**; keeping the union of several lists is called **multi-pass blocking**.

**Worked example (illustrative scores):** total = ns + as + 1.2 × min(ns, as), where ns is the name score and as the address score.

| Candidate | ns | as | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| X: right name, address does not match | 9.0 | 0.0 | 9.0 |
| Y: both match moderately | 4.5 | 4.5 | 14.4 |
| Z: address only | 0.0 | 6.0 | 6.0 |

1. By total the order is Y, X, Z. If we kept only the top 2 by total, Z, an address-only match such as a brand name at the right address, would be lost; the top-by-address list keeps it.
2. Y gets a bonus of 1.2 × 4.5 = 5.4 for agreeing on both fields; X gets none.
3. Exact-name key: "Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc" and "Legacy Marketing Enterprises LLC" both have the key "enterprises legacy marketing" (sorted core words), so the record "Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc)" retrieves both whatever their scores.

**Technical explanation:** The channels (weight; posting cap / budget) are: name words (1; 14,000 / 22,000), address words (1; 10,000 / 18,000), core-name 4-grams (0.45; 2,500 / 15,000), core-name 3-grams (0.22; 1,000 / 6,000) and sound 4-grams (0.18; 800 / 4,000). The name score is ns = name-word IDF sum / (1 + the business's name words)^0.22 + letter-piece and sound sum / (1 + the business's 4-grams)^0.38; the address score is as = address IDF sum / (1 + the business's address words)^0.30; total = ns + as + 1.2 · min(ns, as). Kept per incoming record: the top 12 by total, the top 6 by ns, the top 6 by as (only if as > 0), and every business with the same sorted core-name word set if at most 2,000 businesses share it (Doc 3). This union is multi-pass blocking in ranked form. For every kept candidate the index lookup computes 76 pair features, including 8 retrieval scores: ns, as, total, total divided by the best total, the best total, the second-best total, best minus second, and the raw candidate count. In the all-fold samples the index lookup returns 27.541 (US) and 23.145 (India) candidates per incoming record (Doc B.2).

**How we used it:** Exactly as above; the 76 features feed the quick rule-based filter, the CatBoost ranker and the decision models. Recall at the index lookup on fold 9: 99.3694 % (US) and 98.5068 % (India).

**Expert nuance:** The min term acts as a soft AND: with a plain sum, a strong name-only match could outrank a moderate match on both fields, which is usually the better candidate. The separate lists protect the two recall risks that matter most: a missing or wrong address (the name list) and a brand or renamed business at the right address (the address list). The exact-key channel guarantees that identical core names are always compared, even when their words are too common to pass the caps. The weights, caps and exponents are fixed values reported in the Documentation; the evidence we report for them is the measured recall, not a tuning study.

**Remember:**
- Five channels plus the exact core-name key; total = ns + as + 1.2 · min(ns, as).
- Keep top 12 by total ∪ top 6 by name ∪ top 6 by address ∪ same core name (if at most 2,000 share it).
- The union is what makes retrieval recall-first; 76 features per kept candidate.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why keep separate top lists by name and by address?*
  "A record can match its business on only one side: the right name with no address, or a brand name at the right address. A combined score would bury those, so beside the top 12 overall we keep the top 6 by name and the top 6 by address."
- *What is the exact-name channel for?*
  "It returns every business whose core name, as a sorted word set, equals the record's, if at most 2,000 share it. That guarantees, for example, that 'Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc' and the LLC are both compared even when their words are too common to pass the caps; the later models then separate them."

---

### A1.22 The quick rule-based filter {#a1-22 .concept}

**In one line:** A nearly free, model-less rule drops candidates that are clearly weaker than the record's best one, while keeping special cases that a single score would wrongly drop.

**Simple explanation:** Think of a first interview round where the receptionist uses a checklist: keep the top applicant, anyone close to the top, the best at one particular skill, and a few special profiles; send the rest home. The checklist costs almost nothing, and it shrinks the pile from about 130 to about 22 candidates per business before the expensive interviews begin. Because it is a fixed rule, not a trained model, it is called **deterministic pruning**.

**Worked example (illustrative):** one record's candidates.

| Candidate | Total | Share of best total | Address coverage | Kept? Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Y | 14.4 | 1.00 | 0.60 | yes: best total |
| X | 9.0 | 0.63 | 0.00 | yes: at least 0.6 of the best |
| Z | 6.0 | 0.42 | 0.97 | yes: best address score, and covers at least 0.95 of the record's address |
| W | 5.0 | 0.35 | 0.50 | no |
| V | 4.0 | 0.28 | 0.10 | no |

Real case (Doc D.3): for "TQ COMITE SARL" the index lookup found 16 candidates, the quick filter kept 2, and both entered the shortlist.

**Technical explanation:** A candidate is kept if any of six conditions holds: (1) it has the record's best total (ties kept); (2) its total is at least 0.6 × max(1, best total), where the max(1, ·) guard stops the rule from keeping everything when all scores are tiny; (3) it is the record's best candidate by address score (with as > 0); (4) its address coverage is at least 0.95, coverage being the IDF share of the record's address words found in the business's address; (5) the record's name has at most 3 characters and coverage is at least 0.4 (initials and acronyms, whose name scores are unreliable); (6) it has the same sorted core-name word set and coverage at least 0.3 (Doc 3). The inputs are retrieval statistics the index lookup has already computed, so the cost is linear in the candidates and needs no model call. Conditions 3 to 6 are recall protection for address-only, short-name and same-name candidates. Result: 37,614,782 pairs, 21.7107 per business (US 15.0352, India 23.6328, France 32.7713), against 130.1 per business before pruning in the blocking study of 25 Sep 2026; in the all-fold samples 3.111 (US) and 3.878 (India) candidates per incoming record remain (Doc 3, Doc B.2). The decision models still receive the raw candidate count from before the filter (code).

**How we used it:** Between the index lookup and the CatBoost ranker, on every country. Its measured cost, from the blocking study of 25 Sep 2026 with the decision model of that date: the owner survived for 99.974 % of fold-8/9 records, and fold-9 macro F0.5 moved from 0.990117 to 0.990086 (fold 8: −0.00004) (Doc 3).

**Expert nuance:** Why a rule and not a learned pruner: the ranker would otherwise have to score about 130 candidates per business, while a rule on already-computed statistics is nearly free and its loss was measured. The thresholds were set in that blocking study with the decision model of the time, so the 0.00003 cost estimate belongs to that model and was not re-measured for the final one. A tiny learned model on the 8 retrieval scores might prune more at equal recall, but it adds a model pass and its own training. The rule embodies the cascade principle: cheap tests first, expensive models last.

**Remember:**
- Keep a candidate if any of six simple conditions holds; no model.
- About 130 → 21.71 candidates per business; the owner survived for 99.974 %; fold-9 F0.5 0.990117 → 0.990086.
- Four of the six conditions exist only to protect recall (address-only, acronyms, same name).

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why a hand-written rule before the ranker instead of letting the ranker see everything?*
  "Cost against measured loss: the rule uses scores the index already computed, so it is nearly free, and it cuts about 130 candidates per business to 21.7. On held-out records the true business survived for 99.974 %, and fold-9 F0.5 moved only from 0.990117 to 0.990086."
- *How were the 0.6 and the coverage thresholds chosen?*
  "They come from our blocking study of 25 September, which measured on held-out folds 8 and 9, with the decision model of that date, how many true businesses survive and how exact F0.5 changes. The special conditions keep what a single score would drop: address-only matches, very short names and identical core names."

---

### A1.23 Recall ceiling and the candidate funnel {#a1-23 .concept}

**In one line:** The **recall ceiling** is the share of true matches still present among the candidates after each step; no later model can recover what candidate generation lost.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine panning for gold with a stack of sieves: each layer removes sand, and after every layer we count how many gold grains are left. If gold is lost at layer two, no clever work at layer five can bring it back, except a separate second search. So we counted the gold after every layer: that is the candidate **funnel** with its recall at each stage.

**Worked example (Doc B.2, train fold 9; missed counts derived):**

| Stage | US recall | India recall | Owned records missed (derived) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Index lookup | 99.3694 % | 98.5068 % | about 2,888 of 457,971 (US); about 4,536 of 303,786 (India) |
| Shortlist (quick filter, then top 4), lower to upper bound | 98.8748 % to 99.3628 % | 98.0572 % to 98.4831 % | about 2,918 to 5,153 (US); about 4,608 to 5,902 (India) |

Candidates per incoming record in the all-fold samples: index 27.541 (US) / 23.145 (India) → after the filter 3.111 / 3.878 → shortlist 1.114 / 1.174.

Why recall losses hurt less than precision losses: with perfect precision, a recall of 0.99 still gives F0.5 = 1.25 × 0.99 / (0.25 + 0.99) = 0.998 (pooled; see F-beta).

**Technical explanation:** Recall at stage s = (owned incoming records whose owner is among the stage-s candidates) / (owned incoming records), measured on labelled train fold 9 with the submitted index lookup, quick filter and ranker; the ranker was fitted on folds 0-5, so fold 9 is unseen by it. For the full fold the evidence gives the shortlist recall after the filter as a lower and an upper bound; the fold-9 samples (7,411 US and 7,444 Indian owned records) give exact values: 99.3523 % and 98.3745 % after the filter, 98.8935 % and 97.985 % in the shortlist. The largest loss is the cap of four candidates per record: the top 4 without the filter already gives 98.8814 % (US) and 98.0809 % (India). Second-chance candidates are not included in these numbers; they target the remaining miss types (native-script names, and records whose name differs while the address matches). The final recall is lower than the ceiling, because the decision rule also abstains; the ceiling is an upper bound. For France it cannot be measured, because there are no labels.

**How we used it:** Measuring recall at every candidate stage on held-out labelled data is part of our validation hygiene (Doc 3, Doc B.2): it separates retrieval misses from decision misses, and the two second-chance searches target the retrieval miss types found on train (native-script names the Latin index does not retrieve, and records whose name differs while the address matches) (Doc 3).

**Expert nuance:** The ceiling is counted per owned incoming record (singletons excluded); under the per-business metric a missed record costs only its own business's recall. Separating "retrieval misses" (fixed by better blocking or a second search) from "decision misses" (fixed by better scoring or thresholds) is the main diagnostic value: lowering a threshold cannot help a record whose owner is not among its candidates. The shortlist cap trades recall for reader cost; finer blocking keys would make a larger cap affordable where it loses true businesses (QA 18).

**Remember:**
- Index lookup 99.37 % US / 98.51 % India; shortlist at least 98.87 % / 98.06 % (fold 9).
- The cap of four is the largest loss; the quick filter costs very little.
- Second-chance searches exist because a missing owner cannot be fixed by any threshold.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Where does your pipeline lose the most true matches?*
  "At the shortlist cap of four: on held-out fold 9 the true business is in the index results for 99.37 % of US records and in the shortlist for at least 98.87 %; for India 98.51 % and at least 98.06 %. The quick filter itself is almost free."
- *Why cap the shortlist at four rather than eight?*
  "It is a cost-recall trade-off: four protects the expensive readers, which see 1.17 pairs per record on average. We did not report a curve for other caps; to decide properly we would measure shortlist recall and F0.5 against the cap on fold 9, and finer blocking keys would make a larger cap affordable."

---

### A1.24 Other blocking families: sorted neighbourhood, canopy clustering, LSH / MinHash (not used) {#a1-24 .concept}

**In one line:** These are classic alternative ways to find candidate pairs; we did not use them.

**Simple explanation:**
- **Sorted neighbourhood**: sort all records alphabetically by a key and compare each record only with its few neighbours in the sorted list, like checking only adjacent names in a phone book.
- **Canopy clustering**: use a cheap distance to throw records into overlapping rough groups ("canopies") and compare only within a group.
- **LSH (locality-sensitive hashing) with MinHash**: give each record several random fingerprints built so that similar records are likely to share at least one; compare only records that share a fingerprint.

**Worked example:**

Sorted neighbourhood with key = normalised name and a window of 3 (illustrative): in the alphabetically sorted list, a business written "ganesh traders shree" sits among the thousands of names starting with "ganesh", while the record "shree ganesh traders" sits among the names starting with "shree". They are thousands of rows apart, so a window of 3 never compares them: a word-order change or a first-letter typo breaks the method, which is why it is usually run several times with different keys (for example the name with its words sorted, or the postcode).

MinHash LSH with b = 8 bands of r = 4 rows: the probability that two records with Jaccard similarity J become candidates is 1 − (1 − J^4)^8 (computed):

| Jaccard J | P(candidate) |
|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.013 |
| 0.5 | 0.403 |
| 0.8 | 0.985 |

**Technical explanation:** Sorted neighbourhood (Hernández and Stolfo, 1995) costs O(n log n) to sort plus O(n · w) comparisons for window w; it is sensitive to the key and is normally run in several passes with different keys. Canopy clustering (McCallum, Nigam and Ungar, 2000) uses a cheap distance with a loose threshold T1 and a tight threshold T2 < T1: records within T1 of a centre join its canopy, records within T2 are removed from the pool of future centres, so canopies overlap. MinHash relies on the fact that for a random permutation π, P[min π(A) = min π(B)] = J(A, B); a signature of k min-hashes is split into b bands of r rows, and records sharing any whole band become candidates, giving the S-shaped curve 1 − (1 − J^r)^b with its steepest rise near (1/b)^(1/r) (about 0.59 for b = 8, r = 4). Weighted MinHash variants can include IDF-like weights. In this vocabulary, our method is token, q-gram, phonetic and exact-key blocking with IDF-weighted scoring and a top-k per record, closely related to **meta-blocking**, which weights candidate pairs by the evidence of the blocks they share and keeps the best pairs per record.

**How we used it:** Not used. Our candidate generation is the inverted index with five channels, the exact-name key, the union of top lists and the quick rule-based filter.

**Expert nuance:** The main weakness of these methods at our scale is control: block or bucket sizes are uncontrolled on skewed data (thousands of names share "enterprises"), whereas a ranked top-k per record bounds the output, and plain MinHash weighs every shingle equally, while IDF knows that "legacy" matters more than "enterprises". Their strengths are simplicity and easy distribution (they map naturally onto MapReduce) without an in-memory index. We did not benchmark them, so we do not claim they would be worse; our evidence is our own measured recall.

**Remember:**
- Sorted neighbourhood compares neighbours in a sorted list; it is fragile to word order and first-letter typos.
- MinHash LSH: P(candidate) = 1 − (1 − J^r)^b, a tunable S-curve, with no IDF unless weighted.
- Not used; ours is closest to weighted token and q-gram blocking with a top-k per record (meta-blocking).

**Judge might ask:**
- *Did you consider LSH or sorted-neighbourhood blocking?*
  "We did not use them. An inverted index with IDF weights gives each record a scored, bounded top list, which suits skewed data where some words are shared by thousands of businesses, and it keeps the true business for 99.37 % of US and 98.51 % of Indian held-out records. We did not benchmark the alternatives, so we don't claim they would be worse."

---

### A1.25 Dense vector retrieval with approximate nearest neighbours (not used) {#a1-25 .concept}

**In one line:** **Dense retrieval** turns every name into a vector with a neural encoder and finds the nearest vectors with an approximate search index; we did not use it.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine placing every business on a "meaning map" so that names meaning the same thing land close together, even with no letters in common, for example the same name written in two scripts. Finding candidates then means finding the nearest points on the map. With millions of points, special search structures, a bit like a road network with motorway shortcuts, find near neighbours quickly at the price of occasionally missing one; that is **approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN)** search.

The words you need: an **embedding** is the vector for one text; a **bi-encoder** embeds each side separately, so business vectors can be computed once in advance; **cosine similarity** compares two vectors by their angle; **HNSW** and **IVF-PQ** are two ANN index types; **FAISS** is a widely used ANN library. A **cross-encoder**, like our readers, instead reads both texts together.

**Worked example (illustrative 3-number vectors):**

| Name | Vector |
|---|---|
| Vijay Enterprises | (0.90, 0.10, 0.40) |
| Vijay Ent. | (0.88, 0.12, 0.41) |
| Ajay Traders | (0.20, 0.90, 0.10) |

cos(Vijay Enterprises, Vijay Ent.) = 0.9996; cos(Vijay Enterprises, Ajay Traders) = 0.338. Real encoders use hundreds of numbers per vector: 384 for MiniLM and 768 for E5, which matches the head sizes of 385 and 769 parameters in the Documentation (one weight per number plus a bias). Back-of-envelope memory (derived): 809,986 Indian businesses × 384 numbers × 4 bytes ≈ 1.24 GB in 32-bit floats.

**Technical explanation:** A bi-encoder f maps each text independently into a d-dimensional space and scores a pair by cosine or dot product; business vectors are precomputed, so retrieval reduces to nearest-neighbour search. Exact search costs O(N · d) per query; ANN indexes trade a little recall for speed. HNSW builds a hierarchical navigable small-world graph (parameters M, efConstruction, efSearch) with roughly logarithmic search; IVF clusters vectors with k-means (which groups points around a chosen number of centres) and searches only the few clusters nearest the query (nprobe), and product quantisation compresses vectors into short codes. Bi-encoders are trained contrastively on labelled pairs (pulling the vectors of matching pairs together and pushing non-matching ones apart), using the other pairs of the same batch and deliberately chosen similar-looking non-matches as negatives. A cross-encoder attends across both texts jointly, which is more accurate, but nothing can be precomputed, so it suits re-ranking a shortlist, not retrieval over millions. The usual production answer is hybrid retrieval: a lexical index and a dense index, with the union of their candidate lists.

**How we used it:** Not used, and not benchmarked (QA 1). Retrieval is the inverted index; the readers are cross-encoders that see only the shortlist; a frozen pretrained MiniLM is used only to embed single words for the meaning-similarity "what changed" features.

**Expert nuance:** Dense retrieval is strongest on paraphrases, abbreviations and cross-script names, and weakest on exact digits, house numbers and rare proper nouns, where lexical matching wins; ANN results are approximate and harder to audit, and a good encoder needs fine-tuning. The natural place for it in our pipeline is one more channel in the union of top lists, aimed at brand or "doing business as" names with little word overlap, one of our documented miss types, rather than a replacement for the index. It would be allowed by the rules as long as the encoder is Apache- or MIT-licensed and at most 8B parameters.

**Remember:**
- Bi-encoder plus ANN = precomputed vectors and approximate nearest-neighbour search; cross-encoder = joint reading, shortlist only.
- Not used and not benchmarked, so no claim that it would be worse.
- Best use for us: an extra channel for brand or "doing business as" names, added to the union of lists.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why not embedding (vector) search for blocking?*
  "We did not benchmark a dense retriever, so we can't claim it would be worse. Our index already keeps the true business for 99.37 % of US and 98.51 % of Indian held-out records, deterministically. Dense search would be the natural extra channel for brand or 'doing business as' names that share few words, added to our union of lists rather than replacing it."
- *Would a dense retriever help the Indian-script records?*
  "Plausibly, because a multilingual encoder can place विजय and Vijay close together. Today we handle that with the learned word list and the native-script second-chance search, which added 9,759 links; we have not measured a dense alternative, so it is a hypothesis we would test on labelled Indian folds."

---

### A1.26 Scaling: sharding, bounded work per record and MapReduce-style blocking {#a1-26 .concept}

**In one line:** The pipeline scales by splitting the data into independent pieces (today one per country) and by capping the work per record at every stage, so total cost grows linearly with the number of records.

**Simple explanation:** A grocery chain does not run one giant warehouse for the whole country: each region has its own warehouse and catalogue, every order goes only to its own region, and every order has a maximum number of items. Adding customers then adds work in proportion, not explosively. Our regions are countries: each has its own index, and an incoming record is only ever searched in its own country's index. Each such piece is a **shard**. Work that splits into independent pieces with no communication is called **embarrassingly parallel**. **MapReduce** is a classic framework for such jobs: a map step emits key-value pairs, a shuffle groups them by key, and a reduce step processes each group.

**Worked example:**

Bounded work per incoming record (from the Documentation's caps; the index bound is derived):

| Stage | Bound per incoming record |
|---|---|
| Index lookup | at most 65,000 postings plus 2,000 exact-name matches; keep top 12 + 6 + 6 + the exact key |
| Quick rule-based filter | linear in those candidates, no model |
| Readers | at most 4 pairs (1.17 on average) |
| Decision model | a handful of small tree-model calls per shortlisted pair |

A rough linear extrapolation (QA 2; not a measurement): scoring our 11.69 million shortlist pairs took about 1.4 hours on one 16 GB GPU (every reader except the French E5 reader), so a billion incoming records, about 1.17 billion pairs, would be on the order of 140 GPU-hours, spread across shards.

MapReduce-style blocking (illustrative): map each record to (key, record) for each of its keys ("ganesh", "traders", "pune"); shuffle groups records by key; reduce compares pairs inside each group. If the key "traders" has 50,000 members, one reducer receives an enormous group (**data skew**), so such keys must be capped or dropped, which is the same job our posting-list caps do.

**Technical explanation:** Today all processing is per country, and each country's index fits in memory: every stage needs less than 8 GB of RAM except the address rescue (about 3.2 GB per worker, 13 GB with 4 workers), and the index lookup runs on 8 to 11 threads (code README). Our pattern is "broadcast the index, partition the queries": any number of workers can hold a copy of a country's index and process disjoint slices of incoming records with no shuffle, like a broadcast join (every worker receives a full copy of the smaller table) or a map-only job. Classic key-based MapReduce blocking needs load balancing for skewed keys (splitting or capping large blocks); our caps do it at query time. Finer sharding by country plus state or postcode would shorten posting lists and make a larger shortlist cap affordable, but records with a missing or wrong state then need a fallback search across the whole country, as the native-script rescue already does when the state is unknown or has no match. IDF must be computed consistently across shards (one global value per country, or per shard by design). For streaming, one record would need one index lookup in its shard, on average 1.17 reader pairs and a few small tree models; single-record latency was not measured.

**How we used it:** Everything ran on one machine: one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER 16 GB, a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 32 GB RAM and about 70 GB of disk. A full retrain from raw data took about 11 hours 30 minutes; at inference, index lookup plus quick filter plus ranker took about 1.3 hours and reader scoring about 1.4 hours for the 9.97 million incoming records (code README and clean-run report). The index is split by country only; state or postcode sharding is proposed for scale, not tested (QA 2, QA 18).

**Expert nuance:** Linear scaling assumes bounded work per record and stable data; candidate counts per business are skewed (maximum 3,182), so shards can take uneven time, which dynamic scheduling of record batches absorbs within one machine. New businesses can be appended to posting lists incrementally, while IDF drifts slowly and can be refreshed periodically. Always present the 140 GPU-hours as an extrapolation, not a measurement, and say that single-record latency was not measured.

**Remember:**
- Shard by country today (state or postcode proposed); broadcast the index, partition the records.
- Every stage has a per-record cap, so cost is linear in the number of records.
- The billion-record estimate (about 140 GPU-hours for the readers) is a rough linear extrapolation.

**Judge might ask:**
- *How would this scale to billions of records?*
  "The work per record is bounded at every stage: posting caps and budgets in the index, a fixed number of top candidates, and at most four pairs for the readers, so cost grows linearly and shards run independently. As a rough linear extrapolation, not a measurement, scoring our 11.69 million shortlist pairs took about 1.4 hours on one 16 GB GPU. A billion records would therefore be on the order of 140 GPU-hours, spread across shards."
- *What would you shard on, and what could break?*
  "Country plus state or postcode: shorter posting lists and room for a larger shortlist cap. What breaks is records with a missing or wrong state, so we would keep a fallback search across the whole country, as the native-script second-chance search already does when the state is unknown."

---

## A2 - Concepts: the models {#a2 .chap}

### How to read this part {#a2-how-to-read-this-part .nc}

This part teaches every model in our pipeline from zero, up to the depth a senior applied scientist expects. Read the concepts in order: each one uses words defined in the earlier ones, and every new term is in **bold** where it is first explained. Every concept has the same eight blocks: a one-line summary, a simple explanation with an everyday picture, a worked example you can follow with a pen, the technical explanation, exactly how we used it, expert nuances (trade-offs, traps, alternatives), three things to remember, and the questions a judge might ask with short spoken answers.

Three labels tell you where a number comes from. Numbers about our run or our recipe are exact and come from the submitted Documentation ("Doc"), the code READMEs or the shared fact sheet; **derived** means simple arithmetic on those numbers. **Toy** marks made-up numbers that exist only to teach the arithmetic; they are never results. **Background** marks general knowledge about public models and libraries (for example how many attention heads MiniLM has), checked against the shipped model files where we could; it is not a claim about our results, so you do not need to volunteer it. Spoken answers use the plain names of the talk: business, incoming record, shortlist, quick rule-based filter, CatBoost ranker, the four readers, "what changed" features, LightGBM decision model per country, confident and clear winner, second-chance searches, per-business consistency check, France rules computed by code.

**Words this part borrows from Part A0 (one line each, so you can start here):**
- **Precision**: of the links we made, the share that are right. **Recall**: of the true links, the share we found.
- **F0.5**: one score that combines precision and recall but counts precision more (a wrong link hurts more than a missed one). For one business, F0.5 = 1.25 x correct links / (links made + 0.25 x true links). The competition computes it for every business and averages over all businesses (**macro-average**); a business that truly owns no records scores 1 only if we link nothing to it.
- **Fold**: one of 10 roughly equal parts into which we split the labelled businesses (by a hash of the business id); a model is trained on some folds and checked on another, **held-out** fold it never saw.
- **Epoch**: one full pass over the training data. **Random seed**: the starting number of a random-number generator; a different seed gives different random choices.
- **GPU**: a graphics processor, a chip that does thousands of multiplications in parallel, which makes neural networks (and CatBoost) fast to train.
- **IDF** (inverse document frequency): a rarity score for a word, high for a rare word (a surname) and low for a common one ("services"); for example log((N + 1) / (df + 1)), where N is the number of records and df the number that contain the word.
- **AUC** (area under the ROC curve): the probability that a randomly chosen true pair gets a higher score than a randomly chosen wrong pair; 1.0 means perfect ordering, 0.5 means random.

**Concepts in this part (learn them in this order)**

1. Models, features, labels and loss
2. Logits, the sigmoid and log-loss
3. Overfitting, held-out data and early stopping
4. Decision trees
5. Gradient boosting, step by step
6. The knobs of boosted trees
7. CatBoost: symmetric trees, ordered boosting, categorical encoding
8. LightGBM: histograms and leaf-wise growth
9. Learning to rank: pointwise, pairwise, listwise
10. Text into numbers: tokens, sub-words and embeddings
11. Transformers and attention
12. Pre-training, transfer learning and fine-tuning
13. Bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
14. Inside our reader: pair input, mean pooling and the head
15. MiniLM and knowledge distillation
16. E5 and contrastive pre-training
17. The fine-tuning recipe
18. Number formats: fp32, fp16, bf16 and mixed precision
19. Hard-example selection for reader training
20. Frozen pretrained embeddings as features
21. Self-training with pseudo-labels and replay
22. Blending readers in logit space (France)
23. Stacking: a two-level model with separate folds per layer
24. Early stopping, then refit on more data
25. Seed averaging
26. Calibration: what a model's "probability" means
27. Small models for the second-chance searches

**Where each model sits in our pipeline (orientation map; every term in it is explained in the concepts below)**

| Step of the pipeline | Plain name | Kind of model | Library | Reads | Outputs | Learns from |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ranking the candidates that survive the quick rule-based filter | CatBoost ranker | gradient-boosted trees, binary classifier | CatBoost, on the GPU | 76 numeric features computed by the index lookup for one pair | probability that this business is the record's owner | a 140,000-record pilot of labelled US/India train records, fitted on its fold 0-5 part, early stopping on fold 6 (Doc 4) |
| Reading the shortlist (up to 4 pairs per record) | MiniLM reader, E5 reader | cross-encoders (transformers) | PyTorch + Hugging Face | the raw "name \| address" of the record and of the business, together | one logit (match score) | labelled US/India pairs of folds 0-5 (Doc 4) |
| Reading French shortlist pairs | French MiniLM reader, French E5 reader | the same readers, fine-tuned again | same | same | one logit | confident French pseudo-labels plus labelled US/India pairs (Doc 4) |
| Word-meaning part of the "what changed" features | frozen MiniLM | pretrained encoder, not fine-tuned | sentence-transformers | single words | a vector of 384 numbers per word | not trained by us |
| Deciding | LightGBM decision model, one per country | gradient-boosted trees, mean of 5 seeds | LightGBM | 158 to 217 features (217 US, 211 India, 158 France and default), including ranker probability, reader logits and "what changed" | probability; then the confident + clear-winner rule | folds 6-9 (Doc 4) |
| Second chances | native-script rescue model; address-rescue filter and scorer | gradient-boosted trees | LightGBM | features of the new candidates | probability | India folds 0-7 (native script); folds 6-7 (address) (Doc 4) |

### A2.1 Models, features, labels and loss {#a2-1 .concept}

**In one line:** A model is a formula with adjustable numbers that turns a description of a record pair into a score, and training adjusts those numbers until the scores agree with known answers.

**Simple explanation:** Think of a new bank clerk learning to judge whether two signatures come from the same person. Each case she studies comes with clues she can check (same initials? same slant?) and, in the archive, the true answer. At first she guesses badly; each time she is wrong she adjusts how much weight she gives each clue, and slowly her guesses improve. In machine learning the clues are called **features**, the true answers are **labels**, the clerk's habits are the model's **parameters**, the penalty for a wrong guess is the **loss**, and the process of adjusting is **training**. Learning from examples that come with answers is called **supervised learning**. Using the finished model on new cases, with its habits frozen, is called **inference**.

**Worked example (toy numbers):** Three training pairs, each an incoming record and a candidate business, described by two features.

| Pair | Incoming record | Candidate business | Name similarity (0-1) | Same legal form? (1/0) | Label: is this business the owner? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sharma Traders Pvt Ltd, Pune | Sharma Traders Private Limited, Pune | 0.82 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | Sharma Traders Pvt Ltd, Pune | Sharma Textiles Pvt Ltd, Nagpur | 0.71 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | Boulangerie Martin SARL, Lyon | Boulangerie Martin SAS, Lyon | 0.90 | 0 | 0 |

A very simple model is: score = 3 x similarity + 2 x same_legal - 3. Pair 1 gets 3 x 0.82 + 2 - 3 = 1.46; pair 2 gets 1.13; pair 3 gets -0.30. The order is right for pair 3 but pair 2 (a different business) scores almost as high as pair 1. Training would change the three numbers 3, 2 and -3 (the parameters) to push pair 1 up and pair 2 down. The numbers we choose ourselves, such as how big each adjustment step is, are **hyper-parameters**.

**Technical explanation:** All our learned stages solve **binary classification** on pairs: the input x is a (record, candidate business) pair, the label y is 1 if the business is the record's **owner** (the business it truly belongs to) and 0 otherwise. Training is **empirical risk minimisation**: choose parameters theta to minimise L(theta) = (1/N) * sum_i loss(y_i, f_theta(x_i)) + R(theta), where R is a **regulariser** that discourages overly complex models. Neural networks minimise this by **gradient descent**, theta <- theta - eta * gradient of L, where eta is the **learning rate**; boosted trees minimise it by adding trees (see Gradient boosting). The quantity that matters is not the training loss but **generalisation**: performance on pairs the model never saw. Standard theory assumes training examples are independent; ours are not, because one business owns several records and several candidates share a record. That is why our folds are built per business (see Overfitting, held-out data and early stopping). The pair label also has structure: a record has at most one owner, so at most one candidate in its list has label 1, and some records have none. Finally, the pair-level loss is only a proxy: the competition scores F0.5 per business (defined in the word list at the top of this part), so the decision thresholds are tuned separately on that exact metric (see Calibration).

**How we used it:** Every learned model in the pipeline answers the same yes/no question, "is this business the owner of this incoming record?" (Doc 4). The CatBoost ranker answers it from 76 index features, the readers from the raw text, the LightGBM decision models from 158 to 217 features (217 US, 211 India, 158 France and default), and the second-chance models from features of their own candidates. The ranker, the decision models and the second-chance models were trained from scratch on the provided data; only the readers start from pretrained language models, and a pretrained MiniLM is also used, unchanged, to compare single words (Doc 4, B.5). Labels exist only for the US and India; France has none (Doc 2.1).

**Expert nuance:** The unit of the metric (the business) differs from the unit of the loss (the pair), and that gap shapes the whole design: a model can improve its average pair loss and still lose F0.5, for example if the change that lowers the loss on many easy pairs also lets one extra wrong record be linked to a business that should have an empty row. The shape of the candidate lists matters too: 90.59 % of incoming records have exactly one candidate in the final candidate file (Doc B.1), so much of the difficulty is deciding "link or abstain" rather than "which one". A common misconception is that a better classifier automatically gives a better match file; the decision rule and its thresholds matter as much as the model.

**Remember:**
- One question everywhere: is this business the owner of this record? Label 1 or 0.
- Parameters are learned; hyper-parameters are chosen by us; generalisation is judged on unseen businesses.
- Pair-level loss is a proxy; the competition metric is per business, so thresholds are tuned on it.

**Judge might ask:**
- *What exactly is the label your models learn?* For every model it is the same yes/no question about a pair: is this business the true owner of this incoming record. Labels exist only in the US and Indian training files, so the France decision model learns from US and Indian rows, and the French readers also learn from confident pseudo-labels, that is, very confident predictions of our own models on French records.

### A2.2 Logits, the sigmoid and log-loss {#a2-2 .concept}

**In one line:** A logit is a model's raw score on an unlimited scale, the sigmoid squashes it into a probability between 0 and 1, and log-loss measures how surprised the model was by the true answer.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine a weather forecaster. She can express confidence as a probability ("90 % rain") or as betting odds ("9 to 1"). A **logit** is the logarithm of those odds: 0 means 50/50, +2.2 means about 90 %, +4.6 means about 99 %, and every step of +2.3 multiplies the odds by ten. The **sigmoid** function converts a logit back into a probability. If she says "99 % rain" and it stays dry, she deserves a much bigger penalty than if she had said "60 %". **Log-loss** (also called **binary cross-entropy**, BCE) is exactly that penalty: small when a confident forecast is right, very large when a confident forecast is wrong.

**Worked example (real logits from Doc D.3, the French record "TQ COMITE SARL"):**

| Reader, candidate | Logit z | Probability sigmoid(z) |
|---|---|---|
| MiniLM reader, TQ Parents SARL (same address) | 7.5000 | 0.99945 |
| French MiniLM reader, TQ Parents SARL | 8.9375 | 0.99987 |
| French E5 reader, TQ Parents SARL | 10.8125 | 0.99998 |
| French MiniLM reader, TQ Comite SARL (Pessac, another city) | -1.9219 | 0.128 |
| French E5 reader, TQ Comite SARL (Pessac) | -10.8125 | 0.00002 |

Steps: sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). For z = 7.5, e^(-7.5) = 0.000553, so the probability is 1 / 1.000553 = 0.99945. Notice that 0.99945 and 0.99998 look almost identical as probabilities, yet as logits they are 7.5 and 10.8, a difference of 3.3, which means the odds differ by a factor e^3.3125 = 27.5 (derived). Log-loss for a pair with label 1 is -ln(p): if a reader gave logit 7.5, the loss is -ln(0.99945) = 0.00055; if it gave -1.9219, the loss is -ln(0.128) = 2.06. (Test labels are private, so these labels are hypothetical; the arithmetic is the point.) The US decision-model score 0.965022 in Doc D.1 corresponds to a logit of ln(0.965022 / 0.034978) = 3.32 (derived).

**Technical explanation:** sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) and its inverse logit(p) = ln(p / (1 - p)). Binary cross-entropy for one example is BCE = -[y ln sigmoid(z) + (1 - y) ln(1 - sigmoid(z))]. Its derivative with respect to the logit is simply sigmoid(z) - y, the predicted probability minus the label; this clean gradient is what both gradient boosting and neural-network training use. Log-loss is a **proper scoring rule**: its expected value is minimised by predicting the true probability, which is why a log-loss-trained model is roughly calibrated on its own training distribution (see Calibration). Numerically, computing sigmoid and then log separately loses precision for large |z|; PyTorch's BCEWithLogitsLoss fuses them with the log-sum-exp trick. A boosted-tree model's raw output (the sum of its tree outputs) is also a logit, and LightGBM's binary objective returns sigmoid of that sum. Because logits add, averaging logits corresponds to a weighted geometric mean of odds (see Blending readers in logit space).

**How we used it:** Each reader outputs one logit per shortlist pair (for example 7.5000 above) and was trained with BCE on the logit cast to fp32 (Doc 4; code). The CatBoost ranker is trained with Logloss and outputs a probability; in the code the decision model receives it converted to log-odds, together with its rank (background, code detail). The LightGBM decision models are trained on binary log-loss and output the probability to which the thresholds 0.75 (US, India) and 0.82 (France, default) apply (Doc 4). For France, the decision model's single reader input receives a weighted blend of three reader logits (Doc 4).

**Expert nuance:** Logits from different models are not on a common, calibrated scale, so "logit 7.5" from one reader and from another do not mean the same confidence; the decision model learns how to read each. Trees split on the order of values, so they are (up to binning details) invariant to a monotone transformation of a single input: giving a tree the ranker's probability or its logit leads to essentially the same splits. But derived inputs such as the mean of two readers or a margin between candidates do change with the scale, which is one reason we compute them on logits. Saturation is real: in floating point, probabilities very close to 1 lose resolution, while logits keep it.

**Remember:**
- Logit = log of the odds; sigmoid turns it into a probability; 0 means 50/50.
- Log-loss punishes confident mistakes heavily; its gradient is (probability - label).
- Readers produce logits; decision models produce probabilities that the thresholds apply to.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Why do you keep reader logits instead of probabilities?* Because probabilities saturate: 0.99945 and 0.99998 look the same, but as logits they are 7.5 and 10.8, a 27-fold difference in odds. Keeping logits gives the decision model that information and lets us blend the French readers on a scale where a confident "no" really counts.

### A2.3 Overfitting, held-out data and early stopping {#a2-3 .concept}

*See also [A3.9 Early stopping](#a3-9): early stopping from the training-and-validation side.*

**In one line:** A model overfits when it memorises its training examples instead of learning patterns that carry over, so we always judge it on data it never saw and stop training when that judgement stops improving.

**Simple explanation:** A student who memorises last year's answer key scores perfectly on last year's paper and badly on this year's. That is **overfitting**. The cure is a mock exam with questions she has never seen: a **held-out** (or **validation**) set. In our project the labelled businesses are split into 10 roughly equal parts called **folds**, so "a held-out fold" simply means about one tenth of the businesses, which the model did not train on. **Early stopping** means you keep revising only while the mock-exam score keeps improving, and stop once it has not improved for a while. The opposite problem, a model too simple to learn the pattern at all, is **underfitting**.

**Worked example (toy numbers):** A boosted-tree model is trained round by round; after each round we measure log-loss on the training data and on a held-out fold.

| Rounds (trees) | Training log-loss | Held-out log-loss |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.050 | 0.060 |
| 200 | 0.040 | 0.052 |
| 300 | 0.034 | **0.050** (best) |
| 400 | 0.030 | 0.051 |

Training loss keeps falling, but held-out loss is best at 300 trees and then rises: the extra trees are memorising. With a **patience** of 100 rounds (no improvement for 100 rounds means stop), training stops at round 400 and the model keeps its best 300 trees.

**Technical explanation:** The **generalisation gap** is the difference between training and held-out performance; it grows with model capacity and shrinks with more data and regularisation (the **bias-variance trade-off**). A held-out set is only honest if nothing about it leaked into training: no shared records, no shared businesses, no tuning on it. Because records of one business are strongly related, a record-level random split leaks; we assign the 10 folds per business with a hash of the business id, so all of a business's records sit in one fold (Doc 4). Early stopping is itself a regulariser: it chooses the number of boosting rounds (or training steps) on the validation fold, which makes that fold slightly optimistic afterwards, so final scores must be reported elsewhere. It optimises the pair-level log-loss, not F0.5, which is why decision thresholds are tuned separately on the exact metric.

**How we used it:** The CatBoost ranker stops early with patience 180 on fold 6 (at most 1,600 trees). The LightGBM decision models stop early with patience 100 rounds on fold 8 (at most 3,000 rounds for the US and India, 1,500 for France and the default) (Doc 4; code). The readers do not use early stopping: they train for exactly one epoch (one pass over their training pairs). Our held-out evidence uses a strict protocol: fold 9 is scored by fits on folds 6-8 without the records that touch fold 9, and fold 8 by fits on folds 6, 7 and 9 without the records that touch fold 8; close versions of our decision models score US 0.991212 / 0.991545 and India 0.990046 / 0.990298 (fold 9 / fold 8) (Doc 5).

**Expert nuance:** Our biggest validation limitation, stated plainly: there is no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file. The held-out scores exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules, the final US/India decision models are refitted on folds 6-9, folds 8 and 9 also helped choose thresholds and the consistency check, and France has no labels (Doc 5). The mitigation is that every held-out number comes from fits that never saw the scored fold, and they sit in the same range as the public 0.9913. Overfitting can also happen to a leaderboard: we made 18 uploads and chose the final file using public scores (Doc C.4), which is a mild form of the same problem.

**Remember:**
- Judge a model only on businesses it never trained on; folds are per business.
- Early stopping picks the number of trees on a separate fold (ranker fold 6, decision models fold 8).
- Limitation: no untouched end-to-end validation; held-out scores are in the same range as public.

**Judge might ask:**
- *How do you know your models are not overfitting?* The honest limitation first: we have no fully untouched end-to-end check, because the held-out folds also helped choose the thresholds and the final file includes steps they do not cover. What we do have comes from businesses the scoring fits never trained on: close versions of our decision models score 0.9912 and 0.9915 for the US and 0.9900 and 0.9903 for India on held-out folds, the same range as the public 0.9913.

---

### A2.4 Decision trees {#a2-4 .concept}

**In one line:** A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions about the features that ends in a leaf holding a score.

**Simple explanation:** Think of the game "twenty questions" or a hospital triage chart: "Is the name similarity above 0.8? If yes, does the address overlap a lot?" Each question splits the examples into two groups, and each final group, a **leaf**, stores the average outcome of the training examples that ended there. The tree learns which questions to ask by trying every possible question and keeping the one that best separates matches from non-matches. One question is a **split**; the number of questions on the longest path is the tree's **depth**.

**Worked example (toy numbers):** Eight training pairs with two features.

| Pair | Name similarity | Address coverage | Owner? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.95 | 1.00 | 1 |
| 2 | 0.92 | 0.40 | 1 |
| 3 | 0.88 | 0.97 | 1 |
| 4 | 0.85 | 0.10 | 0 |
| 5 | 0.60 | 0.98 | 0 |
| 6 | 0.55 | 0.20 | 0 |
| 7 | 0.91 | 0.00 | 0 |
| 8 | 0.40 | 0.05 | 0 |

We measure "mixedness" with **Gini impurity**, G = 2p(1 - p), where p is the share of owners in a group (0 = pure). At the root p = 3/8, so G = 2 x 0.375 x 0.625 = 0.469.
- Split A, "name similarity >= 0.8": yes = pairs 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 (3 owners of 5, G = 0.48); no = 5, 6, 8 (G = 0). Weighted impurity = 5/8 x 0.48 = 0.300. Improvement 0.169.
- Split B, "address coverage >= 0.3": yes = 1, 2, 3, 5 (3 of 4, G = 0.375); no = 4, 6, 7, 8 (G = 0). Weighted = 4/8 x 0.375 = 0.1875. Improvement 0.281.

Split B wins, although a human might have asked about the name first. Inside its "yes" branch, "name similarity >= 0.8" then separates pairs 1, 2, 3 (all owners) from pair 5. Two questions, three pure leaves.

**Technical explanation:** Classic trees (CART, "classification and regression trees") are grown greedily: at each node, for every feature and every candidate threshold, compute the impurity decrease (or, in boosting, the gradient-based gain, see Gradient boosting) and take the best split; stop at a maximum depth, a maximum number of leaves or a minimum number of examples per leaf. Searching thresholds naively costs O(n) per feature per node after sorting; histogram methods bin each feature first and search only bin boundaries (see LightGBM). Trees handle features on any scale, need no normalisation, capture interactions (a split inside a split), and are invariant to monotone transformations of a feature. Libraries also handle **missing values** without imputation: LightGBM (and XGBoost) learn a default direction at each split, sending rows with a missing feature to whichever side lowers the loss, while CatBoost by default treats a missing value as smaller than every observed value (its "Min" mode; background, our shipped ranker uses it). A single deep tree has high **variance** (small data changes reshape it), which is why trees are almost always used in ensembles: **bagging** (random forests) averages independent trees, **boosting** adds trees that correct each other.

**How we used it:** We never use a single tree. All our tree models are ensembles: the CatBoost ranker uses up to 1,600 symmetric trees of depth 7; each LightGBM decision model uses trees of up to 127 leaves, up to 3,000 rounds for the US and India; the address-rescue filter uses 200 trees of 15 leaves and its scorer 300 trees of 31 leaves (Doc 4). Missing values matter in our data: in the US worked example the record has no address, so the "what changed" number features are missing for every candidate (Doc D.1), and the LightGBM decision models route those rows by their learned default direction.

**Expert nuance:** Trees split on one feature at a time (axis-aligned), so a relationship like "the difference of two features" must be approximated by many splits unless we compute it as a feature, which is why we engineer margins and differences explicitly. Trees cannot extrapolate: beyond the largest value seen in training, the prediction stays constant, so a French reader logit more extreme than anything in the training rows is simply treated like the most extreme value the model saw (see Blending readers in logit space). Greedy growth is not globally optimal, but in an ensemble that matters little.

**Remember:**
- A tree = nested yes/no questions; each leaf holds a score.
- Splits are chosen by how much they purify the groups (Gini, or gradient gain in boosting).
- Single trees are unstable; we only use boosted ensembles of hundreds to thousands of trees.

**Judge might ask:**
- *Can you explain why the model made one particular decision?* Each decision model is an average of five boosted ensembles, so there is no single readable tree, but every input has a plain meaning, such as "legal form changed" or "one word replaced". In the US example the LLC and PC candidates differ from the record's name only in the legal form, and the decision model gives them 0.000007 and 0.088664 against 0.965022 for the exact name; we did not prepare per-feature attribution plots, so we would not claim exactly how much each input contributed.
