### A3.2 Cross-validation and k folds {#a3-2 .concept}

**In one line:** Cut the labelled data into k equal parts, called **folds**, and let the parts take turns at being the unseen part, or give each part a fixed job.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine a cookery contest with ten judges where you want to test a recipe fairly. You let nine judges help you tune the recipe and keep the tenth blindfolded until the end; then you repeat with a different judge kept aside each time. Every judge is used for testing once and for tuning nine times, so the final verdict does not depend on one lucky or unlucky judge. That rotation is **k-fold cross-validation**. A second use of the same folds is simply bookkeeping: you can say "folds 0 to 5 are for learning, fold 8 is for choosing settings, fold 9 is for reporting", so that every piece of data has a clear job and never does two jobs at once.

**Worked example:**

(toy) Ten businesses, B0 to B9, and k = 5 folds of two businesses each: fold 0 = {B0, B5}, fold 1 = {B1, B6}, fold 2 = {B2, B7}, fold 3 = {B3, B8}, fold 4 = {B4, B9}.

| Round | Train on folds | Test on fold | Score (toy) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1, 2, 3, 4 | 0 | 0.986 |
| 2 | 0, 2, 3, 4 | 1 | 0.991 |
| 3 | 0, 1, 3, 4 | 2 | 0.989 |
| 4 | 0, 1, 2, 4 | 3 | 0.990 |
| 5 | 0, 1, 2, 3 | 4 | 0.988 |

Mean = (0.986 + 0.991 + 0.989 + 0.990 + 0.988) / 5 = 0.9888. The sample standard deviation across folds is about 0.0019, which tells you how much a single split could have misled you.

(ours) Our 10 folds with fixed jobs:

| Folds | Job |
|---|---|
| 0-5 | train the CatBoost ranker (a 140,000-record pilot, its fold 0-5 part), the MiniLM and E5 readers, and the Indic-to-Latin word list used in cleaning |
| 6 | early stopping of the CatBoost ranker |
| 6-7 | fit the decision models (and the address second-chance models) |
| 8 | early stopping of the decision models; choice of the 0.75 threshold and the second-chance thresholds |
| 8 and 9 | choice of the per-business consistency check; held-out scoring |
| 6-9 | final refit of the US and India decision models |
| 0-7 | the native-script second-chance model, trained once on these folds; the word lists that build its training examples leave out each record's own fold (see Cross-fitting) |

**Technical explanation:** k-fold cross-validation estimates the expected performance of a *training procedure*, not of one fitted model: each of the k models trains on (k − 1)/k of the data, so the estimate is slightly pessimistic for a model trained on all of it, and its variance comes both from the test folds and from the overlapping training sets. Because the training sets overlap, the k fold scores are correlated, and there is no unbiased estimator of the variance of the k-fold estimate (a known result of Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004), so the fold standard deviation is only a rough guide. Variants: **stratified** k-fold keeps the class ratio equal in every fold; **group** k-fold keeps every member of a group in one fold (see Group k-fold: folds by business); **time-series** splits never train on the future. When the same folds are used both to tune and to report, the report is optimistic; **nested cross-validation** fixes this with an inner loop for tuning inside an outer loop for reporting, at k × k' times the cost. Cross-validation also produces **out-of-fold (OOF) predictions**: every example scored by the model that did not see it, which is how stacked models are usually trained (see Layer-wise fold separation for stacked models). The cost is k full trainings; typical k is 5 or 10.

**How we used it:** Ten folds assigned per business by a hash of the business id (see Hashing ids into folds). We did not train ten copies of every model and average them; instead the folds are a role system, as in the table above, because our pipeline has several learned layers and the readers are expensive to train. For honest scoring we used a two-way swap: fold 9 is scored by fits on folds 6-8 and fold 8 by fits on folds 6, 7 and 9 (see The held-out evaluation protocol). Fold rotation appears in one cheap place: the word lists used to build the native-script second-chance training examples are rebuilt once per fold, each leaving that fold out (see Cross-fitting); the second-chance model itself is trained once.

**Expert nuance:** The role system buys clean separation between layers at a price: each layer learns from only part of the labels (the readers from 6 of 10 folds, the ranker from a 140,000-record sample of those same 6 folds, the decision models from 4). Our held-out estimate rests on two folds rather than ten, so it is noisier than a full cross-validation, which is why the paired bootstrap matters (see Paired bootstrap intervals). And because fold 8 chose the threshold and folds 8 and 9 chose the consistency check, our setup is closer to "validation reused for reporting" than to nested cross-validation; we disclose that. A full nested scheme would multiply the training of every learned layer, cross-encoders included; we did not attempt it on one GPU in the competition window.

**Remember:**
- k-fold = every example is tested once by a model that did not see it; the average is steadier than one split.
- Our 10 folds are mainly a job system: 0-5 base models, 6-7 decision-model fit, 8 stopping and thresholds, 9 reporting (and, with fold 8, choosing the consistency check).
- Cross-validation estimates a procedure, and reusing folds for tuning makes the estimate optimistic.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why didn't you just run standard 10-fold cross-validation for every model?"  
  **A:** Because the pipeline has layers, and each layer must learn from scores produced on data the layer below never saw; giving folds fixed jobs (0-5 for the ranker and readers, 6-9 for the decision models) does that with one training per model instead of ten, which mattered with cross-encoders on a single GPU. We rotated folds only where it was cheap: the word lists behind the native-script second-chance search leave out each training record's own fold.

---

### A3.3 Data leakage {#a3-3 .concept}

**In one line:** **Leakage** is any route by which information about the answers, or about the evaluation data, reaches training and makes a model look better than it really is.

**Simple explanation:** A student who has secretly seen the exam paper gets a great score, but the score says nothing about what the student knows. Leakage is any way the "exam paper" reaches the model. Sometimes it is obvious, like testing on the training data. More often it is sneaky: two records of the same business end up on both sides of the split; a feature is computed with help from the labels; one model's over-confident score on its own training data is fed to another model; or settings are chosen by looking at test results again and again. The symptom is always the same: an excellent validation score followed by a disappointing real score. Most of the fold design in this part exists to block one leakage route or another.

**Worked example:** Six leakage routes, each with a tiny illustration and our defence.

| Route | (toy) illustration | Our defence (ours) |
|---|---|---|
| Group leakage | "Sharma Traders, 12 MG Road, Pune" owns three incoming records; two land in training, one in validation, so the validation pair looks familiar | folds assigned per business; every record goes with its business |
| Feature (target) leakage | a feature "number of records truly linked to this business" uses the answers | features use only text, model scores and model decisions; the collective features count records whose ranker top choice is that business, not true links |
| Stacking leakage | the reader trained on pair P scores P at 0.9999; a decision model trained on P learns "0.9999 means match" and is fooled later | ranker and readers learn on folds 0-5, decision models on folds 6-9 |
| Learned-resource leakage | a word list learned from all labelled pairs already knows the validation record's own spelling | cleaning word list learned from folds 0-5 only; the second-chance word lists leave out the record's own fold |
| Selection leakage | trying 13 thresholds on fold 8 and reporting fold 8's best | fold 9 reported too; disclosure that folds 8 and 9 also chose settings |
| Test-feedback leakage | uploading 18 files and keeping the best public score | held-out folds as main evidence; disclosure of every public-score decision |

**Technical explanation:** An evaluation estimate is unbiased only if the evaluation data are independent of every fitted object: parameters, preprocessing statistics, learned vocabularies, features, hyperparameters and the final model choice. The standard taxonomy: **target leakage** (a feature is a function of the label or of information that only exists after the outcome); **train-test contamination** (duplicates, near-duplicates or members of the same group on both sides); **preprocessing leakage** (scalers, encoders or vocabularies fitted on data that include the evaluation labels); **temporal leakage** (training on the future); **stacking leakage** (in-sample base-model predictions used as meta-features); and **adaptive leakage** (repeated queries of a holdout). Symptoms include implausibly high scores, a single feature dominating importance, and a validation score that collapses when a suspect input is removed. Detection tools are ablation of suspect inputs, **adversarial validation** (train a classifier to tell training rows from evaluation rows; if it succeeds, the two differ), and re-deriving every learned resource inside the training folds only. One important distinction: computing **label-free** statistics on the test inputs (word frequencies, an index) is **transductive** learning, not label leakage; it is legitimate when allowed and disclosed, but it means the pipeline must recompute those statistics on every new batch.

**How we used it:** The defences in the table are all in the code. Two more details matter. First, the CatBoost ranker's training mask requires both the incoming record and the candidate business to be in folds 0-5, and its early-stopping rows have the record in fold 6 and the candidate in folds 0-6; so no business from folds 7-9 ever appears in ranker training. Second, when we score a fold for evidence, we also drop from training every incoming record that has any candidate in that fold (see The held-out evaluation protocol). Disclosed transductive uses (Documentation, Appendix C): IDF (inverse document frequency, a word weight that is high for rare words and low for common ones) and other token statistics, the search indexes and the competition features are computed on the unlabelled test files; for India a native-script-to-Latin token list is aligned on test records whose first-stage top candidate has probability at least 0.9; for France the geography, the street-type typo table and postcode prefixes are learned from the test files; the two French readers are self-trained on French test pairs; label-free counts on the test records set the size of the extra hard training examples, the France threshold and the French MiniLM reader's blend weight. No test label is used anywhere.

**Expert nuance:** The most dangerous leakage in a competition is not a bug in a feature; it is adaptive leakage through many leaderboard uploads, because it is invisible in any single experiment (see Model selection and public-leaderboard overfitting). The second most common is group leakage, which inflates scores in entity resolution precisely because records of one entity share text. A subtle case in our pipeline is that fold 8 both stopped the decision models and chose the threshold, so fold-8 scores carry a little selection optimism; this is why we report fold 9 next to it and why the Documentation says the folds were reused. Transductive statistics are not leakage of labels, but a judge may still probe them, so name them precisely.

**Remember:**
- Leakage = the answers or the evaluation data reaching training by any route; the result is a score that will not hold.
- Our defences: business folds, separate folds per model layer, word lists learned without the evaluated folds, removal of records touching the scored fold.
- Unsupervised statistics on the unlabelled test files are transductive, allowed and disclosed; no test label is used.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Where could leakage hide in your pipeline, and how did you block it?"  
  **A:** In four places, and three of them are blocked by design. Records of one business on both sides of a split are blocked by folds by business; over-confident scores passed from one model to the next are blocked by training the ranker and readers on folds 0-5 and the decision models on folds 6-9; and learned word lists are built without the evaluated folds. The fourth, reuse of folds 8 and 9 and of public scores for choosing settings, we cannot remove, so we disclose it.
- **Q:** "You compute IDF and the search index on the test files. Isn't that leakage?"  
  **A:** No labels are involved: those are unsupervised statistics on the test inputs, which makes the pipeline transductive, and our documentation lists every such use. The practical consequence is that a new batch of data needs those statistics recomputed, which our inference stages already do.

---

### A3.4 Group k-fold: folds by business {#a3-4 .concept}

**In one line:** Every incoming record must sit in the same fold as its business, so the models are always tested on businesses they have never seen.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine teaching a child to recognise relatives from photographs. If you test with a different photo of the same uncle the child practised on, the child may simply remember that uncle's face rather than learn a general skill. Our "uncles" are businesses: each business owns several incoming records (about 5.75 on average in the test files). If records were split at random, some records of a business would be in training and others in testing, and the model could lean on memory of that particular business, its name, its address, its competitors. **Group k-fold** keeps the whole family together: a business and all its records go into the same fold. Then a good test score really means "works on new businesses", which is what the competition asks.

**Worked example:**

(toy) A training business "Sri Balaji Textiles, 7 Station Road, Salem" owns three incoming records:

| Record | Text |
|---|---|
| R1 | Sri Balaji Textiles Pvt Ltd, 7 Station Rd, Salem |
| R2 | Balaji Textiles, Station Road, Salem |
| R3 | श्री बालाजी टेक्सटाइल्स, Salem |

Record-level random split: R1 and R2 go to training, R3 to validation. During training the decision model sees (R1, Sri Balaji Textiles) = match and (R2, Sri Balaji Textiles) = match, along with the same competing look-alike businesses in Salem. At validation, the pair (R3, Sri Balaji Textiles) shares the business text, the same competitors and the same "other records competing for this business"; the model has effectively been shown the answer. The validation score goes up, but nothing about the model improved.

Business-level split: the business and R1, R2, R3 all get the same fold, say fold 4. If fold 4 is the held-out fold, none of the three records and none of the business's pairs was seen in training.

Two more reasons in our pipeline (ours): the metric is computed per business, so a business must be scored with all of its records together; and the collective features and the per-business consistency check look at all incoming records competing for the same business, which only makes sense if they share a fold.

**Technical explanation:** Standard cross-validation assumes the rows are independent and identically distributed (**i.i.d.**). Clustered data break this: rows within a group are correlated (high **intra-class correlation**), so the effective sample size is closer to the number of groups than to the number of rows, and a record-level split lets the model exploit group identity, which will not be available for new groups. **Group k-fold** assigns folds to groups, never splitting a group; the estimate then targets "performance on new groups". The leak is largest when (a) records of a group are similar to each other and (b) the model has the capacity to memorise group-specific signals, both true for gradient-boosted trees over name and address features. (**Intra-class correlation** is the share of the variation in the data that comes from differences between groups rather than within them; when it is high, a second record of the same business adds little new information.) In our code, an owned incoming record inherits its business's fold; an unowned record (one that belongs to no business) gets a fold by hashing its own id. The decision-model rows are pairs (record, candidate business), assigned by the candidate business's fold, and the held-out protocol additionally removes records whose candidates span folds (see The held-out evaluation protocol).

**How we used it:** Ten folds per business, fold = hash(business id) mod 10 (see Hashing ids into folds). Every training and evaluation step uses these folds. The sizes came out balanced: in held-out scoring, fold 9 had 132,365 US and 87,778 Indian businesses, fold 8 had 132,407 and 88,103 (ours).

**Expert nuance:** Grouping by business is necessary but may not be sufficient. Near-identical businesses (for example branches of one chain, or two businesses with the same name in one city) can fall into different folds and still share text; a stricter scheme would group by connected components of similar names, giving a more pessimistic and arguably more realistic estimate. We did not do that. Also, unowned incoming records can be candidates for businesses in several folds, which is why the held-out protocol removes every record that touches the scored fold. We did not measure how much a record-level split would have inflated our score; to measure it, we would score the same model under both splits and compare.

**Remember:**
- The business is the unit of the metric and of the collective features, so it must be the unit of the split.
- A record-level split would put records of one business on both sides and inflate the score.
- Fold sizes came out balanced: fold 9 US 132,365 vs fold 8 US 132,407.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "How much would a record-level split have inflated your score?"  
  **A:** We did not measure that, so I will not guess a number. The reason we avoided it is structural: one business owns several records, the metric is per business, and the collective features use all records competing for a business; to quantify the inflation we would score the same model under a record split and a business split and compare.

---

### A3.5 Hashing ids into folds {#a3-5 .concept}

**In one line:** Compute fold = hash(business id) mod 10, so every machine and every run puts each business in the same fold without storing a random draw.

**Simple explanation:** A **hash function** is like a very thorough blender for text: you put in an id such as "S1-158550741" and it outputs a huge number that looks random, but the same id always gives the same number. Taking the remainder after dividing by 10 (written "mod 10") gives a fold from 0 to 9. Because the blender mixes so well, about one tenth of the businesses land in each fold. Because the id alone decides the fold, any record that belongs to the business can simply take the business's fold, so the group stays together automatically. And because nothing random is drawn, anyone who runs the code later gets exactly the same folds.

**Worked example:**

(toy hash values; the business ids are the real ones from our US worked example, but the folds shown are invented and are not their real folds)

| Business id | Hash value (toy) | Last digit = hash mod 10 | Fold |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1-158550741 | 9,214,307,552,118,406,233 | 3 | 3 |
| S1-734720318 | 4,551,092,887,310,045,679 | 9 | 9 |
| S1-44256287 | 12,008,553,190,276,431,500 | 0 | 0 |

- An incoming record owned by S1-158550741 gets fold 3 too.
- An unowned incoming record hashes its own id instead.
- A different seed (we used 20260927) gives a completely different but equally random-looking assignment.

(ours) Balance check: fold 9 had 132,365 US businesses and fold 8 had 132,407, a difference of 42 (derived); for India 87,778 and 88,103, a difference of 325 (derived). How big a difference is normal? If each business lands in a fold with probability 0.1, a fold's size has a standard deviation of √(fold size × 0.9), about √(132,000 × 0.9) ≈ 345 for the US, and the difference between two folds has a standard deviation of about √(2 × fold size): √(2 × 132,000) ≈ 514 for the US and √(2 × 88,000) ≈ 420 for India (derived). Differences of 42 and 325 are well inside that, exactly what a good hash should give.

**Technical explanation:** Hash partitioning assigns fold(id) = H_seed(id) mod k. For a well-mixed 64-bit hash the outputs are approximately uniform and independent of any structure in the ids (sequential ids, prefixes), so the fold sizes are jointly multinomial: each is approximately Binomial(N, 1/k) with standard deviation √(N × (1/k) × (1 − 1/k)), and the difference of two folds has variance 2N/k (the negative covariance between folds adds to it). **Modulo bias** (some remainders being slightly more likely because 2^64 is not a multiple of k) is negligible because 2^64 is vastly larger than k. Advantages over shuffling: **stateless** (no stored permutation), **deterministic** across processes and machines, trivially parallel, **stable under growth** (adding new businesses never moves old ones, while a reshuffle would), and **group-consistent** if you hash the group id. Limitations: it is not stratified (class balance is equal only in expectation, which is fine at our sizes), and the result depends on the exact hash implementation. Non-cryptographic hashes are adequate; if stability across library versions matters, a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 of the id is a portable alternative.

**How we used it:** fold = hash of the business id with seed 20260927, mod 10, computed with Polars (the data-frame library our pipeline uses). An owned record inherits its business's fold; an unowned record hashes its own id. Our fold-building code writes a manifest with the seed, the Polars version and a SHA-256 digest (a fingerprint of the file: change one byte and the digest changes completely) of every fold file, because Polars documents that its hash is stable only within one library version.

**Expert nuance:** The seed must be fixed before any experiment; choosing the seed whose split gives the best validation score would be selection leakage in disguise. Hash stability is an easy trap: upgrading a data library can silently change every fold and make old and new experiments incomparable, which is why the manifest records the version and the file hashes. A stricter alternative is to store the fold table itself as a versioned file (we do both: the fold files and their digests).

**Remember:**
- fold = hash(business id, seed 20260927) mod 10; records inherit their business's fold.
- Hashing is deterministic, stateless, group-preserving and stable when new data arrive.
- Library hash functions can change between versions; record the version and file hashes.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why a hash rather than a random shuffle?"  
  **A:** A hash of the business id gives the same folds on every machine and every run without storing anything, keeps each business's records together automatically, and does not move existing businesses when new ones arrive. The folds came out balanced, for example 132,365 and 132,407 US businesses in folds 9 and 8.

---

### A3.6 Layer-wise fold separation for stacked models {#a3-6 .concept}

*See also [A2.23 Stacking: a two-level model with separate folds per layer](#a2-23): stacking from the models side.*

**In one line:** When one model's scores are inputs to another model, the second model must learn from scores that the first model produced on data it never trained on.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine a manager who decides promotions from reports written by team leads. If team leads write about their own favourite projects, every report is glowing; a manager who learns "a glowing report means promote" from such reports will be fooled by over-optimistic reports later. Our CatBoost ranker and readers are the team leads, and the LightGBM decision model is the manager. A reader that has trained on a pair has partly memorised it, so its score on that pair is over-confident. If the decision model learned from such scores, it would learn to over-trust the reader. So the ranker and readers learn on folds 0-5, and the decision models learn on folds 6-9, where every ranker and reader score is a genuine "first sight" score, just like on the test data.

**Worked example:**

(toy) A genuinely hard true match: record "Laxmi Agency, Coimbatore" and business "Sri Lakshmi Agencies, Coimbatore".

| Setting | Reader logit on this kind of pair (toy) | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| The reader trained on this exact pair (in-sample) | +9.0 | 0.9999 |
| A similar pair the reader never saw (out-of-sample) | +1.5 | 0.82 |

If the decision model trains on in-sample scores, nearly every true pair it sees has a logit of +8 or more, so it learns "below +4 means not a match". On the test data, where hard true pairs come in at +1.5, it rejects them. Trained on out-of-sample scores, it sees hard true pairs at +1.5 during training and learns to combine that moderate score with the other features.

(ours) Which folds each layer used:

| Layer | Fit on | Stopping or tuning on |
|---|---|---|
| Indic-to-Latin word list used in cleaning | folds 0-5 | none |
| CatBoost ranker | folds 0-5 (a 140,000-record pilot, both record and candidate in folds 0-5) | fold 6 |
| MiniLM and E5 readers | folds 0-5 | none (one epoch) |
| US and India decision models | folds 6-7, then refit on 6-9 | fold 8 |
| France and default decision models | folds 6-7 | fold 8 |
| Thresholds | none | 0.75 on fold 8; consistency check on folds 8 and 9 |

**Technical explanation:** **Stacked generalisation** (Wolpert, 1992), or **stacking**, trains a **meta-model** (level 1) on the predictions of **base models** (level 0). The meta-features must be out-of-sample, because in-sample predictions have systematically smaller error and higher confidence than predictions on new data; a meta-model trained on them learns the wrong reliability for each base model. There are two standard ways. (a) **Out-of-fold stacking:** train k copies of each base model, each predicting the fold it did not see, so the meta-model can use all labelled rows; at test time a base model refitted on all data is used, which creates a small train-test mismatch, and the cost is k trainings per base model. (b) **Blending, or a layer-wise split:** give the base models and the meta-model disjoint data; one training per base model, a perfect train-test match for the meta-features, but each layer sees less data. Our design is (b). It also matters for non-model resources: the cleaning word list was learned on folds 0-5, so the decision models on folds 6-9 see cleaned text exactly as test records do. The decision model's inputs are the ranker probability and rank, the reader logits, the index lookup's similarity features, the "what changed" features and the competition and collective features; the similarity and "what changed" features are fixed formulas whose word statistics are label-free; their only label-derived ingredient is the Indic-to-Latin word list, learned on folds 0-5, so they too are out-of-sample on folds 6-9.

**How we used it:** Exactly the table above. The decision-model training rows are the training shortlist of incoming records that have a candidate in business folds 6-9, built from the unpruned matcher output, with label "candidate is the owner". The India decision model uses 211 features, the US one 217, and France and the default route 158.

**Expert nuance:** The trade-off is data efficiency: our decision models learn from 4 of the 10 folds, and the readers from 6. Out-of-fold predictions for the readers would let the decision models use all ten folds but would need several reader trainings; the reader-training stage alone (MiniLM and E5 together) took about 2.1 hours in our clean run on one GPU, and out-of-fold reader training would multiply that by the number of folds, which we chose not to spend in the competition window. One mild overlap exists: fold 6 both stopped the ranker and is part of the decision models' training data; early stopping only chooses the number of trees, so the ranker's fold-6 scores are at most very slightly optimistic. Note also that the separation only works if the test-time inputs are produced the same way as the training inputs; this is why France needs care (the French readers were self-trained on French test pairs, see Self-training with pseudo-labels) and why the France blend is fed in logit units (see Blending readers in logit space).

**Remember:**
- A model's scores on its own training data are over-confident; never train the next layer on them.
- Ranker and readers: folds 0-5. Decision models: folds 6-9. Thresholds: folds 8 and 9.
- Layer-wise split = one training per model and identical train and test inputs, at the cost of less data per layer.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why not use out-of-fold predictions so the decision model could learn from all ten folds?"  
  **A:** Out-of-fold scores would need several trainings of each cross-encoder; on one 16 GB GPU the two readers already took about 2.1 hours to train once, so we chose a layer-wise split: readers and ranker on folds 0-5, decision models on folds 6-9. The decision models then see reader scores produced exactly as at test time, and they still learn from four folds of labelled data.

---

### A3.7 Cross-fitting {#a3-7 .concept}

**In one line:** When a learned ingredient (a word list, an encoder, a model score) is used to build training examples, compute it for each record from a version that was learned without that record's fold, so training examples look exactly like test examples.

**Simple explanation:** If students mark their own homework with an answer key they wrote after seeing the answers, every answer looks right, and the marks tell you nothing. **Cross-fitting** is the rule "you may only use an answer key written without your own homework". In our India second-chance search, a name written in an Indian script such as Devanagari (the script of Hindi and Marathi) is rewritten in Latin letters (**transliterated**) with a word list learned from labelled matches. When we built the training examples for the second-chance model, each record was transliterated with a word list learned without its own fold. At test time the word list has never seen the test record either, so the training examples and the test examples are made the same way, and the model learns how reliable the word list really is on unseen names.

**Worked example:**

(toy) Training records of the India second-chance search are spread over folds 0-7. Record R in fold 2 has the native name "बालाजी ट्रेडर्स" and owns the business "Balaji Traders". Suppose R is the only labelled record anywhere that contains the word "बालाजी".

| Word list used to build R's training example | Does it know "बालाजी"? | R's transliterated key | Looks like test time? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Learned from all folds 0-7 (including R itself) | yes, learned from R's own label | (balaji, traders): a perfect key | no: at test time, rare words like this are often unknown |
| Learned from folds 0-7 except fold 2 (cross-fitted) | no | the word is missing or falls back to a generic romanisation | yes |

With the first option the second-chance model learns "keys always match perfectly" and becomes over-confident; with cross-fitting it learns how often keys are incomplete, which is the truth on new records.

**Technical explanation:** Cross-fitting is sample splitting for any fitted component that feeds a later estimator: split the data into K folds; for each fold k, fit the component on the other folds and apply it to fold k; the downstream model is then trained on these out-of-fold values. It generalises out-of-fold predictions (see Layer-wise fold separation for stacked models) to anything learned from labels: target encoders, vocabularies, lexicons, propensity models. The name comes from double or debiased machine learning (Chernozhukov et al., 2018), where cross-fitting removes the over-fitting bias of **nuisance models** (auxiliary models whose outputs feed the quantity you actually care about). The classic everyday example is **target encoding** of a category (replacing a category by the mean label of its rows), which leaks badly unless computed out-of-fold. Cost: K fits of the component. At test time the component is fitted on all training folds, so test inputs are very slightly "better" than training inputs (more data); this mismatch usually errs on the safe side, because the test keys are, if anything, slightly more complete than the keys the model learned to be cautious about.

**How we used it:** The native-script second-chance model (India) was trained on India second-chance candidates of training folds 0-7, retrieved with word lists that leave out the record's own fold (Documentation, Section 4). It links the best candidate if its score is at least 0.88 and it leads the second candidate by at least 0.3; the 0.88 was chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice (see Cost-sensitive threshold selection). At test time the word list is learned from all labelled training records, since no test record has a label to leak. In the final run it scored 649,965 pairs for 171,713 records and added 9,759 links. The separate word list used in the main cleaning step is not cross-fitted; it is simply learned on folds 0-5 only, so every later layer (folds 6-9) sees cleaned text made without its labels.

**Expert nuance:** Cross-fitting removes the optimism of the learned ingredient, but not the optimism of choices made afterwards (the 0.88 threshold was still chosen on fold 8). A common misconception is that out-of-fold treatment is only needed for model predictions; any label-derived preprocessing needs it. A second subtlety is consistency: the procedure that builds training keys and the one that builds test keys must be identical apart from the data the word list was learned on; otherwise the second-chance model learns a distribution it will never see.

**Remember:**
- Cross-fitting = compute each record's learned ingredient from a version fitted without that record's fold.
- Our India second-chance search: word lists leave out the record's own fold; trained on folds 0-7; threshold 0.88 (lead 0.3) with 0.88 chosen on fold 8.
- Any label-derived preprocessing (encoders, word lists) needs it, not only model scores.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why go to the trouble of cross-fitting a word list?"  
  **A:** Because a word list that has learned from a record's own label makes that record's search key look perfect, so the second-chance model would learn to trust keys more than it should; at test time the list has never seen the record. With lists that leave out the record's own fold, the training keys are as imperfect as the test keys, and the model that added 9,759 Indian links learned the true reliability.

---

### A3.8 The held-out evaluation protocol {#a3-8 .concept}

**In one line:** To grade a recipe honestly on fold 9, we retrain it without fold 9 and without any incoming record that touches fold 9, and then compute the exact competition metric on fold 9's businesses (and the same for fold 8).

**Simple explanation:** Think of re-running a whole training camp without the players you want to test, so nobody in the camp has practised against them. There is one extra twist. An incoming record can have candidates in several folds: for example, its true business is in fold 9 and a look-alike candidate is in fold 7. If that record stayed in training through its fold-7 pair, the model would learn "this record is not the fold-7 business", which partly reveals the fold-9 answer by elimination, and the competition features that compare the two candidates would tie them together. So we remove from training every incoming record that has any candidate in the fold being scored. That is the meaning of "held-out" in our numbers.

**Worked example:**

(toy) Four incoming records and their candidate businesses, with each business's fold in brackets. We want to score fold 9.

| Record | Candidates (fold) | In the fit for scoring fold 9? |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | B_a (6), B_b (7) | yes |
| R2 | B_c (9) | no: touches fold 9 |
| R3 | B_d (7), B_e (9) | no: touches fold 9 (even its fold-7 pair is removed) |
| R4 | B_f (8) | yes |

1. Fit the decision model on the fold 6-8 pairs of R1 and R4 only.
2. Use a fixed number of trees: (toy) seed 1 early-stopped at 1,000 trees when fitted on folds 6-7; the new fit on folds 6-8 has 1.5 times as many rows as folds 6-7 (both counted without the records touching fold 9), so it uses 1,000 × 1.5 = 1,500 trees.
3. Score all pairs of R2 and R3, including R3's fold-7 pair, so that "best candidate" and "lead over the runner-up" are computed exactly as at test time.
4. Apply the decision rule (0.75 threshold, 0.4 lead, consistency check) and compute per-business F0.5 for every fold-9 business, including fold-9 businesses whose true records were never retrieved (they count as misses).
5. Average over fold-9 businesses.

(ours) The results:

| Recipe, as measured | Fold 9 | Fold 8 |
|---|---|---|
| India: the final India recipe with 3 of its 5 seeds, with consistency check | 0.990046 | 0.990298 |
| US: the same 3-seed model, scored on US businesses, with consistency check | 0.991212 | 0.991545 |
| France recipe (one fit) applied to US / India at the France operating point, no consistency check: a proxy, not a French score | 0.990508 / 0.989467 | 0.990977 / 0.989850 |

**Technical explanation:** The protocol (Documentation Section 5; code in the evidence folder) is: fold 9 is scored by fits on folds 6-8 without the records touching fold 9; fold 8 by fits on folds 6, 7 and 9 without the records touching fold 8; the number of boosting rounds is fixed at each seed's early-stopping best iteration × n_fit / n_fit(6, 7) (with the same exclusion), so the scored fold is never used for stopping; 3 of the 5 seeds are averaged. The decision uses the production rule: threshold 0.75, lead 0.4, and for the US and India the consistency check (0.68, 0.72, 0.77 for 1, 2 and 3 or more other accepted records). The metric is the exact per-business macro F0.5, where each business's true count comes from the label table, so owners lost by the search are counted as misses: the score includes retrieval losses, not only decision errors. The "touching" exclusion is stricter than group k-fold: it removes cross-fold information carried by records whose candidates straddle folds. Differences between recipes are compared with a paired bootstrap over businesses (see Paired bootstrap intervals).

**How we used it:** This is our main evidence for the decision-model recipes and for the claim, said on the results slide, that "close versions of our decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992 on hidden folds". We are precise about what it does not cover: the final US and India models are refitted on folds 6-9 (so they differ from the evaluated fits); the US number comes from the India recipe applied to US businesses (the final US model trains on US rows only and adds 6 features); the 0.75 threshold was chosen on fold 8 and the consistency check on folds 8 and 9; and the scores exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules. France has no labels, so the France line is only a proxy on US and Indian businesses.

**Expert nuance:** Because the same scaled-iteration rule is used to produce these held-out fits, the protocol also tests the refit rule itself (see Refitting on more folds with scaled iterations), which is a nice property. The weak point is reuse: folds 8 and 9 chose thresholds, so the held-out numbers carry some selection optimism, which is why we call them "evidence in the same range" and not "an unbiased estimate". A simpler protocol (fit on 6-7, stop on 8, score 9) gives an honest fold 9 but not an honest fold 8, since fold 8 was the stopping fold; the swap gives two scores, each from fits that never touched it.

**Remember:**
- Held-out = refit without the scored fold and without every record touching it, fixed tree count, exact per-business F0.5.
- Fold 9 / fold 8: US 0.991212 / 0.991545; India 0.990046 / 0.990298 (3 of 5 seeds).
- It excludes the second-chance searches and the France rules, and folds 8 and 9 also chose thresholds.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "What exactly does 'held-out' mean in your 0.991212?"  
  **A:** The decision model was refitted on folds 6-8 without fold 9 and without any incoming record that has a candidate in fold 9, with a fixed tree count, and then fold 9's businesses were scored with the exact per-business F0.5, our thresholds and the consistency check. It uses 3 of the 5 seeds and excludes the second-chance searches and France rules, and fold 9 also helped choose the consistency check, so it is strong evidence, not an untouched test.

---

### A3.9 Early stopping {#a3-9 .concept}

*See also [A2.3 Overfitting, held-out data and early stopping](#a2-3): overfitting and early stopping from the models side; [A2.24 Early stopping, then refit on more data](#a2-24): early stopping, then refit.*

**In one line:** Keep adding trees (or training steps) only while a score on a separate validation fold keeps improving, and stop when it has not improved for a set number of rounds.

**Simple explanation:** Baking a cake, you test with a toothpick and take it out when it is done, not when the maximum time in the recipe runs out; over-baking ruins it. A boosted-tree model adds small trees one by one. At first each tree fixes real mistakes; later, trees start fitting noise peculiar to the training data, and performance on new data gets worse. **Early stopping** watches the score on a validation fold and keeps the model from the round where that score was best. **Patience** is how many extra rounds you wait in case the score improves again, because validation curves are a little noisy.

**Worked example:**

(toy) A decision model is trained with validation on fold 8, patience 100. The validation measure is **log loss**: for one pair with predicted probability p and label y, loss = −ln(p) if y = 1 and −ln(1 − p) if y = 0. A true pair scored 0.9 costs −ln(0.9) = 0.105; a false pair scored 0.9 costs −ln(0.1) = 2.303, so confident mistakes are punished hard.

| Trees | Training log loss (toy) | Fold-8 log loss (toy) |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.0280 | 0.0300 |
| 400 | 0.0150 | 0.0210 |
| 800 | 0.0090 | **0.0195** (best) |
| 850 | 0.0086 | 0.0196 |
| 900 | 0.0083 | 0.0197 |

Training loss keeps falling, but the fold-8 loss is best at 800 and has not improved for 100 rounds by 900, so training stops at 900 and the model is saved at 800 trees. The "best iteration" is 800.

**Technical explanation:** Early stopping is a form of regularisation: for gradient-boosted decision trees (**GBDT**), the number of trees times the learning rate controls model capacity, and for linear models trained by gradient descent early stopping behaves much like an **L2 penalty** (a penalty on the sum of squared weights, which keeps weights small). The procedure monitors a validation metric each round and keeps the iteration with the best value (best_iteration); training ends after a patience window without improvement or at a maximum round count. The monitored metric should be smooth and **proper** (a **proper scoring rule** is one whose expected value is best when the predicted probability equals the true probability), so log loss is the usual choice; a thresholded metric such as F0.5 is piecewise constant in the scores and too noisy to stop on. Smaller learning rates need more trees but usually generalise slightly better. Two costs: you need a validation fold, and because the stopping point is chosen on that fold, the fold's own score becomes slightly optimistic. With several seeds, each seed has its own best iteration.

**How we used it:**

| Model | Maximum | Patience | Stopping fold | Metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CatBoost ranker | 1,600 trees (depth 7, learning rate 0.075) | 180 rounds | fold 6 | Logloss |
| US and India decision models | 3,000 rounds (learning rate 0.05) | 100 rounds | fold 8 | binary log loss |
| France and default decision models | 1,500 rounds | 100 rounds | fold 8 | binary log loss |
| Readers | no early stopping: one fixed epoch; the learning rate rises over the first 3 % of steps (warm-up), then falls linearly to zero | | | |
| Address second-chance filter / scorer | fixed 200 / 300 rounds | | | |

For the US and India the early-stopped tree count is then scaled up for a refit (see the next concept).

**Expert nuance:** We used fold 8 both to stop the decision models and to choose the 0.75 threshold, so fold-8 numbers carry a little double-use optimism; fold 9 is the cleaner report. Early stopping on log loss and then choosing a threshold for F0.5 is the right split of jobs: the trees are tuned to produce good probabilities, and the decision rule is tuned to the business metric. For the readers we chose a fixed one-epoch budget rather than early stopping; we did not run an epoch sweep, so we cannot say what a second epoch would have done, but their quality on held-out pairs is measured: the E5 reader has AUC 0.998570 and top-1 accuracy 0.993004 (both defined in the word table above) on 509,260 pairs of 437,715 labelled fold-8/9 records, which the readers never trained on.

**Remember:**
- Early stopping keeps the iteration with the best validation loss; patience absorbs noise.
- Ranker: patience 180 on fold 6. Decision models: patience 100 on fold 8, at most 3,000 rounds (US/India) or 1,500 (France).
- Stop on a smooth proper loss (log loss), tune the threshold on the business metric.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why don't your readers use early stopping?"  
  **A:** We gave them a fixed budget of one epoch with a short warm-up and linear decay, which is a common choice when fine-tuning a pretrained encoder on a large set of selected examples. We did not run an epoch sweep, so we cannot quantify the alternative, but their held-out quality is measured, for example the E5 reader's AUC of 0.998570 on fold-8 and fold-9 pairs.

---

### A3.10 Refitting on more folds with scaled iterations {#a3-10 .concept}

*See also [A2.24 Early stopping, then refit on more data](#a2-24): early stopping, then refit, from the models side.*

**In one line:** After early stopping has told you how many trees to use, retrain on all available folds with that tree count scaled up in proportion to the extra data.

**Simple explanation:** Suppose you tested a recipe with half the ingredients and found it needs 20 minutes. Now you cook the full amount, but you no longer have a spare cake to test with a toothpick, so you use a rule of thumb: twice the food, roughly twice the time. Early stopping needs a validation fold; once you want to use that fold for training too, nothing is left to stop on. More data supports a bigger model before it starts memorising, so the refit uses more trees, in proportion to the number of training rows.

**Worked example:**

(toy) For one seed of the US decision model:

| Step | Rows (toy) | Trees |
|---|---|---|
| Fit on folds 6-7, early stopping on fold 8 | 2.0 million | best iteration 1,200 |
| Refit on folds 6-9, no validation | 4.1 million | 1,200 × 4.1 / 2.0 = 2,460 |

(ours) The public results of this step:

| Change | Public score before → after | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| US and India decision models refitted on folds 6-9 | 0.990621 → 0.990676 | kept |
| France decision model refitted on folds 6-9 | 0.990726 with it vs 0.990748 without it | not adopted |

**Technical explanation:** The rule is T_refit = T_best × n(6-9) / n(6-7), applied per seed, with a fixed number of rounds and no validation set. The reasoning: at a fixed learning rate, the number of boosting rounds that a dataset can support before over-fitting tends to grow with its size, because more rows mean more real signal for each extra tree to fit; scaling by the row ratio is a common heuristic (another is multiplying by k/(k − 1) after k-fold cross-validation). It is a heuristic, not a law; it can over- or under-shoot. The gain is more training data for the final model (folds 6-9 hold roughly twice the rows of folds 6-7, since the folds are of similar size); the risk is that the exact refitted model is never validated. In our case the risk is reduced because the held-out protocol uses the same rule: the fold-9 fits on folds 6-8 use the best iteration scaled by n(6-8) / n(6-7), and those fits are what produce our held-out scores (see The held-out evaluation protocol).

**How we used it:** US and India: per seed (1 to 5), fit on folds 6-7 with early stopping on fold 8 (at most 3,000 rounds), then refit on folds 6-9 for best iteration × rows(6-9) / rows(6-7); the five refits are averaged. France and the default route: the early-stopped fit on folds 6-7 is used as it is (at most 1,500 rounds), with no refit, because the France refit scored 0.990726 against 0.990748 without it on the public leaderboard.

**Expert nuance:** After the refit, folds 8 and 9 are inside the training data of the final US and India models, so no labelled fold is left to score those exact models; this is one of the reasons our Documentation says there is no untouched end-to-end validation. The France decision was made on a public difference of 0.000022 (derived), which is tiny and could be noise; when a change showed no public gain, we kept the existing, simpler version. A further subtlety: the 0.75 threshold was chosen on fold 8 and then reused for the refitted models, which have fold 8 in their training data; the held-out fits, which use the same scaled refit rule and the same threshold, are the reassurance that this transfer works.

**Remember:**
- Refit rule: trees = best iteration × rows(6-9) / rows(6-7), because no fold is left for stopping.
- US/India refit kept (public 0.990621 → 0.990676); France refit dropped (0.990726 vs 0.990748).
- The held-out scores use the same scaled rule, so the rule itself is tested.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Isn't refitting without a validation fold risky?"  
  **A:** A little, and that is why we scale the tree count from early stopping by the row ratio instead of guessing, and why our held-out fits use the same rule: fits on folds 6-8 with scaled trees score 0.991212 on US and 0.990046 on Indian fold-9 businesses. On the public board the refit moved US/India from 0.990621 to 0.990676; for France it did not help (0.990726 vs 0.990748), so France keeps the plain fit.

---

### A3.11 Seed averaging {#a3-11 .concept}

*See also [A2.25 Seed averaging](#a2-25): seed averaging from the models side.*

**In one line:** Train the same model several times with different random seeds and average their predicted probabilities, so the randomness of any single training run cancels out.

**Simple explanation:** Ask five equally good doctors for an opinion and average them, and the result is steadier than any one doctor's. Our LightGBM decision models use deliberate randomness: every boosting round uses a random 80 % of the rows, and every tree a random 90 % of the features. A **random seed** is the starting number for that randomness; a different seed gives a slightly different model. Most pairs get the same answer from every seed, but pairs near the 0.75 line can flip between "link" and "no link" from one seed to the next. Averaging five seeds makes those borderline decisions steadier.

**Worked example:**

(toy) One borderline US pair scored by five seeds:

| Seed | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.74 | 0.78 | 0.71 | 0.80 | 0.77 | **0.760** |
| Decision at 0.75 | no | link | no | link | link | **link** |

With a single seed, two runs out of five would reject this pair. The spread across seeds is 0.035 (sample standard deviation); if the seeds were independent, the mean of five would have a spread of 0.035 / √5 = 0.016. Seeds trained on the same data are not independent, so the real reduction is smaller (see the formula below).

**Technical explanation:** If M models each have prediction variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/M: only the uncorrelated part shrinks with M, which is why **subsampling** (bagging of rows, here bagging_fraction 0.8 every iteration, and feature_fraction 0.9) matters; it decorrelates the members. Averaging reduces variance, not bias. We average predicted probabilities (an arithmetic mean); averaging logits is an alternative that weights confident members more. Averaging tends to pull extreme scores slightly inwards, which reduces over-confidence. The cost is M times the training and inference of the tree models, which is small next to the cross-encoders. Picking the single best seed on a validation fold is the wrong alternative: it selects partly on noise and is a mild form of selection leakage.

**How we used it:** The US, India and France decision models are each the mean of seeds 1-5 (LightGBM, learning rate 0.05, 127 leaves, at least 200 rows per leaf, feature fraction 0.9, bagging 0.8 every iteration, L2 1.0). The default route for unseen countries uses a single fit. The address second-chance scorer averages seeds 7, 8 and 9. The held-out table uses 3 of the 5 seeds. Honestly, the effect of the seeds is not isolated: the five-seed models entered the final file in the same upload as the French E5 reader (public 0.991114 → 0.991300), so we do not claim a separate number for them.

**Expert nuance:** Seed averaging is a cheap, low-risk way to stabilise the decision boundary, and it matters more for a precision-oriented rule with a hard threshold, where instability near the threshold turns directly into flipped links. To measure its own effect we would compare one-seed and five-seed decisions on held-out folds 8 and 9 with a paired bootstrap over businesses. A misconception is that averaging always improves the metric; it improves stability, and the metric gain, if any, is usually small.

**Remember:**
- Five seeds, probabilities averaged; row (0.8) and feature (0.9) subsampling makes the seeds differ.
- Averaging reduces variance (only the uncorrelated part), not bias.
- Its own effect is not isolated: it arrived with the French E5 reader (0.991114 → 0.991300).

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why average five seeds rather than keep the seed that scored best on validation?"  
  **A:** Picking the best seed on fold 8 would partly pick fold 8's noise; averaging uses all five, steadies decisions near the 0.75 line, and costs only a few small tree-model calls per pair. Its own gain is not isolated in our evidence, because the five-seed models arrived in the same upload as the French E5 reader.

---

### A3.12 Tuning thresholds on held-out folds {#a3-12 .concept}

**In one line:** Choose the score cut-off for linking by trying several values on a held-out fold and keeping the one that gives the best exact competition score there, not the best AUC.

**Simple explanation:** The decision model gives every candidate a probability, but you still need a rule: "link if the score is above X". If X is too low you make many wrong links (precision falls); if X is too high you miss true links (recall falls). The best X depends on how the scoring works. Our competition scores each business separately with F0.5, whose formula counts a wrong link four times as heavily as a missed one, then averages over businesses, and gives a full point to a business with no true records only if we link nothing to it. So we try candidate values of X on fold 8, compute exactly that score for each, and keep the best. A general-purpose measure such as AUC cannot do this job, because AUC does not depend on X at all.

**Worked example:**

(toy) A held-out fold with four businesses and six incoming records. Each record's best candidate is shown; second candidates are far behind, so the lead rule is always passed.

| Record | Best candidate | Score | Truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| r1 | B1 | 0.95 | correct |
| r2 | B1 | 0.70 | correct |
| r3 | B2 | 0.80 | correct |
| r6 | B2 | 0.85 | wrong (r6 belongs to no business) |
| r5 | B3 | 0.72 | wrong (r5 belongs to no business) |
| r4 | B4 | 0.60 | correct |

True counts: B1 owns 2 records, B2 owns 1, B3 owns 0, B4 owns 1. Per business, F0.5 = 1.25 × TP / (predicted + 0.25 × true), and 1 if predicted = true = 0.

| Threshold | Links made | B1 | B2 | B3 | B4 | Macro F0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.65 | r1, r2, r3, r6, r5 | 2.5 / 2.5 = 1.000 | 1.25 / 2.25 = 0.556 | 0 (wrong link to an empty business) | 0 (missed) | 0.389 |
| 0.75 | r1, r3, r6 | 1.25 / 1.5 = 0.833 | 0.556 | 1 (correctly empty) | 0 | **0.597** |
| 0.90 | r1 | 0.833 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0.458 |

The best threshold here is 0.75. Notice what drives it: protecting the empty business B3 is worth a whole point, which a pair-level measure would barely notice. The AUC of these six scores is one fixed number whichever threshold we pick, because AUC only checks whether true links are ranked above wrong ones; it cannot tell us where to cut.

**Technical explanation:** For one business, F_beta = (1 + β²) × P × R / (β² × P + R) with P = TP / predicted and R = TP / true; with β = 0.5 this simplifies to F0.5 = 1.25 × TP / (predicted + 0.25 × true) = 1.25 × TP / (1.25 × TP + FP + 0.25 × FN), which shows directly that a false positive (FP, a wrong link) weighs four times as much as a false negative (FN, a missed link). The competition averages it over businesses (macro), with the convention that an empty prediction for an empty business scores 1. This metric is **non-decomposable**: the value of a link depends on the other links of the same business, so pair-level summaries (AUC, log loss, pair-level F) can disagree with it. Threshold tuning is therefore a direct search: for each value on a grid, apply the full decision rule on the held-out fold, compute the exact macro metric, and keep the first maximum. A useful sanity rule from theory (shown for F1 by Lipton, Elkan and Narayanaswamy, 2014; the same argument extends to F_beta): for a single global F_beta and calibrated probabilities, the optimal threshold equals F* / (1 + β²), where F* is the best achievable F; for β = 0.5 that is 0.8 × F*, so with F* near 0.99 the optimum is near 0.79. Our 0.75 (US, India) and 0.82 (France) sit on either side of that value; the rule is only a sanity check, because our metric is a per-business average and our scores are not proven calibrated (see Calibration and reliability). Tuning on the same fold you report is optimistic; the usual remedy is to report a second fold.

**How we used it:** Every US and India operating point was chosen on labelled folds, never by AUC: the threshold 0.75 on fold 8 and the per-business consistency check on folds 8 and 9, both for the exact per-business macro F0.5; the second-chance thresholds on fold 8 for the same metric with false positives counted twice; and the address second-chance filter's cut-off by a recall rule, the largest grid value that keeps 98 % of the fold-8 reference links. The lead of 0.4 over the runner-up is one fixed value shared by every country's rule. France has no labels, so its threshold 0.82 was set without labels, from the number of French links per business together with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US and Indian data.

**Expert nuance:** Near the optimum the metric curve is usually flat, so a slightly wrong threshold costs little on the tuning distribution; under a distribution change the optimum can move a lot, which is why France got a stricter value rather than a copied one. Threshold and model interact: if the model changes (for example, five seeds instead of one, or a refit), the score distribution moves a little and the tuned threshold may no longer be exactly optimal; our held-out fits, which use the production threshold on refitted models, are the check. A frequent misconception is "we maximised AUC, so the thresholds are fine"; AUC says nothing about where to cut.

**Remember:**
- Per-business F0.5 = 1.25 × TP / (predicted + 0.25 × true); 1 for a correctly empty business.
- Thresholds were tuned on the exact metric on held-out folds: 0.75 on fold 8; France 0.82 without labels.
- AUC is threshold-free and pair-level; it cannot choose an operating point.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why not pick the threshold by maximising AUC or F1?"  
  **A:** AUC does not depend on the threshold at all, and F1 weighs recall as much as precision, while the competition uses F0.5 per business with a full point for a correctly empty row. So we tuned directly on that exact metric on held-out fold 8, which gave 0.75 for the US and India.

---

### A3.13 Cost-sensitive threshold selection {#a3-13 .concept}

**In one line:** When choosing a threshold, count each wrong link as costing more than the metric says (we counted false positives twice), so the chosen threshold is deliberately more cautious.

**Simple explanation:** Engineers add a safety factor when they are not sure the load on a bridge is exactly what was measured. Our second-chance searches work on records that the main decision model already left unlinked: a riskier group, where the training data come from a slightly different situation than the test data. To build in a safety factor, when we chose their thresholds on fold 8 we pretended that every wrong link cost twice as much as it really does. That pushes the cut-off higher: we accept fewer second-chance links, but the ones we accept are surer.

**Worked example:**

(toy) A second-chance model on fold 8. Simplified units: a true link is worth +1, a false link costs 1 (normal) or 2 (counted twice).

| Threshold | True links | False links | Net, normal cost | Net, false links ×2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.70 | 1,000 | 260 | 740 | 480 |
| 0.80 | 900 | 120 | **780** | 660 |
| 0.88 | 830 | 60 | 770 | **710** |
| 0.95 | 600 | 20 | 580 | 560 |

With the normal cost, 0.80 wins; with false links counted twice, 0.88 wins. You give up 70 true links (900 → 830) to avoid 60 false ones (120 → 60).

**Technical explanation:** In **cost-sensitive** decision theory, you accept a link if p × g > (1 − p) × w × c, where p is the probability that the link is true, g the gain of a true link, c the cost of a false one and w a weight; the break-even probability is p* = w × c / (g + w × c), which rises with w (for g = c, p* goes from 0.5 at w = 1 to 0.67 at w = 2). In our implementation the "gain" is the exact change in per-business macro F0.5 on fold 8, and each false link is counted twice in the predicted count of its business when the candidate thresholds are compared. Two motivations: robustness to **prior shift** (if the share of wrong candidates is higher at test time than in training, false links become more frequent than the training estimate) and a hedge against the optimism of choosing a threshold on the same fold you measure. An alternative is to estimate the test prior and re-weight explicitly; another is to require a lead over the second candidate, which we also do.

**How we used it:** Native-script second-chance search (India): link the best candidate if its score is at least 0.88 and it leads the second by at least 0.3; 0.88 chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice; +9,759 links. Address second-chance search: the scorer's threshold and lead chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice: US 0.86 with lead 0.0, India 0.66 with lead 0.1; the filter keeps a pair if its probability is at least 0.06 (US) or 0.015 (India), the largest grid values that keep 98 % of the fold-8 reference links; +192 US and +2,945 Indian links. The main decision models were tuned on the plain exact metric, without the doubling.

**Expert nuance:** The factor 2 is a judgement call, a safety factor, not an estimated quantity; a judge may call it arbitrary, and the honest reply is that it is a deliberate hedge whose price is a little recall on small add-on modules. Doubling costs makes sense precisely where training and test differ most: the second-chance models act on the leftovers of the main decision, and their training records were themselves selected with earlier decision models. Over-caution has a cost, but for modules that add about 13,000 links out of 5,856,936 (derived), a little lost recall is cheap insurance.

**Remember:**
- Counting false positives twice raises the break-even probability and gives a more cautious threshold.
- Used only for the second-chance searches: 0.88 (native script), 0.86 US / 0.66 India (address).
- It is a safety factor against train-test differences, not a measured cost.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Why count false positives twice for the second-chance searches? Isn't that arbitrary?"  
  **A:** It is a deliberate safety factor: those searches act on records the main model already rejected, a riskier group whose training data differ most from test, so we chose their thresholds on fold 8 as if each wrong link cost double. That gave, for example, 0.88 for the native-script search, which still added 9,759 Indian links.
