### A3.26 Written acceptance checks before keeping a model {#a3-26 .concept}

**In one line:** Before seeing a new model's results, write down the tests it must pass to be adopted, then apply them as written, and disclose any exception.

**Simple explanation:** Teams agree the rules of a match before kick-off, not after seeing the score. If you decide what counts as "better" after you have seen the numbers, it is very easy to find a reason to keep the version you like; scientists call this the **garden of forking paths**. Writing the checks first is called **pre-registration**. It does not make a model good, but it makes your decision honest. And if you break your own rule, you say so plainly, which is what we did for the French E5 reader.

**Worked example:**

(ours) The four written checks of the French E5 reader:

| Check (plain name) | Data | Result | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| US/India quality within tolerance | 509,260 pairs of 437,715 labelled fold-8/9 records | French E5 vs E5: AUC 0.998544 vs 0.998570; top-1 0.993161 vs 0.993004; best F0.5 0.992782 vs 0.992796; allowed drops 0.001 / 0.002 / 0.002 | pass |
| Agreement with held-out French pseudo-labels | 25,192 pairs (12,616 positive) | 0.999206 (E5 reader 0.981304); bar 0.98 | pass |
| Generated labelled French test set | 195,380 pairs (69,910 positive) | best F0.5 0.910516 vs 0.914964 for the E5 reader | fail |
| Expected gain must be safely positive (label-free, final file vs the same pipeline without the French E5 reader) | French links −2,228 / +3,396 (5,437 business rows changed); US, India and candidates identical | point estimate +0.0000302; pessimistic −0.0001806; optimistic +0.0002315 | fail |

The last rule needed two things: the pessimistic estimate above 0, and the point estimate × 0.75 at least 0.00001. Here 0.0000302 × 0.75 = 0.0000226 ≥ 0.00001 (passes), but −0.0001806 is below 0 (fails), so the rule fails.

**Technical explanation:** Good acceptance checks are chosen to catch different failure modes. A **guardrail** or **non-inferiority** check verifies that nothing important got worse beyond a stated tolerance (here, no forgetting on labelled US and Indian data). A **fit** check verifies that the model learned its target (agreement with held-out pseudo-labels). An **external-validity** check tests on data from a different source (the generated French set). An **end-to-end utility** check estimates the effect on the real output, ideally with a **lower confidence bound** above zero so that noise alone cannot pass it. Fixing tolerances and bars before the results removes the freedom to move goalposts. A useful companion practice is a **harness control**: before measuring a change, confirm that an unchanged copy of the pipeline reproduces the previous outputs byte for byte, so any difference is caused by the change alone (our written rule files require this).

**How we used it:** New readers faced written pass-or-fail checks, and our evidence folder also holds rules written in advance for the five-seed decision models and the French readers. The French E5 reader passed two checks and failed two. We kept it because the file containing it had our best public score: a leaderboard-driven decision against our own written rule, and our documentation discloses it as such. It changes French links only (−2,228 / +3,396), and the same upload also added the five-seed decision models, so its own effect on the public score is not isolated. Two later variants, a second French self-training round and a French MiniLM reader with different pseudo-label filters, were not adopted.

**Expert nuance:** A rule that is overridden loses part of its protective value; the remedy is full disclosure, which turns a hidden choice into a documented one that others can judge. Note what each check can and cannot show: the agreement check measures consistency with the teacher, not truth; the generated set measures performance on a simulated distribution; and the expected-gain rule was label-free and wide (from −0.0001806 to +0.0002315), so neither its pass nor its fail is decisive. One precise caveat that our Documentation states itself: the expected-gain rule for the French E5 reader is in our evidence folder with its date, written before any French decision result with the new reader existed, but the original pre-training declaration of its other three checks is not included; their tolerances are restated in a later rule file. If asked about pre-registration in general, say: the rules were written before the results they judge, the files record every deviation, and where an original declaration is missing the Documentation says so.

**Remember:**
- Write the pass/fail tests before the results; apply them as written; disclose exceptions.
- French E5 reader: passed US/India tolerance and pseudo-label agreement; failed the generated French set and the expected-gain rule; kept for the best public score, disclosed.
- Checks target different failures: forgetting, learning, external validity, end-to-end gain.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "If you wrote rules in advance, why did you break one?"  
  **A:** Because the file containing the French E5 reader had our best public score; that was a leaderboard-driven decision against our own written rule, and we disclose it. It passed two checks (US/India AUC 0.998544 against 0.998570; 0.999206 agreement with held-out French pseudo-labels) and failed two (the generated French test set, 0.910516 against 0.914964, and the expected-gain rule, pessimistic −0.0001806), and it changes French links only.

---

### A3.27 Validation hygiene: recall at every stage, assertions and the validator {#a3-27 .concept}

**In one line:** Measure what every stage loses, assert the invariants the output must satisfy, and run the official checker, so errors are caught where they happen rather than discovered at the end.

**Simple explanation:** In a factory you inspect after each machine, not only at the end; if the final product is faulty, you know which machine broke it. For our pipeline: after each candidate-finding step we measure how often the true business is still among the candidates (**recall**), because a business lost early can never be linked later. We also check rules that must always hold: every link we output is also in our candidate list, no record is linked to two businesses, no pair crosses countries, and each output file has exactly one row per test business. Finally we run the organisers' validator. This is unglamorous, but it is what lets a team trust its own numbers.

**Worked example:**

(ours) Recall on a fold-9 sample (share of owned incoming records whose true business is still a candidate), with candidates per incoming record from the all-fold samples:

| Stage | US recall | India recall | US candidates per record | India candidates per record |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index lookup | 99.3658 % | 98.388 % | 27.541 | 23.145 |
| After the quick rule-based filter | 99.3523 % | 98.3745 % | 3.111 | 3.878 |
| Shortlist (at most 4) | 98.8935 % | 97.985 % | 1.114 | 1.174 |

Derived losses: the quick filter costs 0.0135 points of recall in both countries while cutting candidates per record from 27.5 to 3.1 (US) and from 23.1 to 3.9 (India); the cap of four costs 0.4588 points (US) and 0.3895 points (India). So the cap of four is the largest loss, which is exactly what our documentation says, and it tells you where a bigger budget would help most.

(ours) End-to-end cost of the quick filter, measured in the blocking study of 25 Sep 2026: the true business survived for 99.974 % of fold-8/9 records, and fold-9 macro F0.5 moved from 0.990117 to 0.990086 (fold 8: −0.00004).

**Technical explanation:** In record-linkage terms, **pair completeness** is the recall of blocking (the share of true pairs among candidates) and the **reduction ratio** is 1 − (candidate pairs / all possible pairs); our reduction ratio is 0.99999817 on 6,724,569,566,212 same-country pairs. Recall at each stage is a ceiling on final recall, so measuring it localises losses and quantifies the trade-off between candidates per record and recall. Recall alone is not enough: the stronger test is the effect on the end metric, as in the quick-filter measurement. **Invariant assertions** encode properties that must hold whatever the model does; failing loudly at the point of violation is far cheaper than discovering a silent error after an upload. A **metric implementation** must match the official one: our per-business F0.5 code counts each business's true records from the label table, so owners lost by the search are counted as misses. Code-level guards complete the picture: a check that asserts none of the 21 removed data-specific inputs is used by any final decision model, and fold files recorded with their hashes.

**How we used it:** Recall is measured at every candidate step on labelled fold 9 (full fold: index 99.3694 % US / 98.5068 % India; shortlist between 98.8748 % and 99.3628 % US and between 98.0572 % and 98.4831 % India, given as lower and upper bounds). The export asserts that every matched pair is a candidate pair; no pair joins different countries and no incoming record is linked to more than one business; the last stage runs the organisers' validator with `--check-ids`, result PASS: 1,732,544 rows in each file, 100,087 empty and 1,632,457 non-empty rows in the matching file, 125 empty and 1,732,419 non-empty rows in the candidate file. In our written experiment rules, an unchanged copy of the pipeline had to reproduce the previous outputs byte for byte before a change was measured.

**Expert nuance:** Many teams measure only the final score, and then cannot say whether a loss came from retrieval or from the decision. Measuring recall per stage is also what justified our design: the quick filter is almost free, the cap of four is the main loss, and the two second-chance searches target the main remaining miss types (native-script names, and same address with a different name). Recall numbers exclude the second-chance candidates, so they are conservative for the final candidate file.

**Remember:**
- Recall at every step: index 99.37 % US / 98.51 % India on fold 9; the cap of four is the largest loss.
- Assertions: every link is a candidate pair; one business per record; no cross-country pairs; validator PASS.
- End-metric checks beat recall alone: the quick filter moved fold-9 F0.5 only from 0.990117 to 0.990086.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "How do you know your search doesn't silently lose true matches?"  
  **A:** We measure recall at every candidate step on labelled fold 9: 99.37 % of US and 98.51 % of Indian owners survive the index, at least 98.87 % and 98.06 % the shortlist, and the quick filter keeps the true business for 99.974 % of held-out records. The cap of four is the largest loss, and the two second-chance searches target the remaining miss types.
- **Q:** "What guarantees that your output files are internally consistent?"  
  **A:** The export asserts that every link is also a candidate pair, and the output has no record linked to two businesses and no pair that crosses countries. The final stage then runs the organisers' validator with the id check, which passed with 1,732,544 rows in each file.

### A3.28 Determinism and byte-exact reproducibility {#a3-28 .concept}

**In one line:** Running the same code on the same data should give the same output; seeds, pinned versions and stored intermediate results make that possible, but GPU arithmetic can still differ in the last digits.

**Simple explanation:** A recipe followed twice should give the same cake. In computing, hidden sources of randomness can change the result: random sampling and initialisation, the order in which parallel processors finish their sums, and even how Python orders text in a set. A **seed** fixes the random choices. But on a GPU, thousands of threads add numbers in whatever order they finish, and because computers round every result, (a + b) + c is not always exactly a + (b + c). Tiny differences in the CatBoost ranker change a few shortlists, and those ripple through every later stage. So we offer two kinds of reproduction: from the trained models and stored scores, exact to the byte; from the raw data, very close.

**Worked example:**

(toy) Rounding makes order matter. In 32-bit floating point, numbers near 100,000,000 are spaced 8 apart, so:

| Order | Result |
|---|---|
| (100,000,000 + 1) − 100,000,000 | 0 (the + 1 is rounded away) |
| (100,000,000 − 100,000,000) + 1 | 1 |

In **bf16** (a 16-bit number format; our readers were trained with bf16 autocast, which runs most of the arithmetic in it), numbers near 1 are spaced 2^(−7) = 0.0078125 apart, so 1 + 0.001 = 1. Sums done in a different order, or with different padding, therefore differ in the last digits.

(ours) What reproduction achieved:

| Route | Result |
|---|---|
| From the trained weights and the stored arrays of the submitted run (the stages that install the French E5 scores, score the France decision model and export the files) | both files rewritten byte for byte; a fresh extraction of the full archive on 29 Sep reproduced both files byte for byte with the inference-only command |
| Clean run from raw data, 27-28 Sep, every model retrained | validator PASS; identical match list for 99.07 % of businesses; 99.82 % of submitted links reproduced (5,846,344 in common); 12,334,519 candidate pairs; France shortlist 2,122,285 pairs |
| CPU retraining of the India native-script and address second-chance models on the same inputs | byte for byte |
| Output file hashes (SHA-256) | matching file 9183e542…; candidate file e7b4c679… |

**Technical explanation:** Sources of non-determinism: unseeded random number generators (Python, NumPy, PyTorch, LightGBM, CatBoost); Python's **hash randomisation** of strings, which changes the iteration order of sets and dictionaries between runs unless `PYTHONHASHSEED` is fixed; thread scheduling in parallel reductions (sums split across CPU threads, for example with OpenMP); GPU kernels that use atomic floating-point additions or choose algorithms by input shape (in cuBLAS and cuDNN, NVIDIA's GPU maths libraries); **mixed precision** (bf16 keeps only 8 bits of precision, so rounding differences are visible); **batch composition**, because each batch is padded to its longest pair, which changes tensor shapes and therefore kernel choice and summation order even though padded tokens are masked out mathematically; library versions (for example a data library's hash function); and hardware. Remedies: seed everything; force deterministic algorithms where they exist (at a speed cost); train on CPU where feasible; pin library versions and model revisions; store intermediate artefacts with hashes; compare outputs byte for byte. GPU training of CatBoost and bf16 training of transformers are not bit-deterministic in practice, so the realistic standard is "byte-exact from stored artefacts, very close from scratch".

**How we used it:** Seeds: fold hash 20260927; CatBoost ranker 2026; readers torch 0 and numpy 0; decision models 1-5; address second-chance scorer 7, 8, 9; French pseudo-label sampling 11. `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` is required, and the second-chance scripts assert it. The two pretrained encoders are downloaded once at pinned revisions; every later stage runs offline. Input files and outputs are recorded with SHA-256 hashes, and the fold manifest records the data library version and fold-file hashes. In the submitted run, 11,638,504 shortlist pairs carry GPU reader scores reused from earlier scoring runs and 48,813 were scored on the CPU. The French E5 reader's weights were deleted after scoring and its scores on the France shortlist are shipped, so a run from raw data must retrain it, which needs an explicit switch.

**Expert nuance:** Two levels of reproducibility answer two different questions: byte-exact regeneration from stored models proves that the shipped code produced the shipped files (an audit question), while a close retrain from raw data proves the method is stable (a science question); our 99.82 % link agreement answers the second. France differs most in the clean run (identical match lists for 96.72 % of French businesses against about 99.5 % for the US and India). We did not isolate the cause; a plausible reason is that France chains more learned steps on its own earlier scores (both French readers are self-trained on pseudo-labels taken from those scores, and the France rules act on score bands), so a small change early on can compound. A common misconception is that setting a seed makes GPU training deterministic; it fixes the random draws, not the order of floating-point arithmetic.

**Remember:**
- Seeds fix random draws; GPU and bf16 arithmetic still vary in the last digits, which ripples downstream.
- From stored weights and scores: both files byte for byte. From raw data: 99.82 % of links, 99.07 % of businesses identical, validator PASS.
- `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, pinned model revisions, SHA-256 hashes for inputs and outputs.

**Judge might ask:**
- **Q:** "Can someone reproduce your submission exactly?"  
  **A:** Yes, from our trained models and stored reader scores: the inference stages rewrite both files byte for byte, and a fresh extraction of the archive did so too. A full retrain from raw data gives very close files, 99.82 % of links and identical match lists for 99.07 % of businesses with a validator PASS, but not identical ones, because GPU training of the ranker and bf16 training of the readers are not bit-deterministic.
- **Q:** "Where do the differences in a retrain come from?"  
  **A:** A retrained ranker gives slightly different scores, so some shortlists change (12,334,519 candidate pairs instead of 12,293,019) and every later stage follows. France differs most, with identical match lists for 96.72 % of French businesses against about 99.5 % for the US and India; we did not isolate why, but a likely reason is that its readers are self-trained on pseudo-labels taken from earlier scores, so small differences can compound.

## A4 - Our pipeline, step by step, following one record {#a4 .chap}

### How to read this part {#a4-how-to-read-this-part .nc}

Parts A0-A3 taught the building blocks one at a time: what a record and a business are, precision, recall and F0.5, text cleaning, the inverted index and IDF, gradient-boosted trees, cross-encoders, stacking, folds and thresholds, self-training. This part puts them together. We take one incoming record and walk it through every stop of our final, submitted pipeline, in the order the code runs it. At each stop you get the same blocks: **Simple** (an everyday picture), **Our record at this stop** (what happens to the running example), **Technical** (the real mechanism, at the level a senior scientist expects), **Numbers** (the real figures from the Documentation), **Why it exists**, **What it costs**, **Concepts used** (pointers back to Parts A0-A3), **Expert nuance**, and **Judge might ask** (short spoken answers). After the tour we retell the three real worked examples from the Documentation (US, India, France) as numbered walk-throughs, then explain France, which had no labels, in the full concept format, then list traps to avoid and give model answers that explain the whole pipeline in 30 seconds and in 2 minutes.

**Two kinds of numbers.** Read this before anything else.
- **Real numbers** come from the submitted Documentation (tagged "Doc 3", "Doc B.1" and so on), the code README, or the clean-run report. They are the only numbers you may say on stage. A few are marked **derived**: plain arithmetic on Documentation numbers, shown so you can redo it.
- **Illustrative numbers** belong to the running example, which is invented. Its text transformations (cleaning, letter pieces, sound keys) were computed exactly with our shipped normalisation code and the index's definitions, but every count, score and probability attached to it is made up to show the arithmetic. They are always marked "illustrative". **Never quote them to the judges.**

**Words.** We use the plain names of the v3 talk: business, incoming record, shortlist, quick rule-based filter, CatBoost ranker, readers (MiniLM reader, E5 reader, French MiniLM reader, French E5 reader), "what changed" features, LightGBM decision model per country, confident + clear-winner rule, second-chance searches, per-business consistency check, France rules computed by code. Internal code names belong only in the glossary of this study guide.

**Words you will meet in this part (one line each; Parts A0-A3 explain them in depth).**

| Word | Meaning in one line |
|---|---|
| Business | A record of the reference list (Source 1). The thing we link to. |
| Incoming record | A record from Source 2 or Source 3 that we must link to one business, or to none. |
| Candidate / pair | A business we are considering for one incoming record; the two together are a "pair". |
| Blocking | Any cheap step that decides which pairs are worth comparing at all, so we never compare everything with everything. |
| Inverted index | A table from each word (or letter piece) to the list of businesses containing it, like the index at the back of a book. |
| Posting list | The list of businesses stored under one word in the inverted index. Its length is that word's document frequency (df). |
| IDF (inverse document frequency) | A weight that is high for rare words and low for common ones, computed from df. |
| Letter pieces (character n-grams) | Overlapping chunks of n letters: the 3-letter pieces of "dental" are den, ent, nta, tal. |
| Core name | The business name with legal words (inc, llc, pvt, sarl ...) and "and"/"the" removed. |
| Precision / recall | Precision: of the links we make, the share that are right. Recall: of the true links, the share we find. |
| F0.5 | One score combining precision and recall that weighs precision more. |
| Macro average | Score each business separately, then take the plain average over businesses. |
| Fold / held-out fold | One of 10 groups of businesses; a held-out fold is kept away from a model's training and used only to test it. |
| Data leakage | When information from the test side sneaks into training and makes scores look better than they are. |
| Gradient boosting (CatBoost, LightGBM) | A model built from many small decision trees, each one correcting the errors of the ones before it. |
| Early stopping | Stop adding trees (or training steps) when the score on a separate validation fold stops improving. |
| Log loss (binary cross-entropy) | The standard training loss for yes/no predictions: it punishes confident wrong probabilities heavily. |
| Logit / sigmoid | A logit is an unbounded score; the sigmoid 1 / (1 + e^(−logit)) turns it into a probability between 0 and 1. |
| Cross-encoder ("reader") | A transformer language model that reads both texts of a pair together, as one input, and outputs one logit; ours are small ones. |
| Fine-tuning | Further training of a pretrained model on our own labelled examples. |
| Stacking | Training a second model (here the decision model) on the outputs of earlier models plus extra features. |
| Threshold / margin (lead) | The minimum score to accept a link / the minimum gap between the best and the second-best candidate. |
| Pseudo-label / self-training | A model's own very confident guess on unlabelled data, used as if it were a label to train on. |
| Transliteration | Writing a word in another script, for example विजय → vijay. |
| Seed | The number that fixes a model's random choices; different seeds give slightly different models. |

### A4.1 The map: the whole pipeline on one page {#a4-1 .concept}

Everything runs **per country** (US, India, France), and every search stays inside one country. A small configuration file per country, the **country profile**, picks the cleaning rules, readers, decision model, threshold, second-chance searches and rules; the code path is the same for every country (Doc 2.2).

```
incoming record (Source 2 or 3)                          businesses of the same country (Source 1)
        |                                                             |
   [1] normalise text  ----------------------------------->  [1] normalise text, build the index
        |
   [2] index lookup: name words, address words, letter pieces, sounds, exact core name
        |           about 130 candidates per business (blocking study)
   [3] quick rule-based filter (no model)          ->  21.71 per business
        |
   [4] CatBoost ranker -> shortlist (at most 4 per record)  ->  6.75 per business
        |
   [5] readers (cross-encoders) score each shortlist pair
        |
   [6] "what changed" + other features (217 US / 211 India / 158 France)
        |
   [7] LightGBM decision model of that country -> a probability per pair
        |
   [8] confident + clear winner?  yes -> link   no -> stay unlinked
        |
   US / India: [9] native-script second chance (India) -> [10] per-business consistency check -> [11] address second chance
   France:     [12] France rules computed by code
        |
   [13] two output files, checked by the organisers' validator  (7.10 candidates per business in the candidate file)
```

| # | Stop | Runs for | In, then out (real numbers) | Measured cost | Main concepts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Normalisation | all (France adds French rules) | raw text, then cleaned text for the index and features | not timed separately | text normalisation, transliteration |
| 2 | Index lookup | all | 6,724,569,566,212 possible same-country pairs, then about 130.1 candidates per business (blocking study of 25 Sep) | stops 2-4 together on all 9.97 million test records: about 1.3 h | inverted index, IDF, character n-grams, phonetic key |
| 3 | Quick rule-based filter | all | 130.1, then 21.7107 per business (37,614,782 pairs) | no model; held-out F0.5 0.990117 to 0.990086 | rule-based pruning |
| 4 | CatBoost ranker and shortlist | all | 21.71, then 6.75 per business (11,687,317 pairs; at most 4 per record, 1.17 on average) (6.75 and 1.17 derived) | inside the 1.3 h | gradient boosting, top-k with a floor |
| 5 | Readers | all; which readers depends on the country | one logit per reader per shortlist pair | about 1.4 h for two readers per pair (clean run) | cross-encoders, fine-tuning |
| 6 | Features | all | 217 (US), 211 (India), 158 (France, default) features per pair | not timed separately | feature engineering, edit operations |
| 7 | Decision model | one per country | a probability per pair | not timed separately | stacking, LightGBM, seed averaging |
| 8 | Confident + clear winner | all | accepted: US 2,250,036; India 2,726,453; France 887,630 | negligible | threshold, margin, abstention |
| 9 | Native-script second chance | India | 171,713 records searched, +9,759 links | not timed separately | second-stage retrieval, cross-fitting |
| 10 | Consistency check | US, India | US +277 / −284; India +247 / −248 | negligible | count-dependent thresholds |
| 11 | Address second chance | US, India | US +192; India +2,945 links | about 3.2 GB RAM per worker | retrieval cascade, cost-sensitive thresholds |
| 12 | France rules | France | 887,630 accepted, then 867,559 links | not timed separately | deterministic post-model rules |
| 13 | Output and validator | all | 5,856,936 links; 12,293,019 candidate pairs (7.0954 per business); validator PASS | — | validation, reproducibility |

Sources: Doc 2.1, 3, 4, B.1, B.3; times from the clean-run report (CodeREADME 6, clean_run/RESULT.md).

**The idea behind the order.** Cheap steps at the start decide what gets read; expensive models at the end decide what gets linked. Each stage does the cheapest job it can do well, and we measured what each stage loses (QA 1, Script slide 4).

**Judge might ask**
- *Which stage is the most expensive?* "In our clean run from raw data, the two longest inference stages were the index lookup with the quick filter and ranker, about 1.3 hours, and scoring the shortlist with two readers per pair, about 1.4 hours, for 9.97 million records on one machine. On the training side, fine-tuning the MiniLM and E5 readers took about 2.1 hours, and a full retrain from raw data is about 11.5 hours."

### A4.2 The running analogy and our running record {#a4-2 .concept}

#### The post office picture

Imagine a huge post office. About 10 million letters arrive (the **incoming records**), each with a scribbled shop name and address. The post office has a directory of 1.7 million registered shops (the **businesses**). Each letter belongs to at most one shop, or to no registered shop at all, and a shop may receive several letters. The post office is judged shop by shop: a shop is happy only if it gets its own letters and nobody else's, and a shop that should get no letters is happy only if it gets none. Delivering a letter to the wrong shop is worse than holding it back. Every stop below is one desk in this post office.

#### Our record (illustrative, invented for this tour)

An incoming record from Source 2, country US:

| Field | Raw text |
|---|---|
| Name | `Sunrize Dental Care & Implants, LLC` (note the typo: "Sunrize") |
| Address | `0042 North Main Street, Springfield, Illinois` |

Businesses in the US list that it will meet (also invented):

| Label | Business name | Business address |
|---|---|---|
| A | Sunrise Dental Care and Implants LLC | 42 N Main St, Springfield, IL (in this story, the true owner) |
| B | Sunrise Dental Care PC | 1180 Oak Avenue, Peoria, IL |
| C | Sunrise Dental Care | 77 Lake Road, Springfield, IL |
| D | Springfield Smile Clinic | 900 N Main St, Springfield, IL |
| E | Dental Care Implants Studio | 5 Lake Shore Dr, Chicago, IL |

This record is useful because it has a typo, an ampersand, a legal form, a leading zero, a spelled-out state and street type, and competitors that share only the name, only the address, or both. It does not need a second-chance search; the three real examples in section 17 cover those.

---

### A4.3 Stop 0 - Before the record arrives: the task, the score, and what was trained where {#a4-3 .concept}

**Simple.** Before the first letter arrives, the post office must know how it will be judged and must have trained its clerks on old letters whose correct shops are known. It is judged shop by shop, and a wrong delivery hurts more than a held-back letter. The clerks were trained in separate groups on separate piles of old letters, so that the supervisor who checks their work never trusts a clerk on letters that clerk has already memorised.

**Technical.**
- **The task** is many-to-one entity resolution against a reference list: each incoming record (Source 2 or Source 3) links to at most one business (Source 1) or to none; a business can own many records (Doc 2.1).
- **The metric** is F0.5 computed per business and then averaged over all businesses (macro average). Per business: F0.5 = 1.25 · P · R / (0.25 · P + R) = 1.25 · TP / (predicted + 0.25 · true), where TP = correct links, predicted = links we made to that business, true = records it really owns; a business with no true records scores 1 only if we predict nothing for it (Doc 2.1; Code: stack.py `macro`). With beta = 0.5, precision weighs more than recall. Written with error counts, F0.5 = 1.25 · TP / (1.25 · TP + FP + 0.25 · FN) (FP = wrong links, FN = missed links), so inside one business a wrong link weighs four times as much as a missed link in the denominator (derived from the formula).
- **Folds.** All businesses are split into 10 folds by a hash of the business id; every owned incoming record goes with its business, and an unowned record is placed by a hash of its own id (Doc 4; the unowned-record detail is from the code, FACTS C1). This is a group split: records of one business never sit on both sides, which would inflate scores (QA 4).
- **Who trained on what (layer-wise fold separation, a form of stacking without leakage).** "Fit on" = the folds whose labels train the model; "early stopping / tuning" = the fold used to decide when to stop training or to pick a threshold.

| Layer | Fit on | Early stopping / tuning |
|---|---|---|
| Indian-script word list for cleaning | folds 0-5 | — |
| CatBoost ranker | a 140,000-record pilot, its fold 0-5 part | fold 6 |
| MiniLM and E5 readers | labelled pairs of folds 0-5 | none (one epoch) |
| US / India decision models | folds 6-7, then refit on 6-9 (training rows include extra hard examples; describe them only with the QA 15 wording, and only if asked) | fold 8 (at most 3,000 rounds) |
| France / default decision models | folds 6-7, no refit | fold 8 (at most 1,500 rounds) |
| Thresholds | — | 0.75 on fold 8; consistency check on folds 8 and 9 |
| Native-script second-chance model | folds 0-7, word lists that leave out the record's own fold | threshold on fold 8, false positives counted twice |
| Address second-chance models | folds 6-7 | thresholds on fold 8, false positives counted twice |
| French readers | French test pseudo-labels plus labelled US/India pairs | French E5 reader: written checks (Doc B.4) |

(Doc 4, Doc 5; FACTS C2.)

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** Nothing happens to it yet. In our story its true owner is business A, and A truly owns 3 incoming records; the score table below uses that.

**Worked score example (illustrative),** for business A and its 3 true records, plus two cases for a business that owns nothing:

| What we link to A | TP | predicted | true | F0.5 for A |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| exactly its 3 records | 3 | 3 | 3 | 1.25 · 3 / (3 + 0.75) = 1.000 |
| its 3 records plus 1 wrong one | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3.75 / 4.75 = 0.789 |
| only 2 of its 3 records | 2 | 2 | 3 | 2.5 / 2.75 = 0.909 |
| a business with no true records, and we link 1 wrong record | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| a business with no true records, and we link nothing | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 (by the rule) |

One wrong link costs more (1.000 to 0.789) than one missed link (1.000 to 0.909), and a wrong link to an empty business turns 1 into 0. This is why every later stop is **precision first**.

**Numbers (real).** 1,732,544 test businesses (US 663,106; India 809,986; France 259,452) and 9,969,589 incoming records (US 3,817,031; India 4,717,565; France 1,434,993); about 5.75 incoming records per business; labels for the US and India only; France has none (Doc 2.1).

**Why it exists.** Every threshold later on is tuned for this exact per-business metric, not for AUC (area under the ROC curve, a ranking measure that ignores where the threshold sits) (Doc 4), and the fold layering is what lets the decision model trust the reader scores it sees.

**What it costs.** No compute at this stop. The price of the design is data: each model layer learns from only part of the labelled folds (Expert nuance).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Entity resolution; precision and recall; F-beta and macro-averaging; group k-fold; stacking; data leakage.

**Expert nuance.** The fold design is "stacked generalisation with a layer-wise split" rather than the usual out-of-fold predictions: the ranker and readers are trained once on folds 0-5, so their scores on folds 6-9 are honest out-of-sample scores, and the decision models learn only from those folds (FACTS C2). A second benefit: for the US and India, at test time the decision model receives scores from exactly the same ranker and readers, which are also out-of-sample on test records, so the score distributions it learned from match the ones it is applied to; with out-of-fold predictions, the test-time models would differ from the ones that produced the training inputs. The price is that each layer sees less data than a full cross-fitting scheme would give it.

**Judge might ask**
- *About 41 % of incoming records end up unlinked. Isn't that a lot?* "Some incoming records belong to no business in the list, and linking them anyway would be a wrong link. Our final file has 0.5875 links per incoming record, so about 41 % stay unlinked (derived), and 100,087 businesses, 5.8 %, have an empty row; under per-business F0.5 a correct empty row is worth a full point, so we link only a clear winner."

---

### A4.4 Stop 1 - Normalisation (cleaning the text) {#a4-4 .concept}

**Simple.** Before looking anything up, a clerk rewrites the scribbled envelope in one standard style: all small letters, "&" written as "and", "Street" always written "st", "Illinois" always "il", no leading zeros on house numbers. Two envelopes that mean the same thing should now look the same, so that the directory lookup at the next desk finds them. For Indian names written in Devanagari or other scripts, the clerk uses a phrase book learned from old letters to write each word in Latin letters. France gets extra house rules, for example "15B" becomes "15 bis" and "S.A.R.L." becomes "sarl". The cleaned copy is only for searching and comparing; the expert readers later read the original envelope.

**Our record at this stop (computed with our shipped code).**

| | Raw | After cleaning |
|---|---|---|
| Record name | `Sunrize Dental Care & Implants, LLC` | `sunrize dental care and implants llc` |
| Record address | `0042 North Main Street, Springfield, Illinois` | `42 n main st springfield il` |
| Business A name | `Sunrise Dental Care and Implants LLC` | `sunrise dental care and implants llc` |
| Business A address | `42 N Main St, Springfield, IL` | `42 n main st springfield il` |

After cleaning, the two addresses are identical, and the names differ only in "sunrize" against "sunrise". The cleaning cannot fix the typo; the letter-piece and sound channels of the next stop exist for that.

More cleaning examples, also computed with our code:

| Raw | Cleaned | Rule that fired |
|---|---|---|
| `B0B'S Pizza & Grill` (name, US/India rules) | `bob s pizza and grill` | a 0 next to a letter becomes o; & becomes and; punctuation becomes a space |
| `2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN` (French address) | `2 rue suzanne lenglen` | French street type "R" canonicalised |
| `15B Av. Jean Jaurès` (French address) | `15 bis av jean jaures` | glued suffix split, accents removed |
| `N° 7 bd St Michel` (French address) | `7 bd saint michel` | N° prefix removed, st expanded to saint |
| `S.A.R.L. Dupont et Fils` (French name) | `sarl dupont and fils` | dotted legal form collapsed, et becomes and |
| `5ARL Martin & Cie` (French name) | `sarl martin and cie` | "leet" legal form repaired |

**Technical.**
- **US and India rules** (Doc 2.2; Code: prepare.py): lower case; `&` to `and`; every other non-alphanumeric character to a space; in addresses, state names and street abbreviations mapped to one form (street to st, north to n, illinois to il, and so on) and leading zeros dropped from numbers; in names, a `0` next to a letter becomes `o`. Non-ASCII words in addresses (accented letters or other scripts) are always transliterated with unidecode (a library that maps each Unicode character to the closest plain Latin letters).
- **Indian scripts.** Each non-Latin name word goes through an Indic-to-Latin word list learned from labelled training matches of folds 0-5; if the word is missing, a generic transliteration (unidecode) is used. The word list is a co-occurrence alignment: each native-script word of an incoming name is counted against the words of its true business's cleaned name; it gets its best Latin word only if they co-occur at least 3 times (n ≥ 3), the pairing covers at least 0.35 of the native word's occurrences, and its score n / (count of the Latin word + 1)^0.6 is at least 1.8 times the runner-up's (Code: learn_lexicon.py). Dividing by the Latin word's own frequency stops very common words such as "private" or "enterprises", which co-occur with almost every native word, from winning everywhere; the 0.6 power softens that penalty. It is not a neural transliterator.
- **France rules** (Doc 2.2): region, department and city components learned from the unlabelled test files; N°/numéro prefixes removed; `15B` to `15 bis`; bis/ter/quater unified; French street types and their typos canonicalised (the typo table is learned from the test files); st/ste expanded to saint/sainte; dotted and leet legal forms collapsed (`S.A.R.L.` and `5arl` to `sarl`). The code also maps `et` to `and` and unifies a few French abbreviations.
- **The readers read the raw text**, not the cleaned text (Doc 2.2).
- **A country without a profile** gets the US/India rules (Code: profiles/default.json).

**Numbers (real).** Word-list thresholds 3 / 0.35 / 1.8 are fixed values in the code; the word list itself is learned from folds 0-5 (Code: learn_lexicon.py). The French geography and street-type typo table are learned from the unlabelled test files, which the Documentation discloses (Doc C.1). Separately, the pipeline computes an unsupervised native-script-to-Latin word alignment on test records whose first-stage top candidate has probability at least 0.9; it uses no labels and is disclosed in the same item (Doc C.1).

**Why it exists.** The index of the next stop matches exact tokens. Without cleaning, "Street" and "St", "Illinois" and "IL", "0042" and "42" would be different words and the true business would score lower or not be found at all.

**What it costs.** A few string operations per record, done once per record; the Documentation gives no separate time. The real cost is design effort: every rule is a decision about which differences do not matter.

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Text normalisation; Unicode and transliteration; tokens.

**Expert nuance.** Normalisation is lossy on purpose, so it is used only where exact token equality matters (the index and the hand-made features). The readers get the raw strings, so information that cleaning throws away, such as the original script, the brackets in "(Inc)" or capitalisation, is still available to the most accurate model. A second subtlety: the cleaning word list for Indian scripts is learned from labels, so it can only translate words that appeared in labelled training matches, and it keeps one spelling per word; other words fall back to a generic transliteration that may not match the Latin spelling a business uses. The native-script second chance (Stop 9) attacks the same weakness by trying several spellings per name.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why do the readers read raw text if you built careful cleaning rules?* "The cleaning exists for exact token matching in the index and in our hand-made features. The readers are multilingual pretrained models that handle case, punctuation and scripts themselves, so we give them the original text and keep the information that cleaning throws away."
- *How do Indian-script names get into a Latin-script index?* "Each native-script word goes through a word list learned from labelled training matches of folds 0-5: a native word gets a Latin word only if they co-occur at least 3 times and the pairing clearly beats the runner-up; otherwise we fall back to a generic transliteration. For records the main pass still leaves unlinked, the native-script second chance tries up to 64 spellings per name inside the same state."

---

### A4.5 Stop 2 - Index lookup (finding candidates) {#a4-5 .concept}

**Simple.** Comparing every letter with every shop in its country would mean 6.7 trillion comparisons, so the clerk uses the directory's index, like the index at the back of a book: for every word, it lists the shops whose name or address contains that word. The clerk looks up the rare words first, because a rare word like "implants" points to a few shops, while a common word like "street" points to almost everyone and is skipped. There are separate indexes for name words, address words, short letter pieces of the name (so a typo still matches most pieces) and a "sound" version of the name. Each shop collects points for every rare word it shares with the letter, and the clerk keeps the best-scoring shops from several lists, so that a shop matching only by address or only by name is not lost.

**Our record at this stop (text keys computed with our code's definitions; counts and scores illustrative).**

First the record is split into the five channels (Doc 3; Code: matcher.cpp):

| Channel | What is indexed | Our record |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Name words | words of the **core name** (legal words such as inc, llc, pvt, sarl, sas, and "and"/"the", removed) | sunrize, dental, care, implants |
| 2. Address words | words of the cleaned address | 42, n, main, st, springfield, il |
| 3. 4-letter pieces | character 4-grams of the core name written without spaces, `sunrizedentalcareimplants` | 22 distinct pieces: sunr, unri, nriz, rize, ... |
| 4. 3-letter pieces | character 3-grams of the same string | 23 distinct pieces |
| 5. Sounds | 4-grams of a consonant skeleton: core-name words sorted alphabetically, vowels (a, e, i, o, u and y) deleted, repeated letters collapsed, spaces removed: `care dental implants sunrize` becomes `cr dntl mplnts snrz`, then `crdntlmplntssnrz` | 13 distinct pieces |
| plus exact key | the sorted set of core-name words | {care, dental, implants, sunrize} |

How the typo plays out against business A (`sunrise dental care implants`), computed exactly:

| Channel | Shared with A | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Name words | 3 of 4 (dental, care, implants) | "sunrize" matches nothing |
| 4-letter pieces | 18 of 22 | only the 4 pieces around the z differ (nriz, rize, ized, zede) |
| 3-letter pieces | 20 of 23 | only riz, ize, zed differ |
| Sound pieces | 12 of 13 | only snrz against snrs differs |
| Exact key | no | one typo breaks the exact-key channel |

So one wrong letter costs one name word, but most letter pieces and sound pieces still match: that is exactly why those channels exist.

Now the points (illustrative document frequencies; N = 663,106 US businesses is real). The index uses **IDF = ln(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1))**, where df is how many businesses contain the term:

| Term | df (illustrative) | IDF | Used? |
|---|---|---|---|
| implants (name) | 300 | 7.698 | yes |
| dental (name) | 5,000 | 4.895 | yes |
| care (name) | 20,000 | 3.531 | **no**: longer than the name cap of 14,000 |
| sunrize (name) | 0 | — | not in the index at all |
| springfield (address) | 2,500 | 5.584 | yes |
| 42 (address) | 6,000 | 4.714 | yes |
| main (address) | 9,000 | 4.313 | yes |
| il, n, st (address) | 25,000 / 120,000 / 250,000 | 3.315 / 1.876 / 1.295 | **no**: longer than the address cap of 10,000 |

Rarest first, within the address budget of 18,000 postings: springfield (2,500), then 42 (running total 8,500), then main (17,500), all inside the budget.

Business A's scores (word parts only; the real name score also adds the letter-piece and sound points):
- Name-word part: (7.698 + 4.895) / (1 + 4 name words of A)^0.22 = 12.593 / 1.425 = **8.838**
- Address score: (5.584 + 4.714 + 4.313) / (1 + 6 address words of A)^0.30 = 14.611 / 1.793 = **8.150**
- Total: ns + as + 1.2 · min(ns, as) = 8.838 + 8.150 + 1.2 · 8.150 = **26.768**

The last term, 1.2 · min(ns, as), is a bonus that is large only when both the name and the address match. Business B (same-sounding name, Peoria) gets name points but no address points, because its only shared address word, "il", is too common to be used for retrieval, so as = 0 and its bonus is zero; business D (same street, different name) gets address points but few name points. Business A gets both.

**Technical.**
- Written in C++17 with OpenMP (a standard library for running one loop on many CPU cores in parallel), built over the businesses of one country on cleaned text (Doc 3).
- **Scoring is an IDF-weighted set overlap**, not TF-IDF cosine and not BM25: every record is a set of unique terms, there is no term-frequency component (Doc 3; FACTS A2). IDF is smoothed: ln(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1)). Unlike the textbook ln(N / df), this never reaches 0: even a term found in every business keeps a weight of about ln 2 = 0.69, while a term found in exactly one US business gets ln(1 + 663,107 / 2), about 12.71 (derived). (In the 76 features, a record term missing from the index is given IDF 12; Code: matcher.cpp.)
- **Rarest first with caps and budgets.** Query terms are processed from rarest to most common (shortest posting list first); a term is skipped if its posting list is longer than the channel's cap, and a term is also skipped if adding its list would push the channel past its total posting budget. Caps / budgets: name 14,000 / 22,000; address 10,000 / 18,000; 4-grams 2,500 / 15,000; 3-grams 1,000 / 6,000; sounds 800 / 4,000. Channel weights 1 / 1 / 0.45 / 0.22 / 0.18 (Doc 3). So one record touches at most 22,000 + 18,000 + 15,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 = 65,000 posting entries (derived), plus at most 2,000 from the exact-key channel below.
- **Sound key detail** (Code: matcher.cpp): a consonant equal to the previous kept consonant is dropped even when a vowel sits between them, so "lol" becomes "l"; the collapse happens before the spaces are removed, which is why "mplnts snrz" keeps its double s in `crdntlmplntssnrz`.
- **Scores.** Name score ns = name-word IDF sum / (1 + business core-name words)^0.22 + letter-piece and sound sum / (1 + business 4-grams)^0.38; address score as = address IDF sum / (1 + business address words)^0.30; total = ns + as + 1.2 · min(ns, as) (Doc 3). Only the terms actually processed (within caps and budgets) add points. The exponents are length normalisations, in the spirit of BM25's document-length term: a long business name has more chances to contain some of the record's words, and a shared word says less when it is one of many, so the sum is divided by a slowly growing (sub-linear) function of the business's term count. Exponents well below 1 correct for length without punishing long names too hard.
- **Kept per record** (a union of several top lists, which is what makes retrieval recall-first): the top 12 by total, the top 6 by name score, the top 6 by address score (address score > 0), and every business with the **same sorted core-name word set** if at most 2,000 businesses share it (Doc 3).
- **76 pair features** are computed for every kept candidate: 7 string similarities (normalised longest-common-subsequence ratio, 2 · LCS / (len a + len b), computed bit-parallel), set statistics for name words, address words, letter pieces, sound pieces and numbers, length counts, equality flags, IDF overlaps, token alignment, a common-prefix share, exact core-name group sizes, and 8 retrieval scores (Doc 3; FACTS A2).
- No embeddings, no vector search and no learned model in this stage.

**Numbers (real).**
- Same-country comparison space: 6,724,569,566,212 pairs (Doc 3).
- About 130.1 candidates per business out of the index (blocking study of 25 Sep 2026, Doc 3). In all-fold train samples: 27.541 candidates per incoming record (US), 23.145 (India) (Doc B.2).
- Recall on labelled train fold 9 (share of owned records whose true business is among the candidates): **99.3694 % US, 98.5068 % India** (Doc B.2).

**Why it exists.** It turns an impossible all-pairs problem into a small candidate list while keeping almost every true business. It is deterministic, fast and easy to audit.

**What it costs.** The index lookup, the quick filter and the ranker together took about 1.3 hours for all 9.97 million test records in our clean run (stage i1; clean-run report). That stage runs the index and the ranker with 6 threads by default (CodeREADME 2, setting `BLOCK_THREADS`); the 8-11 threads quoted in CodeREADME 1 are for the index runs of the training stages. The work per record is bounded by the caps and budgets, so total cost grows linearly with the number of records.

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Blocking; inverted index; IDF; character n-grams; phonetic keys; recall ceiling.

**Expert nuance.** The cap acts as a stop-word list learned from the data: a word becomes "too common to retrieve with" once it appears in more than 14,000 business names or 10,000 addresses; apart from the small list of legal words (and "and", "the") removed from core names, there is no hand-written stop-word list for retrieval. Common words still count in the 76 features and in the readers; they just do not drive retrieval. The weak spot is a business whose only shared evidence is a common word, or a brand name with no word overlap at all; that is where a dense vector channel would help, which we did not benchmark (QA 1). Also note that the sound key is our own consonant skeleton, not Soundex or Metaphone (FACTS F2).

**Judge might ask**
- *Why an IDF-weighted overlap and not BM25 or TF-IDF cosine?* "Business names and addresses are short and almost never repeat a word, so term frequency carries almost no information; we treat each record as a set of unique terms and sum the smoothed IDF of the shared ones. What we do need is length normalisation so long names do not win by size: we divide by one plus the business's term count, raised to 0.22 for name words, 0.38 for letter pieces and 0.30 for address words."
- *How do you stop common words like "street" or "enterprises" from blowing up the work?* "Rarest terms first, with a cap per list: a term whose posting list is longer than 14,000 businesses for name words or 10,000 for address words is skipped, and each channel has a total budget, so one record touches at most 65,000 posting entries. Common words still count in the later features; they just do not drive retrieval."
- *Why keep separate top lists by name and by address?* "Because a single combined score drops candidates that match on one side only, such as a renamed business at the same address or a moved business with the same name. We keep the top 12 by total, the top 6 by name, the top 6 by address and every business with exactly the same core-name words, and that union keeps the true business for 99.37 % of US and 98.51 % of Indian held-out records."

---

### A4.6 Stop 3 - Quick rule-based filter {#a4-6 .concept}

**Simple.** The index desk hands over a pile of candidate shops for every letter; across the whole post office that is about 130 candidates for every registered shop. Before the senior clerk spends any time, a junior clerk throws out the shops that are clearly weaker than the best one, using a short checklist and no judgement at all. The checklist has safety clauses: never throw out the shop with the best address match, a shop whose address covers almost all of the letter's address, a shop with exactly the same name once words like "LLC" or "Pvt Ltd" are ignored, or a candidate for a very short name such as an acronym. It is almost free and it almost never throws away the right shop.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** Five candidates came out of the index. A candidate is kept if **any** clause holds (Doc 3):

| Candidate | total | total / best | best by address? | address coverage | kept? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A, Sunrise Dental Care and Implants LLC, 42 N Main St, Springfield | 31.0 | 1.00 | yes | 1.000 | **kept** (best total; also best address; also coverage ≥ 0.95) |
| C, Sunrise Dental Care, 77 Lake Road, Springfield | 20.5 | 0.66 | no | 0.422 | **kept** (total ≥ 0.6 × best) |
| B, Sunrise Dental Care PC, 1180 Oak Avenue, Peoria | 12.0 | 0.39 | no | 0.157 | dropped |
| D, Springfield Smile Clinic, 900 N Main St, Springfield | 9.5 | 0.31 | no | 0.777 | dropped (coverage below 0.95) |
| E, Dental Care Implants Studio, 5 Lake Shore Dr, Chicago | 8.0 | 0.26 | no | 0.157 | dropped |

The coverage column is computed from the illustrative IDFs of Stop 2: coverage = the IDF share of the record's address words found in the business's address. For D, every word except "42" is found: (21.097 − 4.714) / 21.097 = 0.777. The "same core name" clause could not fire for any candidate, because the typo "sunrize" gives our record a core-name set that no business has, and the "short name" clause does not apply because the name is long.

**Technical.** No model; every test is a threshold on retrieval statistics the index already computed (Doc 3; Code: prune.py). Keep a candidate if any of:
- (a) it has the record's best total (ties kept);
- (b) total ≥ 0.6 · max(1, best total);
- (c) it is the record's best candidate by address score (address score > 0);
- (d) address coverage ≥ 0.95;
- (e) the record name has at most 3 characters and coverage ≥ 0.4 (initials and acronyms);
- (f) same core-name word set and coverage ≥ 0.3.

Clauses (c) to (f) protect address-only, short-name or acronym, and same-name candidates that a combined score would drop (Doc 3). The `max(1, ...)` in (b) stops the rule from keeping everything when the best total is tiny.

**Numbers (real).**
- 37,614,782 pairs kept, **21.7107 per business**; per country US 15.0352, India 23.6328, France 32.7713 (Doc 3). About 3.77 per incoming record (derived: 37,614,782 / 9,969,589).
- In all-fold train samples: 3.111 (US) and 3.878 (India) candidates per incoming record after the filter (Doc B.2).
- Measured cost (blocking study of 25 Sep, with the decision model of that date): the true business survived for **99.974 %** of fold-8/9 records; fold-9 macro F0.5 moved from **0.990117 to 0.990086**; fold 8 −0.00004 (Doc 3). Fold-9 sample recall: 99.3658 % (US) at the index, 99.3523 % after the filter (Doc B.2).

**Why it exists.** Without it, the CatBoost ranker would score about 130 candidates per business; with it, about 22. A learned pruner would itself need a model pass over all 130.

**What it costs.** Essentially nothing in compute (comparisons on numbers already in memory) and 0.00003 F0.5 on held-out fold 9 (0.990117 − 0.990086, derived).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Blocking; rule-based pruning; the recall-cost trade-off.

**Expert nuance.** Three things to be precise about. First, 130.1 per business comes from the blocking study, not from the final run; the final run reports 21.7107 after the filter (FACTS H2). Second, the decision models were trained on shortlists built from the index output without the filter (Doc 4), so the filter is a test-time cost-saving step. That creates a small train/test difference: at test time the ranker ranks, and the shortlist is cut from, the filtered candidates, so a few context features (ranks, shortlist size) can differ from what the decision model saw in training. The 25 September measurement ran the decision model of that date on filtered candidates, so it captures this effect for that model; the Documentation reports no repeat with the final models, so do not present it as one. Third, the rule's thresholds sit on the index's own scores, so it inherits the index's blind spots: a true business with a low total and a weak address match is dropped here unless clause (e) or (f) protects it.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why a hand-written filter rather than a learned pruner?* "A learned pruner would need a model pass over all of the roughly 130 candidates per business, while our rule reuses statistics the index already computed. Its measured cost is tiny: the true business survived for 99.974 % of held-out records, and fold-9 F0.5 moved from 0.990117 to 0.990086."
- *Where do 0.6 and the coverage thresholds come from?* "From our blocking study of 25 September, which measured how many candidates the rule keeps and the held-out F0.5 with it. The special clauses protect address-only matches, very short names and acronyms, and same-name businesses, which a single score would drop."

---

### A4.7 Stop 4 - CatBoost ranker and the shortlist {#a4-7 .concept}

**Simple.** A senior clerk now looks at the remaining candidates of each letter and puts them in order, most likely first, using the 76 measurements the index desk already wrote down. Only the top candidate always goes forward, plus up to three more if the clerk thinks they have at least a one-in-a-thousand chance. That short list, at most four shops per letter, is the only thing the expensive expert readers will ever see. Most letters end up with just one candidate, because the senior clerk is usually sure.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** The ranker gives A a probability of 0.97 and C 0.006. Rank 0 (A) always goes forward; rank 1 (C) goes forward because 0.006 ≥ 0.001. Our shortlist is {A, C}: two pairs.

**Technical.**
- **Model:** CatBoost on the 76 index features; loss Logloss (log loss); up to 1,600 trees; depth 7; learning rate 0.075 (how much each new tree is allowed to change the prediction); L2 regularisation 5 (a penalty that shrinks leaf values towards zero); early stopping 180 (stop if 180 more trees bring no improvement on the stopping fold); trained on GPU (Doc 4). CatBoost grows symmetric (oblivious) trees by default, and our code does not change that: every node at the same depth uses the same split, so depth 7 means 2^7 = 128 leaves per tree (Code: train_base_v6.py).
- **It is a pointwise binary classifier**, P(candidate is the true business), whose probability we sort by. It is not trained with a learning-to-rank loss such as LambdaMART (Doc 4; FACTS H3).
- **Training data:** a pilot of 140,000 training incoming records (35,000 per country and source), whose fold 0-5 part is fitted; fold 6 is used for early stopping (Doc 4).
- **Shortlist rule:** per incoming record, the top-ranked candidate always, and ranks 2-4 only if the ranker probability is at least 0.001; so at most 4 per record (Doc 3; in code: K = 4, floor 1e-3).
- The ranker's probability and rank are also inputs of the decision model (Doc 4).

**Numbers (real).**
- Shortlist: **11,687,317 pairs**; US 4,098,587; India 5,485,623; France 2,103,107 (Doc 3). That is **6.75 per business** and **1.17 per incoming record** (both derived).
- In all-fold train samples: 1.114 (US) and 1.174 (India) shortlist pairs per incoming record (Doc B.2).
- Recall in the shortlist, train fold 9: US 98.8748 % to 99.3628 % (lower and upper bound), India 98.0572 % to 98.4831 %; without the filter, the top 4 alone keep 98.8814 % (US) and 98.0809 % (India) (Doc B.2). **The largest loss of the whole cascade is the cap of four** (Doc 3).

**Why it exists.** To protect the readers: at most four pairs per record, 1.17 on average, reach the expensive cross-encoders, so their cost stays linear in the number of records.

**What it costs.** Scoring is inside the 1.3 hours of Stop 2. Training the ranker is part of clean-run stage t1 (folds, word list, index and ranker training), about 1.4 hours. In recall, up to about half a percentage point: US 99.37 % at the index against at least 98.87 % in the shortlist. The one exact full-fold comparison is the cap alone, without the filter: US 99.3694 % to 98.8814 %, India 98.5068 % to 98.0809 %, a loss of 0.49 and 0.43 points (derived, Doc B.2).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Gradient boosting; CatBoost; log loss; pointwise ranking; top-k with a probability floor.

**Expert nuance.** The cap of 4 is a ceiling that is rarely reached: about 3.77 candidates per record reach the ranker (derived), yet the shortlist averages only 1.17 per record, and 90.59 % of records end with exactly one candidate in the final candidate file (Doc B.1). So the quick filter and the 0.001 floor do most of the narrowing, while the cap mainly bounds the worst case per record, which is what keeps reader cost linear. The Documentation records no tuning study for the floor (FACTS B.5), so present it as a fixed design value. A pointwise classifier is a reasonable ranker here because the candidate lists are tiny and we also need a usable absolute probability, both for the floor and as an input to the decision model.

**Judge might ask**
- *Is your CatBoost ranker a learning-to-rank model?* "No. It is a pointwise binary classifier, CatBoost with log loss, predicting the probability that a candidate is the true business, and we sort by that probability. We need two things from it: a good order for the top four and an absolute probability for the 0.001 floor, and its probability and rank are also inputs to the decision model."
- *The shortlist costs about half a percentage point of recall. Why accept that?* "It is our largest recall loss: on fold 9 the US goes from 99.37 % at the index to at least 98.87 % in the shortlist, India from 98.51 % to at least 98.06 %. In exchange at most four pairs per record, 1.17 on average, reach the expensive readers, the second-chance searches recover part of the misses, and with finer blocking keys we would have room for a larger cap."

---

### A4.8 Stop 5 - Readers (cross-encoders) {#a4-8 .concept}

**Simple.** Now an expert reader puts the letter and one candidate shop's registration card side by side and reads them together, word against word, then gives one number: how strongly they believe it is the same business. Because they read both texts at once, they notice small but decisive details, like "Inc" turning into "LLC", or the same name in a different city. The readers are small pretrained language models (they already "know" many languages from general text) that we fine-tuned, meaning trained further, on labelled US and Indian examples. For France, two extra readers were trained on French examples that our own models had labelled with very high confidence (Section 18).

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** The reader sees, as one input, the raw record text and the raw business text:

```
record side:   Sunrize Dental Care & Implants, LLC | 0042 North Main Street, Springfield, Illinois
business side: Sunrise Dental Care and Implants LLC | 42 N Main St, Springfield, IL
```

Illustrative outputs: MiniLM reader logit +6.2 for A and −4.8 for C; E5 reader +5.9 for A and −5.3 for C. A **logit** is a score on an unbounded scale; the sigmoid turns it into a probability: sigmoid(6.2) = 1 / (1 + e^−6.2) = 0.998, sigmoid(−4.8) = 0.008.

A real example of why reading both sides matters (France, Doc D.3): for "TQ COMITE SARL, 2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN, NANTES" against the business with the identical name "TQ Comite SARL" in Pessac, another city, the plain MiniLM reader gave +7.125 (a probability of about 0.999, derived), but the French readers gave −1.9219 and −10.8125, and the blend was −3.2008 (about 0.039, derived).

**Technical.**
- **Architecture (all four readers):** each side is encoded as raw `name | address` text; the two sides are fed together as one sequence pair, tokenised (split into sub-word units) with the MiniLM tokenizer, and truncated longest-first to 128 tokens (tokens are cut from whichever side is longer until the pair fits); the transformer's last hidden states, one vector per token, are averaged over the real tokens and not the padding (masked mean pooling); dropout 0.1 (randomly zeroing 10 % of values during training, a regulariser); a linear head turns the averaged vector into one logit (Doc 4). The head is tiny: 385 parameters for MiniLM (a 384-wide weight vector plus a bias) and 769 for E5 (768 + 1).
- **Why cross-encoder.** All tokens of both texts attend to each other in every layer, so the model can compare "Inc" with "LLC" directly. A bi-encoder would compress each side into one vector first and compare the vectors afterwards, which is cheaper (business vectors can be precomputed) but can miss that exactly one word changed (Explainer slide 7). The cost is a full transformer pass per pair, which is why readers see only the shortlist.
- **Training recipe (all four):** binary cross-entropy (log loss on the match / no-match label); AdamW optimiser (Adam with weight decay applied separately from the gradient step; decay 0.01), with the new head learning 5 times faster than the pretrained body; a 3 % linear warm-up (the learning rate rises from 0 over the first 3 % of steps, which protects the pretrained weights from large early updates), then linear decay; bf16 autocast (most matrix maths in 16-bit "brain float", which roughly halves activation memory and speeds up the GPU, while the weights stay in 32-bit); gradient clipping at norm 1.0 (the gradient is rescaled whenever its overall size exceeds 1.0, which prevents unstable steps); one epoch (each training pair seen once); batch 128; length-bucketed batches (pairs of similar length are batched together, so less padding is computed) (Doc 4; code).
- **Training pairs (MiniLM and E5 readers):** labelled US/India train pairs of folds 0-5: every hard record (top ranker probability between 0.003 and 0.9995, a non-owner ranked first, or a second probability above 0.003) plus a random 25 % of the others; candidates 1-4 enter if ranked first, with probability at least 0.001, or if they are the owner; candidates 5-8 only if they are the owner (Doc 4). Learning rate 5e-5.

| Reader | Base model | Parameters | Licence | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MiniLM reader | paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2, fine-tuned | 117,653,760 + 385 | Apache-2.0 | all countries (US, India, France, default) |
| E5 reader | multilingual-e5-base, fine-tuned | 278,043,648 + 769 | MIT | US and India; starting point of the French E5 reader |
| French MiniLM reader | the MiniLM reader, fine-tuned on French pseudo-labels | as MiniLM | Apache-2.0 | France |
| French E5 reader | the E5 reader, fine-tuned on French pseudo-labels, 7,419 steps | as E5 | MIT | France |

(Doc 4, Doc B.5.) Which readers a country uses: US and India, the MiniLM and E5 readers; France, MiniLM + French MiniLM + French E5, blended 0.35 / 0.15 / 0.5 into one score; an unseen country, the MiniLM reader only. The plain E5 reader is not used for France (Doc 4).

**Numbers (real).** Readers score only the shortlist; second-chance candidates are scored by the second-chance models (Doc 4). A larger reader, XLM-R large (about 560 million parameters, MIT), was tried in development and discarded (Doc B.5).

**Why it exists.** It is the most accurate pair judge we have, and the only stage that reads the raw text of both sides together.

**What it costs.** In our clean run, scoring the shortlist with two readers per pair (every reader except the French E5 reader) took about 1.4 hours on one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER 16 GB; retraining and scoring the French E5 reader took about 0.6 hours; fine-tuning the MiniLM and E5 readers took about 2.1 hours (clean-run report). In the submitted run, most reader logits were reused from earlier scoring runs (11,638,504 pairs) and 48,813 pairs were scored on CPU (CodeREADME 6); together these are exactly the 11,687,317 shortlist pairs (derived).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Transformers and attention; cross-encoder versus bi-encoder; fine-tuning; binary cross-entropy; logits and sigmoid; mixed precision; hard-example mining.

**Expert nuance.** A "mini" model with 118 million parameters sounds odd; as general background (not stated in our documents), most of the parameters of these multilingual encoders sit in the large shared vocabulary table, and the MiniLM and E5 base models use the same multilingual SentencePiece vocabulary, which is why one tokenizer serves all four readers. A second point: the training-pair rule deliberately over-samples hard records, so most of the reader's training budget goes to the confusions that reach it at test time (candidates 1-4 mirror the shortlist rule). Owners that the ranker placed fifth to eighth never reach a reader at test time; they are added as hard positives, true matches whose index statistics look weak, so the reader learns to recognise a true match from the text itself. The random quarter of easy records keeps the training data close to the ordinary cases the reader will also see. Third, readers are trained for one epoch only, which limits over-fitting to the training businesses.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why two different readers for the US and India?* "Two different pretrained models make partly different mistakes, and the decision model gets both logits, their mean, and each one's rank and lead within the shortlist, so it can use their agreement. Both are small open models, about 118 million and 278 million parameters, far under the 8-billion limit; the Documentation reports no separate number for the E5 reader's contribution."
- *Which pairs did the readers train on?* "Labelled US and Indian pairs from folds 0-5: every hard record, meaning the ranker was unsure, put a wrong business first, or gave the second candidate more than 0.003, plus a random quarter of the easy ones. Owners the ranker placed fifth to eighth were also included as extra true matches, so the reader learns what a true match looks like even when the index statistics undervalue it."

---

### A4.9 Stop 6 - "What changed" features and the rest of the feature vector {#a4-9 .concept}

**Simple.** Before the supervisor decides, a clerk fills in a form for each candidate. The usual question is "how similar are they?". Our form also asks "what exactly changed?": did a house number change and by how much, were words added, dropped or replaced, how rare and how close in meaning are those words, and did the legal form change, say from Inc to LLC? The reason is that similar-looking edits can mean opposite things: dropping a suffix is typical of a genuine record, while swapping the legal form often means a different company. The form also copies in the readers' scores and how each candidate compares with its rivals for the same letter.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative; the definitions are exact).** Comparing the record's core-name words [sunrize, dental, care, implants] and house number 42 with the two shortlisted businesses:

| "What changed" feature | vs A: sunrise dental care implants, 42 | vs C: sunrise dental care, 77 |
|---|---|---|
| words replaced / added / deleted | 1 / 0 / 0 | 1 / 1 / 0 |
| first new word, first dropped word | sunrize, sunrise | sunrize, sunrise |
| relative position of the first new / dropped word | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| replaced in place (same position)? | yes | yes |
| common words keep their order? | yes (dental, care, implants) | yes (dental, care) |
| character similarity of first new vs first dropped word (RapidFuzz ratio, = 2 · LCS / total length × 100) | 85.7 | 85.7 |
| IDF-weighted Jaccard of the word sets (illustrative IDFs: sunrize 12.0, sunrise 7.0, dental 5.0, care 3.5, implants 7.5) | 16.0 / (16.0 + 12.0 + 7.0) = 0.457 | 8.5 / (8.5 + 19.5 + 7.0) = 0.243 |
| legal-form relation | same (LLC and LLC) | business has none |
| unmatched house numbers | none (42 = 42) | record 42, business 77: difference 42 − 77 = −35, so absolute difference 35, largest negative difference −35 and no positive one; relative difference −35 / 77 = −0.45; digit edit distance 2 ("42" to "77" needs two substitutions); common prefix 0; common suffix 0; digit-length difference 0 |

How the word counts are defined (Code: clean_feats.py): a "new" word is in the record but not in the business, a "dropped" word is in the business but not in the record; replaced = the smaller of the two counts, added = new − replaced, deleted = dropped − replaced. Against C the record has two new words (sunrize, implants) and one dropped word (sunrise), so 1 replaced, 1 added, 0 deleted. The IDF-weighted Jaccard = IDF of shared words / (IDF of shared + new + dropped words).

Read the A column: the IDF-weighted Jaccard alone would punish the typo (a rare "new" word), but the in-place flag and the character similarity of 85.7 say "this looks like a spelling variant", and the readers saw the raw text too. The decision model learns from labels how these signals combine.

**Technical.**
- **The "what changed" block** = 25 generic pair features + the legal-form relation + the number relation (Doc 2.2, Doc 4; Code: clean_feats.py):
  - **Numbers (8 features)** over address digit runs not shared by both records (up to 8 per address): smallest absolute difference between an extra number of the record and a missing number of the business, smallest positive and largest negative difference (record minus business), relative difference of the closest pair ((record − business) / business), Damerau-Levenshtein distance of the two digit strings (the number of single-character insertions, deletions, substitutions or swaps of two neighbours), common prefix and suffix length, digit-length difference. When there is no unmatched pair, the features are left missing (or set to −1), which a tree model can route down its own branch.
  - **Name words (14 features)** on the raw name (lower-cased, accents stripped, transliterated with the training word list, legal-form words and and/et/& removed; up to 8 words): counts of replaced, added and deleted words; relative positions of the first new and first dropped word; an in-place flag; an order flag; character similarity of the first new versus first dropped word; IDF of the first new and first dropped word; maximum and minimum IDF over new words; maximum IDF over dropped words; IDF-weighted Jaccard. IDF here = ln((N + 1) / (df + 1)) over all records of the country, label-free.
  - **Meaning similarity (3 features)** from the pretrained, not fine-tuned, MiniLM encoder applied to single words: cosine similarity (near 1 for words used in similar contexts, near 0 for unrelated words) of the first new versus first dropped word, and the best cosine of each to any word of the other name.
  - **Legal-form relation** (classes such as same, changed, record has none, business has none) and **number relation** of the unmatched digit runs, with forensic legal-form and number comparisons (Doc 4).
- **The rest of the vector** (Doc 4): the 76 index features; reader logits (for the US and India also the E5 logit and the mean of the two readers, each with its rank, best other, margin and top value within the record's shortlist); ranker probability and rank; raw index candidate count; source flag; shortlist size; competition features against the record's other candidates; forensic name, legal-form, number and address comparisons; and, for the US and India only, **collective features** over the other incoming records competing for the same business (4 generic counts, for example how many of them have a different number set or a different legal form, plus 6 value features for the US).
- **Counts:** India 211, US 217 (India + 6), France and default 158 features (Doc 4). Spoken: "about two hundred features per country".
- Design detail: the generic word features ignore legal-form words, so a legal-form change shows up only in the legal-form features and in the readers (Doc D.1).

**Numbers (real).** We removed 21 data-specific inputs and replaced them with 25 generic "what changed" features; a code check asserts that none of the removed inputs is used by a final decision model (Doc 4). On the public leaderboard that switch (upload 14) moved the score from 0.990881 to 0.990934 (Doc B.6).

**Why it exists.** A similarity score treats different edits as the same if they cost the same. We studied how true records differ from their business before building features: true records of a business tend to lose information, by dropping a digit or a suffix, abbreviating or transliterating (Script slide 11). Describing the edit itself lets the model learn which edits are harmless. The features are generic operations, not word lists, so they carry over to France.

**What it costs.** Cheap per pair: string operations, plus one pass of the small pretrained encoder per distinct word of the records involved, computed once and then looked up (Code: clean_feats.py); the Documentation gives no separate time.

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Feature engineering; edit distance (Levenshtein, Damerau-Levenshtein, LCS ratio); IDF; Jaccard; word embeddings and cosine similarity; competition and collective (cross-record) features.

**Expert nuance.** "What changed" features are edit-operation descriptors, which a similarity-only matcher collapses into one number.
