Their strength is interpretability and transfer; their weakness is that the token alignment is a fast proxy (first new word, first dropped word, counts) rather than an optimal edit alignment, so a name with several edits is described only roughly. We ran no clean ablation that removes all "what changed" features (QA 21), and we did not prepare a feature-importance ranking (Explainer slide 11), so do not claim a measured gain beyond the upload-14 comparison.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why describe the differences instead of adding more similarity scores?* "Because two edits with the same similarity can mean opposite things: dropping a legal suffix is typical of a true record, while swapping Inc for LLC often signals a different company. We studied how true records differ from their business before building features, and describing the edit lets the model learn from labels which edits are harmless."
- *A typo looks like a replaced word. Doesn't that punish true matches?* "On its own the word-overlap score would, which is why it is never alone: the same pair also carries 'replaced in the same position' and a character similarity, for a one-letter typo about 86 out of 100, and the readers see the raw text. The decision model learns from labels how these combine; we did not measure the typo case separately."

---

### A4.10 Stop 7 - LightGBM decision model, one per country {#a4-10 .concept}

**Simple.** The supervisor now reads every completed form for the letter, including the experts' opinions and how each candidate compares with the others, and writes one probability per candidate: "how likely is this the right shop?". The supervisor is different for each country, because the countries write addresses and legal forms differently, and France has no answer key at all. The supervisor learned on old letters that the expert readers had never trained on, so they learned how far to trust the experts on letters the experts had not memorised. To be steadier, five supervisors trained with different random choices each give a probability, and we take the average.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** The US decision model gives A 0.93 and C 0.01.

**Technical.**
- **Model:** LightGBM binary classifiers; learning rate 0.05; 127 leaves; at least 200 rows per leaf; feature fraction 0.9 (each tree sees a random 90 % of the features); bagging fraction 0.8 every iteration (each tree sees a random 80 % of the rows); L2 1.0; label "candidate is the true business" (Doc 4). LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise (it always splits the leaf that reduces the loss most, so trees can be deep and uneven, unlike CatBoost's symmetric trees) and finds splits on binned feature values (histograms), which is fast on millions of rows. Leaf-wise growth over-fits easily, so the 200-row minimum per leaf, the L2 penalty and the row and feature subsampling are the regularisers.
- **Training rows:** the train shortlist of incoming records that have a candidate in business folds 6-9, built from the index output without the quick filter (Doc 4). For the US and India the training rows also include extra hard examples; say this only with the QA 15 wording, and only if asked. The ranker and readers were trained on folds 0-5, so their scores on these rows are out-of-sample: this is stacking with a layer-wise fold split (QA 5).
- **Fit protocol** (Doc 4; code):

| Country | Rows | Fit | Seeds | Threshold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US | US rows | fit on folds 6-7, early stopping on fold 8 (at most 3,000 rounds), then refit on folds 6-9 for best iteration × rows(6-9) / rows(6-7) | mean of seeds 1-5 | 0.75, then the consistency check |
| India | US and India rows | same as US | mean of seeds 1-5 | 0.75, then the consistency check |
| France | US and India rows of the normal training set (no French rows) | fit on 6-7, early stopping on 8 (at most 1,500 rounds), no refit | mean of seeds 1-5 | 0.82 |
| Unseen country (default) | as France | single fit | 1 | 0.82 |

- **The refit rule** scales the number of trees by the row ratio because no fold is left for early stopping after refitting on 6-9 (Doc 4). It is a common heuristic, not a guarantee: with more rows, each tree's fitted values are less noisy, so a model can usually take more boosting rounds before it starts to over-fit. Example (illustrative): best iteration 1,000 on folds 6-7 and twice as many rows in folds 6-9 gives 2,000 rounds for the refit.
- **France's reader slot:** the France decision model was trained with MiniLM-reader logits in its reader slot; at test time that slot receives the blend 0.35 MiniLM + 0.15 French MiniLM + 0.5 French E5 (Doc 4).

**Numbers (real).** Accepted links after the decision rule of Stop 8: US 2,250,036; India 2,726,453; France 887,630 before the France rules (Doc B.1, B.3). Held-out exact per-business macro F0.5 for close versions of the decision models (the India recipe with 3 of its 5 seeds, consistency check included; fold 9 / fold 8): US rows 0.991212 / 0.991545, India rows 0.990046 / 0.990298 (Doc 5). These exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules.

**Why it exists.** A reader scores one pair at a time, but the decision is a competition between the candidates of one record. The decision model sees each candidate's rank, lead and best rival, the "what changed" features and all reader and ranker scores together, and it can reorder the ranker (Explainer slide 8).

**What it costs.** Training the US/India decision models, including building their training set, took about 1.0 hour in the clean run (stage t7); inference is a handful of small tree-model calls per pair (five seeds), not timed separately.

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Gradient boosting; LightGBM; stacking; early stopping; refit with scaled iterations; seed averaging; group folds.

**Expert nuance.** Three points. First, the refit on 6-9 for the US and India was chosen on the public leaderboard (0.990621 to 0.990676), and the same refit for France scored lower (0.990726 against 0.990748), so France keeps the 6-7 fit (Doc B.6; QA 5). Second, five seeds reduce the variance created by the row and feature subsampling, but their own effect is not isolated: they entered the final file together with the French E5 reader (QA 6). Third, putting a three-reader blend into a slot trained on one reader's logits creates a mild mismatch between training and test inputs; because the weights 0.35 + 0.15 + 0.5 sum to 1, the blend is a weighted average of logits and stays on a logit scale, but its exact match to the MiniLM distribution was not separately measured.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why put a decision model on top of the readers?* "A reader scores one pair at a time, but the decision is a competition between the candidates of one record. The decision model sees the reader logits together with the ranker probability, the 'what changed' features and each candidate's rank and lead over its rivals, and it reorders the ranker when needed, as in our US example."
- *What data trains the decision models?* "Labelled shortlist pairs of incoming records whose candidates lie in business folds 6-9, so the readers and ranker, trained on folds 0-5, never saw them; the US model uses US rows, the India model US and Indian rows, and the France and default models US and Indian rows with no French rows at all." Only if a judge presses on hard cases (QA 15): "for the US and India the decision models were also trained with extra hard examples: copies of unlinked training records that sit right next to a candidate business, with small name edits; how many to add was set from label-free counts on the test records, never from labels; the France model uses no such examples."

---

### A4.11 Stop 8 - Confident + clear-winner rule {#a4-11 .concept}

**Simple.** The supervisor's rule is short. Take the most likely shop for this letter. Deliver only if you are confident (at least 0.75; 0.82 in France) and it is a clear winner (at least 0.4 ahead of the second most likely shop). Otherwise hold the letter back. A letter goes to at most one shop.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** A has 0.93, C has 0.01.
1. Confident? 0.93 ≥ 0.75: yes.
2. Clear winner? 0.93 − 0.01 = 0.92 ≥ 0.4: yes.
3. Link the record to A.

Counter-example (illustrative): if C had scored 0.60, the lead would be 0.93 − 0.60 = 0.33 < 0.4, and the record would stay unlinked even though A is at 0.93. Two strong candidates mean ambiguity, and ambiguity is where wrong links happen.

**Technical.** Per incoming record: take the candidate with the best decision-model score; accept it only if score ≥ thr and score − second-best score ≥ 0.4; otherwise accept nothing (Doc 4; Code: stack.py `decide`). This is an argmax (pick the highest-scoring candidate) with a reject option (the right to answer "none") on two conditions, an absolute threshold and a margin. If a record has only one candidate, the runner-up counts as minus infinity, so only the threshold matters (Code: stack.py; FACTS H9). Thresholds: 0.75 for the US and India, chosen on fold 8 for the exact per-business macro F0.5; 0.82 for France and the default route, set without French labels (Doc 4, Doc C.1). The 0.4 lead is one fixed value for every country; the Documentation does not record how it was picked (FACTS H8), so do not say it was tuned or that it was never tuned.

**Numbers (real).** US 2,250,036 and India 2,726,453 accepted links; France 887,630 (Doc B.1, B.3). 90.59 % of incoming records have exactly one candidate in the final candidate file (Doc B.1).

**Why it exists.** Under per-business F0.5 a wrong link costs more than a missed one, and a wrong link to a business with no true records turns its score from 1 into 0 (Stop 0).

**What it costs.** Negligible compute. In recall: correct candidates are rejected when a second candidate is too close or the score is below the bar; the Documentation lists this among the common false negatives (Doc 5).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Decision thresholds; reject option (abstention); margin; tuning on the exact metric.

**Expert nuance.** A threshold without a margin would link records where two candidates are almost tied, which is precisely where the errors live (Explainer slide 8). Why is the margin not redundant? The decision model is a binary classifier that scores each pair on its own, so the scores of one record's candidates do not have to add up to 1: two candidates can both score 0.9 (illustrative). If the scores were a proper distribution over the candidates, a best score of 0.75 would already force the runner-up to at most 0.25, a lead of at least 0.5; here only the explicit margin guarantees a gap. The margin is an absolute difference of probabilities, so it interacts with calibration (whether a score of 0.8 really means "right 80 % of the time"): we did not calibrate the scores (no Platt scaling, which fits a logistic curve to held-out scores, and no isotonic regression, which fits a monotone step function) and instead tuned the threshold directly on the exact metric (FACTS F2).

**Judge might ask**
- *How does the 0.4 lead work when a record has only one candidate?* "If there is no runner-up, the runner-up counts as minus infinity, so only the threshold matters; 90.59 % of records have exactly one candidate in the final candidate file. The lead rule bites exactly where it should, on records with two or more plausible businesses."
- *Why not link a record to two businesses if both look right?* "The task says each incoming record belongs to at most one business, so two strong candidates mean ambiguity, not two answers. Under F0.5 one of those two links would be wrong, so the rule abstains unless one candidate leads by at least 0.4."

---

### A4.12 Stop 9 - Native-script second chance (India only) {#a4-12 .concept}

**Simple.** Some letters are held back not because the supervisor was unsure, but because the right shop never reached the desk at all. An Indian name written in Devanagari (the script of Hindi and Marathi) can send the first search to shops with the right name in the wrong towns. So a "lost letters" desk takes each still-unlinked native-script letter, writes the name in Latin letters in several possible spellings, drops words like "Private Limited", and searches only shops in the same state whose name, without such words, is exactly one of those spellings. A small model then picks the best, using the address, and links it only if it is very sure and far ahead.

**Our record at this stop.** Our record is a US record with a Latin-script name, so this stop does not apply. The real India example in section 17 walks through it.

**Technical.** (Doc 3, Doc 4; Code: p5_rescue.py)
- **Who enters:** Indian records with native-script names left unlinked by the decision model.
- **Keys:** legal-word-free word tuples of up to 64 transliterations, from a word list of labelled training matches (alternatives with at least 5 % of a native word's count). In plain terms: a native word may have several Latin spellings in the list; every spelling that accounts for at least 5 % of that word's training occurrences is kept, and the combinations across the words of the name, at most 64, form the search keys.
- **Search:** a key must equal the Latin core-name word tuple of a business exactly, and only businesses in the **same state** are searched (all states if the state is unknown or has no match).
- **Fixed score, top 5 kept:** a weighted sum of same state, first house number found, same digit string of an address segment, share of digit runs found, house-segment similarity, share of place words found, and address token-set ratio (a 0-100 string score that compares the two sets of words, ignoring order and repeats). In code: 2 · same state + 3 · first house number found + 2 · same digit-string segment + 1.5 · share of digit runs found + 0.02 · house-segment similarity (0-100) + 1.5 · share of place words found + 0.01 · token-set ratio (0-100).
- **Decision:** a LightGBM second-chance model scores the 5; link the best if score ≥ 0.88 and its lead over the second ≥ 0.3. The 0.88 was chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice.
- **Training:** India second-chance candidates of train folds 0-7, retrieved with word lists that leave out the record's own fold (cross-fitting), so a record never benefits from its own label.

**Numbers (real).** 649,965 pairs scored for 171,713 records; 578,317 of them were not in the shortlist; **+9,759 links** (Doc 3, B.1).

**Why it exists.** It targets a retrieval failure found on training data: native-script names whose transliteration the Latin index does not retrieve (Doc 3). Lowering the main threshold would not help, because the right business is not among the candidates at all (Explainer slide 12).

**What it costs.** Small: it runs only on unlinked native-script records, and it scores at most 5 candidates each with a small tree model. The Documentation gives no separate time; its CPU retraining reproduced byte for byte (CodeREADME 6).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Second-stage retrieval; transliteration; cross-fitting; cost-sensitive thresholds.

**Expert nuance.** The main index commits to one spelling per native word, a single-hypothesis transliteration; the second chance is a multi-hypothesis search (up to 64 spellings) that stays cheap because it demands an exact core-name match inside one state and keeps only 5 candidates by a hand-weighted address score before any model runs. It only touches still-unlinked records, so it can never undo a link (Script slide 12). It runs before the consistency check, and the check never adds a link for a record that already has a native-script second-chance link (Doc 4). One disclosure belongs here: the training records of both second-chance models were selected with earlier decision models whose inputs we later removed (Doc C.8); if pressed, say exactly that.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why not put every transliteration into the main index?* "The main index already uses one transliteration per word. The second chance tries up to 64 spelling combinations per name, which would multiply the index work for every record; running it only for the 171,713 unlinked native-script records, inside the same state, keeps the cost small and targets the miss type we found on training data."
- *How did you stop the second-chance model from learning from its own labels?* "Cross-fitting: it trains on India candidates of folds 0-7, and each record's candidates are retrieved with a word list that leaves out that record's own fold, so it never benefits from its own label. Its threshold, 0.88, was chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice."

---

### A4.13 Stop 10 - Per-business consistency check (US and India) {#a4-13 .concept}

**Simple.** After the first round of deliveries, a clerk looks at each shop and counts how many other letters were already delivered to it. If a shop already has one or two letters, it is very probably a real, active shop, so a slightly less certain letter is allowed through (the bar drops a little). If a shop already has three or more, one more letter would add little even if right and would still cost a lot if wrong, so the bar goes up a little. Every letter is re-decided once with the bar that fits its shop.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** Suppose business A already has 2 other records accepted by the decision model, so k = 2 and the bar is 0.72. Our record's 0.93 clears it with a lead of 0.92 ≥ 0.4, so the link stays. Two more illustrative cases to see how links move (both with a lead of at least 0.4 over their runner-up):
- A record with best score 0.70 whose business has k = 1 other accepted record: bar 0.68, so it is now **added** (it failed 0.75 in the main decision).
- A record with best score 0.76 whose business has k = 3 others: bar 0.77, so it is now **removed** (it passed 0.75 in the main decision).

**Technical.** (Doc 4) For each record, k = the number of **other** incoming records the decision model accepted for the same business. Accept if score ≥ 0.75 (k = 0), 0.68 (k = 1), 0.72 (k = 2), 0.77 (k ≥ 3), with the same 0.4 lead. The four values were chosen on folds 8 and 9 for the exact metric. k is computed once from the main decision, with no iteration. The check never adds a link for a record that already has a native-script second-chance link.

Why the shape: the break-even of one extra link under per-business F0.5. This is an illustration of the metric's arithmetic, not how the four values were chosen (they were tuned on folds 8 and 9). If an extra link is right with probability p, it is worth adding when p · gain > (1 − p) · loss, that is when p > loss / (gain + loss), the break-even probability. With the formula F0.5 = 1.25 · TP / (predicted + 0.25 · true), and the links already made assumed correct:

| Business situation | F0.5 now | If the extra link is right | If the extra link is wrong | Break-even p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| owns 3 records, 0 links so far | 0 | 1.25 · 1 / 1.75 = 0.714 (gain 0.714) | 0 (loss 0) | 0 |
| owns nothing, 0 links so far | 1 (correct empty row) | not possible | 0 (loss 1.000) | any wrong link costs a full point |
| owns 3 records, 1 correct link | 1.25 / 1.75 = 0.714 | 2.5 / 2.75 = 0.909 (gain 0.195) | 1.25 / 2.75 = 0.455 (loss 0.260) | 0.260 / 0.455 = 0.57 |
| owns 3 records, 2 correct links | 2.5 / 2.75 = 0.909 | 3.75 / 3.75 = 1.000 (gain 0.091) | 2.5 / 3.75 = 0.667 (loss 0.242) | 0.242 / 0.333 = 0.73 |

How to read it. With k = 0 the bar must guard against the second row, a business that owns nothing, where one wrong link turns 1 into 0; so it makes sense to keep the strict main threshold, 0.75, there. With k ≥ 1, the other accepted links are mostly correct, so the business very probably owns records, the empty-row danger largely disappears and the break-even is lower (0.57 here): the bar can drop. As links accumulate, the gain from one more right link shrinks faster than the loss from a wrong one (break-even 0.73 at k = 2), so the bar climbs again. The break-even values assume calibrated probabilities and a known number of true records; our scores are not calibrated (Stop 8), so the tuned bars (0.68, 0.72, 0.77) need not equal them. The arithmetic explains the direction of the shape only.

**Numbers (real).** Final run: US **+277 / −284**; India **+247 / −248** (1 addition skipped because of a native-script link) (Doc B.1).

**Why it exists.** The value of one more link depends on how many links the business already has, because the metric is computed per business.

**What it costs.** Negligible compute; it moves few links.

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Per-business F0.5; count-dependent thresholds; tuning on held-out folds.

**Expert nuance.** Unlike the second-chance searches, this step can remove links. Its thresholds were chosen on folds 8 and 9, the same folds used for the held-out scores, which is one reason we say there is no untouched end-to-end validation (Doc 5). France does not use it.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why is the bar lower with one other link and higher with three or more?* "The four values were tuned on held-out folds 8 and 9 for the exact metric, and the direction follows the metric. With no other link, the danger is a business that truly owns nothing, where one wrong link costs a full point; one or two accepted links make that unlikely, so the bar can drop to 0.68 and 0.72. As links pile up, a right extra link adds little while a wrong one still costs a lot, so the bar rises to 0.77."
- *Can the consistency check remove links?* "Yes, unlike the second-chance searches: in the final run it removed 284 US links and 248 Indian links and added 277 and 247. It never adds a link for a record that already has a native-script second-chance link; one such addition was skipped in India."

---

### A4.14 Stop 11 - Address second chance (US and India) {#a4-14 .concept}

**Simple.** Some letters have a name that has drifted far from the registered name, but an address that still matches. For letters still unlinked after everything else, a clerk searches by the address instead: shops that share one of the letter's rarest house numbers and one of its rarest street words. A first quick model throws out most of these, and a second model links the best survivor only if it is clearly convincing.

**Our record at this stop.** Our record was linked at Stop 8 and kept at Stop 10, so it never reaches this desk: second-chance searches act only on unlinked records. Had it been unlinked, its search keys would have been its rare digit run "42" and its rarest alphabetic address words, and only businesses sharing both kinds of key would come back.

**Technical.** (Doc 3, Doc 4; Code: p5b_addr_rescue.py, addr_lib.py)
- **Retrieval:** businesses that share one of the record's 3 rarest digit runs **and** one of its 3 rarest alphabetic address words (at most 300 per record), ranked by IDF containment (the IDF-weighted share of the record's address words found in the business's address) + 0.5 · coverage (the IDF-weighted share of the business's address words found in the record's); the top 3 not already in the record's shortlist go on (Code: addr_lib.py).
- **Filter:** LightGBM, 10 features, 15 leaves, 200 rounds; it keeps at most 2 per record whose filter probability is at least the filter threshold, the largest value on a grid that still keeps 98 % of the fold-8 reference links (so the filter is tuned for recall).
- **Scorer:** LightGBM, 41 features, 31 leaves, 300 rounds, mean of seeds 7, 8 and 9; link the best kept pair if its scorer probability is at least the link threshold and leads the second kept pair's by at least the margin; threshold and margin chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice (so the scorer is tuned for precision).
- **Parameters** (filter threshold / link threshold / margin): US 0.06 / 0.86 / 0.0; India 0.015 / 0.66 / 0.1.
- **Training:** per country, on address-retrieval pairs of training records that the main decision leaves unlinked, folds 6-7.

**Numbers (real).** US: 3,029,652 retrieved pairs, 1,827 filter survivors, **+192 links**. India: 4,766,484 retrieved pairs, 25,579 survivors (25,558 new candidates), **+2,945 links** (Doc 3, B.1). Together +3,137 (derived).

**Why it exists.** It targets the second miss type found on training data: records whose name differs while the address matches (Doc 3).

**What it costs.** The heaviest step in memory: about 3.2 GB per worker, 13 GB with 4 workers (CodeREADME 1). Most retrieved pairs are scored only by the cheap filter and never written to the candidate file.

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Retrieval cascade (retrieve, filter, score); IDF; cost-sensitive threshold selection; seed averaging.

**Expert nuance.** It is a three-step cascade in miniature: wide cheap retrieval, a recall-tuned filter (98 % of reference links kept), then a precision-tuned scorer. Counting false positives twice when choosing thresholds is a simple cost-sensitive proxy for F0.5's preference for precision; it is not an exact translation of the metric (inside one business F0.5 weighs a wrong link four times as much as a missed one in its denominator, Stop 0, and the macro average adds the empty-row effect). Note also that the US margin is 0.0, so in the US the link threshold alone decides; that is the value the fold-8 search chose. Some choices around it used public feedback: public scores helped calibrate the label-free estimate for transferring the address second chance to the US (Doc C.4).

**Judge might ask**
- *Why require both a rare number and a rare word?* "Requiring both keeps the search small and specific: at most 300 businesses per record, and only the top 3 not already in the shortlist go on. A rare house number alone or a rare street word alone would bring in many unrelated businesses; the pair targets the miss type 'same address, different name'."
- *Why count false positives twice when choosing the second-chance thresholds?* "Because under F0.5 a wrong link costs more than a missed one, and these models act on records the main model already declined, where errors are likely. Counting each false positive twice builds that asymmetry into the choice; it gave the US 0.86, India 0.66, and 0.88 for the native-script search."

---

### A4.15 Stop 12 - France rules computed by code (France only) {#a4-15 .concept}

**Simple.** France had no answer key, so the French branch of the post office adds a short book of house rules after the supervisor. Some rules hold back a letter the supervisor wanted to deliver, for example when the address is the same but one word of the shop name was swapped for a very common word. Others deliver a letter the supervisor held back, but only when the evidence is very specific, for example the shop's name plus one generic suffix such as "groupe" on the shop's own street, with no other compatible shop there. The rules are written as code that reads only the supervisor's scores, the raw text and the address; no person and no AI judges any letter.

**Our record at this stop.** US record, so not applicable. The real French example in section 17 shows a veto.

**Technical and numbers (real; Doc B.3).** The rules run in this order on France shortlist pairs only and add no candidate. p1 and p2 are the best and second-best decision-model scores of the record.

| Step | Rule (plain name) | What it does | Count | France links after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | decision model | confident + clear winner at 0.82 / 0.4 | 887,630 accepted | — |
| 1-2 | category-swap veto; word-substitution veto and rescue | veto: at the same address the business lost a core word and the record gained a category word, or one business word was replaced by a frequent word; rescue: unlinked records with a true-looking name difference, 0.4 ≤ p1 < 0.82, lead ≥ 0.4 | vetoes together −29,021; rescue +5,272 | |
| 3 | residual rescue | unlinked, p2 < 0.05; record name = business name + one generic suffix (for example groupe, france, services) in the conditions listed in Doc B.3; the top business is the only compatible one at the address | +5,846 | 869,727 |
| 4 | street veto | drop a link when none of the business's street-name words appear in the record's address, allowing typos | −826 | 868,901 |
| 5 | generic-word swap veto | same word count, one position where the record has "compagnie" or "services" and the business a non-generic word; same address | −538 | 868,363 |
| 6 | generic-word rescue | unlinked, not vetoed, p2 < 0.05, same address, name differs only by "groupe" or "developpement" in specific positions, p1 in a low band | +332 | 868,695 |
| 7 | cell veto | drop accepted links in seven specific combinations of address relation and name change | −1,322 | 867,373 |
| 8 | acronym rescue | unlinked, not vetoed, 0.4 ≤ p1 < 0.82, same address, the record name holds an initials variant of the business name, unique at that address | +186 | 867,559 (final) |

Check: 887,630 − 29,021 + 5,272 + 5,846 = 869,727 (derived). Counts are actions in execution order, not per-rule accuracies (Doc B.3). The full story, including how the rules were found and checked without labels, is in Section 18.

**Why it exists.** Without labels we cannot train a French decision model; the rules encode precise, checkable conditions where the borrowed US/India model was unsure or risky (Explainer slide 13).

**What it costs.** Cheap per pair; the real costs are disclosure and the risk of fitting the test set (Section 18).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Deterministic post-model rules; label-free validation with control groups.

**Expert nuance.** Limitation first: the rules were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records, including AI-assisted review of sampled pairs, and some parameters were chosen after seeing test results, including public-leaderboard scores (Doc C.2, C.4). So they carry a real risk of fitting the test set, and there is no French F0.5 to measure that risk. Mitigation: each rule is code on decision-model scores, raw text and the address; no test label and no human or AI judgement of any pair is an input when the pipeline runs, and the evidence behind the rules uses no French labels (control groups on the French records, such as same-street records without a house number; for the cell veto, the independence of name noise and address noise, measured on US labels) (Doc B.3, C.2). Technically, each rule is a hand-written region of feature space with a forced decision layered on top of the model: a veto overrides a confident score, and a rescue accepts a record the model left unlinked, under narrow conditions on p1 and p2 (a band for p1, or p2 < 0.05) and, for most rescues, a condition that the business is the only compatible one at that address. Because the rules run in a fixed order and later rules skip records vetoed earlier, the counts in the table are not independent per-rule effects. The cleaner production design is to turn the rule conditions into features and learn them from a small labelled French sample (QA 10).

**Judge might ask**
- *Do the France rules only remove links?* "No. Four of them add links: the word-substitution rescue (+5,272), the residual rescue (+5,846), the generic-word rescue (+332) and the acronym rescue (+186); the others remove links, the largest being the two word-swap vetoes together (29,021 of 887,630 accepted). Net, France goes from 887,630 accepted links to 867,559."

---

### A4.16 Stop 13 - Output and validation {#a4-16 .concept}

**Simple.** At the end the post office writes two logs, one line per shop. The first lists which letters were delivered to each shop. The second lists every shop-letter pair that was seriously considered. A checker makes sure every delivered letter was also on the considered list, and then the organisers' own auditor program checks both logs. Ours passes.

**Our record at this stop (illustrative).** Business A's row in the matching file lists our record (and its other linked records). The candidate file lists our record under A and C, the two businesses of its shortlist. If A truly owns exactly the 3 records we linked, A scores 1.000 (Stop 0).

**Technical.** (Doc 2.2, Doc 3, Doc B.1; CodeREADME 5)
- `matching_results.tsv`: one row per test business with its linked incoming records.
- `candidate_pairs.tsv`: one row per test business with its candidates = the shortlist + native-script second-chance candidates + address second-chance filter survivors not already in it.
- The export asserts that every matched pair is a candidate pair; the last stage runs the organisers' validator `validate_submission.py --check-ids`: PASS.

**Numbers (real).**
- **5,856,936 links**: US 2,250,221; India 2,739,156; France 867,559. Check: US 2,250,036 + 277 − 284 + 192 = 2,250,221; India 2,726,453 + 247 − 248 + 9,759 + 2,945 = 2,739,156 (derived).
- 1,632,457 businesses with at least one link; **100,087 empty rows** (5.8 %, derived); links per business mean 3.3805, median 3, maximum 11 (Doc B.1).
- **12,293,019 candidate pairs**, 7.0954 per business, 1.2331 per incoming record. Check: 11,687,317 shortlist + 578,317 native-script + 1,827 US address + 25,558 India address = 12,293,019 (derived).
- Reduction ratio 0.99999817, so fewer than two pairs in every million possible pairs are written (1.83 per million, derived) (Doc 3).
- No pair joins records of different countries, and no incoming record is linked to more than one business (Doc B.1). Every incoming record except 2 has at least one candidate; 125 businesses have none (Doc B.1).
- Both files have 1,732,544 rows; validator PASS (Evidence: validation_log_package_output.txt).

**Why it exists.** The organisers judge both the match list and the candidate file, so a small candidate file is a goal in itself (Explainer slide 2), and a file that fails the validator scores nothing.

**What it costs.** Writing and validating is quick. Reproducibility: from the trained models, the inference stages rewrite both submitted files byte for byte; a full retrain from raw data (about 11.5 hours, one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER 16 GB, 32 GB RAM, about 70 GB disk) reproduced 99.82 % of the links and passed the validator; it is not bit-identical because GPU CatBoost training and bf16 reader training are not bit-deterministic (CodeREADME 1, 6).

**Concepts used (Parts A0-A3).** Validation hygiene; reproducibility; candidate efficiency.

**Expert nuance.** The candidate file is a union (shortlist + second-chance candidates), so its size, 7.0954 per business, is larger than what the readers saw, 6.75 per business (derived); the export assertion guarantees that the matching file is a subset of the candidate file, so a link can never be "uncandidated". On reproducibility, two different claims must not be mixed up. Byte-identical files need the trained weights and the stored reader logits of the submitted run, because bf16 scores also depend slightly on the device and on how pairs are batched (each batch is padded to its longest pair) (CodeREADME 6). A retrain from raw data gives very close but different files (99.82 % of links reproduced; identical match lists for 99.07 % of businesses), because the GPU training of the ranker and the bf16 training of the readers are not bit-deterministic (Doc A; CodeREADME 6). The regenerated file was never uploaded, so its public score is unknown (clean-run report).

**Judge might ask**
- *How do you guarantee the two output files agree?* "The export asserts that every linked pair is also a candidate pair, and the last stage runs the organisers' validator with ID checks, which passes. Both files have one row for each of the 1,732,544 businesses."
- *Could someone else reproduce your file?* "Yes. From our trained models and stored reader scores, the inference stages rewrite both submitted files byte for byte; a full retrain from raw data, about 11.5 hours on one 16 GB GPU, reproduced 99.82 % of the links and passed the validator. It is not bit-identical because GPU training of the ranker and bf16 training of the readers are not bit-deterministic."

---

### A4.17 The three real examples, retold {#a4-17 .concept}

These are real test records traced through the submitted run (Doc D). Test labels are private, so the examples show **how** the pipeline decides, not whether each link is correct. Say that sentence whenever you present them.

#### A4.17.1 US: the legal form and one word decide (Doc D.1)

Incoming record **S2-672512509**: name "Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc)", **no address**.

1. **Normalisation.** The name becomes "legacy marketing enterprises inc" (computed with our code); with no address, the address channels have nothing to work with.
2. **Index lookup, quick filter, ranker.** The shortlist ends with 4 businesses, ranker ranks 0-3, all with almost the same name:

| Ranker rank | Business | Decision-model score | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc; 46 Lincoln Way, Windsor, CT | **0.965022** | nothing in the name; same legal form |
| 1 | Legacy Marketing Enterprises LLC; 2495 St Paul Boulevard, Unit Unit 5, Irondequoit, NY | 0.000007 | legal form Inc to LLC |
| 2 | Legacy Marketing Enterprises PC; 63189 La Brisa Drive, Joshua Tree, CA | 0.088664 | legal form Inc to PC |
| 3 | Legacy Marketing Industries Inc; 2360 Airbase Road, Louisville, TN | 0.000088 | one word replaced in place (IDF-weighted Jaccard 0.52, meaning similarity of the replaced word 0.77) |

3. **Readers and "what changed" features.** With no address, only the name separates the four. The generic word features ignore legal-form words, so for them the three "Enterprises" names are identical; the legal-form features and the readers tell them apart, and the word-replacement features mark "Industries" (Doc D.1).
4. **Decision model.** It reorders the ranker: the LLC, ranker rank 1, gets the lowest score of all, 0.000007.
5. **Confident + clear winner.** 0.965022 ≥ 0.75, and the lead is 0.965022 − 0.088664 = 0.876 ≥ 0.4, so the record is linked to the Windsor, CT business only.
6. **Consistency check.** It keeps the link: 0.965 clears every bar of the check (0.68 to 0.77).
7. **Address second chance.** Not used: it looks only at unlinked records.
8. **Output.** The Windsor business's row lists this record with two other incoming records; the candidate file lists the record under all four businesses.

**What it teaches.** "What changed" in action: when names are almost identical and there is no address, the type of difference (legal form, one replaced word) decides, and the decision model can overrule the ranker.

**Judge might ask**
- *The ranker put the LLC second; why is it last after the decision model?* "The ranker only sees index statistics, where Enterprises Inc and Enterprises LLC look almost the same. The decision model also sees the legal-form change from Inc to LLC and the reader scores, so it drops the LLC to 0.000007 and keeps the Inc at 0.965."
- *Was it the legal-form features or the readers that made the difference?* "We did not isolate that for this record. Both carry the signal: the legal-form features mark Inc to LLC and Inc to PC, the readers see the raw names, and the generic word features, which ignore legal words, see the three Enterprises names as identical."

#### A4.17.2 India: the native-script second chance (Doc D.2)

Incoming record **S3-309374692**: name "विजय एंटरप्राइजेज प्राइवेट लिमिटेड", address "24/11, Mumbai, महाराष्ट्र".

1. **Main pass.** The shortlist holds three businesses called "Vijay Enterprises Private Limited", in Agra (Uttar Pradesh), Satara (Maharashtra) and Byculla, Mumbai (Maharashtra). The ranker's top-1 probability is only 0.0028, and the decision model scores them 1.9e-6, 6.9e-6 and 7.2e-6: far below 0.75 and below every consistency-check bar (0.68 to 0.77). The record stays unlinked.
2. **Enter the native-script second chance.** The name is in Devanagari and the record is unlinked, so it qualifies.
3. **Transliteration key.** The word list learned from training matches maps विजय to vijay, एंटरप्राइजेज to enterprises, प्राइवेट to private and लिमिटेड to limited, each as the only alternative. Without the legal words, the key is (vijay, enterprises). The address gives the state: Maharashtra.
4. **Second search.** 10 businesses in Maharashtra have the core name "vijay enterprises"; the fixed address score keeps the top 5.
5. **Fixed score of the winner.** "Vijay Enterprises Private Limited", "24/11, Bombay Sarggam, Vallabh Baug Ghatkopar(E), Mumbai, Maharashtra": same state, same house number 24/11 (both digit runs match), address token-set ratio 100 (66.7 for each of the other four; all five are in Mumbai, so the place-word share is 1.0 for each). Fixed score 13.0 = 2 (state) + 3 (first house number) + 2 (same digit-string segment) + 1.5 (all digit runs found) + 2 (house-segment similarity 100 × 0.02) + 1.5 (all place words) + 1 (token-set ratio 100 × 0.01); the next best is 4.78.
6. **Second-chance model.** Score 0.99994; the second best (Bhandup West) 0.0000191; lead 0.99992.
7. **Decision.** 0.99994 ≥ 0.88 and lead ≥ 0.3, so the link is added.
8. **Consistency check.** It runs after this step and would never add a different link for this record, because the record already has a native-script link.
9. **Output.** The record appears in the Ghatkopar business's row; the candidate file lists it under 7 businesses (3 from the shortlist, 5 from the second chance, 1 in both).

**What it teaches.** A retrieval miss cannot be fixed by a lower threshold. The Latin index found the right name in the wrong places; the second search narrowed by transliterated name and state, and the house number 24/11 picked the right business.

**Judge might ask**
- *Why did the main pass give the three exact-name businesses almost zero?* "The names match, but nothing ties those three businesses to this record's address, 24/11 in Mumbai: they are in Agra, Satara and Byculla, and the ranker's best probability was only 0.0028. So the decision model scored them between about 2 and 7 in a million, far below any bar."
- *What if the house number had been missing?* "We did not test that case. The house number is what separated the right business from the other four Mumbai candidates, an address token-set ratio of 100 against 66.7, so without it the lead rule would decide whether anything is linked."

#### A4.17.3 France: a confident link vetoed (Doc D.3)

Incoming record **S2-30376547**: "TQ COMITE SARL", "2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN, NANTES".

1. **Normalisation (French rules).** "2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN" becomes "2 rue suzanne lenglen"; the name becomes "tq comite sarl" (computed with our code).
2. **Index lookup.** 16 candidates.
3. **Quick filter.** Keeps 2.
4. **Ranker and shortlist.** Both enter the shortlist (ranker probabilities 0.9991 and 0.0420, both ≥ 0.001).
5. **Readers.** France uses three readers, blended as 0.35 MiniLM + 0.15 French MiniLM + 0.5 French E5:

| Ranker rank | Business | Ranker prob. | MiniLM | French MiniLM | French E5 | Blend | Decision score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | TQ Parents SARL; 2 Rue Suzanne Lenglen, Nantes, Pays de la Loire | 0.9991 | 7.5000 | 8.9375 | 10.8125 | 9.3719 | **0.999837** |
| 1 | TQ Comite SARL; 2 RUE du Lycee, Pessac, Nouvelle-Aquitaine | 0.0420 | 7.1250 | −1.9219 | −10.8125 | −3.2008 | 0.000098 |

   Blend check for rank 0: 0.35 × 7.5 + 0.15 × 8.9375 + 0.5 × 10.8125 = 9.371875 (derived). The blend rejects the identical-name business in another city, which the plain MiniLM reader alone scored +7.1.
6. **Decision model and rule.** It accepts rank 0: 0.999837 ≥ 0.82 and lead 0.999740 ≥ 0.4.
7. **France rules.** The category-swap veto fires: same house number (2), street token-set ratio 100 ≥ 80, the business name lost the core word "parents", and the record gained the category word "comite". The word-substitution veto also lists the pair ("parents" replaced by the frequent word "comite" at the same address). The link is dropped.
8. **No later rule re-links it.** p1 = 0.999837 is above the rescue band [0.4, 0.82); no residual-rescue pattern applies; the generic-word rescue and the acronym rescue skip records vetoed by the first two rules.
9. **Output.** The record is in no row of the matching file and is listed in the candidate file under both businesses; TQ Parents SARL keeps its link to another incoming record, S2-732760024.

**What it teaches.** Two things at once: the French readers fixed a reader error (identical name, wrong city), and the France rules overruled a very confident model on a risky pattern. Under F0.5, abstaining is cheaper than a wrong link (Script slide 18).

**Judge might ask**
- *Couldn't TQ Parents be the right business?* "It could; the labels are private. The rule is a precision choice: if the link was right we lose a little recall on that business, if it was wrong it would have cost precision, and TQ Parents still keeps its link to another incoming record."
- *Why not link the exact-name TQ Comite SARL in Pessac?* "It sits in another city, Pessac, not Nantes. The plain MiniLM reader liked the identical name, +7.1, but both French readers rejected it, the blend was −3.2, and the decision model gave it 0.000098."

---

### A4.18 France: how we matched with zero labels {#a4-18 .concept}

**In one line:** France had no labels, so we borrowed a decision model trained on labelled US and Indian data, let two French readers teach themselves from their own most confident French guesses, used a stricter bar, and added rules computed by code, all disclosed.

**Simple explanation:** Imagine opening a new branch of the post office in France, where nobody has ever recorded which letter belongs to which shop. You bring your experienced US and Indian supervisor, who knows in general what a genuine letter looks like, but French addresses and company words (SARL, "rue", "bis") are new to them. So you let your expert readers practise on French letters they are extremely sure about, either almost certainly right or almost certainly wrong, and you keep giving them old US and Indian letters with known answers so they do not forget what they learned. Because you cannot check the French answers, you ask for more confidence before delivering (0.82 instead of 0.75). Finally, you write a small book of house rules for situations where the supervisor tends to be over-confident, such as the same address with one name word swapped for a very common word. The honest catch: you can never measure French accuracy directly, you designed the rules after looking at the French letters, and you say so.

**Worked example:**

*Part 1, choosing pseudo-labels for the French E5 reader (rule real, records and logits illustrative).* Confidence p = the average of sigmoid(MiniLM logit) and sigmoid(French MiniLM logit). A positive needs p ≥ 0.97 on the record's best pair and every other pair of that record below 0.5; a negative is the record's highest-p pair among those with p ≤ 0.03, the hardest confident non-match (Doc 4).

| Record | Pair | MiniLM logit | French MiniLM logit | p | Becomes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | best pair | 5.0 (sigmoid 0.9933) | 4.0 (0.9820) | 0.9877 | **positive** (≥ 0.97, and R1's other pair has p = 0.10 < 0.5) |
| R2 | best pair | — | — | 0.80 | not a positive (below 0.97) |
| R2 | pair 2 | — | — | 0.02 | **negative** (the highest p among R2's pairs at or below 0.03) |
| R2 | pair 3 | — | — | 0.001 | not used (a less informative, easier negative) |
| R3 | only pair | — | — | 0.50 | nothing (neither confident match nor confident non-match) |

*Part 2, blending the readers (real numbers, Doc D.3).* For "TQ COMITE SARL" against "TQ Parents SARL": 0.35 × 7.5 + 0.15 × 8.9375 + 0.5 × 10.8125 = 2.625 + 1.3406 + 5.4063 = 9.3719. Against the identical name in Pessac: 0.35 × 7.125 + 0.15 × (−1.9219) + 0.5 × (−10.8125) = −3.2008. The plain MiniLM reader liked both; the blend keeps one and rejects the other.

*Part 3, the stricter bar.* With p1 = 0.84 and p2 = 0.30 (illustrative), a US record would pass (0.84 ≥ 0.75, lead 0.54 ≥ 0.4); a French record also passes (0.84 ≥ 0.82). With p1 = 0.80, the US record passes but the French one does not.

**Technical explanation:** The French part combines six techniques.
1. **Transfer of the decision model.** The France decision model is LightGBM trained only on labelled US and Indian rows of the normal training set (158 features, mean of 5 seeds, fit on folds 6-7 with early stopping on fold 8, no refit), so it encodes generic "what changed" knowledge rather than French specifics (Doc 4).
2. **Self-training with confidence-thresholded pseudo-labels.** A teacher's confident predictions on unlabelled target data become training labels for a student. The French MiniLM reader was fine-tuned on very confident pseudo-labels from an earlier run of our pipeline (best candidate, score at least 0.97, clear lead) and confident non-matches, plus 500,000 labelled US/India pairs. The French E5 reader used the combined confidence of two readers as the teacher (the average of their two probabilities, the rule above), at most 250,000 pairs per class, 5 % of records held out, 474,808 French pairs plus 474,808 labelled US/India pairs, 7,419 steps at learning rate 2e-5 (Doc 4); 949,616 pairs / batch 128 = 7,418.9, so one epoch is 7,419 steps (derived). The risk of self-training is **confirmation bias**: the student can learn the teacher's mistakes, and very confident pseudo-labels are also the easiest cases, so they teach less about the hard ones. The very high confidence bar and the replay of labelled pairs limit, but do not remove, that risk. The held-out pseudo-labels do not limit it: agreement with them (0.999206) only shows that the student reproduces its teacher, not that the teacher is right. That is why the generated labelled French test set was the more independent check, and it failed (Doc B.4).
3. **Replay against forgetting.** Mixing in labelled US/India pairs (about one to one) keeps the fine-tuned readers from drifting away from what they learned on labelled data, a standard defence against catastrophic forgetting during domain adaptation (Script slide 13).
4. **Logit blending into a fixed slot.** The France decision model was trained with MiniLM logits in its reader slot; at test time the slot receives 0.35 MiniLM + 0.15 French MiniLM + 0.5 French E5. Because the weights sum to 1 it is a weighted average of logits. Averaging logits is not the same as averaging probabilities: it is a weighted geometric mean of the odds, so one very confident reader can dominate. In the Pessac example the French E5 reader's −10.8125, with weight 0.5, alone contributes −5.41 and pulls the blend to −3.2008, although the plain MiniLM reader said +7.125. The French MiniLM weight was set by label-free counts on the test records (Doc C.1); 0.35 / 0.15 / 0.5 equals half of the previous blend (0.7 MiniLM + 0.3 French MiniLM) plus half of the French E5 reader.
5. **A stricter operating point.** 0.82 instead of 0.75, set without French labels from the French link volume per business together with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US/India (Doc C.1). The 0.4 lead is unchanged.
6. **Rules computed by code**, after the decision model (Section 15, table). They read only model scores, raw text and the address. Their evidence uses no French labels: control groups on the French records (for example, records on the same street without a house number) and, for the cell veto, the independence of name noise and address noise measured on US labels (Doc B.3). Background from our code's documentation, not the submitted Documentation, use only if asked: the street veto rests on a US fact; among 1,313,608 decidable true US top-1 matches only 48 (0.004 %) have a street name sharing no word with the business's street, while 60,565 of 60,613 (99.92 %) US top-1 pairs with a genuinely different street are wrong.

Checks of the French E5 reader, written before adoption (Doc B.4):

| Check | Result | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| US/India quality within tolerance (509,260 labelled fold-8/9 pairs) | AUC 0.998544 vs 0.998570; top-1 accuracy 0.993161 vs 0.993004; best F0.5 0.992782 vs 0.992796 | pass |
| Agreement with held-out French pseudo-labels (25,192 pairs) | 0.999206 (the E5 reader 0.981304); threshold 0.98 | pass |
| Generated labelled French test set (195,380 pairs) | best F0.5 0.910516 vs 0.914964 for its base model | fail |
| "Expected gain safely positive" rule (final file vs the same pipeline without it) | French links −2,228 / +3,396; pessimistic gain −0.0001806 | fail |

**How we used it:** France flows through the same index lookup (32.7713 candidates per business after the quick filter), the same CatBoost ranker trained on US/India, and a shortlist of 2,103,107 pairs (8.1060 per business) (Doc 3). The three readers are blended 0.35 / 0.15 / 0.5; the France decision model accepts 887,630 links at 0.82 / 0.4; the France rules bring that to 867,559 (Doc B.3). France has no consistency check and no second-chance searches. Final France numbers: 244,207 businesses with at least one link, 15,245 empty rows, 3.3438 links per business (Doc B.1). A diagnostic upload showed how much France matters: emptying every French row of an early file dropped the public score from 0.970125 to 0.839 (Doc B.6). What we tried and dropped, as reported: refitting the France decision model on folds 6-9 (public 0.990726 against 0.990748 without it), a second French self-training round (0.991277 against 0.991300), and the French MiniLM reader retrained with different pseudo-label filters (0.991258) (Doc B.6). The French E5 reader was kept although it failed two of its four written checks, because the file containing it had our best public score; that same upload also added the 5-seed decision models, so its own effect is not isolated (QA 8).

**Expert nuance:** State the limitations first, then the mitigation. **We have no measured French F0.5.** The closest number is a proxy: the France recipe applied to US and Indian records at the France operating point scores 0.990508 / 0.989467 on fold 9 and 0.990977 / 0.989850 on fold 8, which says the recipe is sound on labelled countries, not that it is right in France (Doc 5). **The rules were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records**, including AI-assisted review of sampled pairs, and some parameters were chosen after seeing public-leaderboard results (Doc C.2, C.4); the mitigation is that each rule is code on scores and text, with no test label and no human or AI judgement of any pair as an input. **The French E5 reader failed two written checks** and was kept for a leaderboard reason. A cleaner production design would label a small French sample, turn the rule conditions into features of a French decision model, and set the threshold on labels (QA 10, 18). Alternatives a scientist may raise, such as adversarial domain adaptation or translating French records, are not part of our final approach.

**Remember:**
- No French labels: decision model borrowed from US/India rows; readers self-trained on their most confident French guesses with about one-to-one US/India replay; bar 0.82; rules computed by code.
- 887,630 accepted, then 867,559 after the rules; the two word-swap vetoes removed 29,021.
- Say the three limits plainly: no measured French F0.5; rules designed after looking at test records; French E5 reader kept despite failing two of four checks.

**Judge might ask:**
- *How do you know self-training did not just teach the readers their own mistakes?* "We cannot fully rule it out; that is the known risk of self-training. We limited it with very confident pseudo-labels and an equal number of labelled US and Indian pairs, and US/India quality stayed within tolerance; the 0.999206 agreement with held-out pseudo-labels only shows the student matches its teacher. The more independent check, a generated labelled French test set, failed, 0.910516 against 0.914964, as did our expected-gain rule, and we kept the reader because the file with it scored best on the public board."
- *How did you choose 0.82 without French labels?* "Without labels: we compared the number of French links per business at different thresholds with a threshold sweep on labelled US and Indian fold 8, and chose 0.82, stricter than the 0.75 we use where we have labels. The 0.4 lead stays the same."

---

### A4.19 Traps to avoid when you describe the pipeline {#a4-19 .concept}

1. "About 130 per business" comes from the **blocking study of 25 September**, not the final run. The final run reports 21.7107 after the quick filter.
2. 6.75 per business and 1.17 per record for the shortlist are **derived** (11,687,317 / 1,732,544 and / 9,969,589). The candidate file is 7.0954 per business, 1.2331 per record.
3. The CatBoost ranker is a **pointwise classifier** with log loss. Never say it uses a ranking loss.
4. The quick filter's cost (0.990117 to 0.990086) was measured **with the decision model of 25 September**.
5. **France has no consistency check and no second-chance searches**, does not use the plain E5 reader, and its decision model has **no French rows**.
6. **The second-chance searches never undo a link; the consistency check can** (US −284, India −248).
7. The real order for the US and India is: native-script second chance (India), then the consistency check, then the address second chance. The talk groups the two searches together for simplicity.
8. The readers read the **raw** text; the index and hand-made features use the cleaned text.
9. "1.4 hours of reader scoring" is from the **clean run** (two readers per pair, all except the French E5 reader); the submitted run reused stored logits.
10. Held-out scores (US 0.991212 / 0.991545; India 0.990046 / 0.990298) are for **close versions** of the decision models (the India recipe with 3 of its 5 seeds) and **exclude** the second-chance searches and France rules.
11. The 0.4 lead is **one fixed value for every country**; the threshold 0.75 was tuned on fold 8. Do not claim the lead was tuned, and do not say it was never tuned.
12. The unseen-country route is **untested** on real data.
13. There is **no measured French F0.5**; the France "proxy" numbers are US and Indian records.
14. Never use internal code names on stage. For hard near-identical cases use the QA 15 wording, and only if asked.
15. The cap of four rarely binds (1.17 pairs per record on average); do not say the cap is what cuts the candidates down. The quick filter and the 0.001 floor do most of the narrowing; the cap bounds the worst case.
16. The break-even arithmetic of the consistency check explains only the **direction** of its shape; the four bars were **tuned on folds 8 and 9**. Check the Stop 10 table for the metric's own numbers.
17. Agreement with held-out French pseudo-labels (0.999206) shows that the student matches its teacher; it is **not** evidence of French accuracy.
18. The index stage on test runs with 6 threads by default; the "8-11 threads" in the code README refer to the training-stage index runs.

---

### A4.20 Explain the whole pipeline in one sentence, 30 seconds and 2 minutes {#a4-20 .concept}

**One sentence (about 20 seconds).** "Per country, a cheap index and two pruning steps cut 6.7 trillion possible pairs to about seven candidates per business, small language-model readers and a per-country decision model score them, and we link a record only to a confident, clear winner, with second-chance searches and French rules on top."

**30 seconds (about 80 words).**
"Per country, we clean the text and a C++ inverted index pulls up businesses that share rare words, letter pieces or sounds, about 130 per business. A quick rule with no model cuts that to 21.7, and a CatBoost ranker keeps at most four per record. Cross-encoder readers score each pair, 'what changed' features describe the differences, and a LightGBM decision model links only a confident, clear winner. Second-chance searches, a consistency check and France rules finish it: public F0.5 0.9913."

**2 minutes (about 300 words).**
"We link about ten million incoming records from the US, India and France to 1.7 million businesses, each record to one business or to none. The metric is F0.5 per business, and a business with no true records scores a point only if we link nothing, so we are precision first. The pipeline runs per country and goes from cheap to expensive.

First we clean the text: lower case, abbreviations unified, Indian-script words transliterated with a word list learned from training matches, and French address and legal-form rules. A C++ inverted index then finds businesses that share rare words, letter pieces or sounds, weighted by IDF, with separate lists for name and address so one-sided matches survive. That gives about 130 candidates per business. A quick rule-based filter with no model cuts that to 21.7, at a held-out cost of 0.00003 F0.5, and a CatBoost ranker keeps at most four per record: 6.75 per business.

Cross-encoder readers, fine-tuned multilingual MiniLM and E5, read each record and candidate together. We add 'what changed' features: which numbers changed, which words were added, dropped or replaced, how rare and how close in meaning, and whether the legal form changed. A LightGBM decision model per country turns about two hundred features into a probability, and we link only a confident, clear winner: at least 0.75, or 0.82 in France, and 0.4 ahead of the runner-up.

Then targeted fixes: two second-chance searches for unlinked records, by transliterated name in India and by rare address keys, adding 9,759 and 3,137 links; a per-business consistency check; and for France, which has no labels, self-trained French readers and rules computed by code.

The final file scores 0.9913 on the public leaderboard, and close versions of our decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992 on held-out folds."

If a judge then asks for limitations, add: "We had no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file, France has no labels and its rules were designed after looking at unlabelled test records, and we kept the French E5 reader although it failed two of its four written checks."

# Part B - Q&A bank {#part-b .part}

258 questions in 21 categories, numbered Q1 to Q258 across the whole bank. Every item has the same parts:

- *Why they ask* (grey italics): what the judge is really testing.
- **Say** (in the box): the spoken answer, 20-35 seconds. Direct answer first, then one number, then stop.
- **If they push**: the expert follow-up, only if they ask again. **If they push further** appears where two near-identical questions from the source banks were merged into one item: it is the follow-up of the merged answer.
- **Numbers**: the figures behind the answer, with their sources (Doc = our submitted Documentation, the primary truth; CodeREADME / Evidence / Code = the code package, true but secondary, use only if asked; derived = simple arithmetic on documented numbers; background = correct general knowledge not in our Documentation, use only if asked).

Badges: ★ basic, ★★ probing, ★★★ hard or adversarial; LIKELY = a question we expect the judges to ask. Where an answer is our own reasoning rather than a measurement, it says so; never turn it into a claimed result. A *See also* line at the end of a category points to questions of that category that are answered elsewhere.

## 1. Problem and data (15 questions) {#cat-1 .cat}

### Q1. What exactly is the task, in one sentence? ★ LIKELY {#q1 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check that you can frame the problem precisely before talking about models.

**Say:** We link each incoming record, from Source 2 or Source 3, to at most one business in the reference list, or to none, and one business may own several incoming records. All matching happens inside one country, and the test set has about 10 million incoming records against 1.7 million businesses.

**If they push:** It is many-to-one record linkage against a reference list, not clustering: there is no record-to-record graph to close, so the natural decision is "which business, if any, for this record". The score is computed per business, and both output files have one row per business.

**Numbers:**

- 9,969,589 incoming records; 1,732,544 businesses; US, India, France (Doc 2.1)

### Q2. How large is the data, country by country? ★ {#q2 .q}

*Why they ask:* Scale drives every design choice; they want to see that you know your own numbers.

**Say:** India is the largest, then the US, then France, and every country has between 5.5 and 5.8 incoming records per business. In total that is about 10 million incoming records against 1.7 million businesses.

**If they push:** Per business it is 5.756 in the US, 5.824 in India and 5.531 in France, 5.75 overall. Our output links 3.38 records per business on average, so many incoming records end up unlinked.

**Numbers:**

- US 663,106 businesses / 3,817,031 incoming records; India 809,986 / 4,717,565; France 259,452 / 1,434,993 (Doc 2.1)
- 3.3805 links per business in our output (Doc B.1)

### Q3. What makes this problem hard? ★ LIKELY {#q3 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you understood the real difficulty, not just the mechanics.

**Say:** Three things. Scale: all same-country pairs would be 6.7 trillion. Look-alikes: many businesses share almost the same name, so the decision is between near-identical candidates, and "none of them" must always be an allowed answer. And France came with no labels at all.

**If they push:** On top of that the text is noisy and multilingual: records without an address, abbreviations, names in Devanagari, French conventions such as "15B" or "R" for "Rue". Our India example shows the look-alike problem: three businesses all called "Vijay Enterprises Private Limited", in Agra, Satara and Byculla.

**Numbers:**

- 6,724,569,566,212 same-country pairs (Doc 3)
- France has no labels (Doc 2.1); India example (Doc D.2)

### Q4. What did your data analysis show about how true records differ from their business? ★★ LIKELY {#q4 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to know whether the design came from evidence or from habit.

**Say:** True records of a business tend to lose information: they drop a digit or the legal suffix, abbreviate, or transliterate the name into another script, and some use a brand, website or "doing business as" form. So instead of describing a candidate only by how similar it is, we describe exactly what changed (numbers, words added, dropped or replaced, the legal form) and let the decision model learn which changes are harmless.

**If they push:** That is why retrieval is deliberately tolerant (letter pieces, sound keys, legal words left out of the name lookups) while the decision is strict. In our US example the four candidate names differ only in the legal form or one word, and the decision model gives the "Inc" candidate 0.965022 and the "LLC" candidate 0.000007.

**Numbers:**

- US example scores 0.965022 (Inc), 0.000007 (LLC), 0.088664 (PC), 0.000088 (Industries Inc) (Doc D.1)

### Q5. What are Source 2 and Source 3, and do you treat them differently? ★ {#q5 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check whether you looked at the sources separately or ignored the distinction.

**Say:** They are the two sources of incoming records, and we run both through the same per-country pipeline. The models know the source through a source flag feature, and the CatBoost ranker's training sample was balanced at 35,000 records per country and source.

**If they push:** One code path means one set of thresholds to tune and validate; if the sources behave differently, the trees can split on the flag. We did not build source-specific models.

**Numbers:**

- Ranker pilot of 140,000 incoming records = 35,000 per country and source (Doc 4)

### Q6. What does "France has no labels" change in practice? ★ {#q6 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to see you understand the consequences of a domain with zero supervision.

**Say:** France appears only in the test files, so we can neither train on French labels nor measure a French score. It changed four things: French cleaning rules, two French readers self-trained on confident French pairs, a stricter threshold of 0.82, and France rules computed by code; the France decision model itself learns from US and Indian rows.

**If they push:** A diagnostic upload shows what is at stake: emptying every French row dropped the public score from 0.970125 to 0.839. The France rules were designed by analysing the unlabelled French test records, with some parameters chosen after seeing public scores, and we disclose that. We have no measured French F0.5, and we say so.

**Numbers:**

- France: 259,452 businesses, 1,434,993 incoming records, no labels (Doc 2.1)
- Diagnostic upload 0.970125 → 0.839 (Doc B.6, uploads 4-5)
- France rules designed on unlabelled test records, parameters chosen after seeing test and public results (Doc C items 2, 4)

### Q7. How rare is a true pair in the full comparison space? ★★ {#q7 .q}

*Why they ask:* Extreme imbalance is the classic trap in entity resolution; they test whether you see where it is handled.

**Say:** Extremely rare: each incoming record has at most one owner among hundreds of thousands of businesses in its country, so at most about 1.5 pairs in a million can be true. Blocking is what removes that imbalance: our candidate file has about 1.23 candidates per incoming record.

**If they push:** So the readers and decision models work on short, competitive lists, on average 1.17 shortlisted pairs per record, and are trained as ordinary binary classifiers on those short lists rather than on a one-in-a-million problem. Our candidate file keeps 1.83 pairs per million, the same order as the at most 1.48 per million that can be true at all.

**Numbers:**

- At most 9,969,589 true pairs / 6,724,569,566,212 = 1.48 per million (derived)
- 1.2331 candidates per incoming record (Doc B.1); reduction ratio 0.99999817, so 1.83 per million kept (Doc 3, derived)
- 11,687,317 shortlist pairs / 9,969,589 = 1.17 per record (derived)

### Q8. The test set has 5.75 incoming records per business, but you link only 3.38. Where did the rest go? ★★ {#q8 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check that you understand the "or none" part of the task and your own output.

**Say:** They are records we left unlinked: either they belong to no business, or we were not confident enough to name a clear winner. We make 0.5875 links per incoming record, so about 41 % stay unlinked; with private labels we cannot split that into true non-matches and our abstentions.

**If they push:** The metric scores businesses, not records, so an unlinked record costs us only if it had a true owner, as a missed record; a wrong link would also cost the business that receives it. Of the 1,732,544 business rows, 1,632,457 have at least one link and the busiest has 11.

**Numbers:**

- 5,856,936 links; 0.5875 links per incoming record; about 41 % unlinked (Doc B.1, derived)
- Links per business: mean 3.3805, median 3, max 11 (Doc B.1)

### Q9. Which country was the hardest? ★★ {#q9 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you looked at per-country behaviour rather than one global number.

**Say:** Among the labelled countries, India: the index finds the true business for 98.51 % of Indian held-out records against 99.37 % in the US, and the held-out F0.5 is lower too. France is the hardest to judge, because without labels we cannot measure it at all.

**If they push:** On fold 9 the same India recipe scores 0.990046 on Indian records and 0.991212 on US records. The Indian miss we target is a native-script name that the Latin index does not retrieve, or retrieves only as same-name businesses in other places, as in our Vijay Enterprises example; that is why the native-script second-chance search exists, and it added 9,759 links.

**If they push further:** One visible difference is India's lower recall ceiling: the index finds the true business for 99.37 % of held-out US records but 98.51 % of Indian ones, and the shortlist keeps at least 98.87 % and 98.06 %. Native-script names without a known transliteration are one of our missed-match types, and the native-script search targets them.

**Numbers:**

- Index recall, fold 9: US 99.3694 %, India 98.5068 % (Doc B.2)
- Held-out F0.5, folds 9 / 8: US 0.991212 / 0.991545; India 0.990046 / 0.990298 (Doc 5)
- Native-script second-chance links +9,759 (Doc B.1); miss type (Doc 3, Doc D.2)
- Held-out (Doc 5); recall (Doc B.2)

### Q10. Can you show what a raw incoming record looks like next to its candidate business? ★ {#q10 .q}

*Why they ask:* A quick way to check that you have looked at the data, not just the metrics.

**Say:** Our French example: the incoming record is "TQ COMITE SARL", "2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN, NANTES", and its top candidate is "TQ Parents SARL", "2 Rue Suzanne Lenglen, Nantes, Pays de la Loire". You see capitals, "R" for "Rue", a missing region and one name word that differs; our US example has no address at all.

**If they push:** After our cleaning both addresses become "2 rue suzanne lenglen nantes", so retrieval finds the pair easily; the hard part is the decision, and here a France rule vetoed the link because "comite" replaced "parents" at the same address. That is the general pattern: cleaning and retrieval make true pairs easy to find, and the decision has to tell near-identical candidates apart.

**Numbers:**

- Decision-model score 0.999837, vetoed by the category-swap veto (Doc D.3)
- Cleaned address: output of our French cleaning code on these two strings (Code)

### Q11. What do singletons mean for you, and how do you handle them? ★★ LIKELY {#q11 .q}

*Why they ask:* Singletons are where precision-first scoring bites hardest; Amazon lists them as an edge case.

**Say:** There are two kinds: a business with no true records, and an incoming record that belongs to no business. For the first the only perfect answer is an empty row, and 100,087 businesses, 5.8 %, end with no link; for the second we link nothing unless the best candidate is both confident and a clear winner.

**If they push:** 125 of those empty businesses never received a single candidate; the rest had candidates, but none of those incoming records was linked to them. Without test labels we cannot say how many of the 100,087 are truly empty, only that a correct empty row scores a full point.

**If they push further:** Links per incoming record: 0.5875 overall (US 0.5895, India 0.5806, France 0.6046), so about 41 % are unlinked (derived). We don't know how many test records truly have no owner, because the labels are private. A record that belongs to no business can never raise the score; it can only lower it, by becoming a wrong link on some business.

**Numbers:**

- 100,087 empty rows (Doc B.1); 5.8 % (derived)
- 125 businesses without candidates; 2 incoming records without a candidate (Doc B.1)
- Links per incoming record 0.5875 (Doc B.1); about 41 % unlinked (derived)

### Q12. What exactly do you submit, and how is it checked? ★ {#q12 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check that you know the deliverable and the guard rails around it.

**Say:** Two files, each with one row per test business: the matching file lists the incoming records we link to that business, and the candidate file lists its shortlisted pairs plus the candidates added by the second-chance searches. Our export asserts that every link is also a candidate, and the last stage runs the organisers' validator with ID checks, which returns PASS.

**If they push:** No pair joins two countries and no incoming record is linked to more than one business. From the stored models, our inference stages rewrite both files byte for byte.

**Numbers:**

- 1,732,544 rows in each file (Evidence: validator log)
- 5,856,936 links; 12,293,019 candidate pairs (Doc B.1, Doc 3)

### Q13. Only the links are scored, so why does the candidate file matter? ★★ LIKELY {#q13 .q}

*Why they ask:* Candidate pairs per entity is an explicit judging angle; they test whether you optimised it on purpose.

**Say:** Because candidate efficiency, the number of pairs per business, shows how much work the expensive stages really do and how well the system would scale, and the organisers list candidate pairs per entity as a judging topic. Ours is about 7.10 pairs per business, out of a space of 6.7 trillion pairs.

**If they push:** The file is not padded or trimmed after the decision: it is exactly the shortlist our readers read plus the candidates of the two second-chance searches, 1.2331 per incoming record, and 90.59 % of records have exactly one candidate. To be precise, the CatBoost ranker also scores the 21.71 pairs per business that pass the quick filter, and the address search's filter scores its retrieved pairs; those are not written, and our documentation says so. The recall price is measured: the shortlist still holds the true business for at least 98.87 % of US and 98.06 % of Indian held-out records.

**Numbers:**

- 12,293,019 pairs, 7.0954 per business, reduction ratio 0.99999817 (Doc 3)
- Ranker input 37,614,782 pairs (21.7107 per business) and address-search retrieved pairs are model-scored but not written (Doc 3)
- 1.2331 candidates per record; 9,031,916 records (90.59 %) with exactly one (Doc B.1)
- Shortlist recall lower bounds: US 98.8748 %, India 98.0572 % (Doc B.2)
- "Candidate pairs per entity" is a listed judging topic (DECK_PLAN)

### Q14. Why do you never match across countries? ★ {#q14 .q}

*Why they ask:* They probe whether a hard constraint could silently lose matches.

**Say:** We treat the country as a hard block: all retrieval runs inside one country, and no pair in our files joins two countries. That removes impossible pairs for free, and it lets each country use its own cleaning rules, readers and threshold through a country profile.

**If they push:** The comparison space is then the sum over countries of businesses times incoming records, 6.7 trillion pairs, not the full cross product. If the country field could be wrong in production, we would add a cross-country search for records left unlinked; we did not need or test that here.

**Numbers:**

- 6,724,569,566,212 same-country pairs (Doc 3); no cross-country pair in the output (Doc B.1)

### Q15. What information does each record actually carry? ★ {#q15 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to see that you know how thin the signal is.

**Say:** Very little: an id, a business name, an address and a country, and the source is known from the file. So everything is built from two short text fields, which is why we care so much about exactly how names and addresses differ.

**If they push:** Addresses can be missing, as in our US example, and names can be in Devanagari or carry French legal forms. The readers see each side as raw "name | address" text, with the pair truncated to 128 tokens.

**Numbers:**

- Record fields: id, name, address, country (Code: data loading)
- Reader input truncated to 128 tokens (Doc 4); US record without address (Doc D.1)

## 2. Metric and the precision-first choice (13 questions) {#cat-2 .cat}

### Q16. How is the competition metric computed? ★ LIKELY {#q16 .q}

*Why they ask:* Everything else follows from the metric; they check you can state it exactly.

**Say:** For each business we compare the incoming records we linked to it with its true records and compute F0.5, then we average over all businesses, including those with no true records. A business with no true records scores 1 only if its row is empty.

**If they push:** F0.5 = 1.25·P·R / (0.25·P + R), which per business simplifies to 1.25·TP / (predicted + 0.25·true), and is 1 when both counts are zero. Illustration with made-up counts: 4 true records, we link 3 of them and nothing wrong, so 1.25·3 / (3 + 0.25·4) = 0.9375.

**Numbers:**

- Formula (Doc 2.1; Code: metric function); public score 0.991300 (Doc 5)
