### Q17. Why does F0.5 favour precision? ★ {#q17 .q}

*Why they ask:* Anyone can recite "F0.5"; an expert knows what beta does.

**Say:** In F-beta, beta sets how much recall counts relative to precision; with beta = 0.5 precision weighs more, so a wrong link hurts more than a missed one. That is why every decision in our pipeline is allowed to abstain.

**If they push:** Written as a weighted harmonic mean, 1/F0.5 = 0.8/P + 0.2/R, so precision carries four times the weight of recall. Illustration, a business with 4 true records: missing one gives 0.9375, while finding all four plus one wrong link gives 1.25·4 / (5 + 1) ≈ 0.833.

### Q18. Why does the empty-row rule matter so much? ★★ LIKELY {#q18 .q}

*Why they ask:* This rule is the sharpest edge of the metric; they test whether you designed around it.

**Say:** Because a business with no true records gets a full point only if we link nothing, so one wrong link turns its 1 into 0, the largest loss possible for one business. A correct empty row is worth as much as a perfect match list, and 100,087 of our rows are empty.

**If they push:** With macro averaging these businesses weigh exactly as much as busy ones, so a liberal threshold would be punished hardest here. It is one reason for the clear-winner rule, the stricter French threshold and France rules that remove more links than they add.

**If they push further:** Empty rows: US 38,161, India 46,681, France 15,245. Each empty row scores either one (if the business truly has no records) or zero (if it had some), and we cannot tell which without labels.

**Numbers:**

- 100,087 empty rows (Doc B.1)
- France rules: 31,707 links vetoed, 11,636 added (derived from Doc B.3)
- 100,087 empty rows (Doc B.1); 5.8 % (derived)

### Q19. Why is a wrong link worse than a missed link, beyond the formula? ★★★ {#q19 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want the mechanism, not the slogan.

**Say:** A wrong link usually costs twice: it is a false positive for the business that receives it and, if the record has a true owner, a missed record for that owner. Abstaining costs only the missed record. So when two candidates are close, linking nothing beats guessing.

**If they push:** Our threshold-plus-lead rule encodes this asymmetry, and the second-chance thresholds were chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice, which builds the same asymmetry into their tuning. In our French example the decision model said 0.999837, yet a France rule vetoed the link because one word was swapped at the same address.

**Numbers:**

- Second-chance thresholds: fold 8, false positives counted twice (Doc 4)
- French example 0.999837, vetoed (Doc D.3)

### Q20. What does macro-averaging over businesses imply for your design? ★★ {#q20 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you see that the metric is per entity, not per pair.

**Say:** Every business counts equally, whether it has one true record or eleven, so we cannot buy score by getting the busy businesses right. It also means a pair-level measure such as AUC or log loss is not the thing to optimise at the end: our models train with log loss, but every operating point is chosen on the exact per-business metric.

**If they push:** For a business with a single true record, one decision swings its score between 0 and 1. And because the records of one business interact in its score, we added a per-business consistency check, and our folds are split by business so that all records of a business sit on the same side.

**Numbers:**

- Links per business: median 3, max 11 (Doc B.1)
- Training losses: ranker Logloss, readers binary cross-entropy, decision models binary LightGBM; operating points on exact per-business macro F0.5 (Doc 4); folds per business (Doc 4)

### Q21. How did you choose the decision threshold, and why not tune for AUC? ★★ LIKELY {#q21 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether operating points were set on the right objective and on held-out data.

**Say:** We tuned it directly on the competition metric, exact per-business macro F0.5, on held-out fold 8, which gave 0.75 for the US and India. AUC measures how well all pairs are ranked and has no threshold in it at all, while our decision is at most one link per record, scored per business with empty rows worth 1, so the best threshold can only be read off that exact metric.

**If they push:** The per-business consistency check was tuned on folds 8 and 9 and the second-chance thresholds on fold 8 with false positives counted twice. A real example of AUC and F0.5 disagreeing: on our generated French test set the French E5 reader had the higher AUC, 0.98038 against 0.979415, but the lower best F0.5, 0.910516 against 0.914964.

**If they push further:** The exact metric matters because averaging per business gives small and empty businesses the same weight as large ones, so the best pair-level threshold is not the best business-level one. The honest caveat: fold 8 also appears in our held-out table, so that table is not an untouched test of this choice, as our documentation states.

**If they push further:** Per business, F0.5 = 1.25 · TP / (predicted + 0.25 · true). A business with 4 true records scores 1.0 if all are found, 0.9375 if one is missed, and 0.833 if all are found plus one wrong link, so here a wrong link costs about 2.7 times a miss; at a business with no true records a wrong link costs the whole point. The E5 readers' AUCs are about 0.9985, which says nothing about this trade-off.

**Numbers:**

- Threshold 0.75 (fold 8); consistency check 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77 (folds 8 and 9) (Doc 4)
- Generated French test set: AUC 0.98038 vs 0.979415; best F0.5 0.910516 vs 0.914964 (Doc B.4)
- F0.5 = 1.25 · TP / (predicted + 0.25 · true), 1 if both are 0 (Doc 2.1; formula as in Explainer)
- Worked values 1.0 / 0.9375 / 0.833 (derived)

### Q22. Why require a lead of 0.4 over the runner-up, not just a threshold? ★★ LIKELY {#q22 .q}

*Why they ask:* The lead rule is unusual; they want the reasoning behind it.

**Say:** Because the dangerous case is two candidates that both look right: a threshold alone would link one of them, and a near-tie is where a wrong link is most likely. The lead rule says: link only a clear winner, otherwise link nothing.

**If they push:** In our US example the best scores 0.965022 and the runner-up 0.088664, a lead of 0.876, so it links. For the 90.59 % of incoming records with a single candidate the lead condition passes automatically and only the threshold decides; 0.4 is one fixed lead used in every country, and the US and India threshold next to it was tuned on fold 8 for the exact metric.

**Numbers:**

- Lead 0.4 in every country (Doc 4); US example lead 0.876 (Doc D.1)
- 90.59 % of incoming records with exactly one candidate (Doc B.1)

### Q23. Where does "precision first" show up in your pipeline? ★ LIKELY {#q23 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether the metric really shaped the system end to end.

**Say:** At every decision point: at most one link per record, the best candidate only if it is confident and a clear winner, a stricter 0.82 bar in France, second-chance searches that only touch unlinked records, and France rules that remove more links than they add. Retrieval, by contrast, is recall-first, because a business that is never retrieved can never be linked.

**If they push:** In France the decision model accepted 887,630 links and after the rules 867,559 remain. The second-chance searches never undo a link, while the consistency check and the France vetoes can remove one.

**Numbers:**

- France 887,630 accepted → 867,559 links (Doc B.3, B.1)
- Thresholds 0.75 / 0.82, lead 0.4 (Doc 4)

### Q24. Why is France's threshold 0.82 instead of 0.75? ★★ {#q24 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test how you set an operating point without labels.

**Say:** Because France has no labels, we could not tune its threshold on the metric, so we chose a more conservative point. It was set without labels, from the number of French links per business together with a threshold sweep on US and Indian fold 8.

**If they push:** As a proxy, the France recipe applied to US and Indian rows at 0.82, without the consistency check, scores 0.990508 and 0.989467 on fold 9; that measures the recipe, not French accuracy. We have no measured French F0.5, and the same 0.82 is used for any unseen country.

**Numbers:**

- 0.82 for France and the default route (Doc 4, Doc C item 1)
- Proxy, fold 9: US 0.990508, India 0.989467; fold 8: 0.990977, 0.989850 (Doc 5)

### Q25. If wrong links are so costly, why not link only when you are 99 % sure? ★★ {#q25 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test that you see both sides of the trade-off, not only the precision side.

**Say:** Because missing hurts too: a business with true records and an empty row scores 0, exactly like a business with no true records and one wrong link. The best bar is where per-business F0.5 peaks on held-out data, and for the US and India that was 0.75, not 0.99.

**If they push:** Illustration: a business with 4 true records scores 0.9375 if we miss one of them, but 0 if we refuse all four. The lead rule lets us keep a moderate threshold while still refusing the dangerous near-ties, and the second-chance searches win back some of the records the main decision leaves unlinked.

**Numbers:**

- 0.75 chosen on fold 8 for exact per-business macro F0.5 (Doc 4)

### Q26. Could you have optimised expected F0.5 directly instead of using a fixed threshold? ★★★ {#q26 .q}

*Why they ask:* A senior scientist probes whether you understand the metric's structure, not just a tuned knob.

**Say:** In principle yes: the metric is per business, so the best decision for one record depends on what else is linked to the same business, and a fixed threshold ignores that. Our per-business consistency check is a cheap approximation: it re-decides each record with a bar that depends on how many other records were accepted for that business.

**If they push:** Toy maths: adding a link that is right with probability q to a row with TP = t and D = predicted + 0.25·true raises expected F0.5 only if q ≥ t/D, so a business with 4 true records and 3 correct links already needs q ≥ 0.75, and the break-even moves with the row. The check uses 0.75, 0.68, 0.72 and 0.77 for 0, 1, 2 and 3 or more other accepted records, tuned on folds 8 and 9, and it moved few links (US +277 / −284, India +247 / −248).

**Numbers:**

- Consistency check bars and effect (Doc 4, Doc B.1); break-even q ≥ t/D (derived from the formula)

### Q27. What is your precision-recall trade-off? Did you look at precision and recall separately? ★★ LIKELY {#q27 .q}

*Why they ask:* Amazon lists the precision-recall trade-off under F0.5 as a topic; they want the knobs and the evidence.

**Say:** The trade-off is set by a few knobs: the threshold, the consistency-check bars and the second-chance bars, chosen on held-out folds for the exact metric, plus one fixed 0.4 lead for every country and a more conservative French threshold. Our evaluation code counts false positives and false negatives, but our documentation reports only the combined F0.5, so I do not have separate precision and recall figures to quote.

**If they push:** Recall has a hard ceiling upstream: the shortlist holds the true business for at least 98.87 % of US and 98.06 % of Indian owned records on fold 9, so the decision cannot recover the rest without the second-chance searches. The next thing we would report is a precision-recall curve per country on held-out folds.

**Numbers:**

- Shortlist recall, fold 9: US 98.8748 % to 99.3628 %; India 98.0572 % to 98.4831 % (Doc B.2)
- Knobs and how each was chosen (Doc 4); false-positive and false-negative counts in the evaluation code (Code: metric function)

### Q28. If the metric were F1 instead of F0.5, what would you change? ★★★ {#q28 .q}

*Why they ask:* A counterfactual shows whether you understand the design or only tuned it.

**Say:** We would lower the bar and loosen the lead, because F1 weighs precision and recall equally, so a link pays off at a lower probability of being right. The second-chance searches would become more valuable and the France vetoes less so, and we would re-tune every threshold on held-out folds for F1.

**If they push:** In toy maths, a business with 4 true records and 3 correct links needs an extra link to be right with probability at least 0.75 under F0.5, but only about 0.43 under F1. The pipeline itself would not change, only the operating points and the double weighting of false positives in the second-chance tuning; we have not run that, so I cannot give a measured number.

**Numbers:**

- Break-even q ≥ t / (predicted + β²·true): 3 / 4 = 0.75 for F0.5, 3 / 7 ≈ 0.43 for F1 (derived from the formula, illustration)

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "What does 0.9913 mean in practice?" see [Q180](#q180).

## 3. Normalisation and multilingual text (15 questions) {#cat-3 .cat}

### Q29. What does your text cleaning do? ★ LIKELY {#q29 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check that you know the unglamorous step that sets retrieval recall.

**Say:** For the US and India: lower case, "&" becomes "and", other punctuation becomes spaces, state names and street words are mapped to one short form, leading zeros are dropped, and Indian-script name words are transliterated to Latin. France adds French rules: "15B" becomes "15 bis", street types and their typos are unified, "St" becomes "Saint", and "S.A.R.L." or "5arl" becomes "sarl".

**If they push:** With our cleaning code, a made-up "Suite 0012, 007 Main Street, California" becomes "ste 12 7 main st ca". From our French example, "2 R SUZANNE LENGLEN, NANTES" and "2 Rue Suzanne Lenglen, Nantes, Pays de la Loire" both become "2 rue suzanne lenglen nantes".

**Numbers:**

- Cleaning rules (Doc 2.2); outputs above produced by our shipped cleaning code (Code; first input is an illustration)

### Q30. Why clean the text at all when your readers read the raw text? ★★ {#q30 .q}

*Why they ask:* It sounds contradictory; they test whether you know which component needs what.

**Say:** Because the index lookup needs exact token matches: "Street" and "St", or "Maharashtra" and "MH", must become the same token to find each other. The readers read the raw text instead, because cleaning throws away signals they can use, such as punctuation, capitals and the original script.

**If they push:** So cleaning serves retrieval and the 76 index features, while the "what changed" features use the name lower-cased, accent-stripped and transliterated, with legal-form words removed and described by separate legal-form features. Each component gets the version of the text that suits its job.

**Numbers:**

- Readers read raw text (Doc 2.2); 76 index features (Doc 3)

### Q31. How do you handle names written in Indian scripts? ★ LIKELY {#q31 .q}

*Why they ask:* Multilingual input is a stated challenge; they want the mechanism.

**Say:** In two layers. During cleaning, each native-script name word is mapped to Latin with a word list learned from labelled training matches, with a generic transliteration as fallback; and for records still unlinked, the native-script second-chance search tries Latin spellings of the name within the same state, which added 9,759 links in India.

**If they push:** In our India example the second-chance search's list maps विजय to vijay, एंटरप्राइजेज to enterprises, प्राइवेट to private and लिमिटेड to limited; without the legal words the key is (vijay, enterprises), searched within Maharashtra. The readers also read the Devanagari directly, because their multilingual tokenizer covers it.

**If they push further:** The cleaning word list is a co-occurrence alignment learned on folds 0-5: a native token gets a Latin word if they co-occur at least 3 times, with purity at least 0.35 and a score at least 1.8 times the runner-up; otherwise unidecode is used. It is not a neural transliterator. The second-chance list keeps every alternative with at least 5 % of a token's count and tries up to 64 transliterations. Separately, a label-free word alignment on test records whose top candidate has probability at least 0.9 feeds some name features; our documentation discloses it.

**Numbers:**

- +9,759 links; 649,965 pairs scored for 171,713 records (Doc 3, B.1)
- Transliteration example (Doc D.2)
- Native-script search: 649,965 pairs scored for 171,713 records, +9,759 links (Doc 3, B.1)

### Q32. How was the transliteration word list learned? ★★★ {#q32 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether "learned lexicon" hides something fragile or leaky.

**Say:** From labelled training pairs of folds 0 to 5: for every native-script word in an incoming name, we count which Latin words appear in its true business's cleaned name, and we keep the best Latin word only if the evidence is strong and unambiguous. It is a co-occurrence alignment learned from labels, not a neural transliterator.

**If they push:** A native word gets a Latin word only if they co-occur at least 3 times, that pairing covers at least 35 % of the native word's occurrences, and its score, count / (frequency of the Latin word + 1)^0.6, is at least 1.8 times the runner-up's; the exponent stops very common Latin words from absorbing every native word. The second-chance search uses its own list from training matches, and when its model is trained that list leaves out the record's own fold, so a record never benefits from its own label.

**Numbers:**

- At least 3 co-occurrences, purity ≥ 0.35, score ratio ≥ 1.8, exponent 0.6 (Code: word-list learner)
- Second-chance list: leave-own-fold-out for training (Doc 4)

### Q33. Why not use a neural transliteration model or an LLM for this? ★★ {#q33 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you considered the obvious modern alternative.

**Say:** A word list learned from our own labelled matches is in-domain, deterministic, easy to audit and essentially free at inference, and it only has to serve exact-token retrieval. No LLM runs anywhere in our pipeline.

**If they push:** The multilingual readers already read the native script from the raw text, and the remaining retrieval misses are what the native-script second-chance search targets. We did not benchmark a neural transliterator, so we cannot claim it would be worse; it would be a candidate for words the list does not cover.

**Numbers:**

- No LLM in the pipeline (Doc C item 6)

### Q34. What exactly changes for French text? ★★ {#q34 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want evidence that you adapted to a new address format rather than reusing US rules.

**Say:** French addresses and legal names follow their own conventions, so France gets extra cleaning rules on top of the US and India ones. For example, "N°" prefixes are removed, "15B" becomes "15 bis", "R" and "Rue" both become "rue", street-type typos are fixed with a table learned from the files, "St" becomes "Saint", and dotted or leet legal forms such as "S.A.R.L." or "5arl" collapse to "sarl".

**If they push:** With our cleaning code, the made-up inputs "N° 15B BD Saint Michel, Paris" and "15 bis boulevard St Michel, Paris" both become "15 bis bd saint michel paris", and "S.A.R.L. Dupont & Fils" and "5arl Dupont et Fils" both become "sarl dupont and fils". Region and department parts of an address are recognised from the files and left out of the matching text, which is why both addresses of our French example, one with "Pays de la Loire" and one without, clean to the same string.

**Numbers:**

- French rules (Doc 2.2); outputs and region handling from our French cleaning code (Code; inputs are illustrations)

### Q35. You learned French geography and a typo table from the test files. Isn't that leakage? ★★★ {#q35 .q}

*Why they ask:* Any use of test data raises a flag; they test whether you know the line between labels and text.

**Say:** It does use the unlabelled test text, never test labels, and our documentation discloses it. It is the same kind of statistic as the word-rarity weights of our index, which have to be computed over the businesses we match against anyway.

**If they push:** The geography comes from counting which comma-separated address parts occur together in the test files (regions, departments, cities), with no labels; the typo table maps a word at the street-type position of incoming records that (almost) never occurs in business records to the nearest known street type within one or two edits, skipping ambiguous cases. In the same spirit, one word list used inside some Indian decision-model features is aligned, without labels, on test records whose top candidate the ranker scores at 0.9 or more, and our documentation lists that and every other statistic we compute on the test files.

**Numbers:**

- Disclosure of all statistics computed on unlabelled test files, including the India word list aligned on test records with top ranker probability ≥ 0.9 (Doc C item 1); geography and typo-table learning (Code: French cleaning)

### Q36. How do you handle abbreviations and synonyms such as Street/St or state names? ★ {#q36 .q}

*Why they ask:* Basic, but they check that you used controlled, auditable mappings.

**Say:** With small hand-written tables and no outside data: street words are mapped to one short form (road to "rd", street to "st", avenue to "ave"), state names to their codes (California to "ca", Maharashtra to "mh"), and in names "&" becomes "and". France has its own table of street types and name abbreviations, for example "Etablissements" and "Ets" become one form.

**If they push:** The mapping only has to be applied the same way on both sides, not be linguistically perfect, because it serves exact-token retrieval. Our documentation states that hand-written lists are limited to small word lists, and they ship with the code.

**Numbers:**

- Hand-written lists limited to small word lists (Doc C item 6); tables (Code: cleaning tables)

### Q37. What is the "core name", and why remove legal forms for retrieval? ★★ {#q37 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you see how retrieval and decision split the work on legal-form differences.

**Say:** The core name is the business name without legal-form words such as inc, llc, ltd, pvt, private, limited or sarl, and without "and" and "the". Our name lookups, letter pieces, sound keys and the exact-name key all use it, so dropping or changing a legal form from that list does not block retrieval.

**If they push:** "Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc" and "Legacy Marketing Enterprises LLC" have the same core name, so they are retrieved together, which is why our US example's shortlist holds both. Telling them apart is then the job of the readers and the legal-form features, and the decision model gave 0.965022 to the Inc and 0.000007 to the LLC.

**Numbers:**

- Core name (Doc 3; Code: index lookup, which also applies it to the name-word lookup; its list is inc, incorporated, llc, llp, ltd, limited, pvt, private, corp, corporation, co, company, plc, sarl, sas, sa, sci, sasu, eurl, and, the, so for example "pc" stays in the core name)
- US example scores (Doc D.1)

### Q38. How do you handle typos and spelling variants? ★ LIKELY {#q38 .q}

*Why they ask:* Noisy names and addresses are an explicit judging topic.

**Say:** We handle them in three places. Cleaning fixes known variants such as French street-type typos and leet spellings, the index has letter-piece and sound channels that still match after a typo, and the readers read raw text and tolerate small edits.

**If they push:** Illustrations: "Kreeshna" and "Krishna" have the same consonant skeleton "krshn" in the sound channel, and "Starbucks" and "Star Bucks" share all letter pieces because spaces are removed before the pieces are cut. In names, a zero next to a letter becomes "o", so "C0ffee" becomes "coffee".

**Numbers:**

- Channels (Doc 3); zero-to-o repair (Code: US/India cleaning); examples are illustrations

### Q39. How do you treat numbers: house numbers, leading zeros, "24/11"? ★★ {#q39 .q}

*Why they ask:* Numbers are the strongest and the most fragile evidence in an address.

**Say:** We normalise them carefully because they carry so much evidence: leading zeros are dropped, so "007" becomes "7", punctuation splits a number like 24/11 into 24 and 11, and in France glued suffixes are split and "N°" removed. Then the "what changed" features describe how the numbers differ: absolute and relative difference, digit edit distance, shared prefix or suffix.

**If they push:** The address second-chance search looks up businesses that share one of the record's three rarest digit runs and one of its three rarest address words. In our India example the house number 24/11, with both digit runs matching, is what separated the right "Vijay Enterprises" from four others in Mumbai.

**Numbers:**

- Number features (Doc 4); address search keys (Doc 3); India example (Doc D.2)

### Q40. Do you handle accents and mixed-script names? ★ {#q40 .q}

*Why they ask:* A quick check that real-world text quirks were covered.

**Say:** Yes, word by word: an accented or non-Latin word is transliterated, so "Société" becomes "societe", and in a name that mixes Latin and Devanagari the Latin words stay as they are while the native words go through the learned word list. Addresses are always transliterated generically.

**If they push:** The "what changed" features also strip accents and use the same learned list, and the readers read the original characters.

**Numbers:**

- Word-by-word handling (Code: US/India cleaning)

### Q41. Which tokenizer do the readers use, and does it cover Devanagari and French? ★★★ {#q41 .q}

*Why they ask:* An expert checks whether the multilingual claim holds at the tokenizer level.

**Say:** All four readers use the MiniLM tokenizer, a multilingual SentencePiece vocabulary that covers Latin, accented and Indian scripts, so raw Devanagari and French text is read directly. Each record-business pair is truncated longest-first to 128 tokens.

**If they push:** The E5 readers can share that tokenizer because both base models use the XLM-RoBERTa vocabulary (general background, not stated in our documentation). We do not use E5's "query:" and "passage:" prefixes, because we fine-tune it as a pair reader that reads both texts together, not as an embedding model for retrieval.

**Numbers:**

- MiniLM tokenizer for all readers, 128 tokens, longest-first (Doc 4, B.5)

### Q42. One Hindi word can be written several ways in Latin letters. How do you cope? ★★★ {#q42 .q}

*Why they ask:* One-to-many transliteration is the real difficulty with Indic names; they test whether your word list handles it.

**Say:** Differently for two jobs. The cleaning word list keeps one best Latin spelling per native word, and only when the evidence clearly favours it; the native-script second-chance search keeps every alternative spelling with at least 5 % of the native word's observed spellings and tries up to 64 combinations per name.

**If they push:** So the main index lookup stays precise and cheap, and the second chance covers spelling variety for records that are still unlinked. Where neither list knows a word, the name falls back to a generic transliteration, and the multilingual readers still read the original script.

**Numbers:**

- Alternatives with at least 5 % share, up to 64 transliterations (Doc 3)

### Q43. Your state table maps both Tennessee and Tamil Nadu to "tn". Isn't that a bug? ★★★ {#q43 .q}

*Why they ask:* An adversarial check that you know your own lookup tables and their failure modes.

**Say:** It would be if we matched across countries, but we never do: retrieval runs inside one country, so in the US "tn" can only mean Tennessee and in India only Tamil Nadu. The same holds for Georgia and Goa ("ga") or Minnesota and Manipur ("mn").

**If they push:** The general rule is that a normalisation collision is harmless when a block above it separates the cases, and the readers see the raw text anyway. Within a country a mapping only needs to be applied the same way on both sides: "Washington Street" becoming "wa st" looks odd but still matches itself.

**Numbers:**

- State table (Code: cleaning tables); all retrieval within one country (Doc 3)

## 4. Blocking and candidate generation (13 questions) {#cat-4 .cat}

### Q44. Why do you need blocking at all? ★ LIKELY {#q44 .q}

*Why they ask:* The basic framing question for the whole retrieval stage.

**Say:** Comparing every incoming record with every business in its country would be 6.7 trillion pairs, which no model can score. Blocking cheaply picks a few likely businesses per record; our final candidate file keeps about 7.10 pairs per business, a reduction ratio of 0.99999817.

**If they push:** That keeps 1.83 pairs in every million (derived), or 1.23 per incoming record, against at most 1.48 in a million that can be true at all, since each record has at most one owner. And the shortlist still keeps the true business for roughly 99 % of US and 98 % of Indian held-out records.

**Numbers:**

- 6,724,569,566,212 pairs; 12,293,019 kept; 7.0954 per business; ratio 0.99999817 (Doc 3)
- 1.2331 candidates per incoming record (Doc B.1); 1.83 and 1.48 per million (derived); shortlist recall (Doc B.2)

### Q45. Walk me through your candidate funnel. ★ LIKELY {#q45 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want the count at each step and to see where cost and recall go.

**Say:** Four steps, from cheap to expensive: the inverted index finds about 130 candidates per business, a quick rule-based filter with no model drops the clearly weaker ones, the CatBoost ranker keeps at most four per incoming record, and the two second-chance searches add a few for records left unlinked. We end at about 7 per business.

**If they push:** In numbers: 130.1 per business in our 25 September blocking study, 21.7107 after the filter (37,614,782 pairs), 6.75 in the shortlist (11,687,317 pairs, derived) and 7.0954 in the final file (12,293,019 pairs). Per incoming record that is 1.2331 candidates, and 90.59 % of records have exactly one.

**Numbers:**

- Funnel (Doc 3); per record and single-candidate share (Doc B.1)
- Per country final: US 6.1836, India 7.5180, France 8.1060 per business (Doc 3)

### Q46. How does your inverted index work? ★★ {#q46 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether "inverted index" is understood or just a buzzword.

**Say:** Like the index at the back of a book: for every word, letter piece or sound key it stores the list of businesses that contain it. For an incoming record we walk the lists of its rarest terms first, add each term's rarity weight to every business on the list, and keep the best-scoring businesses. It is written in C++ with OpenMP and built per country on the cleaned text.

**If they push:** The rarity weight is IDF = log(1 + (N + 1)/(df + 1)); with N = 663,106 US businesses, a term found in 10 businesses weighs about 11.0 and one found in 10,000 about 4.2 (derived), so one rare shared word outweighs two common ones. There is no term-frequency part, because a short name is a set of words: the score is an IDF-weighted overlap, not TF-IDF cosine or BM25.

**Numbers:**

- IDF formula (Doc 3); 11.0 and 4.2 (derived, illustration)

### Q47. What are the five channels, and why so many? ★★ {#q47 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether each channel has a reason to exist.

**Say:** Name words, address words, 4-letter and 3-letter pieces of the core name, and a sound key of the name. Each catches a different miss: words for clean matches, letter pieces for typos, abbreviations and split or joined words, sounds for spelling variants, and the address channel for records whose name changed but whose address did not.

**If they push:** The channel weights are 1, 1, 0.45, 0.22 and 0.18, so letter pieces and sounds mostly matter when the words fail. On top, an exact-name key pulls in every business with the same sorted core-name word set when at most 2,000 businesses share it.

**Numbers:**

- Channels, weights, exact key up to 2,000 (Doc 3)

### Q48. What exactly is the sound channel? Soundex? ★★ {#q48 .q}

*Why they ask:* A precise follow-up that separates people who know the code from people who read about it.

**Say:** Not Soundex or Metaphone: a simple consonant skeleton. We delete the vowels and "y", collapse repeated letters, and index 4-letter pieces of what remains.

**If they push:** Illustrations: "Krishna" and "Kreeshna" both become "krshn" and share the pieces "krsh" and "rshn"; "Smith" and "Smyth" both become "smth". Repeats are collapsed after the vowels are dropped, so consonants that meet across a removed vowel also merge; the key is language-agnostic, which suits transliterated names where vowel spelling varies a lot, and it has the smallest weight, 0.18.

**Numbers:**

- Vowels removed, repeated letters collapsed, 4-grams, weight 0.18 (Doc 3; "y" also removed: Code: index lookup)

### Q49. How is the retrieval score computed, and why the min term? ★★★ {#q49 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether the scoring function was designed or copied.

**Say:** Each candidate gets a name score and an address score, each a sum of rarity weights of shared terms divided by a power of the business's term count, and the total is name plus address plus 1.2 times the smaller of the two. The min term rewards candidates that match on both name and address over ones that match only one of them strongly.

**If they push:** Toy example: name 10 and address 0 gives a total of 10, while name 5 and address 4 gives 5 + 4 + 1.2 × 4 = 13.8, so the balanced candidate ranks higher although its plain sum, 9, is lower. The length exponents, 0.22 for name words, 0.38 for letter pieces and 0.30 for address words, stop long names or addresses from winning just because they have more terms to match.

**Numbers:**

- ns, as and total = ns + as + 1.2·min(ns, as) with the exponents above (Doc 3); toy example is an illustration

### Q50. What are posting-list caps and budgets, and why use them? ★★★ {#q50 .q}

*Why they ask:* Bounded work per query is the core of any scaling argument for an inverted index.

**Say:** A very common term has a huge list of businesses: walking it costs a lot and tells us little. So each channel skips any term whose list is longer than a cap and stops adding terms once a budget of list entries is spent, always starting from the rarest. That bounds the work per record, whatever the record looks like.

**If they push:** Caps and budgets: name 14,000 / 22,000, address 10,000 / 18,000, 4-letter pieces 2,500 / 15,000, 3-letter pieces 1,000 / 6,000, sounds 800 / 4,000, so at most 65,000 list entries per record (derived). In effect it is a stop-word list learned automatically from document frequency.

**Numbers:**

- Caps and budgets (Doc 3); 65,000 (derived: sum of the budgets)

### Q51. Which candidates does the index keep per record, and why several lists? ★★ {#q51 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether retrieval is genuinely recall-first.

**Say:** The top 12 by total score, the top 6 by name score, the top 6 by address score, and every business with exactly the same core-name word set if at most 2,000 share it. Taking the union of several ranked lists makes retrieval recall-first: a business that matches only on the address, or only on the name, still gets in.

**If they push:** On held-out fold 9 this keeps the true business for 99.3694 % of US and 98.5068 % of Indian owned records, with about 27.5 and 23.1 candidates per record in our samples. Each pair also gets 76 features (string similarities, overlaps, rarity overlaps and retrieval scores) for the later steps.

**Numbers:**

- Kept lists (Doc 3); recall and candidates per record (Doc B.2)

### Q52. What does the quick rule-based filter do, and why no model? ★★ LIKELY {#q52 .q}

*Why they ask:* Pruning before any model is unusual; they want the rule and its measured cost.

**Say:** It keeps a candidate if any one of six simple conditions holds, such as having the record's best score, scoring at least 60 % of the best, or covering at least 95 % of the record's address. A model would first have to score all of the roughly 130 candidates per business; the rule is nearly free, and its measured cost is tiny.

**If they push:** The six: best total; total at least 0.6 times the best; best address score; address coverage of at least 0.95; a name of 3 characters or fewer with coverage at least 0.4; the same core name with coverage at least 0.3, where coverage is the rarity-weighted share of the record's address words found in the business's address. The last four keep address-only, acronym and same-name candidates that one combined score would drop, and in the blocking study the true business survived for 99.974 % of fold-8/9 records while fold-9 F0.5 moved only from 0.990117 to 0.990086.

**Numbers:**

- Six conditions; 130.1 → 21.7107 per business (Doc 3)
- Owner kept 99.974 %; fold 9 0.990117 → 0.990086; fold 8 −0.00004 (Doc 3)

### Q53. How do you know blocking does not lose true matches? ★ LIKELY {#q53 .q}

*Why they ask:* Recall is the hidden ceiling of every entity-resolution system; they want measured evidence.

**Say:** We measure recall at every candidate step on labelled fold 9: the index keeps the true business for 99.37 % of US records and 98.51 % of Indian ones, and the shortlist loses about half a percentage point more, mostly to the cap of four. The quick filter is almost free.

**If they push:** In the fold-9 samples the filter moves US recall from 99.3658 % to 99.3523 % and India from 98.388 % to 98.3745 %; the shortlist's full-fold lower bounds are 98.8748 % and 98.0572 %. These numbers use a ranker that never saw fold 9 and exclude the second-chance candidates, which target the remaining miss types: native-script names, and the same address with a different name.

**Numbers:**

- Recall table, fold 9 (Doc B.2)

### Q54. What is your blocking recall in France? ★★★ {#q54 .q}

*Why they ask:* An adversarial probe of the unlabelled country.

**Say:** We cannot measure it: France has no labels, so our recall tables exist only for the US and India. What we can say is that France uses the same index with French cleaning rules, and the system keeps more alternatives there: 32.77 candidates per business after the filter against 15.04 in the US.

**If they push:** In the final file France has 8.106 candidates per business and 1.4656 per incoming record, against 6.18 and 1.0742 in the US. With a small labelled French sample, recall at every step is the first thing we would measure.

**Numbers:**

- After the filter: France 32.7713, US 15.0352 per business (Doc 3)
- Final: France 8.1060 / 1.4656, US 6.1836 / 1.0742 per business / per record (Doc 3, B.1)

### Q55. Why do some businesses have hundreds or thousands of candidates? ★★★ {#q55 .q}

*Why they ask:* Skew in the candidate distribution is where blocking systems blow up.

**Say:** Because our caps are per incoming record, not per business: a business that many records retrieve, for instance one whose name is made of common words, collects many candidates. The median is 7 per business, but 125 businesses have more than 100 and one French business has 3,182.

**If they push:** Cost stays bounded because the shortlist adds at most four pairs per record, whatever the business. Crowded businesses are where many records compete for the same business: the collective features and the per-business consistency check in the US and India look at exactly that, and the clear-winner rule still requires each link to stand out among that record's own candidates.

**If they push further:** 125 businesses have more than 100 candidates (US 3, India 32, France 90), with a maximum of 3,182 in France; overall median 7, 99th percentile 17. At the other end, 125 businesses have no candidate at all. Links per business never exceed 11. Our documentation has no breakdown of why each crowded business is crowded.

**Numbers:**

- Candidates per business, median / p90 / p99 / max: all 7 / 11 / 17 / 3,182 (Doc B.1)
- 125 businesses with more than 100 candidates (US 3, India 32, France 90) (Doc B.1)
- Collective features and consistency check, US and India only (Doc 4); "common words" is the mechanism, not a profiled finding
- Candidates per business, all: median 7, p90 11, p99 17, max 3,182 (Doc B.1)

### Q56. Did you consider classic blocking such as sorted neighbourhood, canopy clustering or MinHash LSH? ★★ {#q56 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check your awareness of the entity-resolution literature and your reasons.

**Say:** We did not use them. Our word and letter-piece inverted index retrieves by any shared rare word, letter piece or sound rather than by agreement on one key, and the rarest-first caps act like stop-word removal, so a true pair only needs one rare shared term to be found.

**If they push:** Sorted neighbourhood depends on one sort key, so a typo in the first letters can separate a true pair, which our letter-piece and sound channels tolerate; MinHash LSH approximates the Jaccard overlap of letter-piece sets probabilistically, while our lists compute an exact rarity-weighted overlap, deterministically. Canopy clustering needs a cheap similarity plus thresholds, which is close to what our weighted overlap and top lists already do; we did not benchmark these alternatives.

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "Why CatBoost for the ranker, and how is it trained?" see [Q71](#q71); "Why at most four candidates per record?" see [Q72](#q72); "Why not embedding-based (vector) blocking?" see [Q195](#q195); "What do the second-chance searches add to the candidate file?" see [Q118](#q118).

## 5. Scale, efficiency and cost (11 questions) {#cat-5 .cat}

### Q57. What exactly is bounded per record? ★★★ {#q57 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether "linear" is backed by real caps in the code.

**Say:** Every stage has a per-record cap: a budget on how many index list entries we walk, a fixed number of top candidates per list, and at most four pairs for the readers. So total work is the number of records times a constant, plus building the index, which is linear in the number of businesses.

**If they push:** The budgets add up to at most 65,000 list entries per record (derived), the candidates are the top 12 + 6 + 6 plus at most 2,000 same-name businesses, and on average we are far below that: about 27.5 and 23.1 index candidates per record in our US and Indian samples. After that only 1.17 pairs per record reach the readers.

**Numbers:**

- Budgets and kept lists (Doc 3); candidates per record in samples (Doc B.2); 1.17 (derived)

### Q58. Where does inference time go after retrieval and reading? ★★ {#q58 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you know your profile, not just the total.

**Say:** Very little goes anywhere else: once the readers are done, every remaining stage takes minutes. In our clean run, features took about 17 minutes, the decision models about 4, the address second-chance search about 10, and writing and validating the files about 6.

**If they push:** In that run all inference stages together took about 3.9 hours of wall clock, including about 0.6 hours to retrain and run the French E5 reader, which a run from our stored models replaces by loading the shipped French E5 scores. These figures come from the clean run's stage timeline (derived), not from a dedicated benchmark.

**Numbers:**

- Stage start times (Evidence: clean_run/stage_timeline.txt; durations derived)

### Q59. How many model evaluations does a single incoming record trigger? ★★ {#q59 .q}

*Why they ask:* Per-record cost is the unit that matters when you multiply by billions.

**Say:** On average: about 23 to 28 index candidates with cheap features, about four CatBoost ranker scores, and 1.17 shortlisted pairs, each read by two readers (three in France) and scored by five small LightGBM models. So the expensive readers run only a few times per record.

**If they push:** Derived from the documentation: 37,614,782 ranker pairs / 9,969,589 records = 3.77 per record, and the index gives 27.541 (US) and 23.145 (India) candidates per record in the all-fold samples. Records still unlinked may also get a second-chance search, which is cheap by comparison.

**Numbers:**

- 37,614,782 filtered pairs (Doc 3); 3.77 per record (derived); sample counts (Doc B.2)
- Readers per country and five-seed decision models (Doc 4)

### Q60. How would you shard the index? ★★ {#q60 .q}

*Why they ask:* Sharding is the concrete step behind any billion-scale claim.

**Say:** Today the index is split by country. At billions we would split by country and then by state or postcode, so each shard's lists and score arrays stay small, and run the shards in parallel.

**If they push:** The risk is records with a missing or wrong state; the native-script second-chance search already handles that by falling back to all states when the state is unknown or has no match, and we would do the same for unlinked records. Smaller shards would also leave room for a larger cap than four where the cap loses true businesses.

**Numbers:**

- State fallback of the native-script search (Doc 3)

### Q61. At a hundred times the data, what breaks first? ★★★ {#q61 .q}

*Why they ask:* A senior engineer wants you to find your own bottleneck before they do.

**Say:** The index, not the readers: reader cost just needs more GPUs, but each index thread keeps score arrays the size of its country's business list, and as lists grow, more common terms hit the caps and are skipped, which could cost recall for records made of common words. Both point to the same fix: shard by state or postcode so each index stays small.

**If they push:** The address second-chance search is the other memory-heavy step, about 3.2 GB per worker today. We have not run at that scale, so these are limits we see in the design, not measured failures.

**Numbers:**

- Per-thread score arrays (Code: index lookup); 3.2 GB per worker (CodeREADME 1)

### Q62. How much memory and disk does it need? ★ {#q62 .q}

*Why they ask:* Resource footprint is part of cost.

**Say:** Every stage needs less than 8 GB of RAM except the address second-chance search, which uses about 3.2 GB per worker, 13 GB with the default four workers, so the whole pipeline fits in 32 GB. A full run writes about 70 GB of intermediate files.

**If they push:** The trained weights are about 2.1 GB, and the full archive with code, weights, encoders and stored reader scores is 3,285,958,103 bytes. Most stages use up to 6 CPU threads; the index lookup uses 8 to 11 in the training stages and some decision-model fits 8 to 12.

**Numbers:**

- RAM, threads, disk, weights (CodeREADME 1, 6); archive size (GitHub README)

### Q63. How much does the cascade save compared with reading every index candidate? ★★ {#q63 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you can put a number on the efficiency argument.

**Say:** About 19 times fewer pairs for the readers: they read the shortlist, about 6.75 pairs per business, instead of the roughly 130 index candidates per business. And thanks to the quick filter, the CatBoost ranker scores 37.6 million pairs rather than every index candidate.

**If they push:** By linear extrapolation from the 1.4 hours our readers took on the shortlist, reading all index candidates would be on the order of 27 GPU-hours (derived, not measured). The 130 figure comes from our 25 September blocking study, not from the final run.

**Numbers:**

- 130.1 / 6.7458 = 19.3 (derived from Doc 3); 27 GPU-hours (extrapolation)

### Q64. Is the CatBoost ranker worth it, or could the readers read everything the filter keeps? ★★ {#q64 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether each stage pays for itself.

**Say:** The ranker cuts the readers' input from 21.71 to about 6.75 pairs per business, roughly three times fewer, using only cheap tabular features. The price is the cap of four, our largest recall loss, about half a percentage point of US recall on fold 9.

**If they push:** By linear extrapolation from the 1.4 hours the readers took on the shortlist, reading all filtered pairs would be on the order of 4.5 GPU-hours (derived, not measured). The ranker's probability and rank are also inputs of the decision model, so it is more than a gate.

**Numbers:**

- 21.7107 → 6.7458 per business (Doc 3, derived); recall 99.3694 % → 98.8814 % (Doc B.2)

### Q65. How expensive is training the readers? ★★ {#q65 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether fine-tuning cost allows fast iteration.

**Say:** Cheap enough to iterate on one GPU. The reader stage, which trains the MiniLM and E5 readers for one epoch each on labelled US and Indian pairs and then scores the decision models' training pairs with them, took about 2.1 hours, and fine-tuning the French E5 reader on 949,616 pairs took about 16 minutes.

**If they push:** One epoch, bf16 mixed precision, batches of 128 and length-bucketed batches keep it cheap: grouping pairs of similar length means each batch is padded only to its own longest pair. The readers also train only on hard records plus a random 25 % of the easy ones.

**Numbers:**

- 2.1 h for the reader stage, training plus scoring of the decision models' training pairs (Evidence: clean_run/RESULT.md; stage content: Code: run_all.sh); about 16 min for 949,616 pairs (Code: French E5 training)
- Training recipe and data selection (Doc 4)

### Q66. What did you do to make the index lookup fast? ★★★ {#q66 .q}

*Why they ask:* An engineering-depth probe on the stage that touches every record.

**Say:** It is C++17 with OpenMP: records are processed in parallel batches, each thread keeps its own dense score arrays and resets only the entries it touched, and terms are hashed to 64-bit keys. The rarest-first walk with caps means we never traverse the longest lists.

**If they push:** The string similarities among the 76 features use a bit-parallel longest-common-subsequence computation, much faster than a dynamic-programming table for short names. Results are written in shards that the filter and ranker consume as they appear.

**Numbers:**

- C++17 with OpenMP (Doc 3); implementation details (Code: index lookup)

### Q67. Can it run without a GPU? ★★ {#q67 .q}

*Why they ask:* Cost and deployment flexibility.

**Say:** Training needs a GPU, because the CatBoost ranker and the readers are trained on it. Inference could run on CPU at lower throughput: in our submitted run 48,813 shortlist pairs were in fact scored on CPU, but we have not timed a CPU-only run.

**If they push:** At inference, index lookup, quick filter, ranker scoring, LightGBM decision models, second-chance searches and the France rules already run on CPU. Besides the readers, only the word-meaning features use the GPU when one is present, and that step falls back to CPU.

**Numbers:**

- 48,813 pairs scored on CPU; 11,638,504 with reused GPU scores (CodeREADME 6)
- GPU needed for training and reader scoring (CodeREADME 1); ranker scoring on CPU threads, word-meaning encoder on GPU if available, else CPU (Code: blocking job, feature stage)

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "How would this scale to billions of records?" see [Q208](#q208); "How long does it take to run, and on what hardware?" see [Q221](#q221); "Could this run online, one record at a time?" see [Q210](#q210); "Why small readers, and no LLM?" see [Q194](#q194) and [Q199](#q199); "How do you make sure the output is reproducible?" see [Q222](#q222).

## 6. The CatBoost ranker and the shortlist (12 questions) {#cat-6 .cat}

### Q68. What does the CatBoost ranker do, and why does it sit between the quick filter and the readers? ★ LIKELY {#q68 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to see that every stage of the cascade has one clear job and a cost reason for being where it is.

**Say:** The ranker orders the candidates that survive the quick rule-based filter, so that only the best few reach the expensive readers. It is a gradient-boosted tree model on similarity numbers the index has already computed, so scoring a pair costs almost nothing compared with a transformer pass. We keep at most four candidates per incoming record, 1.17 on average, and the ranker's probability and rank also feed the decision model.

**If they push:** It turns 37,614,782 filtered pairs into an 11,687,317-pair shortlist, so the readers run on about 31 % of the pairs the ranker scores (derived). The cheap model decides what gets read; the expensive models decide what gets linked.

**Numbers:**

- 37,614,782 pairs, 21.7107 per business after the quick filter (Doc 3)
- Shortlist 11,687,317 pairs: 6.75 per business, 1.17 per incoming record (Doc 3; per-business and per-record values derived)

### Q69. Why not let the ranker do all the pruning and skip the quick rule-based filter? ★★ {#q69 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether each stage is justified by cost, and whether you measured its price.

**Say:** Without the filter the ranker would have to score everything the index returns, roughly six times more pairs. The filter needs no model and costs almost nothing in accuracy: the true business survived it for 99.974 % of held-out records. So a free rule makes the coarse cut and the learned ranker makes the fine one.

**If they push:** In the blocking study of 25 September the index gave 130.1 candidates per business and the filter left 21.7107 in the final run; with the decision model of that date, fold-9 macro F0.5 moved from 0.990117 to 0.990086 (fold 8: −0.00004). Its special clauses keep what a single combined score would drop: the record's best address match, an almost complete address match, very short names and acronyms, and businesses with exactly the same core name.

**Numbers:**

- 130.1 → 21.7107 candidates per business (Doc 3)
- Owner kept for 99.974 % of fold-8/9 records; fold-9 F0.5 0.990117 → 0.990086 (Doc 3)

### Q70. What features does the ranker see? ★★ {#q70 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check that you know what information exists at each stage, and therefore what each stage can and cannot catch.

**Say:** Only the 76 pair features the C++ index computes: string similarities of names and addresses, overlaps of words, letter pieces, sound pieces and numbers, IDF-weighted overlaps, and the retrieval scores themselves, including how far the candidate is behind the record's best. It sees no reader score and none of the "what changed" features; those arrive later, in the decision model.

**If they push:** In detail: 7 string similarities (a normalised longest-common-subsequence ratio, 5 on name forms and 2 on address forms); intersection, Jaccard, overlap-coefficient and intersection-over-max statistics for name words, address words, 3-grams, 4-grams, sound grams and numbers; length counts, equality and empty flags, IDF overlaps, token-alignment scores, a common-prefix share, exact core-name group sizes, and 8 retrieval scores (name, address, total, total over best, best, second, best minus second, raw candidate count).

**Numbers:**

- 76 pair features (Doc 3; composition from Code: matcher.cpp)

### Q71. How was the ranker trained, and on which records? ★★ {#q71 .q}

*Why they ask:* A first-stage model trained on the wrong records leaks into everything downstream; they check the split.

**Say:** It is CatBoost with a Logloss objective, so strictly a pointwise classifier whose probability we sort by. It was trained on a pilot of 140,000 labelled US and Indian training records, fitted on the part in folds 0 to 5, with early stopping on fold 6. It is never fitted on folds 6 to 9 on purpose, because the decision models train there on its scores; fold 6 only decides when the ranker stops adding trees.

**If they push:** Up to 1,600 trees of depth 7 (CatBoost's default symmetric trees, so 128 leaves each), learning rate 0.075, L2 regularisation 5, early stopping after 180 rounds, on GPU; the pilot holds 35,000 records per country and source, with all their index candidates as training pairs. Our documentation reports no study of a larger training sample, so we make no claim about one.

**If they push further:** It is a pointwise binary classifier with log loss, not a listwise ranking loss, and a probability on an absolute scale is what lets the shortlist use an absolute floor of 0.001 for ranks 2 to 4. We did not run a head-to-head against other boosted-tree libraries for this step; its settings were up to 1,600 trees, depth 7, learning rate 0.075.

**Numbers:**

- 140,000 records, 35,000 per country and source; folds 0-5 fit, fold 6 early stopping (Doc 4)
- 1,600 trees, depth 7, learning rate 0.075, L2 5, early stopping 180 (Doc 4)
- Ranker settings and training data (Doc 4); floor 0.001 (Doc 3)

### Q72. Why at most four candidates per incoming record? ★★ LIKELY {#q72 .q}

*Why they ask:* Every cap is a trade-off; they want both the cost side and the recall side, with a measurement.

**Say:** It is a cost-recall trade-off, and it is our largest recall loss, which we measured rather than assumed. On held-out fold 9, the index finds the true business for 99.37 % of US records and the shortlist still holds it for at least 98.87 %. In return, the readers see on average little more than one pair per record instead of the three to four that survive the filter.

**If they push:** For India the same step goes from 98.51 % to at least 98.06 %. The cap bounds the transformer passes per record, which keeps cost linear; at larger scale we would shard the index by state or postcode to afford a larger cap where it loses owners, and the second-chance searches recover part of what the index and the cap miss.

**If they push further:** Ranks 2 to 4 are kept only if the ranker gives them at least 0.001, so the shortlist averages 1.17 pairs per record (derived), not four. For India the same step goes from 98.5068 % to 98.0809 %, and the second-chance searches exist to win back the miss types the index and the cap leave behind.

**Numbers:**

- Fold 9, index → shortlist: US 99.3694 % → 98.8748-99.3628 %; India 98.5068 % → 98.0572-98.4831 % (Doc B.2)
- Candidates per record in the all-fold samples: after filter 3.111 (US) / 3.878 (India); shortlist 1.114 / 1.174 (Doc B.2)
- Index 99.3694 % vs top four without the filter 98.8814 % (US); 98.5068 % vs 98.0809 % (India) (Doc B.2)

### Q73. What is the 0.001 floor for ranks two to four, and why always keep the top candidate? ★★ {#q73 .q}

*Why they ask:* Small design details reveal whether you understand where cost and recall are spent.

**Say:** The top-ranked candidate always enters the shortlist, whatever its probability; ranks two to four enter only if the ranker gives them at least 0.001. Keeping the top one means every record with any candidate is read by the readers, so a weak ranker score can still be overturned. The floor stops us paying reader cost for candidates the ranker considers hopeless, and together with a confident ranker it leaves most records with a single candidate.

**If they push:** 90.59 % of incoming records have exactly one candidate in the final candidate file. Our documentation does not record a separate sweep for the 0.001 value; what we measured is recall after the shortlist. In the India example the top ranker probability was only 0.0028: the readers and the decision model still examined that record, rejected its candidates, and it went on to the native-script second-chance search.

**Numbers:**

- 90.59 % of records with exactly one candidate; 1.2331 candidates per record (Doc B.1)
- Ranker top-1 probability 0.0028 in the India example (Doc D.2)

### Q74. How exactly did you measure the recall of the shortlist, and why do you quote a range? ★★ {#q74 .q}

*Why they ask:* Blocking sets the ceiling of the whole system, so they test the rigour of the measurement.

**Say:** On labelled train fold 9, with the submitted index, the quick filter and a ranker fitted on folds 0 to 5, we counted the share of owned incoming records whose true business is still among the candidates after each stage. The range exists because, for the full fold, the evidence gives the top four without the filter exactly but the filter-then-top-four result only as a lower and an upper bound. On fold-9 samples of about 7,400 owned records per country we have exact values at every step, for example 98.8935 % for the US shortlist.

**If they push:** The full-fold bounds are 98.8748 % to 99.3628 % (US) and 98.0572 % to 98.4831 % (India); the exact top four without the filter is 98.8814 % and 98.0809 %. The samples show the filter itself costs little (US 99.3658 % at the index, 99.3523 % after the filter) and the cap of four is the larger loss; second-chance candidates are not included in these figures.

**Numbers:**

- Owned records in fold 9: US 457,971, India 303,786 (Doc B.2)
- Fold-9 samples: US 99.3658 → 99.3523 → 98.8935 %; India 98.388 → 98.3745 → 97.985 % (Doc B.2)

### Q75. In the US example the ranker put the LLC second, but the decision model put it last. Is the ranker wrong? ★★ {#q75 .q}

*Why they ask:* They probe whether you understand the division of labour in a cascade.

**Say:** No: the ranker's job is only to keep the owner inside the top four, not to make the final order. It sees index similarities, and on those the Inc, LLC and PC names are nearly identical. The decision model adds the readers and the legal-form features, so it scores the LLC 0.000007 against 0.965022 for the Inc.

**If they push:** The ranker's probability and rank are themselves inputs of the decision model, so it learns from labels how far to trust the ranker and when the readers and "what changed" features should override it. A cascade is judged on whether the owner survives each stage, not on whether each stage agrees with the last.

**Numbers:**

- Decision-model scores: Inc 0.965022, LLC 0.000007, PC 0.088664, Industries 0.000088 (Doc D.1)

### Q76. The readers are much stronger than the ranker. Why still give the ranker's probability to the decision model? ★★ {#q76 .q}

*Why they ask:* A stacking question: they test whether you know that a weaker model can still add information.

**Say:** Because it summarises different evidence: the ranker condenses the 76 index similarities, including address and number overlap and the retrieval scores, into one number learned from labels, while the readers read raw text. When the two agree the decision is easy; when they disagree, the decision model learns from labels which one to trust in that situation. It enters as log-odds, together with its rank, best rival and lead within the record's shortlist.

**If they push:** Trees pick up such interactions cheaply, for example a high reader score combined with a weak address overlap. We have not prepared a feature-importance ranking, so we do not claim how much weight it carries; the US example shows the decision model is free to overrule the ranker's order.

### Q77. The ranker was trained only on US and Indian labels. Doesn't that hurt France? ★★★ {#q77 .q}

*Why they ask:* Domain mismatch at the first learned stage is a silent recall risk; they want to see you know where it bites.

**Say:** It can, and we cannot measure it, because France has no labels. Two things limit the risk: the ranker's inputs are language-independent similarity numbers computed on French-cleaned text, and the shortlist keeps the top candidate plus any rank up to four above 0.001, so the French readers and decision model re-score whatever survives. The remaining risk is an owner falling below rank four, which only French labels would reveal.

**If they push:** France does pass more candidates through: 32.7713 per business after the filter and 1.4656 per incoming record in the candidate file, against 15.0352 and 1.0742 for the US. With a small labelled French sample, shortlist recall is the first thing we would measure, exactly as in our recall table.

**Numbers:**

- After filter: France 8,502,590 pairs (32.7713 per business), US 9,969,935 (15.0352) (Doc 3)
- Candidates per incoming record: France 1.4656, US 1.0742 (Doc B.1)

### Q78. Why a learned ranker at all? Why not cut to four by the index score? ★★ {#q78 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether each learned component earns its place over a simpler heuristic.

**Say:** The index score is one hand-weighted formula; the ranker learns from labels how to combine all 76 signals, for example a weak name match with a perfect address, so the owner is more likely to land in the top four. It also gives an absolute probability we can floor at 0.001 and pass to the decision model. Our documentation does not report top-four recall by the raw index score alone, so we cannot quote the gain as a number.

**If they push:** The comparison we would run: on fold 9, top-four recall by the index total versus by the ranker, with the filter fixed. What we do have is the recall with the ranker: at least 98.87 % (US) and 98.06 % (India) in the shortlist.

### Q79. If you had to improve recall at the shortlist, what would you do first? ★★ {#q79 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to see you can turn a measured weakness into a concrete plan.

**Say:** The cap of four is our largest measured recall loss, so we would start there, but only where it bites: shard the index by state or postcode so lists are shorter, then afford a larger cap where the cap loses true businesses. We would also consider giving the ranker a few cheap "what changed" signals, such as the legal-form relation, since today it sees only index similarities. Each change would be judged by the same per-stage recall table on fold 9 and by reader pairs per record.

**If they push:** Today the gap is 99.37 % at the index against at least 98.87 % in the shortlist (US) and 98.51 % against at least 98.06 % (India), so at most about half a percentage point is recoverable at this step. Owners the index never finds need a different retrieval channel, which is the job of the second-chance searches.

**Numbers:**

- Index and shortlist recall, fold 9 (Doc B.2)

## 7. The readers (cross-encoders) (15 questions) {#cat-7 .cat}

### Q80. What exactly is a "reader" in your pipeline? ★ LIKELY {#q80 .q}

*Why they ask:* The basic check that you can explain your core model in one breath.

**Say:** A reader is a cross-encoder: a small multilingual transformer that reads the incoming record and one candidate business together, as one input, and outputs one match score. Because both texts sit in the same sequence, every word of one side can attend to every word of the other, so it notices small decisive differences such as Inc becoming LLC. We feed it the raw text, "name | address" for each side, cut to 128 tokens.

**If they push:** The encoder's last hidden states are averaged over the real tokens (masked mean pooling), then dropout 0.1 and a linear layer give one logit. Reading jointly means nothing can be pre-computed per business, so every pair costs a full transformer pass, which is why readers see only the shortlist, about 1.17 pairs per record. Raw rather than cleaned text lets the reader see what cleaning removes or rewrites: case, punctuation, native script and the exact spelling of the legal form.

**Numbers:**

- 128-token limit, longest-first truncation, dropout 0.1, one logit (Doc 4)

### Q81. Why put the name and the address into one text instead of reading them separately? ★★ {#q81 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you understand what joint attention buys you.

**Say:** Because the decision depends on how name and address agree together, not separately: the same name in another city is usually another business, while a slightly different name at exactly the same address can be the same one. One sequence lets attention connect the record's city to the business's city and the two names in the same pass. Our French example fits this: a business with exactly the same name, but in Pessac instead of Nantes, was rejected by the French readers.

**If they push:** Within each side the "|" marks the boundary between name and address; between the two sides the tokenizer's pair encoding inserts separator tokens, and we pass no segment ids, so the separators and positions tell the model which text is the record and which the business. Separate name and address models would lose the interactions between fields, which the decision model would then have to reconstruct from two coarse scores.

### Q82. Why MiniLM and E5? ★★ LIKELY {#q82 .q}

*Why they ask:* Model selection under constraints (licence, size, languages, compute) is a core applied-science judgement.

**Say:** We needed multilingual models for Indian scripts such as Devanagari and for French, under open licences, small enough to score millions of pairs on one GPU. The MiniLM reader starts from a model of about 118 million parameters under Apache-2.0 and the E5 reader from one of about 278 million under MIT, both far below the competition's size limit. Two differently pretrained encoders give the decision model two partly independent opinions; for the US and India it sees both logits and their mean.

**If they push:** paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 is a distilled multilingual paraphrase model and multilingual-e5-base a contrastively pretrained retrieval encoder; as readers both are fine-tuned end to end with a fresh one-logit head. A larger xlm-roberta-large reader, about 560 million parameters, was tried during development and discarded; no stage uses it.

**Numbers:**

- 117,653,760 (Apache-2.0) and 278,043,648 (MIT) parameters, plus a 385- / 769-parameter head (Doc B.5)

### Q83. Your E5 readers use the MiniLM tokenizer. Isn't that a bug? ★★★ {#q83 .q}

*Why they ask:* An expert who reads the documentation notices this and checks that you understand tokenisation.

**Say:** No: both base models use the same XLM-RoBERTa SentencePiece vocabulary, so the MiniLM tokenizer produces exactly the token ids the E5 model expects. That lets the same tokenised pairs serve every reader. We also do not add E5's "query:" and "passage:" prefixes, because each reader is fine-tuned end to end with its own head for pair classification.

**If they push:** Our documentation states it directly: all readers tokenise the pair with the MiniLM tokenizer. The E5 prefixes matter for its original retrieval use, where one embedding space must separate queries from passages; a cross-encoder with a new classification head learns the task through fine-tuning without them.

### Q84. Why mean pooling and not the [CLS] token? ★★ {#q84 .q}

*Why they ask:* A detail question to check you understand the architecture you actually used.

**Say:** Both base models were pretrained as sentence encoders with mean pooling, so averaging the token vectors matches how their representations were trained. We take the attention-masked mean of the last hidden states, so padding does not dilute it, then dropout and a one-logit linear head. We have no comparison with [CLS] pooling to quote.

**If they push:** For a cross-encoder the head must summarise interactions spread over both texts, and a mean over all real positions is a stable summary; since the whole encoder is fine-tuned, it also adapts to the pooling we chose.

### Q85. How were the readers trained, and why only one epoch? ★★ {#q85 .q}

*Why they ask:* Training details show whether you can reproduce and debug the model, and whether defaults were checked.

**Say:** Standard full fine-tuning: binary cross-entropy on labelled US and Indian pairs from folds 0 to 5, AdamW, the whole encoder trained and the new head at five times the encoder's learning rate, with a short linear warm-up, bf16 mixed precision and gradient clipping. One epoch, because the training set is large and the encoders are already strong, so in our reasoning one pass adapts them while limiting memorisation of the training businesses' strings; we have no epoch sweep to quote, so we do not claim one epoch is optimal.

**If they push:** Learning rate 5e-5 for the encoder and 2.5e-4 for the head, weight decay 0.01, 3 % warm-up then linear decay, batch 128, clip norm 1.0; with bf16 autocast the weights and the optimiser stay in fp32 and only the forward computations run in bf16, which needs no loss scaling because bf16 has fp32's exponent range. Batches come from chunks of 100 batches sorted by length and then shuffled, which cuts padding without fixing the order; on held-out folds 8 and 9 the E5 reader reaches AUC 0.998570 on businesses it never saw.

**If they push further:** The recipe: binary cross-entropy; AdamW with weight decay 0.01 and a five times higher learning rate on the head; 3 % linear warm-up then linear decay; bf16 autocast; gradient clipping at 1.0; batch 128; learning rate 5e-5 (2e-5 for the French fine-tunes); longest-first truncation to 128 tokens; length-bucketed batches to cut padding. What we would measure next: the per-business F0.5 of the whole decision after one versus two epochs, since the reader's AUC is already near its ceiling.

**Numbers:**

- BCE, AdamW (weight decay 0.01, head ×5), 3 % warm-up, bf16, clipping 1.0, 1 epoch, batch 128, learning rate 5e-5 (Doc 4)
- E5 reader AUC 0.998570, top-1 accuracy 0.993004 on held-out fold-8/9 pairs (Doc B.4)
- One epoch, batch 128, 128 tokens (Doc 4)

### Q86. Which pairs did you train the readers on? Did you mine hard examples? ★★ LIKELY {#q86 .q}

*Why they ask:* Training-data selection usually matters more than architecture; they want to see you focused on the decision boundary.

**Say:** Yes. We took every "hard" training record, where the ranker was unsure or ranked a wrong business first, plus a random quarter of the easy ones. For those records we used the candidates the shortlist would keep, plus the true business even when the ranker had put it as low as rank eight.

**If they push:** Hard means a top ranker probability between 0.003 and 0.9995, a non-owner ranked first, or a second candidate above 0.003; candidates 1-4 are kept if ranked first, at least 0.001 or the owner, and candidates 5-8 only if the owner. Easy pairs teach little, but keeping 25 % of them stops the reader from training on a sample that is all borderline, which would distort its scores on the many easy test pairs (our reasoning, not a measured ablation).

**If they push further:** A hard record has a top ranker probability between 0.003 and 0.9995, or a non-owner ranked first, or a second-best probability above 0.003. Candidates 1-4 enter if ranked first, if their probability is at least 0.001 (the shortlist floor) or if they are the owner; candidates 5-8 only if they are the owner. The MiniLM and E5 readers use the same pairs, from labelled US and India folds 0-5. The reasoning: easy records are already settled by the ranker, so the reader's capacity goes where the ranker is uncertain.

**Numbers:**

- Hard records: top probability in (0.003, 0.9995), a non-owner first, or second probability > 0.003; plus 25 % of the others (Doc 4)
- Hard record: top probability in (0.003, 0.9995), a non-owner ranked first, or second probability > 0.003; plus a random 25 % of the others (Doc 4)

### Q87. How good are the readers on their own? ★★ LIKELY {#q87 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want a number for the component, and to see you know the difference between pair-level and business-level metrics.

**Say:** On held-out pairs of labelled folds 8 and 9, the E5 reader alone has AUC 0.998570 and puts the right candidate first 99.3 % of the time. These are pair-level numbers on businesses it never trained on; the competition score is per business, after the decision model, so they are not directly comparable with our leaderboard score.

**If they push:** Its best pair-level F0.5 is 0.992796, on 509,260 pairs of 437,715 records. These figures come from the French E5 reader's written check, where the plain E5 reader was the reference; our documentation has no equivalent table for the MiniLM reader, so we do not quote one.

**If they push further:** On 509,260 pairs of 437,715 labelled fold-8/9 records: E5 reader AUC 0.998570, top-1 accuracy 0.993004, best F0.5 0.992796 (measured on these reader pairs at the best cut-off, not the per-business macro metric); French E5 reader 0.998544, 0.993161 and 0.992782. In our French example the MiniLM reader alone scored the wrong-city business +7.1, which is why no reader decides alone.

**Numbers:**

- E5 reader, folds 8-9: AUC 0.998570, top-1 accuracy 0.993004, best F0.5 0.992796 (Doc B.4)
- Reader quality (Doc B.4)

### Q88. If the readers are that good, why do you need a decision model? ★★ LIKELY {#q88 .q}

*Why they ask:* This tests whether you see matching as a comparative decision rather than a pair classification.

**Say:** A reader scores one pair at a time, but the decision is a competition: among a record's candidates and, for the US and India, among records competing for the same business. The decision model sees the reader logits next to the ranker, each candidate's rank and lead within the shortlist, the "what changed" features and the collective features, and gives one probability on which we set an operating point for the exact metric. A reader also cannot see corpus-level facts, such as how rare a dropped word is across the country.

**If they push:** Transformers are unreliable at arithmetic on digit strings, so exact number differences come in as features. Even with pair-level AUC near 0.999, a record can have two plausible candidates, and choosing between them, or abstaining, needs the comparison that the decision model's context features and the lead rule provide.

### Q89. How do the reader scores enter the decision model? ★★ {#q89 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test the stacking interface: raw scores, probabilities, or derived context.

**Say:** As raw logits plus context within the record's shortlist: for each reader, the candidate's rank, the best other candidate's logit, the margin to it and the top value. For the US and India both the MiniLM and E5 readers go in, plus their mean with the same context; France has a single reader slot filled by a blend of three readers.

**If they push:** For one feature on its own a tree is invariant to monotone transforms, but differences and means (margins, the two-reader mean) behave differently in logit space, where they add up as log-odds evidence. The ranker probability also enters as log-odds.

### Q90. What is a logit, and what does a reader score of 7.5 mean? ★ {#q90 .q}

*Why they ask:* A basic check that you can read your own numbers.

**Say:** A logit is the raw output before the sigmoid: the log-odds that the pair is a match. A logit of 0 means 50 %, and 7.5 means about 99.94 %. We keep logits rather than probabilities because they spread out the region near certainty, where the important differences sit.

**If they push:** In the French example the MiniLM reader gave the same-name business in Pessac +7.125 (about 99.9 %), while the French E5 reader gave it −10.8125 (about 0.002 %). Averaging probabilities would hide how strongly the French reader disagreed, while averaging logits keeps it, which is one reason a logit blend suits us.

**Numbers:**

- Logits 7.125 (MiniLM) and −10.8125 (French E5) for the Pessac business (Doc D.3); percentages derived with the sigmoid

### Q91. Why does France not use the plain E5 reader? ★★ {#q91 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check that you know exactly which models run where.

**Say:** For France the E5 reader is replaced by its French version, the French E5 reader, which started from the E5 reader and was fine-tuned on French pseudo-labels with labelled US and Indian replay. The France decision model has one reader slot, and it receives a blend of the MiniLM reader, the French MiniLM reader and the French E5 reader. The US and India use the MiniLM and E5 readers, and an unseen country uses only the MiniLM reader.
