**Say:** Paired, on the same held-out businesses, never by comparing absolute scores from different samples. Absolute held-out scores move by two to three ten-thousandths between fold eight and fold nine, so only a paired comparison can resolve smaller differences, and our evaluation code computes paired bootstrap intervals over businesses for that.

**If they push:** Fold 8 minus fold 9: US +0.000333, India +0.000252 (derived). The bootstrap resamples businesses 2,000 times. The public board gives one number per upload, so we cannot resample it, which is another reason not to over-read small public differences.

**Numbers:**

- US 0.991545 − 0.991212 = 0.000333; India 0.990298 − 0.990046 = 0.000252 (derived from Doc 5)

### Q160. Why only two held-out folds instead of full ten-fold cross-validation? ★★ {#q160 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether your evaluation design follows from your training design.

**Say:** Because of the layer split: folds zero to five are reserved for the ranker and readers, so the decision models can only be trained and tested within folds six to nine. Within those, six and seven are always in the fit, and we rotate eight and nine as the held-out fold, which gives two separate checks of every setting.

**If they push:** Rotating six and seven into the held-out role as well would add two more checks, and we would do that with more time. Folds 0-5 cannot serve as held-out folds for the decision models without out-of-fold reader scores, which would need several copies of each reader.

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "Why tune thresholds on the exact metric instead of AUC or log loss?" see [Q21](#q21); "How did you choose the 0.75 threshold and the 0.4 lead?" see [Q21](#q21) and [Q111](#q111); "How did you set the French threshold of 0.82 without labels?" see [Q131](#q131).

## 14. Edge cases (11 questions) {#cat-14 .cat}

### Q161. How do you handle a business that owns many incoming records? ★★ {#q161 .q}

*Why they ask:* Many-to-one linking is what makes this different from one-to-one matching; they test whether your decisions are coordinated per business.

**Say:** Each record is decided on its own, and then the per-business consistency check adjusts the bar using how many other records were already accepted for the same business. For the US and India, records competing for the same business also feed collective features. In our file a business has about 3.4 links on average and at most 11.

**If they push:** The bar is 0.75, 0.68, 0.72 or 0.77 for 0, 1, 2 or 3+ other accepted records, with the same 0.4 lead, chosen on folds 8 and 9. The shape matches the metric: if a business already has k correct links and one more true record, one extra link pays off only if its chance of being right exceeds k / (k + 0.25 · (k + 1)), which is 0.67, 0.73 and 0.75 for k = 1, 2, 3 and approaches 0.8 for large k (derived from the F0.5 formula, treating the score as a calibrated probability; the bars themselves were tuned on folds 8 and 9). With no other links the bar stays at 0.75, because there a wrong link can ruin an empty row. Net effect: US +277 / −284, India +247 / −248. No record is ever linked to two businesses.

**Numbers:**

- Consistency check 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77 (Doc 4); effect (Doc B.1)
- Links per business: mean 3.3805, median 3, max 11 (Doc B.1)

### Q162. What do you do with a country you have never seen? ★ LIKELY {#q162 .q}

*Why they ask:* Generalisation beyond the test countries is part of the brief; they want a concrete fallback and honesty about testing.

**Say:** It takes a default route: the US and India cleaning rules, the multilingual MiniLM reader only, a decision model with 158 features that exist in every country, trained on labelled US and Indian rows, and the stricter 0.82 threshold, with no second-chance searches or rules. Honestly, it is untested on real data, because the test set had only the US, India and France.

**If they push:** The index and its rarity weights are built per country from that country's own businesses, so retrieval needs no labels. The proxy row in our held-out table is this same decision-model recipe as a single fit, run on labelled US and Indian rows at 0.82: 0.990508 and 0.989467 on fold 9; but those are countries it was trained on, not a new one. For a real new market we would add a country normaliser, self-train readers as for France, and label a small sample to set the threshold.

**Numbers:**

- Default route: 158 features, single fit, 0.82 / 0.4 (Doc 4)

### Q163. How do you handle chains: the same brand at several addresses? ★★ LIKELY {#q163 .q}

*Why they ask:* Chains are the classic hard case for business matching; names agree, only the location differs.

**Say:** The address decides. Branches share the name, so the readers and the address and number features carry the difference, and the clear-winner rule refuses to link when two branches score close. Branches of a chain at nearby addresses are still one of our known wrong-link types, so we reduce the problem rather than remove it.

**If they push:** Retrieval keeps every business with the same core name (if at most 2,000 share it) plus the best candidates by address score, so every branch can be retrieved; the quick filter keeps same-name branches with some address overlap, and the ranker passes at most four on. Two index features count how many businesses share that exact core name, which tells the model the name is shared. Our India example shows the mechanism: three same-name businesses in Agra, Satara and Byculla score below one in a hundred thousand, and the second-chance search picks the one with the same house number, 24/11.

**Numbers:**

- Same-core-name channel: up to 2,000 businesses (Doc 3)

### Q164. What if the reference list itself contains duplicates? ★★★ {#q164 .q}

*Why they ask:* Reference data is rarely clean; they check that duplicates cannot make you split or double-count links.

**Say:** We don't merge businesses; each one keeps its own row. If a record matches two near-identical businesses equally well, neither can be 0.4 ahead of the other, so we link nothing, which costs a little recall but puts no wrong link on either. Our documentation doesn't report a count of duplicate businesses, so I can't say how often this happens.

**If they push:** The candidate file still lists the record under both. The same-core-name channel retrieves such businesses together (unless more than 2,000 share the name), and identical text gives them near-identical ranker scores, so they normally reach the shortlist together. What we would measure: the number of same-country business pairs with identical cleaned name and address, and how often the lead rule abstains between them; a production system might add a deduplication step for the reference list, which the competition format did not ask for.

### Q165. How do you handle name variations: abbreviations, legal forms, typos? ★★ {#q165 .q}

*Why they ask:* Noisy names are the core of the task; they want the mechanism at each stage, not just "we normalise".

**Say:** In three layers. Cleaning maps spellings to one form, for example "&" to "and" and, in France, "S.A.R.L." to "sarl"; the index has letter-piece and sound lists, so a typo still retrieves the business; and the "what changed" features describe which words were added, dropped or replaced and whether the legal form changed, so the model learns which changes are harmless.

**If they push:** Letter pieces are character 3- and 4-grams of the core name (legal words removed); the sound key removes vowels, including y, and collapses repeated letters, then indexes its 4-grams. France also collapses leet legal forms ("5arl" becomes "sarl"), and in US and Indian names a zero next to a letter is read as the letter o. The word features deliberately ignore legal-form words, so among the "what changed" features a legal-form change shows up only in the legal-form relation, and the readers see it in the raw text, as in our US example (Inc against LLC against PC).

### Q166. And address variations? ★★ {#q166 .q}

*Why they ask:* Addresses carry most of the disambiguating signal; they check you handle formats and numbers, not just strings.

**Say:** Cleaning brings addresses to one form: state names and street abbreviations are mapped and leading zeros dropped, and in France "15B" becomes "15 bis", street types and their typos are canonicalised, and "st" becomes "saint". Then the number features compare house numbers directly, how far apart they are and how many digits differ, instead of treating the address as plain text.

**If they push:** France also removes "N°" and "numéro" prefixes, unifies bis, ter and quater, and learns region, department and city components from the unlabelled test files. The quick filter keeps any candidate whose address covers at least 95 % of the record's address, weighted by rarity. The France street veto tolerates typos: Damerau distance at most 1, or 2 for words of 8 or more characters.

**Numbers:**

- Address coverage ≥ 0.95 keeps a candidate (Doc 3)

### Q167. What if a record has no address? ★★ {#q167 .q}

*Why they ask:* Missing fields are common; they check you neither crash nor silently lower the bar.

**Say:** Then only the name can decide, and the bar does not drop. Our US example has no address: the shortlist holds four businesses with nearly the same name, and the decision model, using the legal-form and word-change features and the readers, gives 0.965 to Enterprises Inc and at most 0.089 to the others, so it is linked to that one.

**If they push:** The number features become missing values; LightGBM learns at each split which side missing values go, so "no address" is information, not an error. The number relation also has explicit classes for "record has no number" and "business has no number". Retrieval then relies on the name lists, and the address second-chance search cannot run without digits.

**Numbers:**

- 0.965022 vs 0.088664, lead 0.876 (Doc D.1)

### Q168. What if only the house number or the state is missing? ★★★ {#q168 .q}

*Why they ask:* Partial addresses are the realistic case; they want to know which parts of the pipeline degrade and how.

**Say:** Without a house number, a record on a street with several businesses is genuinely ambiguous, and that is one of our known missed-match types, because the clear-winner rule often refuses to link. Without a state, the native-script search falls back to searching all states. In France, the street veto skips pairs it cannot decide, so missing information does not by itself remove a link.

**If they push:** In France the word-substitution rescue accepts the same, an empty or an unnumbered address, and the residual rescue covers "business name plus one generic suffix" with no house number on the same street, provided that business is the only compatible one at the address. The address search needs digits: it takes businesses that share one of the record's three rarest numbers and one of its three rarest address words.

### Q169. How do you handle very short names and acronyms? ★★★ {#q169 .q}

*Why they ask:* Short names break most similarity scores in both directions; they test whether you treat them specially.

**Say:** Carefully, because they fail in both directions. The quick filter keeps a candidate for a record name of three characters or fewer if enough of its address matches, and in France an acronym rescue links a record whose name is an initials version of the business name at the same address, when that business is the only such one there. The opposite case, an acronym that differs by one initial at another address, is a known wrong-link type, and one part of the France cell veto removes it.

**If they push:** Quick filter: name of at most 3 characters with address coverage at least 0.4. Acronym rescue: one upper-case token of 2-5 letters, best score in [0.4, 0.82), +186 links. Cell veto: an acronym with one different initial away from the business's address, 74 links vetoed; a letter edit of an initialism at the same address, 65.

**Numbers:**

- Acronym rescue +186; cell veto parts 74 and 65 (Doc B.3)

### Q170. What about brand names, websites or "doing business as" names that share few words with the business? ★★★ {#q170 .q}

*Why they ask:* A lexical retriever's blind spot; they test whether you know where your recall goes.

**Say:** That is a known weak spot. Our retrieval is built on words, letter pieces and sounds, so a record that shares almost no words with its business may never be retrieved, and we list it among our main missed-match types. The address second-chance search recovers some of these when the address matches, and a dense vector retrieval channel would be the natural addition.

**If they push:** The address search takes businesses sharing one of the record's three rarest numbers and one of its three rarest address words, then two LightGBM models filter and score them: +192 links in the US and +2,945 in India. We did not benchmark a dense retriever, so we don't claim it would be better; it would be an extra list in the index lookup, not a replacement.

### Q171. If a record has only one candidate, does the lead rule mean anything? ★★★ {#q171 .q}

*Why they ask:* A precise reviewer notices that a margin is undefined without a runner-up and checks what your code does.

**Say:** No, for those records only the threshold applies: with no runner-up, the lead condition passes automatically. About nine in ten incoming records have exactly one candidate in our final candidate file, so for most records the confidence threshold does the work, and the lead matters where there is real competition.

**If they push:** 9,031,916 records, 90.59 %. The decision model still sees context, such as how many candidates the index originally returned and the shortlist size, so a lone survivor of a crowded list is not treated like a truly unique match. In the code the runner-up of a single-candidate record is set to minus infinity.

**Numbers:**

- 90.59 % with exactly one candidate (Doc B.1)

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "What happens to an incoming record that has no matching business?" see [Q11](#q11); "And a business that owns no incoming records?" see [Q18](#q18); "How do you handle transliteration, names written in Indian scripts?" see [Q31](#q31); "Some businesses have thousands of candidates. Why, and is that a problem?" see [Q55](#q55).

## 15. Results and error analysis (9 questions) {#cat-15 .cat}

### Q172. What is your final result? ★ LIKELY {#q172 .q}

*Why they ask:* The opener; they want the number and whether it is backed by offline evidence.

**Say:** Our final file scores 0.9913 F0.5 on the public leaderboard, up from 0.968 for our first scored baseline. On held-out folds, close versions of our US and Indian decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992, so the public number is in line with what we measured offline.

**If they push:** Exactly 0.991300, upload 16 of 18. The file has 5,856,936 links and 12,293,019 candidate pairs (7.10 per business), and it passes the organisers' validator.

**Numbers:**

- Public 0.991300; first scored baseline 0.968212 (Doc 5, B.6)

### Q173. Where did the improvement from 0.968 to 0.9913 come from? ★★ LIKELY {#q173 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to know which ideas actually moved the score, and whether you can tell a bundle of changes from an ablation.

**Say:** Two steps did most of it: our first LightGBM decision-model submission and the France adaptation, which together took the public score from about 0.970 to 0.9906. After that each kept upload added less than two ten-thousandths: the consistency check, the US and India refit, the address second-chance searches, more France rules, generic "what changed" inputs, and finally the five-seed models with the French E5 reader.

**If they push:** Upload log: 0.970125 (upload 4) → 0.982561 (6, first decision model) → 0.990556 (7, France adaptation with the first four France rules) → 0.990621 → 0.990676 → 0.990748 → 0.990788 → 0.990881 → 0.990934 → 0.991114 → 0.991300 (the not-adopted France refit, 0.990726, is left out). The steps after upload 7 range from +0.000040 to +0.000186 (derived). Most uploads bundle several changes, so this log is not an ablation.

**Numbers:**

- Full upload table (Doc B.6)

### Q174. What are your most common wrong links? ★★ LIKELY {#q174 .q}

*Why they ask:* Error analysis shows whether you understand your model's failures, which matters more than the score.

**Say:** Three kinds: names at the business's own address with one generic word replaced or added or the legal form changed; acronyms that differ from the business name by one initial at another address; and branches of a chain at nearby addresses. The "what changed" features, the clear-winner rule and, in France, the vetoes each target one of these.

**If they push:** In France the two word-swap vetoes removed 29,021 of 887,630 accepted links (3.3 %, derived), the street veto 826, the generic-word swap veto 538 and the cell veto 1,322. In our US example the legal-form change from Inc to LLC is scored down to 0.000007, although the ranker had put it second.

**Numbers:**

- France rule counts (Doc B.3)

### Q175. And your most common missed matches? ★★ LIKELY {#q175 .q}

*Why they ask:* The other half of error analysis; they check where recall goes and what you did about it.

**Say:** True businesses that retrieval never found or that the cap of four cut off; native-script names without a known transliteration; brand or website names with little word overlap; records without a house number on a street with several businesses; and correct candidates rejected because a second one was too close. The second-chance searches, the consistency check and the France rescues each recover part of these.

**If they push:** In France, correct candidates below the conservative 0.82 are a further source. Recall on held-out fold 9: index 99.3694 % (US) and 98.5068 % (India); shortlist at least 98.8748 % and 98.0572 %. Links recovered: native-script +9,759; address +192 and +2,945; France word-substitution rescue +5,272, residual rescue +5,846, generic-word rescue +332, acronym rescue +186.

**Numbers:**

- Recall (Doc B.2); links (Doc B.1, B.3)

### Q176. Where in the pipeline do you lose the most? ★★★ {#q176 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether you measured loss per stage instead of only at the end.

**Say:** Before the decision model, the largest measured loss is the cap of four candidates per record: on held-out fold nine the index finds the true business for about 99.4 % of US records, and the shortlist keeps about 98.9 %. After that we do not have a stage-by-stage breakdown of the final metric, because our held-out scores cover only the main decision.

**If they push:** The fold-9 samples give exact values: US 99.3658 % at the index, 99.3523 % after the quick filter, 98.8935 % in the shortlist; India 98.388 %, 98.3745 % and 97.985 %. So the filter costs about 0.01 percentage points and the cap about 0.4-0.5 (derived). Top 4 without the filter on the full fold gives 98.8814 % and 98.0809 %, almost the same: the cap, not the filter, is the loss.

**Numbers:**

- Fold-9 samples (Doc B.2); per-stage differences (derived)

### Q177. Is your remaining error mostly precision or recall? ★★★ {#q177 .q}

*Why they ask:* A good scientist knows which side of the trade-off their errors sit on, or says they do not.

**Say:** We did not report precision and recall separately, so I can't give a measured split. What we know is the recall ceiling: roughly one percent of US and two percent of Indian owned records are out of reach before the decision model runs. Since our operating points deliberately give up recall for precision, we would expect missed links to be the larger part, but that is a hypothesis we would check by computing per-business precision and recall on a held-out fold.

**If they push:** The ceiling is one minus the shortlist recall: about 1.1 % (US) and 2.0 % (India) of owned fold-9 records, before any threshold (derived from the fold-9 samples). The second-chance searches win back part of it, because their candidates come from outside the shortlist. Under F0.5 the best operating point usually sits where precision exceeds recall, because a wrong link costs more than a miss.

### Q178. How much does each refinement contribute? ★★ {#q178 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to know if the extra machinery earns its complexity.

**Say:** In links, the two second-chance searches add about thirteen thousand and the France rules remove a net of about twenty thousand, while the consistency check is close to neutral. We don't have a separate held-out F0.5 for each refinement; the metric evidence is the public step when each was added, and most uploads bundled several changes.

**If they push:** Native-script +9,759; address +192 and +2,945; consistency check US +277 / −284, India +247 / −248, so it changes about 500 links in each direction even though the net is small; France 887,630 accepted → 867,559 after the rules (31,707 vetoed and 11,636 rescued, derived). The cleanest public step is the India address search alone: 0.990676 → 0.990748.

**Numbers:**

- 12,896 second-chance links; France net −20,071 (derived from Doc B.1, B.3)

### Q179. Walk me through a case where you deliberately chose not to link. ★★ {#q179 .q}

*Why they ask:* A concrete example tests whether you understand your own precision logic end to end.

**Say:** The French record TQ Comite SARL in Nantes. The decision model was very confident about TQ Parents SARL at exactly the same address, but the only difference is that the core word "parents" was replaced by a common category word, "comite", and our France rule vetoes exactly that pattern at the same address. So we link nothing; test labels are private, so this shows how we decide, not that the call was right.

**If they push:** Decision score 0.999837 and lead 0.999740, so it passed 0.82 and 0.4. The other candidate, TQ Comite SARL in Pessac, has the identical name but another city: the MiniLM reader liked it (+7.125), the French readers rejected it (−1.92 and −10.81), blend −3.20, decision score 0.000098. The category-swap veto fires and the word-substitution veto also lists the pair; the score is above the word-substitution rescue band [0.4, 0.82), and the later rescues skip records vetoed by those two rules, so nothing re-links it. TQ Parents keeps its link to another incoming record.

**Numbers:**

- Worked example (Doc D.3)

### Q180. What does 0.9913 mean in practical terms? ★ {#q180 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check you can translate a metric into what it says about the output.

**Say:** It is the average, over the businesses the leaderboard scores, of a per-business score that is one when that business's list of linked records is exactly right, so the average shortfall per business is under one percent. Because the score weighs precision more, wrong links cost more than misses, and a business with no true records scores zero after a single wrong link.

**If they push:** The public score alone does not show how that shortfall is spread: it could be a few businesses scoring zero or many scoring slightly below one. Per business, F0.5 = 1.25 · P · R / (0.25 · P + R); the test files hold 1,732,544 businesses.

**If they push further:** We cannot turn it into an error count, because labels are private and the metric mixes precision and recall per business. The held-out scores exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules, so there is no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file.

**Numbers:**

- 1,732,544 test businesses (Doc 2.1); average shortfall 1 − 0.991300 = 0.0087 (derived)
- Public 0.991300, upload 16 (Doc 5, B.6); first scored baseline 0.968212 (Doc B.6)
- Held-out folds 9 / 8: US 0.991212 / 0.991545; India 0.990046 / 0.990298 (Doc 5)

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "How does performance differ between countries?" see [Q9](#q9); "Show me the "what changed" features deciding a real case." see [Q97](#q97); "Do you have an ablation showing the "what changed" features help?" see [Q102](#q102); "How good are the readers on their own?" see [Q87](#q87); "Can your results be reproduced?" see [Q222](#q222).

## 16. Limitations and what we would do differently (13 questions) {#cat-16 .cat}

### Q181. What is the biggest limitation of your work? ★★ LIKELY {#q181 .q}

*Why they ask:* Senior scientists trust teams that name their own weak points before anyone else does.

**Say:** We never had a fully untouched end-to-end test of the final file. Our held-out scores cover the main decision models, but they exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules, the same folds also helped choose thresholds, and France has no labels at all. The mitigation is that held-out scores of close versions of our models sit in the same range as the public score.

**If they push:** One more detail from our documentation: the final US and India decision models are refitted on folds 6-9, so the shipped models are not the exact ones scored. Held-out fold 9 / fold 8: US 0.991212 / 0.991545, India 0.990046 / 0.990298.

**Numbers:**

- Section 5 disclosure (Doc 5)

### Q182. The France rules were designed by looking at the test set. Isn't that overfitting? ★★★ LIKELY {#q182 .q}

*Why they ask:* The most adversarial question you can get; they want the admission first, then the safeguards.

**Say:** Partly, yes, and we disclose it. The rules were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records, and some parameters were chosen after seeing public scores. What limits the damage is that each rule is code on model scores, raw text and the address, with no test label and no human or AI judgement of any pair as an input; the largest action, the two word-swap vetoes, removes 29,021 of 887,630 accepted French links.

**If they push:** The evidence for the rules is label-free: control groups on the French records, and for the cell veto a check on US labels that name noise and address noise are independent. The analysis included AI-assisted review of sampled pairs, about 1,000 pairs in five samples plus smaller checks. In production we would turn the rule conditions into features and learn them from a small labelled French sample.

**Numbers:**

- 29,021 of 887,630 (3.3 %, derived) (Doc B.3)

### Q183. Why did you keep the French E5 reader when it failed two of its checks? ★★★ LIKELY {#q183 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you follow your own rules, and whether you are honest when you did not.

**Say:** Because the file containing it had our best public score: a leaderboard-driven decision against our own written rule, and we disclose it as such. It passed the US and Indian quality check and agreed 99.92 % with held-out French pseudo-labels, but it was slightly worse than its base model on our generated French test set and failed our rule that the expected gain must be safely positive. It changes French links only, and the same upload also added the five-seed models, so its own effect is not isolated.

**If they push:** Generated French test set: best F0.5 0.910516 against 0.914964, although the blend that includes it beat the blend without it, 0.90843 against 0.898031. Gain rule: point estimate +0.0000302, pessimistic −0.0001806, optimistic +0.0002315, and the rule required the pessimistic estimate to be above zero. It changed French links by −2,228 / +3,396 (5,437 business rows); US, India and candidates were identical.

**If they push further:** It passed the US/Indian quality tolerance (AUC 0.998544 against 0.998570) and agreement with held-out French pseudo-labels (0.999206 against a 0.98 bar). The gain rule's pessimistic estimate was −0.0001806; it changes French links only (−2,228 / +3,396), and the same upload also added the five-seed models, so its own public effect is not isolated.

**Numbers:**

- Written checks (Doc B.4); disclosure (Doc C.3)
- Gain estimate: point +0.0000302, pessimistic −0.0001806, optimistic +0.0002315 (Doc B.4)

### Q184. Your pipeline computes statistics on the test files. Isn't that a form of leakage? ★★★ {#q184 .q}

*Why they ask:* They probe the line between unsupervised use of test inputs, which is common, and using test outcomes, which is not.

**Say:** It uses the unlabelled test records, never their labels, and our documentation lists every such use. Rarity statistics, the blocking indexes, competition features, a native-script word alignment on very confident test matches and the French geography are computed from test text, and the French readers self-train on French test pairs. That is normal in production, where the reference list and the incoming stream are available at run time, but it makes our evaluation transductive, and label-free counts on the test records also set the French threshold and the French reader blend weight.

**If they push:** Transductive means the system is fitted with access to the unlabelled records it is scored on: it uses no labels, but it can adapt to quirks of this one snapshot. The native-script alignment uses test records whose first-stage top candidate has probability at least 0.9. The generated French test set was built from the French test businesses and used only for evaluation. No external data, lookup or API is used anywhere.

**Numbers:**

- Test-data disclosure (Doc C.1); external resources (Doc C.6)

### Q185. If a strict reviewer looked at your evidence, what would they say is missing? ★★★ {#q185 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you know the difference between what you showed and what you assumed.

**Say:** Four things: an end-to-end held-out score of the final file, a measured French F0.5, clean ablations such as removing all "what changed" features or isolating the five seeds, and a single-record latency measurement. We also did not prepare a feature-importance ranking. Each of these is something we would measure rather than claim.

**If they push:** What we do have: recall at every candidate stage on fold 9, the measured cost of the quick filter, held-out per-business F0.5 of the main decision, written checks for new readers, the public upload log, and byte-for-byte reproduction from the trained models and stored reader scores.

### Q186. How much does the cap of four candidates cost you? ★★ {#q186 .q}

*Why they ask:* A fixed cap is an obvious engineering compromise; they check you measured it and know how you would relax it.

**Say:** It is our largest measured recall loss: on held-out fold nine about 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points of owners are found by the index but fall outside the shortlist of four. We kept four to protect the expensive readers; with finer blocking, such as state or postcode shards, we would have room to raise the cap where it loses true businesses.

**If they push:** Fold-9 samples: US 99.3523 % after the filter → 98.8935 % in the shortlist; India 98.3745 % → 97.985 %. The second-chance searches add candidates from outside the shortlist: 578,317 native-script pairs not in it, and 1,827 (US) and 25,558 (India) new address candidates. Our documentation reports no results for other cap values, so I won't quote a gain for five or six.

**Numbers:**

- Recall (Doc B.2); second-chance candidates (Doc 3)

### Q187. Don't your hand-written word lists make the system brittle in a new language? ★★★ {#q187 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test how much of the system is general and how much is tuned to these three countries.

**Say:** Partly, yes. The France rules and part of the cleaning depend on small hand-written word lists, for example French street types and generic words like "groupe" or "services", so a new language needs its own lists. The core, the index lookup, the readers and the "what changed" features, is mostly language-independent, which is why the default route keeps it and drops the France rules; learning the rule conditions from a small labelled sample would reduce that dependence further.

**If they push:** Our documentation limits hand-written lists to small word lists for cleaning, decision-model features, the India native-script search and the France rules; there is no external data, geocoder, postal or business table. The street veto, for example, depends on a list of French street types and stop words, and the legal-form relation needs each country's legal-form words.

**Numbers:**

- External resources (Doc C.6)

### Q188. You say the data-specific features were removed. Are they completely gone? ★★★ {#q188 .q}

*Why they ask:* A probing follow-up on your feature clean-up; they check for indirect dependencies.

**Say:** As inputs of the final decision models, yes: we replaced 21 data-specific inputs with 25 generic "what changed" features, and a code check asserts that none of the removed inputs is used. An indirect dependence on those inputs remains, and our documentation discloses it: the training records of the two second-chance models were selected with earlier decision models that still had them.

**If they push:** Two training features of those second-chance models, counts of links already accepted at the business, also come from those earlier models' decisions. The 21 apply to the US and India models; the France and default models exclude 16 from their base list. To remove the dependence we would re-select those training records with the final decision models and retrain the two second-chance models; we have no measurement of whether that changes anything.

**Numbers:**

- 21 removed (US/India), 16 (France/default), 25 generic added (Doc 4); disclosure (Doc C.8)

### Q189. What did you try that did not work? ★★ LIKELY {#q189 .q}

*Why they ask:* Negative results show judgement; they also check that you can let go of ideas.

**Say:** Four things we tried and dropped: a larger XLM-R reader, refitting the France decision model on more folds, a second French self-training round, and retraining the French MiniLM reader with different pseudo-label filters. The last three each scored slightly lower on the public board than the version we kept.

**If they push:** France refit 0.990726 against 0.990748; second French round 0.991277 against 0.991300; French MiniLM retrain 0.991258 against 0.991300. XLM-R large (MIT, about 560 million parameters) was discarded during development; our documentation records no number for it, so we don't quote one. All three public differences are small enough that they may be noise.

**Numbers:**

- Dropped items (Doc B.5, B.6)

### Q190. Why didn't the second French self-training round help? ★★★ {#q190 .q}

*Why they ask:* They test whether you understand iterative self-training and can say "we don't know" cleanly.

**Say:** We don't know for certain; we did not diagnose it. It scored 0.991277 against 0.991300 for one round, a small difference that may be noise. A plausible reason is that a second round mostly re-learns the first round's own confident guesses, so errors can compound while little new information is added.

**If they push:** This is the confirmation-bias risk of self-training: the more the teacher is the student's own earlier version, the less independent the pseudo-labels are. What we would measure: how many second-round pseudo-labels differ from the first round's, and whether the second-round reader does better or worse on the generated labelled French test set; neither number is in our documentation, so I won't guess.

**Numbers:**

- Upload 17: 0.991277 vs 0.991300, not adopted (Doc B.6)

### Q191. Your pipeline has many moving parts. Isn't that a maintenance burden? ★★ {#q191 .q}

*Why they ask:* Production scientists care about operating cost, not only accuracy.

**Say:** Yes, it is a long pipeline, and that is a real cost. The upside is that each stage has its own measurement, recall at each candidate step, a held-out threshold or a written check, so a regression can be traced to one stage. In a production version we would fold the second-chance searches into one decision model and turn the France rules into learned features, which removes the most bespoke parts.

**If they push:** There is one code path for every country; a country profile only selects the cleaning rules, readers, decision model, threshold, second-chance searches and rules. Training and inference run from one entry script, and the organisers' validator is the last stage. A full retrain takes about 11.5 hours on one GPU.

**Numbers:**

- About 11 h 30 min full retrain (CodeREADME 1, 6)

### Q192. What would you do differently? ★★ LIKELY {#q192 .q}

*Why they ask:* The reflection question; they want specific, prioritised lessons tied to your own limitations.

**Say:** First, keep an untouched end-to-end validation fold, including the second-chance searches, from day one. Second, add finer blocking keys such as state or postcode, which gives room for a larger cap than four where the cap loses true businesses. Third, label a small French sample, to replace the hand-written rules with learned features and set the French threshold on real labels; and fourth, fold the second-chance searches into one decision model.

**If they push:** Also: a dense retrieval channel for brand and "doing business as" names, clean ablations of the "what changed" features and the seeds, and a single-record latency measurement.

### Q193. If this went to production at Amazon, what would you do first? ★★ {#q193 .q}

*Why they ask:* They check whether you can move from a competition mindset to an operational one.

**Say:** First, a small labelled sample for every country we serve, starting with France, to measure F0.5 directly and set thresholds on real labels. Then we would time single-record latency, since the work per record is bounded but we have not measured it, and add monitoring of links per business and score distributions per country, to catch drift before it costs precision.

**If they push:** For scale, we would split the index by state or postcode as well as by country and run the shards in parallel; the cost per record is bounded at every stage, so it grows linearly with volume. As a rough linear extrapolation, not a measurement, a billion incoming records would mean about 1.17 billion reader pairs, on the order of 140 GPU-hours spread across shards.

**Numbers:**

- Scaling estimate (QA 2; extrapolation, not a measurement)

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "How confident are you in the French part?" see [Q137](#q137); "Your documentation says AI coding assistants were used. What did they do?" see [Q229](#q229).

## 17. Why not X? Alternatives we did not use (14 questions) {#cat-17 .cat}

### Q194. Why not simply ask a large language model whether two records match? ★★ LIKELY {#q194 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to see that small models were a deliberate choice (cost, control, competition rules), not a default.

**Say:** No LLM runs anywhere in our pipeline. The rules cap every model at 8 billion parameters, and even after blocking we score 11.7 million shortlist pairs, so a generative call per pair would cost far more than our readers, which have about 118 and 278 million parameters. Small fine-tuned readers plus a decision model that compares all candidates of a record were accurate enough: close versions of our decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992 on hidden folds.

**If they push:** Our decision is a competition between up to four candidates with a tuned threshold and a 0.4 lead, so it needs a numeric score for every candidate; an LLM judge could give one through its token probabilities, but at the price of a forward pass through a model tens of times larger than our readers for each of 11.7 million pairs. During development, AI assistants helped write code and review sampled pairs when we designed the France rules, which we disclose, but no human or LLM judgement of any pair is an input to the pipeline. In production, an LLM could earn a place offline, for example pre-screening the uncertain band before human review, judged against a labelled audit sample like any other model.

**Numbers:**

- 11,687,317 shortlist pairs (Doc 3)
- MiniLM 117,653,760 and E5 278,043,648 parameters (Doc B.5)
- Held-out US 0.991212 / 0.991545, India 0.990046 / 0.990298, fold 9 / fold 8 (Doc 5)
- "No LLM runs in the pipeline" (Doc C.6)

### Q195. Why an inverted index for blocking, and not embedding (vector) search with an approximate-nearest-neighbour index? ★★ LIKELY {#q195 .q}

*Why they ask:* Dense retrieval is the modern default; they test whether we considered it and know how we would judge it.

**Say:** We did not benchmark a dense retriever, so we cannot claim it would be worse. Our index keeps the true business for 99.37 percent of US and 98.51 percent of Indian held-out records, it is deterministic, cheap and easy to audit, and its separate lists for name words, address words, letter pieces and sounds already catch typos and abbreviations. A vector index would be a natural extra channel for brand or "doing business as" names that share few words with the business.

**If they push:** In our view, embeddings are weakest exactly where our hard cases are: two names that differ only in the legal form or a single word get almost the same vector, so a dense channel would add recall for paraphrase-like names, not precision. We would add it as an extra candidate list unioned with the index output, train it contrastively with hard negatives mined from our own index, and judge it by the same per-stage recall table on fold 9, by candidates per business and by held-out F0.5, because extra candidates compete for the same four shortlist places.

**If they push further:** Rare exact tokens such as house numbers and unusual name words are what sparse matching captures best, and its misses can be explained term by term. We would add dense retrieval as a sixth channel and measure the recall gain at each step before paying for the embeddings and an approximate-neighbour index.

**Numbers:**

- Index recall, train fold 9: US 99.3694 %, India 98.5068 % (Doc B.2)
- About 130 candidates per business from the index, blocking study of 25 Sep (Doc 3)
- Index recall, fold 9 (Doc B.2)

### Q196. Why a cascade of five zones instead of one end-to-end model? ★★ {#q196 .q}

*Why they ask:* Checks that we understand the cost-accuracy trade-off of a cascade and can justify its extra parts.

**Say:** One end-to-end model would have to score every pair, 6.7 trillion within countries, or trust a single retrieval score. A cascade lets each stage do the cheapest job it can do well, and we can measure what each stage loses: the index, the quick rule-based filter and the shortlist each have a recall number on a held-out fold. The decision model exists because the final decision is a competition between candidates, which a model that sees one pair at a time cannot see.

**If they push:** The price of a cascade is that errors compound: a true business cut by the cap of four can never be linked by the main decision, and only the two second-chance searches can bring back their two miss types, which is why we report recall per stage. A retriever and reader trained jointly is possible, but it needs negatives drawn from the retriever during training and much more compute; we did not try it.

**Numbers:**

- 6,724,569,566,212 same-country pairs (Doc 3)
- Per business: about 130 (index) → 21.7107 (filter) → 6.75 (shortlist, derived) → 7.0954 (candidate file) (Doc 3)

### Q197. Why cross-encoders as readers, and not a bi-encoder (two embeddings and a cosine)? ★★ {#q197 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we understand the architectural difference, not just the model names.

**Say:** A bi-encoder squeezes each record into one vector before comparing, so it can miss that exactly one word or the legal form changed; a cross-encoder reads both texts in one sequence, so every token can look at the other side. The cost is that nothing can be precomputed per business, so a cross-encoder runs once per pair; that is affordable only because the shortlist sends on average 1.17 pairs per incoming record to the readers.

**If they push:** Bi-encoders win at retrieval because business vectors can be indexed once; cross-encoders win at the final judgement. In our US example, "Legacy Marketing Enterprises Inc" and "... LLC" differ by one token; the readers and the legal-form features separated them, and the decision model gave the LLC 0.000007 against 0.965022 for the Inc.

**Numbers:**

- 1.17 shortlist pairs per incoming record (derived: 11,687,317 / 9,969,589, Doc 3)
- US example: 0.965022 vs 0.000007 (Doc D.1)

### Q198. Did you consider Ditto, DeepMatcher or other published entity-matching models? ★★ {#q198 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests awareness of the entity-resolution literature and where our design sits in it.

**Say:** Our readers are in the same family as Ditto: a pretrained transformer fine-tuned as a cross-encoder on serialised record pairs, here "name | address" on each side. We did not benchmark Ditto or DeepMatcher themselves. What we added around the reader goes beyond a pairwise matcher: a per-country decision model that compares all candidates of one record, the "what changed" features, and a tuned threshold with a clear-winner lead.

**If they push:** DeepMatcher predates pretrained transformers and summarises each attribute with recurrent or attention layers; Ditto adds tricks such as marking spans with domain knowledge, summarising long attributes and data augmentation. Our attributes are short, so summarising matters little, and we put domain knowledge into explicit features instead of the input text; we chose multilingual base models because India has native-script names and France has French text.

### Q199. Why not bigger readers, such as XLM-R large or a 7-billion-parameter model? ★★ {#q199 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether model size was a deliberate cost-accuracy choice and whether we over-claim.

**Say:** We tried a larger reader, XLM-R large with about 560 million parameters, during development and dropped it; our documentation records no comparison number, so I will not claim it was worse, only that it did not enter the final pipeline. Reader cost grows with model size and is paid on every shortlist pair, and the hardest part of our problem is choosing between near-tied candidates, which the decision model handles with features a reader does not see.

**If they push:** Our readers have 117.7 million and 278.0 million parameters, far below the 8-billion cap, under Apache-2.0 and MIT licences. With more compute we would rerun the comparison properly: same shortlist, the same decision-model recipe refitted on the larger reader's scores, per-business F0.5 on held-out fold 9, and GPU-hours per million pairs.

**Numbers:**

- XLM-R large, MIT, about 560 M parameters: tried and discarded (Doc B.5)
- 117,653,760 and 278,043,648 parameters (Doc B.5)

### Q200. Why separate models per country rather than one global model? ★ LIKELY {#q200 .q}

*Why they ask:* A global model is simpler to run; they check that per-country models are justified, not accidental.

**Say:** The countries differ in format, French addresses and legal words and Indian scripts, and in labels: France has none. The code path is the same for every country; a country profile only selects the cleaning rules, readers, decision model, threshold, second-chance searches and rules. We share where it helps: the India decision model and the France decision model both train on US and Indian rows.

**If they push:** One model with a country feature could share more, but the operating points would still be per country: France, with no labels to tune on, uses a more conservative 0.82, against 0.75 tuned on fold 8 for the US and India. Per-country models also let us retrain or roll back one country without touching the others; the closest thing we have to a global model is the unseen-country route, trained on US and Indian rows with the MiniLM reader only, which is untested on real data.

### Q201. Why no graph clustering or transitive closure, as in classic deduplication? ★★★ {#q201 .q}

*Why they ask:* Entity resolution is often framed as clustering; they test whether we understood the structure of this task.

**Say:** In our view this task does not need it: each incoming record links to at most one business in a reference list, so there is no record-to-record graph to close. Transitive closure also chains errors: one wrong edge would merge two whole groups. The cross-record logic we do need is per business: the collective features look at all records competing for the same business, and the per-business consistency check adjusts the bar by how many other records that business already accepted.

**If they push:** If we had to deduplicate incoming records among themselves, correlation clustering would be the principled choice, but this task does not score that. If the business list itself contained duplicates, deduplicating it would be a separate step before matching. This is our reasoning; our documentation does not discuss clustering.

### Q202. Why not a one-to-one assignment, for example the Hungarian algorithm? ★★ {#q202 .q}

*Why they ask:* Assignment methods are a standard tool for linking two lists; they check we know when it does not fit.

**Say:** Because the structure is many-to-one: one business owns several incoming records, on average 3.38 links per business in our final file and up to 11. A one-to-one assignment would force us to drop true records. Taking each record's best candidate, only if it is confident and a clear winner, already guarantees at most one business per record.

**If they push:** A capacitated version, b-matching or min-cost flow, fits the many-to-one shape, but it needs a capacity per business, and how many records a business owns is exactly what we do not know. The business-side coupling we handle more softly, for the US and India: the consistency check lowers the bar to 0.68 when one other record of the business is already accepted and raises it to 0.77 with three or more, with the thresholds tuned on folds 8 and 9.

**Numbers:**

- Links per business: mean 3.3805, max 11 (Doc B.1)
- Consistency check: 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77 for 0 / 1 / 2 / 3+ other accepted records (Doc 4)

### Q203. Why not active learning, or simply labelling some French pairs? ★★ {#q203 .q}

*Why they ask:* Labelling a few hundred pairs is often the cheapest fix; they test whether we thought about it.

**Say:** We had no French labels, and hand-labelling French test pairs would have meant labelling the test set, so we did not: no human or LLM judgement of any pair is an input to our pipeline. Instead, for France we used self-training on very confident pseudo-labels. In production, labelling a small French sample is the first thing we would do.

**If they push:** We did review sampled unlabelled French pairs, with AI assistance, when designing the France rules, and we disclose that, but those reviews never became labels or pipeline inputs. In production we would choose pairs by uncertainty, for example records whose best candidate lies between 0.4 and the 0.82 threshold or that fail the 0.4 lead, and use the labels to set the French threshold and to replace the hand-written France rules with learned features. We would also label a random slice, because uncertainty sampling alone gives a biased estimate of precision.

### Q204. Why IDF-weighted word overlap in the index, and not BM25 or TF-IDF cosine? ★★ {#q204 .q}

*Why they ask:* Probes whether we know classic retrieval scoring and chose ours for a reason.

**Say:** Names and addresses are short, so a word almost never repeats inside one record; we treat each record as a set, and the score is the sum of the IDF weights of shared terms with our own length normalisation. BM25 adds term-frequency saturation, which has little to work on in such short text, and a length normalisation, where we use our own. The design choice we leaned on instead is scoring name and address separately and rewarding candidates that match on both.

**If they push:** IDF = log(1 + (N + 1) / (df + 1)); the name score divides the name-word IDF sum by (1 + tokens)^0.22 and adds a letter-piece term, and the total adds 1.2 × min(name score, address score). Terms are taken rarest first with posting-list caps, which works like stop-word removal learned from frequency and bounds the work per record; we did not benchmark BM25, so this is a design argument, not a measured comparison.

**Numbers:**

- Channel weights 1 / 1 / 0.45 / 0.22 / 0.18; caps and budgets per channel, e.g. name 14,000 / 22,000 (Doc 3)

### Q205. Why not classic Fellegi-Sunter probabilistic record linkage? ★★★ {#q205 .q}

*Why they ask:* It is the textbook method; they test whether we can relate our model to it.

**Say:** Our decision model is a supervised version of the same idea: turn a vector of field comparisons into a match probability. In its usual form, Fellegi-Sunter estimates a weight per comparison assuming the fields are independent given the match status; with labels for the US and India we can learn interactions directly, such as "the legal form changed and the address is the same". For unlabelled France we chose self-training plus a decision model trained on US and Indian labels.

**If they push:** An unsupervised Fellegi-Sunter model fitted by EM is the textbook option when labels are missing, as in France; we preferred to transfer a model learned with US and Indian labels because, in our view, the signals that matter interact, which the independence assumption ignores. Boosted trees also handle missing comparisons natively: in our US example the record has no address, so the "what changed" number features are missing and the name and legal form decide.

### Q206. Why add second-chance searches instead of just lowering the threshold? ★★ {#q206 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we diagnosed the type of error before choosing the fix.

**Say:** Because these misses are mostly retrieval failures: the right business is not among the candidates at all, so no threshold can link it. A targeted second search fixes the miss types we found on training data, native-script names and records whose name differs while the address matches. It only looks at records that are still unlinked, so it never undoes a link.

**If they push:** Lowering the main threshold would add wrong links among the candidates we already have, and under F0.5 a wrong link costs more than a missed one. The second-chance thresholds were chosen on fold 8 with false positives counted twice: 0.88 for the native-script search, which also needs a 0.3 lead, 0.86 for the US address search, and 0.66 with a 0.1 lead for the Indian address search.

**Numbers:**

- +9,759 native-script links (India); +192 (US) and +2,945 (India) address links (Doc B.1)

### Q207. Why not machine-translate the Indian and French records into English first? ★★ {#q207 .q}

*Why they ask:* Translation is an obvious idea for multilingual data; they test whether we know why it fits names badly.

**Say:** Business names are mostly proper nouns, so they need transliteration, not translation: विजय has to become "vijay", not a translated word. We learned an Indic-to-Latin word list from labelled training matches, and the readers are multilingual and read the raw text, including Devanagari and French accents. In our view a translation model would add cost and a new source of errors at the very step where one changed word decides the match; we did not test one.

**If they push:** The word list keeps a native word's Latin form only if it appears at least 3 times with that word in true matches and clearly beats the runner-up, otherwise we fall back to unidecode; it is a simple co-occurrence alignment learned from labels, not a neural transliterator. In the India example, the second-chance search's word list mapped all four words of the name, each with a single alternative.

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "Why train the CatBoost ranker with a plain classification loss and not a learning-to-rank loss?" see [Q142](#q142).

## 18. Taking it to production at Amazon scale (13 questions) {#cat-18 .cat}

### Q208. Amazon has billions of records. What would the deployed system look like? ★★ LIKELY {#q208 .q}

*Why they ask:* The core production question: does the design scale, and where would it break?

**Say:** The work per record is bounded at every stage, posting-list caps in the index, a fixed number of top candidates per list and at most four pairs per record for the readers, so cost grows linearly and shards run independently. Today we split by country; at billions we would split by country and state or postcode, keep each shard's index in memory and run the readers on a pool of GPUs. As a rough linear extrapolation, not a measurement, a billion incoming records means about 1.17 billion reader pairs, on the order of 140 GPU-hours spread across shards.

**If they push:** Finer shards lose recall when the state is missing or wrong, so we would keep a fallback to the country-wide index, as our native-script search already does: it searches the record's state and falls back to all states when the state is unknown or has no match. The posting-list caps are absolute numbers: a word whose list is longer than the cap is skipped, and in much larger shards more words cross that line, so we would re-measure recall per stage on a labelled sample before trusting the extrapolation.

**Numbers:**

- Reader scoring of the shortlist, two readers per pair: about 1.4 h on one 16 GB GPU (Evidence: clean_run/RESULT.md)
- About 140 GPU-hours per billion records: extrapolation (QA 2)

### Q209. New records and new businesses arrive every day. Can this run incrementally? ★★★ {#q209 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we know which parts of the pipeline depend on global statistics.

**Say:** Most of the per-record path can: clean the text, look up the shard index, rank, read at most four pairs, score and decide. What needs care are the parts computed over the whole data: the IDF weights and the index, the per-business collective features and consistency check, and the learned word lists. We would run the per-record path as a stream and recompute the global parts in periodic batches, re-deciding only the businesses they affect.

**If they push:** A new business must go into the posting lists, and it can change the answer for earlier records that had no good candidate, so we would re-query recently unlinked records against new businesses; it can also create a near tie for a record that is already linked, so linked records that retrieve the new business would be re-decided too. In our view IDF drifts slowly, so a periodic rebuild is enough, and because folds are a hash of the business id, new businesses fall into training folds automatically; we have not built or measured an incremental version.

### Q210. What is the latency for a single incoming record? ★★ LIKELY {#q210 .q}

*Why they ask:* Online matching needs a latency budget; they check whether we know ours and are honest if we do not.

**Say:** We have not measured single-record latency; our runs were batch jobs. The path per record is short: one index lookup in its shard, the ranker over a few filtered candidates, on average 1.17 reader pairs, and a handful of small tree-model calls per pair, so streaming is plausible in principle. The second-chance searches only run for records left unlinked and could run asynchronously.

**If they push:** In batch, the index lookup with the filter and ranker took about 1.3 hours and reader scoring about 1.4 hours for 9.97 million records on one machine. For an online service we would measure p50 and p99 per stage; the reader is the stage to watch, because a cross-encoder pass cannot be precomputed per business.

**If they push further:** For streaming we would keep the index and the business-side statistics in memory and refresh the rarity weights periodically rather than per record; the collective features and the per-business consistency check would need each business's current set of competing and accepted records. Those are design ideas, not things we built or timed.

**Numbers:**

- After the filter: 3.111 (US) / 3.878 (India) candidates per record in the all-fold samples (Doc B.2)
- Index + filter + ranker about 1.3 h; reader scoring about 1.4 h (Evidence: clean_run/RESULT.md)
- 1.17 shortlisted pairs per record (derived from Doc 3)

### Q211. How would you monitor this in production and detect drift without labels? ★★ LIKELY {#q211 .q}

*Why they ask:* Models decay silently; they want concrete signals, not "we would monitor it".

**Say:** We would track label-free health numbers per country against the baselines of our final run: 0.5875 links per incoming record, 5.8 percent of businesses empty, 1.23 candidates per record, the share of records whose best candidate fails the threshold or the lead, and how often each France rule fires. A sudden move in these signals that the input or a model has changed. A small labelled audit sample each period then gives the real precision.

**If they push:** We already used this kind of statistic to set the French threshold without labels: French link volume per business, compared with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US and Indian data. For drift in the text itself we would watch the share of native-script names, of records without an address, and of words missing from the learned word list.

**Numbers:**

- 0.5875 links per incoming record; 100,087 empty rows (5.8 %, derived); 1.2331 candidates per record; 90.59 % with exactly one candidate (Doc B.1)
- France: the two word-swap vetoes removed 29,021 of 887,630 accepted links (Doc B.3)

### Q212. Where would human reviewers fit in? ★★ {#q212 .q}

*Why they ask:* Real entity-resolution systems mix automation with review; they test whether we know where review adds most value.

**Say:** Between "link" and "no link". Records whose best candidate is fairly likely but not confident, or confident but not a clear winner, would go to a review queue instead of being dropped. Two of our France rescues already work in such a band: they consider only records whose best score is between 0.4 and 0.82, so that band is a natural first queue.

**If they push:** We would size the queue by counting records per band per day and order it by risk: a link that would be the first one for its business matters most, because if that business truly has no records, one wrong link takes its score from 1 to 0. Reviewer answers become labels, exactly the small French sample we lack, and they feed threshold tuning and retraining.

### Q213. How would you add a new country or language? ★★ LIKELY {#q213 .q}

*Why they ask:* Amazon operates in many marketplaces; they test whether the design generalises beyond three countries.

**Say:** On day one it takes our default route: the decision model trained on US and Indian rows, the multilingual MiniLM reader and the conservative 0.82 threshold; that route is untested on real data because the test set had no such country. Then we would repeat the France recipe: a country cleaner for its address format and legal words, self-trained readers on very confident pseudo-labels mixed with labelled pairs, and a small labelled sample to set the threshold.

**If they push:** Everything is driven by a country profile, a small JSON file that names the cleaner, readers, decision model, threshold, second-chance searches and rules, so the pipeline itself does not change; the new work is the country's cleaner, its word lists and the training. If the country uses another script, we would learn a transliteration word list from the first labelled matches, as we did for India.

### Q214. What does it cost to run, and where would you cut cost first? ★★ {#q214 .q}

*Why they ask:* At Amazon scale cost decides whether a design ships.

**Say:** On one consumer GPU, an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER with 16 GB, a full retrain takes about 11.5 hours; at inference the two longest stages are the index with the ranker, about 1.3 hours, and the GPU readers, about 1.4 hours. The cheapest saving is caching: a reader score belongs to a pair, so an incremental run only scores new pairs. Our own submitted run did exactly that: 11,638,504 shortlist pairs reused stored scores and only 48,813 were scored fresh.

**If they push:** Next we would try distilling the two readers into one, lower-precision inference, and skipping the second reader when the first is decisive, each judged by held-out per-business F0.5 against GPU-hours; we have not measured any of these. The tree models are cheap: in the clean run the decision-model scoring stage took about four minutes (derived from the stage timeline).

**Numbers:**

- Full retrain about 11 h 30 min; about 70 GB disk (CodeREADME 1)
- 11,638,504 reused vs 48,813 CPU-scored shortlist pairs (CodeREADME 6)
- Decision-model stage about 4 min (derived from Evidence: clean_run/stage_timeline.txt)

### Q215. How would you measure precision and recall in production when labels are scarce? ★★★ {#q215 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we know the difference between label-free proxies and real accuracy.

**Say:** With a small labelled audit sample that is never used for tuning: whole businesses sampled by country and score band, with every candidate record of each labelled, so we can compute the same per-business metric. Label-free proxies help between audits, but they measure consistency, not correctness. We learned that directly: our French E5 reader agreed 99.92 percent with held-out French pseudo-labels, yet on a generated labelled French test set it scored slightly below its base model.

**If they push:** Stratifying by score band, then reweighting by band size, estimates precision where it is uncertain without labelling thousands of easy cases; recall also needs a random sample of incoming records, including unlinked ones, because a true record that never became a candidate is invisible in the output. For differences between versions we would use a paired bootstrap over businesses, as our evaluation code does.

**Numbers:**

- Agreement 0.999206; best F0.5 0.910516 vs 0.914964 on the generated French set (Doc B.4)

### Q216. How often would you retrain, and how would you keep the training layers separate? ★★★ {#q216 .q}

*Why they ask:* Stacked systems break quietly when one layer is retrained without the others.

**Say:** We would keep the same layered split: the ranker and readers learn on one part of the businesses and the decision models on another, assigned by a stable hash of the business id, so new businesses fall into a part automatically. The tree models are cheap and could be retrained often; the readers are expensive and would change less often. Any reader update forces a refit of the decision model, because its inputs change.

**If they push:** Our France decision model is an exception we would not repeat in production: it was trained with the MiniLM reader's score in its reader slot but receives a blend of three readers at test time without a refit; the blend keeps the input on the same logit scale, and France's threshold was set separately, without labels. Every new model would pass written acceptance checks before release, like the ones our French E5 reader faced, for example AUC within 0.001 and top-1 accuracy within 0.002 of its base model on labelled US and Indian pairs; and, unlike that reader, which we kept although it failed two of its four checks, a failed check would block the release.

### Q217. Different teams want different precision-recall trade-offs. Can you move the operating point? ★ {#q217 .q}

*Why they ask:* Production users differ; they check the design is configurable and that we know how to choose a point.

**Say:** Yes, without retraining: the threshold and the lead are settings in each country's profile. We tuned 0.75 for the competition metric, F0.5, on fold 8; a team that wants suggestions for human review would use a lower bar, and fully automatic merging a higher one. The choice should come from a held-out curve of precision and recall per threshold, not from intuition.

**If they push:** The threshold and the lead interact: the lead guards against near ties between candidates, which we expect to be the riskiest links, so for a review queue we would lower the threshold before touching the lead, and check both on a held-out curve. Under F0.5 a wrong link weighs four times as much as a missed link in the formula; a recall-oriented metric such as F2 reverses that weighting and would move the best operating point lower.

### Q218. How would you explain a particular link to an auditor or a seller? ★★ {#q218 .q}

*Why they ask:* Explainability matters when links affect customers or sellers.

**Say:** Every decision can be traced from stored values: which candidates were found, their scores, the lead over the runner-up, the "what changed" features and any rule that fired. In our US example, "Legacy Marketing Enterprises (Inc)" was linked to the Inc in Windsor at 0.965, while the LLC, whose name differs only in the legal form, scored 0.000007. In France, a link the model scored 0.9998 was vetoed by a readable rule: same address, but the word "parents" was replaced by "comite".

**If they push:** The index and the quick filter are deterministic, so "why was this business not even considered" also has an exact answer, and the candidate file lists every business that the decision model or a second-chance model scored for the record. For the tree model we would add per-decision feature attributions, for example SHAP values, which LightGBM can compute for trees directly; we did not prepare them for this submission.

### Q219. Would you keep the hand-written France rules in production? ★★★ {#q219 .q}

*Why they ask:* Hand rules are a maintenance and overfitting risk; they test whether we see that.

**Say:** Not as they are. They were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records, their parameters were chosen after seeing test results, including public scores, and they depend on French word lists, so they are brittle. In production we would turn each rule's condition into a feature, learn it from a small labelled French sample, and keep a rule only if it still helps on held-out data.

**If they push:** Two things make them manageable meanwhile: each rule is code on model scores and raw text, with no test label and no human or LLM judgement as an input, and each rule's firing count is recorded in the run report, for example the two word-swap vetoes removed 29,021 of 887,630 accepted French links, so a change in firing rate is an alert. The largest France risk remains that we have no measured French F0.5.

### Q220. What if bad actors create records that copy a real business's name at a nearby address? ★★★ {#q220 .q}

*Why they ask:* Production systems face adversarial inputs; they test whether our precision safeguards carry over.

**Say:** Near-identical candidates are exactly what our decision rule is built for: the "what changed" features describe the one word, number or legal form that differs, and we only link a clear winner, at least 0.4 ahead of the runner-up. When two businesses are too close, the record stays unlinked, which is the cheaper mistake under F0.5.

**If they push:** For the US and India the decision models were also trained with extra hard examples: copies of unlinked training records that sit right next to a candidate business, with small name edits; how many to add was set from label-free counts on the test records, never from labels, and the France model uses no such examples. In production we would add signals a competition does not have, such as account history, and send high-impact near ties to human review.

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "What if the business list itself contains duplicates?" see [Q164](#q164).

## 19. Reproducibility, engineering and rules (12 questions) {#cat-19 .cat}

### Q221. What hardware did you use, and how long does it take? ★ LIKELY {#q221 .q}

*Why they ask:* A sanity check on cost and feasibility, and on whether we know our own numbers.

**Say:** One desktop machine: an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti SUPER with 16 GB, a Ryzen 7 9800X3D and 32 GB of RAM, on Windows 11. A full retrain from raw data takes about 11.5 hours of compute and about 70 GB of disk. At inference, the index lookup with the filter and ranker took about 1.3 hours and reader scoring about 1.4 hours for almost 10 million records.

**If they push:** Every stage needs less than 8 GB of RAM except the address second-chance search, about 3.2 GB per worker or 13 GB with four workers, and most stages use at most 6 CPU threads. The only network access is the first stage, which downloads the two pretrained encoders at pinned revisions; everything after it runs offline.

**Numbers:**

- 11 h 30 min retrain; 70 GB disk; RAM < 8 GB except address search 13 GB with 4 workers (CodeREADME 1)
- Longest clean-run stages: folds, word list, index and ranker training 1.4 h; MiniLM and E5 reader training 2.1 h; first French scoring + French MiniLM reader fine-tune 2.0 h; test index + filter + ranker 1.3 h; reader scoring 1.4 h (Evidence: clean_run/RESULT.md)

### Q222. Can someone reproduce your submitted file exactly? ★★ LIKELY {#q222 .q}

*Why they ask:* Reproducibility is a submission requirement and a sign of engineering discipline.

**Say:** Yes, at two levels. From our trained models and stored reader scores, the inference stages rewrite both submitted files byte for byte; a fresh extraction of the full archive on 29 September reproduced both, with matching SHA-256 hashes. From raw data, a clean run of every stage passed the organisers' validator and reproduced 99.82 percent of the submitted links.

**If they push:** In that clean run 99.07 percent of businesses had an identical list of linked records; France agreed least, 96.72 percent: its shortlist changed most (2,122,285 pairs instead of 2,103,107), and both self-trained French readers were retrained in that run as well. The regenerated file was never uploaded, so its leaderboard score is unknown.

**If they push further:** Clean run of 27-28 September: identical match list for 99.07 % of businesses, 5,846,344 links in common, about 11.5 hours of compute on one RTX 4070 Ti SUPER 16 GB. A fresh extraction of the full archive on 29 September reproduced both files byte for byte. The stored reader scores are needed because bf16 scores depend slightly on the device and on how pairs are batched and padded. The French E5 reader's weights were deleted after scoring; its logits are shipped, and a flag retrains it for a run from raw data. The regenerated file was never uploaded, so its public score is unknown.

**Numbers:**

- 99.82 % of links reproduced (5,846,344 in common); 99.07 % identical match lists (CodeREADME 6; Evidence: clean_run/RESULT.md)
- SHA-256: matching 9183e542…, candidates e7b4c679… (CodeREADME 5)
- Reproduction (CodeREADME 6; Evidence)

### Q223. Why is a run from raw data not bit-identical? ★★ {#q223 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we understand sources of non-determinism in GPU training.

**Say:** Two GPU training steps are not bit-deterministic: the CatBoost ranker trained on the GPU, and the readers trained in bf16 mixed precision. A slightly different ranker changes some shortlists, and every later stage follows from them. Even bf16 reader scores depend slightly on the device and on which pairs share a batch, because each batch is padded to its longest pair, which changes the shapes of the computation and so the order of the floating-point sums.

**If they push:** On a GPU, parallel reductions and atomic additions sum in a varying order, and floating-point addition is not associative, so two training runs drift apart; that is why byte-exact reproduction needs the stored reader scores as well as the weights. The CPU-trained parts we re-checked are deterministic: retraining the India native-script and India address second-chance models on the same inputs reproduced their files byte for byte, and the pipeline requires a fixed Python hash seed.

### Q224. Which pretrained models did you use, under which licences, and how big are they? ★ LIKELY {#q224 .q}

*Why they ask:* Direct check of the competition rules: open licence and at most 8 billion parameters.

**Say:** Two, both from Hugging Face at pinned revisions: multilingual MiniLM-L12, Apache-2.0, 117.7 million parameters, and multilingual E5-base, MIT, 278.0 million. All four readers are fine-tuned from these two; the ranker, decision models and second-chance models are trained from scratch on the provided data. Our largest model is under 4 percent of the 8-billion-parameter limit.

**If they push:** The MiniLM encoder is also used without fine-tuning to embed single words for the meaning-similarity features. A larger XLM-R reader, MIT and about 560 million parameters, was tried and discarded and is not downloaded or used. The libraries are open source, mostly BSD, MIT and Apache-2.0, plus text-unidecode used under the Artistic License; their licences are listed in our documentation and their pinned versions in the requirements file.

**Numbers:**

- 117,653,760 (Apache-2.0) and 278,043,648 (MIT) parameters (Doc B.5)
- 278,043,648 / 8,000,000,000 = 3.5 % (derived)

### Q225. Did you use any external data, lookup table or API? ★ LIKELY {#q225 .q}

*Why they ask:* External lookup was banned; they want a clear, confident no.

**Say:** No. No geocoder, postal table, business registry, API or other external data; the only network access downloads the two pretrained encoders. Hand-written lists are limited to small word lists for cleaning, features, the India second-chance search and the France rules, and the Indic-to-Latin word list is learned from labelled training matches.

**If they push:** No LLM runs in the pipeline, and every model, including any model used to produce training data, has at most 8 billion parameters. Our documentation states all of this in its disclosures.

### Q226. Did you use the test data in any way? ★★★ LIKELY {#q226 .q}

*Why they ask:* The key integrity question; they want a complete disclosure without having to drag it out.

**Say:** Yes, without labels, and it is all disclosed. The pipeline computes unsupervised statistics on the test files, such as word rarity, the search indexes and competition features and, for France, the geography and a street-type typo table, and it self-trains the two French readers on confident pseudo-labels of French test pairs. The France rules were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records, including AI-assisted review of sampled pairs, and their parameters were chosen after seeing test results, including public scores.

**If they push:** Label-free counts on the test records also set the French threshold, the French MiniLM reader's blend weight and, for the US and India, how many extra hard training examples to add; for India, a native-script word alignment is computed on test records whose first-stage top candidate has probability at least 0.9. During development, a generated labelled French test set made from the French test businesses was used for evaluation only. We never had test labels, and no human or LLM judgement of a pair is an input.

### Q227. Pretrained encoders already contain world knowledge. Isn't that external information? ★★★ {#q227 .q}

*Why they ask:* An adversarial probe of the "no external data" claim.

**Say:** They are general-purpose multilingual language models under open licences, and the rules allow such models up to 8 billion parameters. We never query them for facts: after fine-tuning on the provided data they only read a pair and output a score, and the frozen MiniLM encoder only embeds single words for one feature group.
