And nothing leaves the machine at inference: after the first stage downloads the encoders, everything runs offline.

**If they push:** What a pretrained encoder brings is language, for example that "Enterprises" and "Industries" are related but different words, and a vocabulary that splits Devanagari and French text into word pieces. Like any language model it may have seen some business names during pretraining, but we never ask it about a business: it only scores the two texts in front of it, and we used no lookup of any kind.

### Q228. Who did what in your team? ★ {#q228 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want to know the presenter's own role and that the team understands the work.

**Say:** We are a team of three, Monika, Hemachand and I, and we built and checked the pipeline together; I am presenting it today. The documentation, code and evidence files are our shared work, and all three of us stand behind them. **[TO FILL IN** before 7 October: one accurate sentence, agreed with Monika and Hemachand, on the split of work. Our documents do not record roles, so do not improvise one on stage.**]**

**If they push:** We are happy to share a breakdown afterwards; the full method, code and disclosures are in our documentation and repository.

### Q229. Did you use AI tools to build this? ★★ {#q229 .q}

*Why they ask:* They want a straight, factual answer; our documentation already discloses it.

**Say:** Yes, and our documentation discloses it: AI coding assistants wrote and ran code and analysis scripts during development. For three later France rule changes, the cells of the cell veto, the acronym rescue and the lower bound of the generic-word rescue, they also chose the cells and thresholds and wrote the rule code, which we adopted. No LLM runs in the submitted pipeline.

**If they push:** Their output went through the same checks as the rest of our work: held-out folds where labels exist, label-free tests and public scores for the France rules, written acceptance checks for new readers, and the organisers' validator. We can walk through any part of the code and the reason for each choice.

**If they push further:** The three changes were the cell-veto cells, the acronym rescue and the lower bound of the generic-word rescue. Every rule is code on model scores and raw text; no human or AI judgement of a pair is an input.

**Numbers:**

- Disclosure (Doc C.5); models (Doc B.5)

### Q230. Why is the index written in C++, and how is the code organised? ★★ {#q230 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests engineering judgement: where performance mattered and how the system is structured.

**Say:** The index lookup is the only stage that compares every incoming record against large posting lists, so we wrote it in C++17 with OpenMP threads; everything else is Python with LightGBM, CatBoost and PyTorch. One shell entry script runs the training stages and then the inference stages in a fixed order, and a JSON profile per country selects the parts.

**If they push:** The index takes query terms rarest first, skips any term whose posting list is longer than the cap and stops a channel when its budget is used up, which keeps the work per record bounded. It also computes the 76 features per candidate in the same pass; its string similarity is a longest-common-subsequence ratio computed with a bit-parallel algorithm. After a failure the script can be re-run from the failed stage onwards.

### Q231. With 18 leaderboard uploads, how did you keep track of what each change did? ★★ {#q231 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests experiment discipline and honesty about leaderboard use.

**Say:** Every upload is logged in our documentation with its time, what changed and its public score, from the first scored baseline at 0.968212 to the final file at 0.991300, including the three changes we tried and did not adopt. Thresholds that could be tuned with labels were set on held-out folds, and new readers had written pass-or-fail checks; the evidence files ship with the code.

**If they push:** The log is also how we disclose leaderboard influence honestly: the US and Indian refit was kept on public evidence, 0.990621 to 0.990676, the France refit was dropped, 0.990726 against 0.990748, and the final file was chosen among the uploads by public score.

### Q232. What safety checks protect the output files? ★★ {#q232 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether the pipeline guards itself against silent errors.

**Say:** The export asserts that every linked pair is also in the candidate file, and the last stage runs the organisers' validator with ID checks, which passes. The final file has no pair across countries and no incoming record linked to more than one business. Stored French reader scores are installed only if the France shortlist matches the one they were scored on, checked by its SHA-256 hash.

**If they push:** A clean end-to-end run from a fresh folder found four issues, a Windows runtime-library clash, an over-strict assertion, a full disk, and that French-score check stopping as designed, and all fixes are in the package. A code check also asserts that none of the 21 data-specific inputs we removed is used by a final decision model, and the validator log shows 1,732,544 rows in each file.

## 20. Rapid-fire ML fundamentals a scientist may probe (15 questions) {#cat-20 .cat}

### Q233. Explain gradient boosting in two sentences. Why boosted trees, and not a neural network, for the decision model? ★ LIKELY {#q233 .q}

*Why they ask:* A basic competence check, and whether we can justify the model family for our data.

**Say:** Gradient boosting adds decision trees one at a time: each new tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current log-odds, which for log loss is simply the label minus the predicted probability, and it is added with a small learning rate. We chose it because our decision model has about two hundred tabular features of mixed scales, often missing; a record with no address, for example, has no "what changed" number features. And the key signals are interactions such as "legal form changed and same address", which trees capture directly.

**If they push:** LightGBM and CatBoost take a second-order step, each leaf value is minus the sum of gradients over the sum of Hessians plus the L2 term, and LightGBM learns a default direction for missing values at each split. Our settings: learning rate 0.05, 127 leaves, at least 200 rows per leaf, feature fraction 0.9, bagging 0.8, L2 1.0, mean of five seeds; a neural network could use the same features, but on tabular data like this boosted trees are usually as accurate with far less tuning, and we did not benchmark one.

### Q234. You use both CatBoost and LightGBM. What is the difference, and why both? ★★ {#q234 .q}

*Why they ask:* Checks that we know the libraries beyond their names.

**Say:** CatBoost by default grows symmetric trees, the same split across a whole level, so depth 7 gives 128 leaves, fast scoring and some built-in regularisation; we train it on the GPU as the ranker over the 76 index features. LightGBM grows trees leaf by leaf, always splitting the leaf that reduces the loss most, on binned histograms, which suits our larger feature sets on CPU. Both are gradient-boosted trees, and we did not compare swapping them.

**If they push:** The ranker uses at most 1,600 trees, depth 7, learning rate 0.075, L2 5 and early stopping after 180 rounds without improvement; the decision models use 127 leaves and stop after 100 rounds without improvement (the patience is set in the code). Leaf-wise growth can overfit, and the minimum of 200 rows per leaf guards against that.

### Q235. What does attention do inside your readers, and why is a cross-encoder expensive? ★★ {#q235 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests transformer basics and whether we connect them to cost.

**Say:** Self-attention lets every token build its representation as a weighted mix of all tokens in the sequence, with weights from query-key similarity, softmax of Q·Kᵀ divided by √d, applied to the values. Because a cross-encoder puts the record and the business in one sequence, "Inc" on one side can attend directly to "LLC" on the other, in each of the 12 layers. The price is that nothing can be precomputed per business, so every pair needs a full forward pass, and attention's cost grows with the square of the sequence length; that is why we cap pairs at 128 tokens and read only the shortlist.

**If they push:** At 128 tokens the linear layers still cost more than the attention itself, so the real saving comes from reading fewer pairs. We pool by the masked mean of the last hidden states, ignoring padding, then apply dropout 0.1 and a linear head to one logit: 385 parameters for MiniLM, 384 weights plus a bias, and 769 for E5. Mean pooling matches how both base models were pretrained as sentence encoders (background knowledge, not in our documentation).

### Q236. Did you use contrastive learning anywhere? ★★ {#q236 .q}

*Why they ask:* Contrastive training is central to modern matching; they check we know what it is and where it would fit.

**Say:** Not in our own training: all four readers are fine-tuned with binary cross-entropy on labelled or pseudo-labelled pairs. Contrastive learning pulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matching ones apart in an embedding space, usually with in-batch negatives and an InfoNCE loss; it is how bi-encoders such as E5 are pretrained (background knowledge), and we start from those pretrained weights. Our negatives come from the ranker instead: the non-owner candidates it ranked highest, taken from every hard record, where the ranker was unsure or wrong, plus a random 25 percent of the other records.

**If they push:** If we added a dense retrieval channel, we would train it contrastively with hard negatives mined from our own index, because random in-batch negatives are far too easy for business names.

### Q237. Are your probabilities calibrated? Does it matter? ★★★ LIKELY {#q237 .q}

*Why they ask:* A threshold is only meaningful if we understand what the score means; this separates practitioners from tutorial users.

**Say:** We did not calibrate them, for example with Platt or isotonic scaling, and we did not measure calibration; instead we tuned the threshold directly on the exact per-business F0.5 on a held-out fold. For a threshold alone that is enough: any order-preserving recalibration just moves the best threshold with it and selects the same links. Calibration matters when a threshold has to transfer to data whose scores are distributed differently, which is France's situation.

**If they push:** The 0.4 lead is a difference of probabilities, so unlike the threshold it does change under recalibration; that is one reason our operating points stay tied to a specific model. The France decision model was trained with the MiniLM reader's score in its reader slot but receives a three-reader blend at test time, and France has no labels to tune on, so its threshold, a more conservative 0.82, was set from French link volume per business, compared with a fold-8 threshold sweep on US and Indian data.

### Q238. How did you deal with class imbalance? ★★ LIKELY {#q238 .q}

*Why they ask:* Matching is extremely imbalanced; they test whether we handled it consciously.

**Say:** Mostly by blocking: across the 6.7 trillion possible pairs a true pair is extremely rare, but the shortlist keeps at most four pairs per record, 1.17 on average on the test files, with at most one owner, so positives are no longer rare where the models are trained. We use plain, unweighted log loss and handle the cost asymmetry at decision time, with thresholds tuned for F0.5 and false positives counted twice when setting the second-chance thresholds.

**If they push:** For the readers we chose which pairs to train on instead of reweighting: every hard record, where the ranker was unsure or wrong, plus a random 25 percent of the other records, so the training effort goes to informative pairs. Reweighting classes would mostly shift the log-odds by a constant, which a threshold tuned on the metric largely absorbs anyway.

**If they push further:** Shortlist size in the labelled all-fold samples: 1.114 candidates per record for the US and 1.174 for India. The LightGBM objective is plain binary log loss with no class weights. Reweighting classes would mainly rescale the predicted probabilities and so move the best threshold, which we tune on the exact metric anyway. The French E5 reader's pseudo-labels are capped at 250,000 per class.

**Numbers:**

- Shortlist candidates per incoming record, all-fold samples: US 1.114, India 1.174 (Doc B.2)

### Q239. Walk me through the F0.5 maths. Why does one wrong link hurt so much? ★ LIKELY {#q239 .q}

*Why they ask:* The metric drives every design choice; they check we can do the arithmetic, not just name it.

**Say:** Per business, F0.5 = 1.25 × correct links / (links we made + 0.25 × true links), then we average over all businesses. A business with no true records scores 1 only if we link nothing, so one wrong link takes it from 1 to 0. Example: a business with three true records; linking two correct ones scores 1.25 × 2 / (2 + 0.75) = 0.91, while linking all three plus one wrong scores 1.25 × 3 / (4 + 0.75) = 0.79.

**If they push:** In counts, F_β = (1 + β²)·TP / ((1 + β²)·TP + β²·FN + FP), so with β = 0.5 a missed link weighs 0.25 against 1 for a wrong link. Macro averaging gives every business equal weight, so a business with no true records, which scores either 1 or 0, counts as much as the busiest one; that is why we link only a confident, clear winner, and we leave 100,087 rows empty.

### Q240. What kind of cross-validation did you use, and how does it prevent stacking leakage? ★★ {#q240 .q}

*Why they ask:* Leakage is the most common reason for over-optimistic results in stacked models.

**Say:** Grouped by business: ten folds from a hash of the business id, and every record goes with its business, so no business sits on both sides. The layers use different folds: the ranker and readers learn on folds 0 to 5 and the decision models on 6 to 9, so the decision model never sees reader scores on records the readers trained on, where they would be over-confident. To test a change we score fold 9 with fits on folds 6 to 8 that also drop every record touching fold 9, and fold 8 the same way.

**If they push:** The textbook alternative is out-of-fold stacking: train k readers, each scoring the fold it did not see, so every record gets an honest score and both layers use all the data. It costs k reader trainings on the GPU; our layer split gives the same guarantee more cheaply, at the price of each layer seeing less data.

### Q241. How did you control overfitting in the decision model? ★★ {#q241 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests regularisation knowledge and honesty about where overfitting can still hide.

**Say:** Through regularisation, early stopping and honest evaluation: at least 200 rows per leaf, 90 percent of features and 80 percent of rows per iteration, L2 of 1.0, learning rate 0.05, and early stopping on fold 8. We also removed 21 data-specific inputs and replaced them with 25 generic "what changed" features, which should transfer better to new data. On held-out folds 8 and 9, close versions of our decision models score between 0.990 and 0.992.

**If they push:** In our view the larger remaining risk is in our selection, not inside the model: thresholds were chosen on folds 8 and 9, which are also our evaluation folds, the final file was chosen among 18 uploads by public score, and the France rules were designed on the unlabelled test records. Held-out and public scores in the same range limit that risk, but do not remove it.

**Numbers:**

- Held-out US 0.991212 / 0.991545, India 0.990046 / 0.990298 (Doc 5)

### Q242. 127 leaves is a lot. How do you think about bias and variance here? ★★★ {#q242 .q}

*Why they ask:* Checks whether we can reason about capacity rather than copy default settings.

**Say:** Many leaves lower bias: the model can represent interactions like "number changed, same street, legal form unchanged". We pay for that in variance and control it with at least 200 rows per leaf, row and feature subsampling, L2, and by averaging five seeds. Seed averaging reduces the variance that comes from the random subsampling, not the variance from having a finite training set.

**If they push:** Honestly, the seeds' own effect is not isolated: the held-out table uses three of the five seeds, and the five-seed models entered the final file together with the French E5 reader (public 0.991114 to 0.991300), so we claim no separate number for them.

### Q243. Early stopping, then a refit with more rounds: is scaling the iterations by the row count justified? ★★★ {#q243 .q}

*Why they ask:* Probes whether we understand the refit heuristic and its limits.

**Say:** It is a heuristic, not a law. We fit on folds 6 and 7, find the best number of trees by early stopping on fold 8, then refit on folds 6 to 9 for that number times rows(6-9) / rows(6-7), because no fold is left to stop on and, at a fixed learning rate, more data usually supports more trees. For the US and India it helped on the public board, 0.990621 to 0.990676; for France it did not, 0.990726 against 0.990748, so France keeps the 6-7 fit.

**If they push:** The refitted model can no longer be evaluated on folds 8 or 9, which is one reason we have no untouched end-to-end validation; our held-out numbers come from fits that leave the scored fold out, using the same iteration rule.

### Q244. Why blend the French readers in logit space rather than averaging probabilities? ★★ {#q244 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests understanding of how to combine model outputs.

**Say:** A logit is log-odds, so a weighted sum of logits adds evidence: a reader that is very sure carries more weight than one that is only fairly sure, whereas in probability space every confident "no" is squashed into the narrow range near zero. In our French example, the business with the identical name in another city got +7.1 from the MiniLM reader, −1.9 from the French MiniLM reader and −10.8 from the French E5 reader; the 0.35 / 0.15 / 0.5 blend gives −3.2, and the decision model scored it 0.000098.

**If they push:** With weights that sum to one, the blend is a weighted geometric mean of the odds. Averaging probabilities with the same weights would give about 0.37, a much weaker "no" (our own arithmetic on those three logits). The blend also keeps the input on the scale the France decision model was trained on, a single reader logit. The French MiniLM reader's weight was set from label-free counts on the test records, and 0.35 / 0.15 / 0.5 equals half of the earlier blend, 0.7 MiniLM and 0.3 French MiniLM, plus half the French E5 reader.

**Numbers:**

- 0.35 × 7.1250 + 0.15 × (−1.9219) + 0.5 × (−10.8125) = −3.2008 (Doc D.3)
- Probability average with the same weights ≈ 0.369, logit about −0.54 (derived from Doc D.3)

### Q245. How do the readers handle Devanagari, French accents and long records? ★★ {#q245 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests tokenisation basics in a multilingual setting.

**Say:** They read the raw text, not our cleaned text, through a multilingual subword tokenizer, so Devanagari, accents and capital letters all reach the model as word pieces. Each pair is "name | address" on both sides, truncated to 128 tokens longest-first, which trims the longer side before the shorter one. Business names and addresses are short, so truncation should rarely bite, though we did not measure how often it does.

**If they push:** The E5 readers also use the MiniLM tokenizer; as background knowledge, both base models share the XLM-RoBERTa SentencePiece vocabulary, which is why one tokenizer serves both. The cleaned text, with transliteration and unified abbreviations, is used by the index and the hand-made features instead.

### Q246. Your reader recipe: why AdamW, warm-up, bf16 and only one epoch? ★★ {#q246 .q}

*Why they ask:* Checks that the fine-tuning settings were understood, not copied.

**Say:** AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive step, so the decay is not distorted by Adam's per-parameter scaling, and the new linear head gets five times the encoder's learning rate because it starts from random weights. A 3 percent linear warm-up avoids large early updates that would damage the pretrained weights while Adam's statistics are still noisy. bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so it cuts memory and time on a 16 GB GPU without loss scaling, and one epoch over a large labelled set limits both overfitting and cost.

**If they push:** After the warm-up the learning rate decays linearly to zero. Gradient clipping at 1.0 guards against rare large gradients, and length-bucketed batches, pairs of similar length together, cut padding waste. For scale: the French E5 reader trained 7,419 steps of batch 128, about 16 minutes on our GPU (noted in its training script).

### Q247. Self-training can reinforce its own mistakes. How did you limit confirmation bias? ★★★ {#q247 .q}

*Why they ask:* Pseudo-labelling is risky; they test whether we understand its failure mode.

**Say:** We cannot rule it out, because France has no labels, but for the French E5 reader we limited it in four ways. Only very confident pseudo-labels: positives at least 0.97 with every other candidate of the record below 0.5, so ambiguous records were skipped, and negatives at most 0.03. The teacher was the averaged confidence of two other readers, not the student itself, and we mixed in as many labelled US and Indian pairs, 474,808 of each, to anchor it. We also held out 5 percent of records to check agreement.

**If they push:** The teacher is not fully independent, since one of its two readers, the French MiniLM reader, was itself self-trained on French pseudo-labels. And agreement with pseudo-labels measures consistency, not correctness: the reader agreed 0.999206 but scored slightly below its base model on the generated labelled French test set, 0.910516 against 0.914964. A second self-training round did not help either: it scored 0.991277 on the public board against 0.991300, so we did not adopt it.

## 21. Curveballs and reflection (11 questions) {#cat-21 .cat}

### Q248. What was the hardest bug you hit? ★★ {#q248 .q}

*Why they ask:* Reveals real hands-on experience and how we debug.

**Say:** The nastiest was silent: in a clean run from a fresh folder, the freshly compiled C++ index exited with no output at all. On Windows it had loaded an incompatible runtime library from Git for Windows, found earlier on the system path; the fix was to ship the compiler's own runtime libraries next to the executable. It taught us to test the whole package from scratch, not just our working folder.

**If they push:** The subtler issue was numerical: bf16 reader scores change slightly with batch composition, because each batch is padded to its longest pair, so byte-exact reproduction needs the stored scores, not just the weights. That clean run found four issues in total, and all fixes are in the package.

### Q249. What surprised you most? ★★ {#q249 .q}

*Why they ask:* Shows whether we learned from the data rather than just executing a plan.

**Say:** How cheap the quick rule-based filter was. With no model at all it cuts the index output from about 130 to 21.7 candidates per business, and on held-out records the true business survived 99.974 percent of the time while F0.5 moved only from 0.990117 to 0.990086. A simple rule, measured carefully, removed most of the work for almost no loss.

**If they push:** A second surprise was the French example: the business with exactly the same name but in another city was liked by our original reader, +7.1, and rejected by both French readers, firmly by the French E5 reader at −10.8; it is one example, not a measurement, but it suggests self-training taught them to weigh the address. And a diagnostic upload showed how much France weighs: emptying every French row dropped the public score from 0.970125 to 0.839.

### Q250. With ten times the compute, what would you do? ★★ LIKELY {#q250 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we know where our system is limited and can prioritise.

**Say:** Spend it where we measured the largest loss, the cap of four candidates: on fold 9 the index finds the true business for 99.37 percent of US records, but the shortlist keeps at least 98.87 percent. We would let the readers see more candidates where the ranker is unsure and measure the gain. Second, train the readers out-of-fold, so the decision models can learn on all ten folds instead of four.

**If they push:** Third, rerun the larger-reader comparison properly on the same shortlist and held-out fold, and try a dense retrieval channel judged by the per-stage recall table. Each of these is a plan with a measurement attached, not a result we have.

### Q251. What is the most important thing you learned? ★ LIKELY {#q251 .q}

*Why they ask:* An open question to see whether we can name a real, transferable insight.

**Say:** Study how true records differ from their business before building features. True records tend to lose information, they drop a digit or a suffix, abbreviate or transliterate, and describing exactly what changed gave the decision model the right language. The second lesson is validation first: measure what each stage loses, tune on the exact metric, and write the acceptance checks before seeing the results.

**If they push:** Describing the change, rather than the word, also made the features generic: when we replaced data-specific inputs with the final generic "what changed" inputs, the public score moved from 0.990881 to 0.990934, so on the public board generality cost nothing. We did not run a clean ablation that removes all "what changed" features.

### Q252. Explain this to a business stakeholder in thirty seconds. ★ LIKELY {#q252 .q}

*Why they ask:* Senior scientists must explain work to non-experts; they test clarity.

**Say:** Every day, records about businesses arrive from many sources, with typos, abbreviations and different scripts, and each must be attached to the right business in our catalogue, or to none. We first pull up about seven possible matches per business out of trillions of combinations, then a careful model attaches a record only when one match is clearly right. When it is not sure, it leaves the record alone, because a wrong attachment does more damage than a missing one; on the competition's strict score we reached 0.9913.

**If they push:** The real business decision is where to set the bar: lowering it attaches more records, but under this score each extra wrong attachment costs more than a missed one. The bar is a setting per country, so it can follow what the business can tolerate.

### Q253. Give me your approach in one sentence. ★ LIKELY {#q253 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we can compress the whole system without losing the key idea.

**Say:** We keep about seven candidates per business, make one careful decision per record, and link nothing whenever we are not sure. That is how 6.7 trillion possible pairs became a score of 0.9913.

**If they push:** The technical version: a recall-first inverted index and a quick rule cut the space, a CatBoost ranker keeps up to four candidates, multilingual cross-encoders read each pair, and a LightGBM decision model per country links only a confident, clear winner, with second-chance searches for missed candidates and self-training for France.

### Q254. Which part of your solution are you least confident about? ★★ {#q254 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests honesty and whether we know our own weak spots.

**Say:** France. It has no labels, so we have no measured French F0.5; its readers are self-trained, its rules were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records, some rule parameters were tuned with public-leaderboard feedback, and we kept the French E5 reader although it failed two of its four written checks. What we can say is that every rule is code on model scores and raw text with no labels as inputs, and that we disclose the rest.

**If they push:** Second on the list is the unseen-country route: it is built like France, with the MiniLM reader only and the 0.82 threshold, but the test set had no such country, so it is untested on real data.

### Q255. If you had to remove one component, which would it be? ★★★ {#q255 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests whether we know the contribution of each part, and whether we over-claim.

**Say:** We have no full ablation of every component, so I would decide with a held-out test, not by instinct. By link counts the smallest pieces are the French acronym rescue, 186 links, the US address second-chance search, 192, and the per-business consistency check, which changes about a thousand decisions out of about 8.5 million US and Indian records. But small counts do not mean small value: under per-business F0.5 one wrong link can zero a business.

**If they push:** The two US and Indian pieces were selected on held-out evidence: the consistency check's thresholds on folds 8 and 9, the address search's thresholds on fold 8 with false positives counted twice; the acronym rescue, like every France rule, has no labelled evidence. The part we would least like to remove is the clear-winner rule, because it is what stops us choosing between near-identical candidates.

**Numbers:**

- Consistency check US +277 / −284, India +247 / −248, 1,056 changed decisions in total (Doc B.1; total derived)
- US address-rescue links +192 (Doc B.1); France acronym rescue +186 (Doc B.3)
- US + India incoming records 8,534,596 (derived from Doc 2.1)

### Q256. Are the differences between your leaderboard uploads statistically meaningful? ★★★ {#q256 .q}

*Why they ask:* A scientist's reflex: is the signal bigger than the noise?

**Say:** Some are probably not, and we treat them carefully. The late steps are tiny, the second French round was 0.000023 below our final file and the last gains from 0.991114 to 0.991300 add up to 0.000186, and without labels or a known public subset we cannot put an error bar on them. That is why we present leaderboard-driven choices as a disclosed limitation, not as evidence.

**If they push:** On held-out folds we compare versions with a paired bootstrap over businesses, 2,000 resamples, because both versions are scored on the same businesses and pairing removes the variance from which businesses are easy. The differences come from relatively few businesses: for example, adding the French E5 reader changed 5,437 business rows.

### Q257. What limits your score? Where are the remaining errors? ★★ {#q257 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests error analysis: do we know what is left to fix?

**Say:** Two ceilings. Retrieval: the shortlist holds the true business for roughly 99 percent of US and 98 percent of Indian held-out records, and the rest can only come back through the second-chance searches. Decision: the wrong-link types we found are names at the business's address with one generic word replaced or added or the legal form changed, acronyms that differ by one initial at another address, and branches of a chain at nearby addresses.

**If they push:** Known misses are native-script names without a known transliteration, brand or website names with little word overlap, records without a house number on a street with several businesses, and correct candidates rejected because a second one is too close. Each of our components targets one of these, and none removes it completely.

### Q258. Looking back, which decision would you reverse? ★★★ {#q258 .q}

*Why they ask:* Tests mature self-criticism without undermining the work.

**Say:** Not keeping an untouched end-to-end validation fold from the start. Because folds 8 and 9 also chose our thresholds and the final file was picked by public score, we cannot give one clean number for the whole pipeline. The model decision I would revisit is keeping the French E5 reader against our own written rule: a rule only helps if you follow it, or change it before you see the result.

**If they push:** For balance: it passed the checks on US and Indian quality and on agreement with held-out French pseudo-labels, AUC 0.998544 against 0.998570 on US and Indian pairs and 0.999206 agreement, and it changes French links only, 2,228 removed and 3,396 added. It entered the final file together with the five-seed decision models, so its own effect on the public score is not isolated.

*See also, answered elsewhere:* "With one more month, what would you change?" see [Q192](#q192).

Quick filter (Doc 3): keep a candidate if any of six conditions holds (best total; total at least 0.6 times the best; best address score; address coverage at least 0.95; name of at most 3 characters with coverage at least 0.4; same core name with coverage at least 0.3).

## (b) A-Z glossary {#c-glossary .csec}

279 technical terms, each with a one-line simple definition and links to where it is taught (the first link is the main place). Terms marked "not used by us" are ones a judge may ask about.

### A {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **Abstention (reject option)** | Choosing to link nothing when no candidate is good enough or clearly best; under F0.5 this is often the cheaper mistake. | [A1.7](#a1-7), [A3.15](#a3-15) |
| **Abugida (matra, virama)** | A script such as Devanagari where each consonant carries a vowel "a"; vowel signs (matras) replace it and the virama removes it. | [A1.10](#a1-10) |
| **Accent stripping** | Removing accents (é becomes e) so that differently typed spellings match. | [A1.9](#a1-9) |
| **Accumulator** | The running score of each business while the index is being looked up for one record. | [A1.20](#a1-20) |
| **Acronym rescue** | France rule that links a record whose name is an initials version of the business name at the same address, if that business is the only such one there. | [A4.15](#a4-15) |
| **Activation function (ReLU, GELU)** | The small non-linear function each neural-network unit applies after its weighted sum. | [A0.14](#a0-14) |
| **AdamW** | The optimiser used for the readers: Adam's per-weight step sizes plus weight decay applied separately from the gradient step. | [A0.9](#a0-9), [A2.17](#a2-17) |
| **Adaptive overfitting** | Overfitting to a test set by making many choices based on its score, such as repeated leaderboard uploads. | [A3.25](#a3-25), [A0.10](#a0-10) |
| **Address normalisation and parsing** | Bringing addresses to one form: street types, state names, house numbers, French "bis" and "ter". | [A1.11](#a1-11) |
| **Address second-chance search** | For unlinked US and Indian records, a second search by rare numbers and rare address words, followed by a filter model and a scorer model. | [A4.14](#a4-14), [A2.27](#a2-27) |
| **Adversarial validation** | Training a classifier to tell training rows from evaluation rows; if it can, the two differ. | [A3.3](#a3-3) |
| **Ambiguity rejection** | Abstaining when the top two candidates are close; our clear-winner lead. | [A3.15](#a3-15) |
| **Approximate nearest neighbours (ANN)** | Fast search for the closest vectors that accepts a small chance of missing the exact best; used in dense retrieval, not by us. | [A1.25](#a1-25) |
| **Argmax** | The candidate with the highest score among a record's candidates. | [A0.3](#a0-3) |
| **Attention** | The transformer mechanism that lets each token build its meaning from a weighted mix of all other tokens. | [A2.11](#a2-11) |
| **AUC** | The chance that a random true pair scores higher than a random false pair; it measures ranking and has no threshold. | [A1.6](#a1-6), [A0.4](#a0-4) |
| **Autocast (mixed precision)** | Running most maths in a cheaper 16-bit format while keeping the weights in 32-bit. | [A2.18](#a2-18) |

### B {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **Backpropagation** | The method that computes, layer by layer, how much each weight of a network should change to reduce the loss. | [A0.9](#a0-9) |
| **Bagging** | Training several models on random resamples of the data and averaging them, to reduce variance. | [A0.13](#a0-13) |
| **Base rate** | The share of examples that are positive, for example the share of candidate pairs that are true matches. | [A0.6](#a0-6) |
| **Batch (mini-batch)** | A group of training examples processed together in one optimisation step; ours are 128 pairs. | [A0.9](#a0-9), [A2.17](#a2-17) |
| **bf16** | A 16-bit number format with the same exponent range as 32-bit floats: faster and smaller, slightly less precise. | [A2.18](#a2-18) |
| **Bias (in the bias-variance sense)** | Error from a model that is too simple to capture the pattern. | [A0.10](#a0-10), [A2.3](#a2-3) |
| **Bi-encoder** | A model that turns each text into a vector separately and compares the vectors; good for retrieval, weaker for fine decisions. | [A2.13](#a2-13), [A1.25](#a1-25) |
| **Binary cross-entropy (log loss)** | The standard training loss for yes/no predictions; it punishes confident wrong probabilities very heavily. | [A0.8](#a0-8), [A2.2](#a2-2) |
| **Blending (logit space)** | A weighted average of several models' logits; for France 0.35 MiniLM + 0.15 French MiniLM + 0.5 French E5. | [A2.22](#a2-22), [A3.22](#a3-22) |
| **Blocking** | Any cheap step that decides which pairs are worth comparing at all, so that we never compare everything with everything. | [A1.19](#a1-19) |
| **BM25** | A classic search-ranking formula with term-frequency saturation and length normalisation; we use a simpler IDF-weighted overlap. | [A1.16](#a1-16) |
| **Boosting** | Building models one after another, each new one correcting the errors of those before it. | [A0.13](#a0-13), [A2.5](#a2-5) |
| **Bootstrap (paired)** | Resampling businesses with replacement many times to get an uncertainty interval for the difference between two models scored on the same businesses. | [A3.17](#a3-17) |
| **Business** | A record of the reference list (Source 1): the thing we link to. The test files hold 1,732,544. | [A1.1](#a1-1) |

### C {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **Calibration** | Whether a score of 0.8 really means "right 80 % of the time"; we did not calibrate, we tuned thresholds on the exact metric. | [A2.26](#a2-26), [A3.14](#a3-14) |
| **Candidate** | A business that our search proposes for one incoming record; record plus candidate is a pair. | [A1.1](#a1-1) |
| **Candidate file** | The output file listing, for each business, the pairs we considered: the shortlist plus second-chance candidates (7.0954 per business). | [A4.16](#a4-16) |
| **Canopy clustering** | A blocking method that groups records with a cheap distance and two thresholds; not used by us. | [A1.24](#a1-24) |
| **Capacity** | How complex a pattern a model can fit (depth, leaves, trees, epochs); it moves the model along the bias-variance curve. | [A0.10](#a0-10) |
| **Cascade** | A cheap model applied to many items, then a more expensive one to the few survivors; our whole pipeline is one. | [A2.27](#a2-27), [A4.1](#a4-1) |
| **Catastrophic forgetting** | A model losing what it learned before when it is fine-tuned on new data; replay prevents it. | [A2.12](#a2-12), [A3.21](#a3-21) |
| **CatBoost** | A gradient-boosted tree library with symmetric trees and ordered boosting; our ranker uses it. | [A2.7](#a2-7) |
| **CatBoost ranker** | Our first learned model: it orders each record's candidates by the probability that each is the owner, and the shortlist keeps at most four. | [A4.7](#a4-7), [A2.9](#a2-9) |
| **Category-swap veto** | France rule that drops a link when, at the same address, the business name lost a core word and the record gained a category word. | [A4.15](#a4-15) |
| **Cell veto** | France rule that drops accepted links falling in seven specific address × name-change combinations. | [A4.15](#a4-15) |
| **Character n-grams (letter pieces)** | Overlapping chunks of n letters; the 3-letter pieces of "dental" are den, ent, nta, tal. | [A1.12](#a1-12) |
| **Classification** | Predicting a category, for example "match" or "not a match". | [A0.3](#a0-3) |
| **Class imbalance** | Far more negative examples than positive ones; blocking removes most of it before our models run. | [A0.6](#a0-6) |
| **Clear winner (lead, margin)** | The best candidate must be at least 0.4 ahead of the runner-up before we link it. | [A3.15](#a3-15), [A1.7](#a1-7) |
| **Code point** | The number of one Unicode character, written U+00C9 and so on. | [A1.9](#a1-9) |
| **Collective features** | Features computed over the other incoming records that compete for the same business (US and India only). | [A4.9](#a4-9) |
| **Combining mark** | A character that attaches to the previous one, such as an accent or an Indic vowel sign. | [A1.9](#a1-9) |
| **Comparison space** | All possible pairs; 6,724,569,566,212 within countries for our test files. | [A1.19](#a1-19) |
| **Concept shift** | What counts as a match for a given input changes between training and use. | [A3.24](#a3-24) |
| **Confident + clear-winner rule** | Link the best candidate only if its score is at least the threshold (0.75 or 0.82) and it leads the runner-up by at least 0.4. | [A4.11](#a4-11), [A3.15](#a3-15) |
| **Confirmation bias (self-training)** | A self-trained model reinforcing its own or its teacher's mistakes. | [A2.21](#a2-21), [A3.20](#a3-20) |
| **Confusion matrix** | The table of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. | [A0.4](#a0-4), [A1.3](#a1-3) |
| **Consistency check (per business)** | A re-decision for US and Indian records with a bar that depends on how many other records the business already accepted. | [A3.16](#a3-16), [A4.13](#a4-13) |
| **Contrastive learning** | Training embeddings so that matching texts end up close together and non-matching ones far apart; how E5 was pretrained. | [A2.16](#a2-16) |
| **Core name** | The business name without legal-form words (inc, llc, pvt, sarl ...) and without "and" and "the". | [A1.8](#a1-8) |
| **Cosine similarity** | How similar two vectors are, by the angle between them: 1 means the same direction. | [A0.16](#a0-16) |
| **Cost-sensitive threshold selection** | Choosing a threshold where some errors count more; our second-chance thresholds count each false positive twice. | [A3.13](#a3-13) |
| **Country profile** | A small configuration file per country that picks the cleaning rules, readers, decision model, threshold, second-chance searches and rules. | [A4.1](#a4-1), [A4.4](#a4-4) |
| **Covariate shift** | The inputs change between training and use while the task stays the same, as when France's blend replaces one reader. | [A3.24](#a3-24), [A2.22](#a2-22) |
| **Cross-encoder (reader)** | A transformer that reads both texts of a pair together, as one input, and outputs one score. | [A2.13](#a2-13), [A2.14](#a2-14) |
| **Cross-fitting** | Producing a learned component's output for a record with a version that never saw that record, so training looks like test. | [A3.7](#a3-7) |
| **Cross-validation (k-fold)** | Splitting the data into k folds and rotating which fold is held out. | [A3.2](#a3-2) |

### D {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **Damerau-Levenshtein distance** | Edit distance that also counts swapping two neighbouring characters as one edit. | [A1.13](#a1-13) |
| **Data augmentation** | Creating extra training examples by transforming existing ones. | [A3.19](#a3-19) |
| **Data leakage** | Information from the test side or the label sneaking into training, which makes scores look better than they are. | [A3.3](#a3-3), [A0.2](#a0-2) |
| **Data skew** | One key with a huge group (a very common word) overloading one worker; posting-list caps prevent it in our index. | [A1.26](#a1-26) |
| **Decision model (LightGBM, per country)** | The final model: it turns about two hundred features into a probability that the candidate is the owner. | [A4.10](#a4-10), [A2.8](#a2-8) |
| **Decision rule** | The rule that turns scores into actions (link or not). | [A0.5](#a0-5) |
| **Decision tree** | A model that asks a series of yes/no questions about the features and ends in a leaf with a prediction. | [A0.12](#a0-12), [A2.4](#a2-4) |
| **Deduplication** | Finding duplicates inside one list; not our task, which links to a reference list. | [A1.1](#a1-1), [A1.2](#a1-2) |
| **Default route (unseen country)** | What a country without a profile gets: US/India cleaning, the MiniLM reader, a decision model trained on US and Indian rows, threshold 0.82. | [A3.24](#a3-24), [A4.4](#a4-4) |
| **Dense retrieval** | Finding candidates by embedding similarity instead of shared words; not used by us. | [A1.25](#a1-25) |
| **Determinism** | Getting exactly the same output when a run is repeated; GPU and bf16 training are not bit-deterministic. | [A3.28](#a3-28) |
| **Dice coefficient** | Twice the shared items divided by the two list lengths added together. | [A1.17](#a1-17) |
| **Document frequency (df)** | The number of records that contain a term; IDF is computed from it. | [A1.16](#a1-16) |
| **Domain adaptation (unsupervised)** | Adapting a model from a labelled domain (US, India) to an unlabelled one (France). | [A2.21](#a2-21), [A2.12](#a2-12) |
| **Domain shift** | The data a model meets in use differ from the data it learned from; France is our case. | [A3.24](#a3-24) |
| **Dropout** | Randomly switching off units during training so that a network does not rely on any single one. | [A0.11](#a0-11), [A2.14](#a2-14) |
| **Dynamic programming** | Solving a big problem by filling a table of small sub-problems, each computed from neighbours already filled in. | [A1.13](#a1-13), [A0.15](#a0-15) |

### E {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **E5 reader** | Our reader fine-tuned from multilingual-e5-base (278 million parameters, MIT); used for the US and India. | [A2.16](#a2-16), [A4.8](#a4-8) |
| **Early stopping** | Stop adding trees or training steps when the score on a separate validation fold stops improving. | [A3.9](#a3-9), [A0.10](#a0-10) |
| **Edit distance (Levenshtein)** | The number of single-character insertions, deletions or substitutions that turn one string into another. | [A1.13](#a1-13) |
| **Embarrassingly parallel** | Work that splits into independent pieces that need no communication, such as our per-country runs. | [A1.26](#a1-26) |
| **Embedding** | A list of numbers (a vector) that represents a word or text, so that similar meanings get similar vectors. | [A0.16](#a0-16), [A2.10](#a2-10) |
| **Empirical risk minimisation** | Training as minimising the average loss over the training examples plus a regulariser. | [A2.1](#a2-1) |
| **Empty row** | A business with no linked records; it scores 1 if the business truly has no records and 0 otherwise. | [A1.5](#a1-5), [A1.7](#a1-7) |
| **Ensemble** | Several models whose predictions are combined. | [A0.13](#a0-13) |
| **Entity resolution (record linkage)** | Deciding which records refer to the same real-world thing. | [A1.1](#a1-1) |
| **Epoch** | One full pass over the training data; our readers train for one epoch. | [A0.9](#a0-9) |
| **Exact-key blocking** | Retrieving every business with the same sorted core-name word set (if at most 2,000 share it). | [A1.21](#a1-21), [A4.5](#a4-5) |
| **Expected loss** | The average loss of a model on new data from the deployment distribution: what validation tries to estimate. | [A3.1](#a3-1) |
| **Exponent and mantissa** | The parts of a floating-point number: the exponent sets the range, the mantissa sets the precision. | [A2.18](#a2-18) |

### F {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **False negative / false positive** | A true link we missed / a wrong link we made. | [A0.4](#a0-4), [A1.3](#a1-3) |
| **F-beta, F0.5** | A single score combining precision and recall; beta = 0.5 weighs precision more, so a wrong link hurts more than a missed one. | [A1.4](#a1-4), [A0.4](#a0-4) |
| **Feature, feature vector** | A clue written as a number; the list of all clues for one pair. | [A0.2](#a0-2) |
| **Fine-tuning** | Further training of a pretrained model on our own task and data. | [A0.17](#a0-17), [A2.12](#a2-12) |
| **Focal loss** | A variant of log loss that down-weights examples the model already gets right; not used by us. | [A0.6](#a0-6) |
| **Fold** | One of 10 groups of businesses used to separate training from checking. | [A0.7](#a0-7), [A3.2](#a3-2) |
| **fp16 / fp32** | 16-bit and 32-bit floating-point formats; fp16 has a small range, fp32 is the precise default. | [A2.18](#a2-18) |
| **France rules computed by code** | Fixed vetoes and rescues on French shortlist pairs, computed from scores, raw text and addresses after the decision model. | [A4.15](#a4-15), [A3.23](#a3-23) |
| **French E5 reader** | The E5 reader fine-tuned on French pseudo-labels plus labelled US/Indian pairs; kept although it failed two of four written checks. | [A4.18](#a4-18), [A3.20](#a3-20) |
| **French MiniLM reader** | The MiniLM reader fine-tuned on confident French pseudo-labels plus 500,000 labelled US/Indian pairs. | [A4.18](#a4-18), [A2.21](#a2-21) |
| **Funnel (candidate funnel)** | The candidate counts at each step: about 130 → 21.71 → 6.75 → 7.10 per business. | [A1.23](#a1-23) |

### G {.gl}

| Term | Simple definition | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| **Garden of forking paths** | Many small analysis choices made after seeing data, which together make results look better than they are. | [A3.26](#a3-26), [A3.25](#a3-25) |
| **Generalisation** | Doing well on new data, not just on the training data. | [A0.1](#a0-1), [A2.3](#a2-3) |
| **Generic-word rescue** | France rule that links an unlinked record at the business's address whose name differs from the business name only by "groupe" or "developpement" in specific positions, when the model's score is in a low band. | [A4.15](#a4-15) |
| **Generic-word swap veto** | France rule that drops a link when one name word was replaced by "compagnie" or "services" at the same address. | [A4.15](#a4-15) |
| **Gini impurity** | A measure of how mixed the labels in a tree node are; splits try to reduce it. | [A0.12](#a0-12), [A2.4](#a2-4) |
| **GOSS** | LightGBM's sampling of rows by gradient size (keep large gradients, sample small ones). | [A2.8](#a2-8) |
| **Gradient** | The direction in which a small change of each parameter increases the loss fastest. | [A0.9](#a0-9), [A2.5](#a2-5) |
| **Gradient boosting (GBDT)** | Adding small decision trees one at a time, each fitted to the remaining errors (the negative gradient of the loss). | [A2.5](#a2-5), [A0.13](#a0-13) |
| **Gradient clipping** | Capping the size of a gradient step (ours at 1.0) to avoid rare huge updates. | [A0.9](#a0-9), [A2.17](#a2-17) |
| **Gradient descent** | Repeatedly stepping parameters against the gradient to reduce the loss. | [A0.9](#a0-9) |
| **Group k-fold** | Cross-validation where whole groups (for us, businesses with their records) stay in one fold. | [A3.4](#a3-4) |

| **Word-substitution veto and rescue** | France rule: drop a link when a business word was replaced by a frequent word at the same address; rescue true-looking name differences in a score band. | [A4.15](#a4-15) |

## (d) The honest-limitations answers in one place {#c-limits .csec}

The pattern is always the same: **say the limitation plainly first, then the mitigation, then stop.** These are disclosed in our Documentation (Section 5 and Appendix C), so saying them is a strength, not a risk. The full answers are in the linked questions.

| # | Limitation (say it first) | Mitigation (then this) | Full answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **No untouched end-to-end validation of the final file.** The held-out scores exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules, folds 8 and 9 also chose thresholds and the consistency check, and the final US / India models were refitted on folds 6-9. | Held-out per-business F0.5 from fits that leave the scored fold out: US 0.991212 / 0.991545, India 0.990046 / 0.990298, the same range as the public 0.9913. | [Q181](#q181) |
| 2 | **France has no labels, so we have no measured French F0.5.** | French readers self-trained with labelled US / Indian replay; a stricter 0.82 threshold; the France recipe on labelled US / Indian rows at 0.82 scores 0.990508 / 0.989467 on fold 9 (a proxy, not a French score). | [Q158](#q158) |
| 3 | **The France rules were designed after analysing the unlabelled French test records**, including AI-assisted review of sampled pairs, and some parameters were chosen after seeing test results, including public scores. | Each rule is code on model scores, raw text and the address; no test label and no human or AI judgement of any pair is an input; the evidence is label-free control groups; the largest action removes 29,021 of 887,630 accepted French links. | [Q182](#q182) |
| 4 | **We kept the French E5 reader although it failed two of its four written checks** (the generated French test set and the expected-gain rule). | It passed US / Indian quality (AUC 0.998544 vs 0.998570) and pseudo-label agreement (0.999206); it changes French links only (−2,228 / +3,396); it was a leaderboard-driven decision and we disclose it. | [Q183](#q183) |
| 5 | **Public-leaderboard feedback influenced selections**: 18 uploads, the final file chosen by public score, the refit kept and the France refit dropped on public scores. | US / India thresholds came from held-out folds; held-out scores sit in the same range; the late public gains were small (0.991114 → 0.991300). | [Q153](#q153) |
| 6 | **The pipeline computes statistics on the unlabelled test files** (word rarity, indexes, French geography, self-training, the French threshold from link volume), so our evaluation is transductive. | No test labels are ever used, every such use is listed in our Documentation, and in production the reference list and the incoming stream are available at run time anyway. | [Q184](#q184) |
| 7 | **The unseen-country route is untested on real data.** | It is conservative by design: the MiniLM reader, a decision model trained on labelled US / Indian rows, threshold 0.82; a new market would get its own cleaner, self-trained readers and a small labelled sample. | [Q162](#q162) |
| 8 | **No clean ablation of the "what changed" features and no feature-importance ranking.** | Closest evidence: generic inputs replacing data-specific ones moved the public score 0.990881 → 0.990934; we would run grouped permutation importance on held-out folds. | [Q102](#q102) |
| 9 | **Single-record latency was not measured**; our runs were batch jobs. | Work per record is bounded at every stage (on average 1.17 reader pairs per record); batch: about 1.3 h index + ranker and 1.4 h readers for 9.97 million records. | [Q210](#q210) |
| 10 | (Only if pressed.) **The two second-chance models' training records were selected with earlier decision models** whose inputs included data-specific features we later removed. | Disclosed in our Documentation; the fix would be to re-select those records with the final decision models and retrain. | [Q188](#q188) |

**One sentence that covers the first four, for when time is short:** "We had no untouched end-to-end validation of the final file, France has no labels and its rules were designed after looking at unlabelled test records, and we kept the French E5 reader although it failed two of its four written checks; all of this is disclosed, and close versions of our models score in the same range on held-out folds."

## (e) If you don't know: how to answer gracefully {#c-dontknow .csec}

Senior scientists respect "we did not measure that" far more than a guessed number. A confident, honest non-answer followed by what you *would* measure is a good answer.

**Phrases that work.**

| Situation | Say |
|---|---|
| The number was never measured | "We did not measure that, so I won't guess. What we would measure is ... on a held-out fold, with the exact per-business F0.5." |
| The number exists but you do not remember it | "I don't want to misquote it; it is in Section ... of our Documentation, and I'm happy to send it right after." |
| A good idea you did not try | "That's a good idea, and we didn't try it. We'd judge it the same way as everything else: same shortlist, held-out fold 9, per-business F0.5, and a paired bootstrap over businesses." |
| The question is unclear | "Just to make sure I answer the right question: do you mean ... or ...?" |
| It touches a weakness | "Honestly, that is a limitation: ... What limits the damage is ..." |
| You are asked for a comparison we lack (for example dense retrieval, BM25, XLM-R large, a ranking loss) | "We did not benchmark it, so I can't claim ours is better. Our reason for the choice was ..., and here is how we'd compare them." |
| Something was decided on public scores | "That one was a leaderboard-driven decision, and our Documentation discloses it." |
| A question on near-identical look-alike businesses or hard negatives | Use the wording of [Q115](#q115) exactly, and add nothing. |
| Team roles | Use the one sentence agreed with Monika and Hemachand before 7 October ([Q228](#q228)). |
| AI assistance | Answer briefly and factually, as in [Q229](#q229). |
| You are running long | "The short answer is ...; I'm happy to go deeper if useful." Then stop. |
| You realise you misspoke | "Let me correct that: the exact number is ..." Correcting yourself is fine. |

**What never to say.**

- Anything about near-identical look-alike businesses beyond the agreed wording of [Q115](#q115), and never raise the topic yourself.
- Internal code names or rule letters (see the [code-name table](#c-names)), or a record id such as "S1-...".
- A number that is not in the [numbers table](#c-numbers) or in a question's **Numbers** list; never quote toy or illustrative numbers.
- "About 130 per business in the final run" (it is from the blocking study of 25 September; the final run reports 21.7107 after the quick filter).
- "The ranker uses a ranking loss" (it is a pointwise classifier with log loss).
- "The 0.4 lead was never tuned" or "the 0.4 lead was tuned" (say: one fixed value for every country; the threshold was tuned on fold 8).
- "Our held-out scores are an end-to-end test" (they exclude the second-chance searches and the France rules).
- "The French readers are 99.9 % accurate" (0.999206 is agreement with their own teachers' pseudo-labels, not accuracy).
- Any break-even story for the consistency check's bars (say: the four bars, 0.75 / 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.77, were tuned on folds 8 and 9).
- "One LightGBM call per record" (say: a handful of small tree-model calls per pair, five seeds).

**Three breaths before any hard question.** (1) What is the judge really testing? (2) Which one number proves my answer? (3) Is there a limitation I should say first?
